title: LSAT 180 Mastery
description: A twelve-module, year-long LSAT preparation pathway. Develop diagnostic review, argument analysis, formal logic, assumptions, evidence evaluation, flaw diagnosis, inference, principles, advanced reading, argumentative writing, pacing, full-simulation planning, targeted error repair, rare-error refinement, and test readiness with original practice. A 180 is an aspirational target, not a guaranteed outcome.
author: Erudior
changelog: Initial release: twelve modules with 58 lessons, 712 original questions, 352 cards, 250 glossary entries, 45 references, and six complete argumentative-writing prompts. Develop diagnostic reasoning, logical analysis, advanced reading, writing, pacing, error repair, and readiness evaluation. Preserve the distinction between original raw results and exact-form official practice reports, with guidance for the intended administration.
disclaimer: Original Erudior preparation, independent of LSAC. This course is not an official LSAT practice test or a validated score predictor. Its original baseline reports raw results only. The app's generic bank timer and completion threshold are not LSAT timing or an LSAT passing score.

lessons.title: Start here — reasoning baseline in the app
lessons.body:
## What this starting point can tell you

This course begins with an **[[untimed learning baseline]]**: twelve original questions that help you notice how you reason before studying the foundation lessons. Six concern short arguments and six concern reading passages. Some will feel easy; others introduce skills taught later. You are collecting a starting record, so an unfamiliar task is useful information rather than a reason to stop.

The questions are Erudior learning material. They are not official LSAT questions, a complete test, or a calibrated predictor of your eventual score. The small sample also gives limited evidence about any individual skill. Three questions sharing a passage are related observations, not three independent demonstrations that you understand every kind of reading. Use your responses to choose something concrete to practice.

Complete this baseline before reading the other lessons or its answer explanations. If you have already seen any items, record that exposure. You can still learn from them, but the result is a review result rather than an untouched baseline. There is no benefit in concealing a previous attempt from yourself.

The course also retains a separate manual worksheet, **Original baseline — questions only**, with sixteen different items labeled B01–B16. This app baseline uses AB01–AB12. Choose one starting set and keep its record distinct; the other can provide additional original practice. Do not combine their denominators or treat them as equivalent forms.

## Set up a fair learning session

Choose a setting in which you can read comfortably. Use the text size and access tools you normally need, and note any assistance or interruptions. This is untimed: the lesson's suggested study minutes are a planning estimate, not a deadline. If you need a break, take it and record it. You are measuring your reasoning under described conditions, not testing your ability to tolerate an inaccessible format.

Prepare a simple record with the date, whether the questions are new, and the conditions. For each item, record its AB01–AB12 label, your selected answer text, whether you were sure or uncertain, and a brief reason. Answer letters may move between attempts; the item label and answer text make the record useful later. Do not consult explanations, a search engine, or another person for answers during this first attempt.

If you cannot decide, you may make a best choice and mark it as a guess. A correct guess still receives raw credit; its uncertainty belongs in a separate review column. Leaving an item unanswered is also informative. Keep unanswered items in the denominator when describing this twelve-item set.

## Take the baseline in the app

Skip the optional warm-up on this page so it does not expose questions before your first attempt. Use this lesson's **Take the quiz** button for the twelve baseline items. The ordinary course-wide Exam option draws from the larger bank; it is not this assessment or an official LSAT simulation.

During the first pass, choose answers and use the numbered Answer sheet controls to move between questions. Leave **Check answer** unused until you have recorded all twelve choices. Checking early reveals feedback that may affect later questions, especially those sharing a passage. The numbered controls let you move without revealing feedback. Record confidence in your own worksheet before submitting; you can also flag uncertain items.

When you are ready, use **Finish quiz**. The results give your raw total and the two baseline topic subtotals. Read explanations only after preserving your first-pass record. If you accidentally checked an answer early, write that down and call the affected work practice. Accurate labeling makes the data useful without pretending the session was untouched.

The app also displays its normal lesson-quiz completion threshold. That is a course workflow marker, not an LSAT passing score or a judgment of readiness. You can return to the lesson list and begin Recognizing arguments and evidence even if you have not reached that threshold. A later retry may complete the lesson, but it must not replace the original entry in your baseline log.

## Read a raw report without inventing a scale

A **[[raw score]]** is simply the number answered correctly. Here the report is correct out of twelve overall, plus correct out of six for each of the two broad skill groups. A **[[scaled score]]** uses a test-specific scoring process; this original set does not have one. Never turn its percentage into a number between 120 and 180.

The App baseline score and review sheet reference gives the exact item map and a blank record. Use the subtotal labels to locate a starting lesson, then inspect the actual mistakes. An identical subtotal can arise from different causes: one learner might misread qualifying words, while another might mistake a reported opinion for the author's view.

### Example 1: Correct, uncertain, and unanswered

Imagine a learner gets four of the six short-argument questions right and three of the six reading questions right. One reading item was unanswered. First add the correct counts: four plus three gives seven. Report **7/12**, with **4/6** for Logical Reasoning and **3/6** for Reading Comprehension. The unanswered item remains part of twelve, so the total is not seven out of eleven.

Next suppose two of those seven correct answers were guesses. Keep the raw total at seven. Separately record two uncertain-correct answers, four wrong answers, and one unanswered item. These categories explain why seven correct does not necessarily mean seven skills are secure. A useful next action is to review one wrong and one uncertain item and identify the evidence each decision needed.

### Example 2: A retry does not erase a first attempt

Suppose the same learner studies the explanations and scores eleven out of twelve when repeating the set three days later. First keep both dated entries. Label seven out of twelve as the first attempt and eleven out of twelve as a repeated set after feedback. The improvement shows successful review of these questions, but familiarity may have helped.

Next choose fresh questions practicing the same weak skills. Compare the reasoning, conditions, and results without assuming two sets have identical difficulty. If fresh performance also improves and the learner can reject plausible alternatives, there is stronger evidence of transfer. There is still no defensible conversion from either original set to an official scaled score.

## Decide what to do next

After review, choose one action that describes a reasoning behavior: identify the supported claim before evaluating an argument; keep the direction of a conditional rule; or label each speaker's viewpoint before choosing a passage answer. Avoid an action as vague as "read harder." A specific behavior can be practiced and checked.

The remaining lessons teach argument structure, diagnostic review, and reading structure. Work through them even if this short baseline went well; twelve items cannot establish mastery of the course. Your first official timed baseline is a separate task using authorized official material and that form's instructions. The Exam format reference identifies the current format and the announced August 2027 transition so your eventual timing practice matches your intended administration.

## Common mistakes

Do not check each response before recording the rest of the baseline. Do not replace your first result with the best retry. Do not subtract uncertain correct answers from the raw score, or omit unanswered items to improve the percentage. Do not treat the app's completion threshold as an official exam standard. These mistakes make the report harder to interpret.

## Key points

- Record a first attempt before feedback, including uncertainty and conditions.
- Report overall correct out of twelve and each skill group out of six.
- Preserve the difference between fresh and repeated questions.
- Use the result to choose a practice action; it is not a scaled-score estimate.

lessons.title: Recognizing arguments and evidence
lessons.body:
If you already completed the app baseline AB01–AB12, retain that as your starting record and continue. The linked reference “Original baseline — questions only” is a separate manual set, B01–B16, which can serve as an alternative starting route or later practice. If you choose it for a fresh starting record, record your choices before studying the worked examples or opening its separate key. Both original untimed sets report raw accuracy, not an official LSAT score. You can also begin learning now and label a later attempt as practice.

Before you try to reason quickly, learn to describe reasoning accurately. A paragraph can contain true facts, impressive vocabulary, and a confident recommendation without giving adequate support for that recommendation. Your first task is to separate what the author asks you to accept from the reasons offered for accepting it.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to identify an argument's conclusion and premises, distinguish support from description, and explain one gap without inventing facts. All examples in this lesson describe fictional situations. Work without a time limit; the explanation you can give matters more than how quickly you select an answer.

## Claims and their jobs

A **[[claim]]** is a statement that can be true or false. “The reading room closes at six” is a claim. “When does it close?” is a question rather than a claim. An **[[argument]]** offers one or more claims as reasons for accepting another claim. It need not involve disagreement or anger.

The supported claim is the **[[conclusion]]**. A supporting claim is a **[[premise]]**. **[[Evidence]]** is information offered to support a claim; observations, records, and comparisons can function as evidence. These labels describe a statement's job in a particular argument. The same statement can be a conclusion in one paragraph and a premise in another.

Consider: “The reading room should open earlier because students are waiting outside before the doors open.” The recommendation is the conclusion. The observation about waiting students is the premise. Whether earlier opening is affordable is a further issue. Identifying the conclusion does not require agreeing with it.

Conclusions can describe, predict, or recommend. They can appear at the beginning, middle, or end. A recommendation such as “we should extend service” is still a claim the author wants accepted.

## A repeatable reading method

Use three passes through a short argument:

1. Identify the claim the author wants to establish. Ask, “What am I supposed to believe or do?”
2. Identify the stated support. Ask, “What reasons does the author actually give?”
3. Examine the connection. Ask, “Could those reasons be true while the conclusion fails, or is less certain than the author says?”

When identifying structure, preserve the author's wording and level of certainty. “This might help” and “this will solve the problem” are different conclusions. When evaluating the connection, provisionally accept the stated premises and examine what follows. This does not certify that the premises are true in the real world.

Words such as “therefore” and “because” are useful clues, not automatic answer keys. “Since the renovation, attendance has risen” uses “since” to mark time. It does not, by itself, say that the renovation caused the increase. Read the relationship between claims before assigning labels.

## Reports, explanations, and support chains

“The workshop has six tables and two windows” reports information without using one fact to establish another. An explanation instead addresses why an accepted event happened: “The workshop closed early because a pipe burst.” If everyone accepts that the closure happened, the speaker is explaining its cause.

Context can change the task. A speaker might argue that a pipe burst, using a maintenance report as evidence. The word “because” does not settle whether the passage is primarily explaining an accepted event or supporting a disputed claim. Ask what the speaker treats as established and what needs support.

Arguments can also contain an **[[intermediate conclusion]]**: a claim supported by earlier premises and then used to support a further conclusion. In “The windows admit rain, so the room needs repairs; therefore, we should request a repair estimate,” the need for repairs is intermediate. The request for an estimate is the main conclusion. The middle claim has two jobs; calling it a premise of the final step does not erase its role as a conclusion of the earlier step.

### Example 1: Reading the limits of a comparison

Read this fictional proposal:

> The town added shade canopies to two bus stops in May. In June, those stops were cooler at noon than two nearby stops without canopies. Therefore, canopies can reduce the heat experienced by people waiting at bus stops.

Step 1: State the conclusion. The author claims that canopies can reduce heat at bus stops. The conclusion is a causal possibility, not a claim that canopies remove every heat problem.

Step 2: Identify the premises. Canopies were added to two stops, and the covered stops were cooler than the comparison stops. The difference in temperatures is the evidence offered for the causal claim.

Step 3: Examine the comparison. Could another difference help explain the result? Perhaps the covered stops also had more tree shade, or their measurements were taken on cooler days. These are possibilities to investigate, not facts supplied by the passage. An **[[assumption]]** is an unstated claim the reasoning relies on. The author needs the comparison to be informative about the canopies' contribution rather than merely reflecting unrelated differences.

Step 4: State a proportionate assessment. The observed difference may support the proposal, but this comparison alone does not isolate the cause. Do not jump to the opposite conclusion that canopies are ineffective. A gap in a particular argument is not proof that its conclusion is false.

Step 5: Choose a useful follow-up. Ask whether the stops were measured under comparable weather and shade conditions. Asking whether the town has a popular bus logo would not address the identified gap. Good scrutiny targets the connection between the actual evidence and conclusion.

### Example 2: Checking a reversed relationship

Consider a different argument:

> Every member of the conservatory orchestra studies music theory. Lena studies music theory. Therefore, Lena is a member of the orchestra.

Step 1: The conclusion is that Lena belongs to the orchestra. The premises are the rule about members and the statement about Lena's studies.

Step 2: Read the rule in its stated direction. Membership guarantees studying music theory. The rule does not say that studying music theory guarantees membership. Students outside the orchestra could study the subject too.

Step 3: Construct a **[[counterexample]]**: a possible case that satisfies the premises but defeats the proposed conclusion. Imagine that every orchestra member studies music theory and Lena takes the same class independently, without joining the orchestra. Both premises remain true while the conclusion is false.

Step 4: Explain the result. The conclusion does not follow from these premises alone. We have not discovered that Lena is definitely outside the orchestra; she might belong. We have shown only that these reasons do not establish membership.

Step 5: Compare a valid direction. If the premises said that every member studies music theory and Lena is a member, concluding that Lena studies music theory would follow. The difference is the direction of support, not the subject matter or the number of sentences.

## Preserve quantity and certainty

**[[Scope]]** is the range of people, cases, places, or times covered by a claim. Moving from observations about two stops to a claim about every stop expands scope. A stronger conclusion needs enough support for that expansion.

“Some volunteers attended training” establishes that at least one did. It does not establish that some failed to attend; all might have attended. Similarly, “the device sometimes works” does not, by itself, establish that it sometimes fails. Ordinary conversation can suggest “not always,” but do not treat that suggestion as a guaranteed logical consequence.

Preserve certainty as well. Evidence that a proposal might help is not automatically evidence that it must help. Reject a stronger claim because its extra commitment lacks support, not simply because it contains a word such as “all.” Universal conclusions can be justified when the premises justify them.

## Guided practice: name the missing step

Read: “Three members of the book club like the new venue. Therefore, every club member likes that venue.” Before reading further, write the conclusion, the premise, and a possible case showing the gap.

The conclusion concerns every member; the premise concerns three members. A club with other members who dislike the venue would fit the premise while defeating the conclusion. You need not claim that those dissatisfied members actually exist. The possibility shows why the stated evidence does not establish the universal claim.

Now revise the conclusion to fit the evidence: “At least three members like the new venue.” That follows directly. “The venue is unsuitable” does not. Explaining why an argument fails and proving its opposite are different tasks.

## Common mistakes

Do not identify the conclusion by sentence position alone. Do not count each sentence containing “because” as an argument without considering its purpose. Do not confuse a claim the author quotes with a claim the author endorses. If an author reports a critic's view and then challenges it, track whose position each claim expresses.

Avoid inventing facts while evaluating support. Say that an alternative is possible, then explain why the premises leave it open. Finally, do not replace “not established” with “false,” or replace “some” with “some but not all.” These changes add conclusions the text has not earned.

## Key points

- Identify the conclusion before evaluating its support.
- Separate stated premises from unstated assumptions.
- Track intermediate conclusions when support has several steps.
- A counterexample can expose a gap without proving the opposite conclusion.
- Preserve the quantity, scope, and certainty of each claim.

lessons.title: Establishing your diagnostic baseline and error log
lessons.body:
## Choose and label your starting set

The first lesson offers a twelve-item baseline in the app, labeled AB01–AB12, with six short-argument and six reading questions. The separate manual references contain sixteen different questions, B01–B16, with eight in each group. The worksheet instructions below refer to that sixteen-item set. Choose one for your initial record and use the other as separately labeled practice; their item mixes differ. Do not combine them or replace one denominator with the other. The app baseline has its own score-and-review reference.

A **[[baseline]]** is a recorded starting point under stated conditions. It helps you choose what to practice; it does not define your potential. By the end of this lesson, you should be able to report a practice result honestly, preserve your original reasoning during review, and turn one mistake into a specific learning task.

If you chose the manual route and have not yet read the arguments or reading lessons, take the original 16-item baseline reference before studying them. Otherwise, record what you have already studied, including any app-baseline attempt. The assessment is still useful, but you cannot reconstruct an untouched starting point afterward. Its eight reasoning and eight reading questions are original Erudior practice, not a standardized diagnostic or an official LSAT form.

## Separate the measurements

As checked on November 3, 2026, the standard multiple-choice LSAT has four 35-minute sections: two scored Logical Reasoning sections, one scored Reading Comprehension section, and one unscored section of either type. A 10-minute intermission follows the second section. LSAT Argumentative Writing is separate and unscored; the standard allocation is 15 minutes for prewriting and 35 for writing. Approved accommodations may alter timing. Check the [LSAC test specifications](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/register-lsat/accommodations/specifications-lsat-and-lsat-argumentative-writing) and [writing information](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/about/lsat-argumentative-writing) before official practice or registration.

Target-date note, checked November 3, 2026: the four-section format applies through June 2027. [LSAC announces a different format from August 2027](https://www.lsac.org/lsat-will-look-little-different-starting-august-2027): Reading Comprehension first, with 52 minutes, followed by two 45-minute Logical Reasoning sections, with 10-minute breaks between sections and unscored questions embedded within them. Choose official practice for your intended administration. LSAC plans new-format practice for February 2027; this note does not claim it is already available.

Three labels prevent misleading comparisons:

- An original Erudior learning baseline reports correct answers out of the questions offered. It has no LSAT score conversion.
- An authorized official-practice test may provide a scaled practice result through its own scoring tool or form-specific conversion. Record that it was practice, including the conditions used.
- An official LSAT score is a result issued for an administered LSAT. Completing a practice form does not produce that credential.

Your **[[raw score]]** is the number correct. A **[[scaled practice score]]** is a practice result calculated using the appropriate official form's scoring method. Do not multiply an original-set percentage into the LSAT scale, borrow another form's conversion, or infer an admissions outcome. None of those operations establishes a valid relationship between the measures.

## Make the first attempt interpretable

Open the baseline questions without opening the separate key. Use a notebook or a document you control for responses; this reference does not automatically save answers or an error log. Record the date, set name, previous exposure, timing conditions, interruptions, and access supports used. You may use your usual accessibility supports. Describe them neutrally so future comparisons have context.

This original baseline is untimed. Record elapsed time if useful, but do not turn it into a speed contest. For later official practice, follow the applicable instructions and approved timing rather than assuming everyone's test conditions must be identical.

For each question, record your selected answer and a **[[confidence rating]]** before checking: high means you can justify it and reject the strongest rival; medium means you have a reason but unresolved doubt; low means a guess or little usable justification. These are working labels, not calibrated probabilities.

Keep unanswered questions visible. **[[Accuracy]]** for this set is correct divided by all 16 offered questions. Report reasoning and reading separately out of eight as well. Attempted-item accuracy can be an additional statistic if clearly labeled, but it must not replace the full-set result. Otherwise, leaving difficult questions blank can make the headline result look better without improving performance.

### Example 1: Report the result before interpreting it

Mira attempts 14 of the 16 questions and leaves two blank. She gets six of eight reasoning questions and five of eight reading questions correct. Fourteen attempts minus 11 correct leaves three attempted errors.

1. Preserve the original answer sheet. The first-attempt result is 11/16, or 68.75%; report 68.8% if rounding to one decimal place.
2. Record the components: reasoning 6/8, reading 5/8, three wrong selections, and two unanswered. The components explain more than a single percentage.
3. If recording attempted-item accuracy, label 11/14, approximately 78.6%, explicitly. It answers a different question and does not replace 11/16.
4. Record relevant conditions: untimed, one interruption, no previous exposure, and the supports used. Another session with different conditions is not a controlled experiment.
5. Choose a review priority after examining the mistakes. The one-question difference between reasoning and reading does not establish a lasting weakness. Eight items per area are too small a sample to support that conclusion confidently.

No step converts 11/16 into an LSAT-scaled score. The useful outcome is a specific review plan, not a numerical prediction beyond the evidence.

## Review without rewriting history

**[[Blind review]]** means reconsidering your answers before seeing the key or explanations. Copy your first-attempt responses into a separate column, then revisit uncertain items. Write the evidence for your choice, the strongest alternative, and what distinguishes them. Record changes in a review column rather than overwriting the original answer.

Afterward, consult the key and explanations. You now have distinct records: what you chose initially, what you chose with further reflection, and what you learned after feedback. Improvement during blind review is useful evidence about a question, but it does not prove that time alone caused the initial error. Familiarity, another reading, and chance can also matter.

An **[[error log]]** records a correctable reasoning process. Include the item ID, task, original choice and confidence, relevant wording, error hypothesis, corrected reasoning, and a follow-up task. Use labels as prompts for investigation:

- Concept gap: a needed distinction was not understood.
- Misread: a word or the requested task was overlooked.
- Scope: the chosen claim exceeded what the text supported.
- Timing: recorded time conditions plausibly affected the process.
- **[[Uncertain correct]]**: the selected answer was right, but its justification was weak.

More than one label may apply. “Timing” alone does not explain what to change. A correct answer also needs review when the justification is a guess or rejects the wrong alternative for an invalid reason.

### Example 2: Turn a plausible cause into a practice task

During a practice set, Jo reads a passage about a trial in two branches of a library. Jo chooses an answer stating that the program works in every branch. The correct choice limits the finding to the observed trial. Jo had marked the original answer high confidence.

1. Preserve the original answer and confidence. Lowering the recorded confidence after feedback would conceal the mismatch the log is meant to reveal.
2. Locate the failure: evidence about two branches was expanded to every branch. Label the error “scope,” and note the specific quantifier change.
3. Write a correction: “Match the population in my answer to the population supported by the text.” Avoid a vague promise to concentrate harder.
4. Rework the item and explain why the broad answer exceeds the evidence. This rehearses the correction; remembering the key is not fresh evidence of learning.
5. Later attempt new questions requiring the same distinction. This tests **[[transfer]]**: using a learned method on unfamiliar material. Record whether Jo independently notices the scope issue.

If Jo also ran short of time, add that observation. Do not assume speed caused the scope mistake merely because the session was timed. Repeated patterns across fresh work provide stronger guidance than one convenient explanation.

## Guided practice: make the report useful

Before continuing, write a report for this fictional attempt: 12 correct, two wrong selections, two unanswered; later blind review changes one wrong selection to correct and one correct selection to wrong. What is the original raw result? What is the review result? Which responses need investigation?

The original result stays 12/16. The review result is also 12/16: one gain and one loss cancel numerically. Review both changed answers, the remaining error, the unanswered items, and any uncertain correct responses. An unchanged total can hide an important change in reasoning.

Now write one error-log entry for overlooking the word “EXCEPT” in a question. A useful follow-up is to restate several new question tasks accurately before answering. Memorizing unrelated vocabulary would not address this particular error.

## Common mistakes

Do not erase first-attempt evidence with a corrected answer. Do not use only attempted questions in an unlabeled headline percentage. Do not call familiarity with repeated items transfer, or treat one small set as a reliable ability estimate. Keep official practice, original practice, blind review, and post-feedback correction separate in your records.

Allow time for analysis between sets. A modest schedule can include a first attempt, a review session, focused instruction, and fresh follow-up questions. Adjust it to the observed need and your available study time; completing more sets without understanding mistakes does not resolve those mistakes.

## Key points

- Label the source, timing, supports, and previous exposure of each attempt.
- Report manual B01–B16 out of sixteen, with each group out of eight; report app AB01–AB12 out of twelve, with each group out of six.
- Preserve first responses before blind review and before feedback.
- Use an error log to connect specific evidence, a corrected method, and fresh practice.
- A practice score or ambitious target cannot guarantee a future LSAT score or admission outcome.

lessons.title: Reading for structure instead of memorizing details
lessons.body:
In Recognizing arguments and evidence, you separated an argument's reasons from its conclusion. A reading passage asks you to retain that relationship across several paragraphs and sometimes several speakers. By the end of this lesson, you should be able to map a passage, identify its central claim, distinguish its author's position from a reported view, and defend an inference using particular words in the text.

If you want an unfamiliar starting measure and have not already taken one, choose either the app baseline AB01–AB12 or the manual worksheet B01–B16 before studying this lesson. Otherwise, preserve your earlier result and record the skills you have already practiced. The passages below are original teaching examples; their invented situations do not require outside knowledge.

## Build a map you can use

A passage's **[[topic]]** is its subject: urban gardens, shipping routes, or museum labels. Its **[[main point]]** is the central claim the passage develops about that subject. A topic names an area; a main point says something that could be supported, challenged, or qualified. “Museum labels” is a topic. “Labels can help visitors interpret unfamiliar objects, but attendance alone cannot measure that benefit” is a main point.

After each paragraph, write a brief **[[paragraph function]]** label: introduces a disputed explanation, supplies evidence, answers an objection, or narrows a proposal. About five words is often enough; five is not a rule. A useful label captures a relationship rather than listing nouns. “Describes three survey results” locates material, but “Survey results challenge attendance measure” explains why it matters.

Keep a second note for the exact evidence you might need to revisit. A structural map helps locate details; it does not replace careful reading of them. When a question asks what happened in one study, return to that study and preserve its dates, groups, and qualifications. Do not answer a detail question with a general impression of the author's argument.

## Identify whose view you are reading

An **[[author viewpoint]]** is the position the writer adopts toward the issue. A **[[reported view]]** belongs to a person or group described in the passage. “Some critics argue that…” introduces a view without making it the author's. Look for the response: endorsement, objection, a concession, or a distinction between cases.

A **[[concession]]** acknowledges something that favors another position without necessarily accepting that position as a whole. In “The proposal has merit, but its costs are underestimated,” the writer accepts merit and raises a problem. Neither complete rejection nor unconditional endorsement captures both parts.

Words such as “however” and “although” signal relationships, but they do not settle the answer by themselves. Ask what claim comes before the shift, what comes after, and whose voice supplies each. A passage may explain a debate without choosing a winner; do not force a strong opinion onto a restrained description.

### Example 1: Follow a qualified explanation

Read this three-paragraph passage:

> A town commissioned street murals after several shop owners predicted that murals alone would prevent vandalism. The first report recorded less vandalism on the decorated blocks than on nearby undecorated blocks. Supporters took the difference as confirmation of their prediction.
>
> A later review found that the decorated blocks also received nightly maintenance visits. On decorated blocks where those visits subsequently stopped, vandalism increased again despite the murals remaining in place. The review did not compare blocks receiving maintenance alone with blocks receiving both maintenance and murals.
>
> The initial report therefore cannot establish that murals alone prevented vandalism. Maintenance deserves investigation as part of the explanation, although the evidence does not determine whether murals contributed any additional benefit.

Step 1: Name the topic without treating it as the answer. The topic is murals and vandalism. “Murals prevent vandalism” is the supporters' claim, not yet the author's conclusion.

Step 2: Map the paragraphs. The first presents a claim and apparent support. The second introduces a competing factor and identifies a missing comparison. The third limits the original conclusion and leaves an open question. This structure is claim, complication, qualified conclusion.

Step 3: State the author's main point. The initial evidence does not isolate the effect of murals; maintenance may matter, and the murals' additional contribution remains unsettled. Notice the difference between uncertainty and a negative result. “The murals had no effect” would answer a question the passage explicitly leaves open.

Step 4: Test a tempting inference. Does the increase in vandalism establish that maintenance always prevents vandalism? No. The passage concerns particular blocks and does not establish what happens everywhere. Does it establish that murals were still present on those blocks when vandalism increased again? Yes: that detail is explicitly stated. The second paragraph is the right place to check it.

## Match the strength of the evidence

An **[[inference]]** is a claim supported by the passage even when not repeated word for word. It needs a textual reason. Before selecting an answer, point to the sentence or combination of sentences that licenses it. “This is plausible in the real world” is insufficient when the task asks what follows from this passage.

The **[[scope]]** of a claim includes the people, places, times, or circumstances it covers. Evidence about one town does not automatically establish a rule for every town. A **[[qualification]]** limits a claim, as “under these conditions” or “in this sample” does. Preserve those limits when paraphrasing.

Treat “some” as at least one unless the passage supplies a further restriction. “Some projects succeeded” establishes success in at least one case; by itself it establishes neither that every project succeeded nor that some failed. Similarly, “sometimes works” does not alone prove “always works” or “does not always work.” A stronger everyday suggestion is not the same as a conclusion required by the words.

A **[[counterexample]]** is a case that contradicts a general claim. If a claim says every mural remains undamaged for a year, one mural damaged within its first year refutes that claim, provided it falls within the stated category. It does not prove that every mural is damaged. Strong words are not automatically wrong: “all” is appropriate when the evidence actually supports it.

## Compare two passages on the same question

For **[[comparative reading]]**, first map each passage separately. Then choose a shared question and compare each writer's answer. Agreement about one benefit can coexist with disagreement about how to measure it. Similar subject matter alone establishes neither agreement nor conflict.

### Example 2: Find agreement without erasing a difference

Passage A:

> Digitizing a regional archive lets readers inspect documents without traveling. That expanded access is valuable. The number of remote users should therefore be one measure of a digitization project's success, though it should not be the only measure.

Passage B:

> Remote access is a real benefit of digitizing archives. Yet a project that scans only familiar documents may make neglected collections harder to discover. Evaluators should examine which materials become searchable as well as how many readers connect.

Step 1: Map A. It identifies a benefit, then recommends remote-user numbers as one evaluation measure. Its final qualification prevents “user numbers are sufficient” from being an accurate paraphrase.

Step 2: Map B. It accepts the access benefit, raises a selection concern, and recommends checking searchable coverage along with use. B questions an incomplete evaluation, not the value of all digitization.

Step 3: Ask a shared question: is remote access valuable? Both explicitly answer yes. “Only A values remote access” is contradicted by B's first sentence.

Step 4: Identify what is different. B develops a specific concern about collection coverage that A does not discuss. Silence is not rejection: A might accept B's recommendation. Therefore “A opposes checking collection coverage” is unsupported. A defensible comparison says B adds an evaluation concern to a benefit both acknowledge.

## Guided practice

Read this short passage before checking the explanation:

> A library's first report credited longer opening hours with increased attendance. A later report found that attendance had begun rising before the hours changed. The librarian concluded that longer hours could not explain the entire increase, while leaving open whether they explained part of it.

Write three notes: the passage's structure, its main point, and one claim it does not establish. Then ask whether the librarian rejects every possible effect of longer hours.

Check your reasoning: the structure is initial explanation, timing complication, narrower conclusion. The main point limits how much of the increase longer hours can explain. It does not establish that longer hours had no effect, because a partial effect remains open. It also does not identify the earlier increase's cause. “Something else must be considered for that earlier rise” is different from naming an unsupported alternative.

## Check a word in its context

For a word-in-context question, start with the surrounding sentence and its role in the argument. A familiar dictionary meaning may not fit this use. Substitute a proposed meaning and check whether the sentence still expresses the same relationship. For example, "The small survey offers limited support, so the researcher treats the conclusion as tentative" contrasts suggestive evidence with certainty. Here tentative means held pending stronger support, not disproved or deliberately false. The surrounding reason determines the sense. Keep that restriction when comparing choices; do not assume a claim will become certain merely because it is currently open to revision.

## Common mistakes

- Choosing an answer that repeats passage vocabulary but reverses the relationship between claims.
- Treating the first speaker's position as the author's position before reading the response.
- Turning a possibility into a certainty, or missing evidence into proof of absence.
- Assuming “some” means “some but not all,” or assuming a qualification makes every strong answer wrong.
- Treating a second writer's additional concern as a disagreement when the first writer never addresses it.
- Relying on a paragraph label when the question requires checking an exact detail.

## Key points

- Separate the subject from the central claim made about it.
- Map paragraph functions and track each speaker's commitments.
- Use the map to locate evidence, then inspect the relevant wording.
- Preserve scope and qualifications; explain what supports an inference.
- Compare writers on the same question, distinguishing disagreement from silence.

lessons.title: Main and intermediate conclusions
lessons.body:
Module 1 introduced premises and conclusions. Now you will work with passages that contain several supported claims, not just one reason followed by one recommendation. Your job is to identify the claim the argument ultimately supports and explain how the other statements contribute.

By the end, you should be able to identify a conclusion at any sentence position, distinguish a main conclusion from an intermediate one, and restate a conclusion without making it stronger. Work through the examples before answering the lesson questions. All situations are fictional, and no specialist knowledge is needed.

## Identify the target of the supplied argument

A **[[main conclusion]]** is the claim that the argument as a whole aims to establish. Other claims support it, directly or through another step. An **[[intermediate conclusion]]** receives support from earlier reasoning and then serves as support for a further claim. A **[[premise]]** is a reason offered for a conclusion; an intermediate conclusion is therefore also a premise in a later step.

These are roles, not judgments about truth or importance. A weakly supported recommendation can still be the main conclusion. An accurate observation can remain a premise. Do not replace the author's recommendation with the conclusion you think the evidence ought to support.

“Main” also refers to the argument supplied. An organization may have a broad goal, such as encouraging local participation, while its argument supports a narrower recommendation to move one meeting. The broad goal is not automatically the main conclusion. Ask which claim the actual reasons are being used to establish, not which aim would matter most in life.

## Follow support instead of sentence order

**[[Support direction]]** is the movement from a reason to the claim it is offered to justify. To test a proposed relationship, complete this sentence: “The author offers this as a reason to accept that.” Use the passage's intended reasoning, even if you later identify a gap.

Consider: “The notice should be rewritten. Several readers mistook the closing date for the opening date.” The observation supports the recommendation, although the recommendation appears first. Reversing the sentence order would not reverse the support.

Indicators such as “therefore” show an inferential step, but that step may produce an intermediate conclusion. A passage can say “therefore” twice. Neither the first occurrence nor the last sentence is automatically the main conclusion. Check whether the resulting claim is then used to support another claim.

A simple map can use numbered statements and a table:

| Statement | What supports it? | What does it support? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | No reason supplied here | Statement 3 |
| 2 | No reason supplied here | Statement 3 |
| 3 | Statements 1 and 2 | Statement 4 |
| 4 | Statement 3 | No further conclusion in this argument |

Here 3 is intermediate and 4 is main. “No reason supplied here” means the passage treats the statement as a starting point; it does not prove that the statement needs no justification anywhere else.

### Example 1: The main conclusion appears first

Read the whole proposal before assigning roles:

> For this autumn's collection, the seed bank should rent the smaller refrigerated room. The collection contains ninety crates, and the smaller room holds one hundred. Both available rooms maintain the required temperature. The larger room costs more, and the collection is not expected to grow before winter. Paying for its extra space would therefore add expense without meeting an additional storage need this autumn.

Step 1: Locate the decision being defended. The first sentence recommends the smaller room for a particular collection and season. The rest explains why that choice meets the stated needs.

Step 2: Identify the supporting facts. The crate count and capacity support adequate space. The temperature claim addresses another requirement. The cost difference and expected lack of growth support rejecting the extra capacity.

Step 3: Examine the final sentence. It follows from the space, cost, and growth claims, so it is a conclusion. It also supports the first sentence's rental recommendation. That makes it intermediate, despite its position after “therefore” at the end of the passage.

Step 4: Restate the support direction. “The larger room would add expense without meeting an additional storage need” is offered to support “rent the smaller room.” The rental recommendation is not offered as evidence that extra capacity meets no additional storage need. This is the useful direction of the relationship.

Step 5: Compare plausible answers. “The collection contains ninety crates” is a premise. “Paying for the larger room would add expense without meeting an additional storage need this autumn” captures the intermediate assessment. “The seed bank should always rent the cheapest room” invents a standing rule. The main conclusion remains the specific recommendation about this autumn's collection.

Step 6: Keep analysis separate from agreement. You could ask whether either room has an unmentioned reliability problem. That would evaluate the recommendation's support; it would not make the crate count the argument's main conclusion.

### Example 2: A chain contains more than one supported claim

Consider this report:

> The workshop tested three prototype shelves. Its log records a different material for each prototype, although the published comparison lists the materials as identical. Material choice can affect the load a shelf supports. The published comparison therefore conceals a potentially relevant difference. Its ranking cannot, on this record alone, be attributed solely to the designs. For that reason, the team should repeat the comparison using the same material before selecting a design.

Step 1: Identify the final proposal. The team should repeat the comparison under a common material condition before choosing a design. This is the decision the report's reasoning supports.

Step 2: Find the starting evidence. The log records different materials, the publication labels them identical, and material can affect load. These statements are presented as premises rather than defended with further reasons in this passage.

Step 3: Mark the first intermediate conclusion. The claim that the published comparison conceals a potentially relevant difference follows from those premises. It summarizes why the discrepancy matters rather than merely repeating one observation.

Step 4: Mark the next supported claim. The ranking cannot be attributed solely to design on this record. That assessment is supported by the material problem and then used to justify repeating the test. It is another intermediate conclusion.

Step 5: Check the chain. The material evidence supports an assessment of the comparison; that assessment supports caution about attributing the ranking; the attribution problem supports the retesting proposal. The passage does not argue from “we should retest” back to “the materials differed.”

Step 6: Preserve the limits. The author does not say that design had no effect or that the prototypes are equally good. Nor does the author recommend discarding every workshop result. Those claims are stronger or broader than the supplied recommendation. A conclusion answer must identify the actual target, even if a different proposal also seems sensible.

## Paraphrase without changing the claim

A **[[paraphrase]]** restates a claim while preserving its meaning. A good conclusion answer may use different words, but it must keep the relevant **[[scope]]**: which people, objects, circumstances, and time period the claim covers. It must also preserve a **[[qualification]]**, a restriction on the claim's strength or conditions.

“The labels may reduce some filing errors” is not equivalent to “the labels will eliminate filing errors.” The first concerns a possible partial benefit; the second guarantees complete success. Conversely, “the labels should be tested” is a recommendation to investigate, not a conclusion that they already work.

Conditional recommendations need their conditions. “If the route remains available, the group should use it” does not recommend using it when it becomes unavailable. Keep the condition even if removing it makes an answer sound simpler.

Do not demand exact wording, however. “Choose the smaller room for the autumn collection” faithfully restates Example 1's recommendation. The test is preservation of commitments, not repetition of a distinctive phrase.

## Guided practice: two conclusions, one main target

Read this passage and classify the supported claims before continuing:

> The display cabinet needs a new lock: the current key no longer turns, and the technician has ruled out repairing the mechanism. A replacement cabinet is unnecessary because its case and shelves are sound. The museum should therefore replace the lock rather than the whole cabinet.

The need for a new lock is supported by the key and technician statements. The judgment that a replacement cabinet is unnecessary is supported by the condition of the case and shelves. Both judgments support the final recommendation to replace only the lock.

Each intermediate conclusion contributes something different: one supports taking action, and the other limits the action's extent. The main conclusion combines those points into a specific proposal. “The museum should preserve all old equipment forever” may sound related to conserving resources, but it is not the claim defended here.

Now explain the structure aloud without using sentence positions: “These facts support this assessment; that assessment supports this proposal.” If your explanation instead says “this comes last,” return to the support relationships.

## Common mistakes

Do not choose the broadest or most dramatic statement merely because it seems important. Do not promote an intermediate conclusion to main status just because it follows “therefore.” Do not downgrade a first-sentence recommendation simply because its reasons appear later.

A quoted speaker can have a conclusion that the passage's author rejects. Keep ownership clear. Some passages also contain separate arguments; map each before assuming every sentence supports one target. The lesson questions supply enough context to identify the requested role.

Finally, do not confuse structure with validity. You can accurately identify an intended conclusion without accepting it. Describe the argument first, then evaluate whether its reasons are adequate.

## Key points

- Main and intermediate conclusions are identified by support roles, not sentence position.
- An intermediate conclusion receives support and supplies support.
- Identify the target within the supplied argument, not an imagined wider goal.
- Preserve scope, certainty, and conditions when paraphrasing.
- Explain how the premises support your selected conclusion.

lessons.title: Background, concessions, and opposing views
lessons.body:
In Module 1, you learned to separate premises from conclusions. Longer arguments also include scene-setting facts, someone else's reasoning, and points the author grants while resisting a broader proposal. Sorting those statements accurately prevents a common error: treating every sentence in a paragraph as support for the author's final position.

This lesson develops a more precise habit. Identify the argument you are analyzing, track whose claim each sentence expresses, and explain how the author uses it. By the end, you should be able to distinguish background from support, describe a concession without turning it into surrender, and limit what a response to an objection actually establishes. All situations and figures below are fictional.

## Locate the argument before classifying its parts

A **[[statement role]]** is the job a claim performs in a particular piece of reasoning. “The building opened in 1920” has no permanent label. It may introduce a setting, supply evidence for a preservation proposal, or report a disputed historical assertion. Its subject matter does not determine its role.

Start by writing the author's main conclusion in a short sentence. Keep its limits: a four-week pilot is different from permanent adoption. Then ask how each statement connects to that conclusion, directly or through another claim.

A paragraph may contain more than one argument. An opponent's premise supports the opponent's conclusion; the author may quote both to challenge that reasoning. Calling the quoted premise “support” without saying whose conclusion it supports loses the structure you need.

## Distinguish background from actual support

**[[Background]]** sets the context without being offered as a reason for the conclusion being analyzed. Consider: “The center opened in 1998. Its only evening class has a long waiting list. We should offer a second session.” The opening date locates the center historically. The waiting list supplies the stated reason for another session.

Do not invent a bridge such as “old centers deserve more classes” to turn the date into a premise. Conversely, do not dismiss a date automatically. In “The grant covers centers opened before 2000; this center opened in 1998; therefore, it meets that eligibility condition,” the date is essential support.

Removing a sentence can be a useful check, but it is not a definition. A paragraph may supply two independent reasons; deleting one leaves the other intact, yet the deleted reason was still a premise. Look for the actual supporting relationship, not merely whether the remaining paragraph still sounds persuasive.

A detail can also explain a term or identify the people involved without supporting the recommendation. Context matters to understanding a passage even when it is not evidence for its conclusion.

## Track attribution separately from endorsement

**[[Attribution]]** identifies who makes a claim. **[[Endorsement]]** means the author accepts it. “A consultant argues that the new timetable will eliminate delays” attributes a prediction; it does not by itself show that the writer shares it. Even accepting that the consultant made the prediction is different from accepting that the prediction is true.

Read the author's response. Agreement, criticism, and suspended judgment are different positions. A **[[reported claim]]** can later become a premise the author adopts, but the adoption needs support in the wording. “The consultant is right about the staffing shortage” endorses that point. “Whether the consultant is right remains unknown” does not.

An **[[objection]]** offers a reason against a claim, proposal, or inference. A **[[rebuttal]]** responds to an objection or argument. The response might dispute a premise, challenge the connection to its conclusion, or show that a narrower proposal avoids the difficulty. It need not establish that every part of the opponent's position is false.

### Example 1: Map two arguments without combining their voices

Read this passage:

> The town archive moved into a former bank in 1998. Several committee members oppose evening opening because, they say, every record is already available online. But the catalog lists 400 records that are unavailable online, and requests for these records often come from people whose work overlaps the archive's opening hours. The claim that evening access would merely duplicate online access is therefore unsound. The archive should run a four-evening pilot to test demand and staffing before deciding about regular evening hours.

Step 1: Name the author's final proposal: run a limited pilot before a decision about regular hours. The writer is not recommending permanent evening opening immediately.

Step 2: Map the committee's reasoning. Its reported premise is that every record is online; its opposition to evening opening rests on that premise. The writer reports this claim and then disputes it. Do not place “every record is online” in the author's evidence column.

Step 3: Identify the author's evidence. The 400 records unavailable online contradict the universal online-access claim. The requests from people who work during opening hours also give a reason to investigate whether evening access meets an unmet need.

Step 4: Place the remaining statements. The 1998 move supplies background as used here. The judgment that the duplication argument is unsound is supported by the records unavailable online; it also helps answer an objection to the pilot.

Step 5: Limit the result. Refuting that objection does not prove that a pilot is affordable or that permanent evening hours are desirable. The author also offers a demand-related reason and recommends investigation. A faithful map distinguishes the rebuttal, the positive support, and the limited conclusion instead of treating one defeated objection as a complete proof.

## Conceding a point does not concede the whole argument

A **[[concession]]** grants a point that might count against the author's preferred position. The author can accept a cost, limitation, or risk while rejecting the opponent's proposed response. “The project will cost more than expected” does not mean “we should abandon it” unless the author also accepts the reasoning connecting those claims.

A concession may do additional work. An accepted limit can become support for revising a plan: “The large venue is unaffordable, so we should use the smaller one.” The cost claim is a concession to a concern and a premise supporting the narrower recommendation. Roles can overlap because they describe relationships.

Words such as “admittedly,” “although,” and “however” can mark these moves, but classify the actual claim. “However” might introduce an objection, a reply, or a qualification. It does not automatically reverse every claim that precedes it.

### Example 2: Find the conceded evidence and the disputed response

Read this passage:

> Neighbors argue that the museum should abandon its proposed concert series because courtyard concerts would be too noisy. The courtyard trial exceeded the noise target agreed for this project, and I accept that this location is unsuitable. However, the indoor trial stayed below the same target. The museum should therefore offer four indoor concerts with continued monitoring, instead of canceling the entire series. If the indoor events exceed the target, they should pause while the arrangement is reconsidered.

Step 1: Separate the neighbors' position from the writer's. The neighbors recommend abandoning the series. The writer recommends a limited indoor series with a condition for pausing it. Both positions concern noise, but their recommended actions differ.

Step 2: Identify the concession. The writer accepts the courtyard result and explicitly agrees that the location is unsuitable. Saying that the writer dismisses the neighbors' concern would contradict the passage.

Step 3: Show how that accepted point enters the reasoning. The courtyard problem supports rejecting that location. The indoor result supplies positive evidence for trying a different location. Thus the concession is also part of the explanation for changing the proposal.

Step 4: Preserve the limits. One indoor trial does not guarantee that every future concert will meet the target. The monitoring and pause condition reflect that uncertainty. Nor does the writer claim that noise is the only issue that could matter.

Step 5: State the disagreement accurately. The writer grants the location problem but disputes the inference from that problem to canceling every version of the series. The passage does not support “the writer accepts the neighbors' entire argument” or “the writer proves that the neighbors' concern was imaginary.”

## Guided practice: explain the relationship in words

Read: “A workshop organizer says a second session is impossible because no instructor is available. The coordinator points to an instructor who has accepted the proposed time. The coordinator concludes only that this staffing objection does not rule out a second session; room availability still needs checking.”

First identify the claim the coordinator rejects. Then state one conclusion the passage leaves open.

The coordinator rejects the premise that no instructor is available. The accepted instructor is counterevidence to that universal claim. The coordinator does not conclude that a second session is fully feasible: the room issue remains unresolved. A successful rebuttal removes this stated barrier without resolving every other barrier.

Now consider adding: “The workshop first met in a school cafeteria.” Unless the argument connects that history to staffing or rooms now, it remains background. Its topical relevance to the workshop does not supply the missing connection.

## Common mistakes

Avoid sorting statements by whether you personally believe them. Role analysis describes the reasoning presented, including unsupported claims and objections the author rejects. Also avoid equating quotation with disagreement: authors can quote a view they accept, challenge, or leave unresolved.

Do not force one exclusive label onto a statement with two stated functions. Identify the particular relationship the question asks about. Finally, rejecting one objection does not prove the proposal, and conceding one disadvantage does not establish that the opponent's recommendation follows.

## Key points

- Identify whose argument and which conclusion a role description concerns.
- Classify background and premises by their use, not their topic or position.
- Keep attribution distinct from author endorsement.
- A concession can also support a narrower or conditional proposal.
- State exactly what a rebuttal establishes and what it leaves unresolved.

lessons.title: Arguments and causal explanations
lessons.body:
You can identify a conclusion and distinguish an author's position from a reported view. Now use those skills to ask what a passage is trying to accomplish. Is the writer establishing that something happened, explaining why an accepted event happened, or defending a proposed explanation? Similar sentences can do different jobs in those settings.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to identify the immediate purpose of a passage, describe an explanation that is itself supported by an argument, and keep the order of events separate from the order of reasoning. All situations below are fictional. The task is to read the supplied context, not to supply technical knowledge about the devices or institutions described.

## Start with what is being taken as established

An **[[argument]]** offers reasons for accepting a conclusion. A **[[causal explanation]]** identifies a cause or process to account for an event treated as established in the discussion. In an argument about whether a concert was canceled, cancellation is the claim needing support. In a discussion about why an acknowledged cancellation occurred, cancellation is the starting point.

“Established” here means accepted for the present discussion. It does not mean impossible to question, officially certified, or independently verified by the reader. Two people could share a mistaken belief and still be trying to explain it. Describing their purpose does not certify their facts.

Use three questions:

1. What claim does the speaker treat as settled?
2. What remains in question: whether an event occurred, why it occurred, or whether a proposed cause is correct?
3. What information is offered to answer that remaining question?

Do not decide from a single connector. “Because” can introduce a reason to believe a claim or a cause offered to explain an event. An explanation may be an unsupported assertion, and an argument may support a causal explanation. The categories describe roles in context; they are not two boxes into which every whole passage fits exclusively.

## Separate a proposed cause from support for it

An **[[explanatory hypothesis]]** is a proposed account of why something happened. “Perhaps the timer malfunctioned” identifies a possibility. It does not become verified merely because it would make the event understandable.

A writer can then argue for that hypothesis. The accepted event supplies the problem to be explained; additional observations may support the proposed explanation. The overall passage is now an argument for an explanatory conclusion. Calling it an argument does not remove its explanatory purpose.

Keep two questions separate: “What is the writer claiming?” and “How well do the stated reasons support it?” A weak argument is still an argument. A mistaken explanation is still being offered as an explanation. For a role or purpose question, identify the attempted relationship before evaluating its quality.

### Example 1: The same sentence, two immediate purposes

Consider the sentence:

> The display went dark because its power supply failed.

Context A: Talia and Noor both watched the display go dark. Noor asks, “Why did that happen?” Talia replies with the sentence above. No further evidence is supplied.

Context B: Noor has not seen the display and doubts that it went dark. Talia cites two accepted facts: in this fictional model, failure of the display's sole power supply always makes the display go dark, and a test record confirms that the supply failed. Talia then uses the sentence above to answer Noor's doubt.

Step 1: Identify what is settled in A. Both speakers accept that the display went dark. Talia is trying to account for that event by naming a cause. Her immediate purpose is explanatory.

Step 2: Identify what is unsettled in B. Noor doubts the event itself. Talia offers the supply failure and the stated operating rule as reasons to accept that the display went dark. Here, the event is a conclusion supported by an argument.

Step 3: Preserve what the examples actually supply. Context B gives an explicit rule and a confirmed failure. You do not need to assume that real displays behave this way. Context A does not supply those supporting facts, so its cause is asserted rather than established by the excerpt.

Step 4: Avoid a false contrast. The sentence in B still describes a causal connection. Its argumentative function comes from using that connection to establish a contested event. It does not become “noncausal” merely because it functions as an argument.

Step 5: Imagine a new question. If Noor in A asks, “What makes you think the power supply failed?”, Talia would need support for that causal account. The conversation could move from giving an explanation to defending it. Track the current question rather than permanently labeling the sentence.

## Keep event order and support order distinct

**[[Chronology]]** is the order in which events occur. **[[Logical support]]** is the relationship in which information gives a reason to accept a claim. An earlier event may cause a later event, while evidence observed later helps establish what happened earlier.

Suppose a pipe cracked overnight and water later appeared on the floor. A morning inspection finds the crack and a trail of water beneath it. The physical explanation runs from the earlier crack toward the later water. The investigator's reasoning starts with the later observations and supports a claim about the earlier event. This is not a claim that the water or the inspection traveled backward in time and caused the crack.

| Question | Relevant relationship |
|---|---|
| What happened first? | The sequence of events |
| What produced the later event? | The proposed causal process |
| Why accept the account? | Evidence supporting the causal claim |

A timeline alone does not supply the entire third relationship. “The bell rang after the door opened” states an order. “Opening the door caused the bell to ring” adds a causal claim. That claim may be true, but it needs support beyond the word “after.” Conversely, reasoning from a later observation to an earlier event is not automatically a mistake. Evaluate the evidential connection, not the direction of the calendar.

### Example 2: An explanation becomes an argued conclusion

Read this report:

> Everyone on the committee agrees that the hall's bell rang unexpectedly at midnight. A scheduled performance cannot explain it: the hall had no performance scheduled that night. The maintenance log records a command from the old timer at midnight. After that timer was replaced, no unexpected ringing occurred during the next three nights. The manager concludes that the old timer probably contributed to the midnight ringing.

Step 1: Identify the accepted event. The unexpected ringing is agreed upon. The report is not primarily trying to establish that a sound occurred.

Step 2: Identify the proposed explanation. The manager attributes a probable contribution to the old timer. The word “probably” matters, as does “contributed.” Neither word claims that the timer was conclusively identified as the only possible cause.

Step 3: Locate the support. The recorded command connects the timer to the relevant time. The later absence of unexpected ringing after replacement provides another observation the manager treats as relevant. These facts make the passage an argument for an explanatory conclusion, not merely a bare statement of a cause.

Step 4: Assess the excluded alternative narrowly. No scheduled performance rules out that particular account as described. It does not, by itself, prove a timer fault. The report does not say that scheduled performances and timer faults are an exhaustive list of possible causes.

Step 5: Keep the remaining uncertainty precise. Three subsequent nights without ringing do not establish that unexpected ringing can never recur. The report also does not describe every other condition before and after replacement. These limits matter if someone strengthens the conclusion to “the timer was certainly the sole cause.” They do not require replacing the manager's qualified conclusion with “the timer played no role.”

Step 6: Summarize the purpose in one sentence: the writer uses records and subsequent observations to support a proposed explanation of an accepted event. That summary captures both the explanatory target and the argumentative structure.

## Guided practice: compare purpose before judging strength

Read these two short passages:

Passage A: “The committee agrees that the seedlings wilted. Asked why, the gardener suggests that the greenhouse's ventilation failed. The gardener offers no observations about the ventilation.”

Passage B: “Whether the ventilation failed is disputed. An inspection record reports that its fan did not turn during the relevant period. The gardener cites that record as evidence that the ventilation failed.”

Before continuing, write what each passage treats as settled, what it tries to establish or explain, and what support it supplies.

Check your reasoning: A takes the wilting as established and proposes an explanation without giving evidence for that proposal. B offers a record in support of a contested ventilation claim. Identifying B as an argument does not show that its evidence proves everything about the ventilation system. The passage tells you how the record is being used.

Now consider a third sentence: “The seedlings wilted after a cloudy week.” By itself, this reports timing. It does not explicitly argue that clouds caused wilting. If a writer adds “therefore, the clouds caused the wilting,” the writer has made a causal argument whose support you can evaluate. Your task changes when the discourse changes.

## Common mistakes

- Treating every sentence containing “because” as having the same function.
- Assuming an event accepted in a discussion has been independently verified.
- Calling a supported causal explanation either an explanation or an argument, when it can be both.
- Confusing evidence observed later with a claim that a later event caused an earlier one.
- Treating an intelligible possibility as a confirmed cause.
- Assuming that excluding one explanation establishes another, without an exhaustive set of alternatives.
- Answering a purpose question with “the reasoning is weak” instead of describing what the writer attempts.

## Key points

- Ask what is settled and what remains in question.
- Distinguish establishing an event from accounting for an accepted event.
- An explanatory hypothesis can itself be the conclusion of an argument.
- Event chronology and logical support are different relationships.
- Preserve uncertainty, causal contribution, and the limits of any excluded alternative.

lessons.title: Linked and independent support
lessons.body:
Identifying a premise is only a start. A longer argument can use two premises together, offer several separate reasons, or build one conclusion on another. To evaluate it efficiently, first reconstruct those relationships. Otherwise, you may attack a detail the conclusion does not depend on or mistake the loss of one reason for the collapse of the whole argument.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to distinguish linked, independent, and serial support; describe a mixed argument in words; and separate a map of the author's reasoning from a judgment about its strength. All policies and situations below are fictional. You need no outside facts.

## What a support connection represents

An **[[argument map]]** records which claims are offered as reasons for which other claims. A **[[support connection]]** means "this is offered as a reason for that." It does not automatically mean "this caused that," "this happened earlier," or "this proves that beyond doubt." Label the claims before drawing connections, and preserve the author's qualifiers.

**[[Linked support]]** occurs when premises work together as one line of reasoning. A general rule and the fact that brings a particular case under that rule are a familiar pair. Neither statement alone delivers the intended inference under the information supplied.

**[[Independent support]]**, sometimes called convergent support, consists of separate lines of reasoning for the same conclusion. Removing one line can leave another reason standing. The remaining reason need not settle the issue by itself. "Independent" describes the argument's support structure; it does not guarantee that the evidence comes from unrelated sources or is statistically independent.

Both patterns operate against **[[shared background]]**: assumptions or rules held fixed while comparing the offered reasons. Be explicit about that background. A claim that works as a separate reason under an accepted rule may need to be paired with that rule in a fully written deduction.

## A cautious removal check

Temporarily set one premise aside without assuming its opposite. Ask what the remaining statements, with the same stated background, still support.

- If an intended inference needs the statements together, that line is linked.
- If a separate line still offers a reason for the same conclusion, that line can be independent of the removed line.
- If one derived claim is then used to support another, you have a chain as well.

This **[[removal check]]** is a reading aid, not a mechanical verdict. A premise may retain some relevance after its partner is removed, even though the author's complete line no longer works. Different reasonable reconstructions can expose ambiguity. In a question, prefer the structure most clearly supported by the wording rather than adding missing rules to force a preferred diagram.

### Example 1: A linked rule and its application

An exhibition coordinator writes:

"Every work classified as fragile must be transported in a padded crate. Lark is classified as fragile. Therefore, Lark must travel in a padded crate. Since the crate will not fit in the small van, we should use the larger van, which is available and can hold it."

1. Identify the first target: Lark must travel in a padded crate. The general requirement and Lark's classification jointly support it.
2. Set aside the classification. The rule tells you what fragile works need, but the remaining text no longer establishes that Lark belongs to that category.
3. Restore the classification and set aside the rule. Being fragile may suggest caution in ordinary life, but the stated requirement for a padded crate is no longer established by this passage.
4. Identify the next target: use the larger van. The crate requirement becomes an **[[intermediate conclusion]]**, used with claims about vehicle capacity and availability.
5. Separate structure from evaluation. These claims make the larger van a supported choice; they do not establish that it is the cheapest or only possible transport option.

The first part has this shape. The full statements are in the example above.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Linked premises in the transport argument
  accDescr: The fragile-work rule and Lark's classification are used together to support the conclusion that Lark needs a padded crate.
  P1["Fragile-work rule"] --> J["Use both premises"]
  P2["Lark is fragile"] --> J
  J --> C["Lark needs a crate"]
```

The extra joining box is not a new fact. It represents the instruction to use both premises together. Do not count the box as a third premise or confuse the diagram's visual layout with the order of sentences.

## Chains and mixed structures
