Sometimes a sentence remains genuinely ambiguous. Do not resolve it by importing an elaborate assumption. Check whether another paragraph clarifies it and whether the question can be answered from evidence that is clear. Your explanation should acknowledge the actual limits of the text.

### Example 1: Read an editorial decision precisely

Consider this original passage:

> (1) In an edition of the fictional poet Sera Venn, editor Arin uses two notebooks. One contains dated drafts; the other contains undated fair copies. Arin prints the dated drafts chronologically and places the fair copies in a separate section.
>
> (2) Several fair copies share titles with dated drafts. Arin flags each pair of same-title texts so readers can compare their punctuation and wording. These pairs make differences easy to locate, but their presentation does not establish which member was written later.
>
> (3) A clean transcription is not necessarily a final revision, Arin cautions. The edition therefore identifies the notebook supporting each printed reading without claiming that every difference reveals a step toward the poet's final intention.

Step 1: Answer a detail question. Where are the fair copies printed? Paragraph (1) places them in a separate section. “Interspersed chronologically among the drafts” imports a dating decision that the passage does not report.

Step 2: Resolve the reference in paragraph (2). “These pairs” refers to the same-title draft and fair-copy combinations just described. It does not refer to pairs of notebooks or pairs of punctuation marks. The action of comparing the two texts supports that reading.

Step 3: Interpret “flags.” The stated reason is to help readers compare variants. Marking them for attention fits. Declaring them unreliable does not: the paragraph supplies no such judgment, and the edition prints readings from both notebooks.

Step 4: Test an inference. Does a fair copy necessarily represent the later version? Paragraphs (2) and (3) prevent that conclusion. The editor withholds a relative date and distinguishes a clean copy from a final revision. This does not prove that no fair copy is later; the passage leaves particular sequences unresolved.

Step 5: Keep accuracy separate from completeness. “Arin prints dated drafts chronologically” is true, but it does not answer where the fair copies appear. A choice can accurately report the passage and still fail the question asked.

## Connect paragraphs without changing their subjects

A **[[cross-paragraph inference]]** draws on information from more than one paragraph. First identify each needed claim. Then state the connection in an ordinary sentence. Check that the claims concern compatible people, groups, dates, and circumstances. Two facts about different samples cannot silently become two facts about one sample.

Preserve **[[scope]]** and **[[qualification]]** throughout the connection. “All recordings included in the comparison met the noise limit” says something about included recordings. It does not say that every recording made during the survey met the limit. Similarly, permission to include a record differs from its actual inclusion.

For a must-follow task, try to imagine the premises remaining true while the proposed answer fails. For a best-supported task, compare the positive support for each choice and retain the text's degree of confidence. Either way, distinguish missing evidence from evidence that something did not happen. A study that never measured long-term durability cannot establish either long-term success or long-term failure simply by being silent.

### Example 2: Link a survey rule to its reported results

Read this invented survey account:

> (1) A marsh team visited every pond on its selected route and made one dawn recording at each. The report's comparison table uses only recordings whose background-water noise was below a specified limit. The team made no second recordings.
>
> (2) At three visited ponds, the only recording exceeded that noise limit. Staff retained these files in the survey archive but omitted them from the comparison table. No separate listening review of those files was performed.
>
> (3) The report compares audible calls in the included recordings. It does not estimate the number of animals at the omitted ponds, and it does not treat an omitted recording as a recording containing no calls.

Step 1: Locate the rule in paragraph (1). A recording needs sufficiently low background noise to enter the comparison table. Being made during a route visit does not alone secure inclusion.

Step 2: Add the cases from paragraph (2). Three visited ponds have only recordings above the limit. With no second recordings, those ponds contribute no recording to this table. The same ponds were visited; omission from a comparison is not omission from the field route.

Step 3: Draw the bounded conclusion. The table does not contain a recording from every pond visited. That follows by combining the route procedure with the three excluded cases. You do not need to invent additional ponds or assume how many animals lived there.

Step 4: Reject an unwarranted explanation. “Those three ponds contained no calling animals” is unsupported. Excessive background noise explains exclusion, and paragraph (3) expressly distinguishes exclusion from a zero-call result. Neither presence nor absence at those ponds is settled by the account.

Step 5: Identify the right evidence for a different detail question. Were the noisy files discarded? Paragraph (2) says they were archived. A reader remembering only “excluded” might incorrectly turn exclusion from one table into destruction of the underlying records.

## Guided practice

An invented craft survey reports:

> (1) The survey lists workshops that admitted visitors on the inspection day. Closed workshops were not entered, even when a sign advertised public visits on other days.
>
> (2) For every listed workshop, inspectors recorded entrance width and whether steps interrupted the entrance route. They did not inspect internal rooms.

Before reading further, identify one explicit detail, one supported inference, and one unsupported extension. Also explain what information you would revisit before describing a workshop as accessible throughout.

Check: entrance width was recorded for every listed workshop. Combining the two paragraphs supports that those recorded entrance measurements concern workshops admitting visitors that day. The record does not establish accessibility throughout any workshop, because interior rooms were not inspected and no full accessibility criterion is supplied. A public-visiting sign also does not establish inclusion if the workshop was closed on the inspection day.

## Common mistakes

- Matching a familiar phrase while changing its speaker, subject, time, or comparison group.
- Treating an accurate detail as the answer to a different question.
- Quoting an anchor without the sentence that limits it or identifies its referent.
- Turning “not measured,” “not included,” or “not reported” into “did not occur.”
- Assuming that a conventional dictionary meaning must fit a word in this passage.
- Combining paragraphs through an unstated identity or causal assumption.

## Key points

- Identify the requested claim before searching for its evidence.
- Use a textual anchor with enough context to preserve meaning and attribution.
- Paraphrase accurately; keep scope, quantities, and qualifications intact.
- Explain the connection supporting an inference, including connections across paragraphs.
- Distinguish a wrong claim, an unsupported extension, and a true statement that answers the wrong question.

lessons.title: Integrating reading skills in untimed sets
lessons.body:
The earlier lessons separated skills so you could inspect each one. A complete reading set asks you to coordinate them. You need a workable understanding of the passage, a precise reading of each question, and evidence for each answer. This lesson brings those tasks together without imposing a speed target. Its original passages are instructional practice, not a calibrated measure of an official LSAT score.

The goal is controlled flexibility. A main-point question needs a whole-passage account; a detail question may turn on one qualified sentence. Use the same passage map to find your way, then choose the evidence and level of explanation that the particular task requires.

## Read once for a usable structure

During the initial reading, identify the subject, the issue connecting the paragraphs, and the major changes in direction or speaker. Build a brief **[[passage map]]** in your own words. Keep unfamiliar names or technical details available for later retrieval rather than attempting to reproduce every sentence from memory.

The map should remain revisable. An early paragraph may report a proposal that the author later modifies. A final paragraph may summarize a descriptive distinction rather than announce a new conclusion. After reaching the end, check whether your first impression fits the entire passage.

Then state a provisional main point and the author's **[[primary purpose]]**. The main point expresses the passage's central claim or account. Purpose describes what presenting that account accomplishes: explaining a distinction, defending a qualified proposal, revising an interpretation, or tracing a development. Neither needs an elaborate sentence. Both need enough coverage to include the important relationships.

## Match the question to the right operation

For organization or function, connect a passage part to the larger development. For viewpoint, identify whose commitment is at issue and its exact object. For tone, inspect evaluative wording and reasons without borrowing a reported speaker's emotion. For a detail or inference, locate a **[[textual anchor]]** and explain the support it supplies.

Before reading the choices closely, try a short answer in your own words. This is a working hypothesis, not a commitment to defend at all costs. If the choices expose a detail you overlooked, return to the passage and revise. A prephrased answer is useful only while it remains accountable to the text.

Compare the whole of each choice. One accurate clause cannot rescue a second clause that changes the speaker, exaggerates certainty, or adds a result. Conversely, do not reject a supported answer simply because its wording differs from yours. The relevant test is whether it expresses the right relationship at the right scope.

### Example 1: Coordinate several questions about one account

Read this original passage:

> (1) A fictional harbor association catalogues its tools by the workshop responsible for maintaining them. A tool used by several workshops still appears under the workshop assigned its maintenance. This arrangement helps members locate the person to contact when a tool needs repair.
>
> (2) New apprentices often begin with a task, such as rounding a wooden edge, rather than with the name of a workshop. To help them, the association adds an index organized by use. One tool can appear under several uses, and each entry points back to its existing catalogue record. No tools change location as part of the project.
>
> (3) The two arrangements answer different questions. The original catalogue identifies maintenance responsibility; the additional index helps readers find tools for a task. Adding the index need not imply that the original organization was mistaken.

Step 1: Map the structure. Paragraph (1) explains the original arrangement and its purpose. Paragraph (2) introduces a different user need and a supplementary index. Paragraph (3) clarifies why the two arrangements can coexist.

Step 2: State the main point. Organizing tools by responsible workshop and indexing them by use serve different needs. “The association moved its tools” contradicts an explicit detail. “The association abandoned maintenance records” turns a supplement into a replacement.

Step 3: Answer a function question. The apprentice example in paragraph (2) explains why a use-based entry point would help. It does not show that apprentices are unable to repair tools, a separate ability the passage never discusses.

Step 4: Check an inference. Several index entries can refer to one tool, because a tool may have several uses and entries point to its existing record. An increase in entry count would therefore not, by itself, establish an increase in the number of tools. The connection is between entries and objects, not between tools and workshop locations.

Step 5: Describe purpose and tone. The passage explains the complementary purposes of two organizational systems. Its treatment is explanatory, without contempt for the original catalogue or enthusiasm about relocating the collection. Neither attitude appears in the stated reasons.

## Keep an evidence record that diagnoses the mistake

An **[[evidence ledger]]** is a brief review record connecting an answer with its task, textual support, and reasoning. It can be kept in your own notes. It helps distinguish failure to find relevant text from failure to interpret text you already found.

For an uncertain or missed question, record:

- The question ID or a short description of the task.
- Your first answer, confidence, and reason, saved before review.
- Your blind-review answer and reason, saved separately before any feedback.
- The paragraph and phrase that support the answer you now defend.
- The connection between that evidence and the question.
- The particular error in the strongest competing choice.
- Any feedback-assisted correction, labeled and added without overwriting the earlier records.

Use the answer's content in your notes, not just a displayed letter that may change with choice order. “I missed the author's limitation on the study population” is more useful than “I should read carefully.” It identifies what to check on another passage.

### Example 2: Review a tempting explanation without changing the evidence

Consider another invented passage:

> (1) A guide to the fictional language Nalin describes one greeting ending used at formal public welcomes. A visitor later hears a different ending in informal conversations among younger speakers. Some observers call the difference evidence that a new generation has replaced the older form.
>
> (2) Researcher Ilen records those same younger speakers at public welcomes. They use the ending described in the guide there, while retaining the other ending in the recorded informal conversations. Ilen has not recorded older speakers in either setting.
>
> (3) Ilen argues that context needs investigation before the informal ending is treated as evidence of generational replacement. The observations do not show how older speakers would speak informally, and they do not make a guide to formal welcomes inaccurate merely because informal conversation differs.

Step 1: Separate the viewpoints. Some observers propose generational replacement. Ilen responds with observations that make context relevant and leave older speakers' behavior unmeasured. Reporting the replacement claim does not make it Ilen's conclusion.

Step 2: Answer a detail question. The public-welcome recordings concern the same younger speakers heard informally. Replacing them with a separate group would alter the comparison. Older speakers were not recorded, so neither ending can be assigned to them from these data.

Step 3: Draw a bounded inference. The documented younger speakers use both endings across the recorded settings. This follows from connecting paragraphs (1) and (2). It does not establish that all younger speakers do so or that age plays no role in any language change.

Step 4: Compare possible attitudes. Ilen is cautious about the replacement explanation and supplies a reason for that caution. Calling Ilen hostile to younger speakers invents an attitude toward people. Calling Ilen certain about older speakers' informal usage ignores the acknowledged gap.

Step 5: Build a useful ledger entry. Suppose your first answer said that Ilen had proved the guide obsolete. The anchor is paragraph (3), where the guide's scope remains formal welcomes. The error is a scope shift from one setting to every setting. A later repair should explain that shift rather than merely memorize that the guide survives criticism.

## Keep first attempts and review separate

For an initial set, preserve your choices before opening explanations. Rereading without solutions can support **[[blind review]]**; changing an answer after reading its explanation is feedback-assisted correction. Both can teach you something, but they provide different evidence about what you could do independently.

Several questions about one passage are several assessment items, not several independent first readings. Familiarity with the passage can help on later questions. Seeing an explanation for one item can also reveal information useful for another. Record that exposure when interpreting the result.

Repeated module-review questions are useful for retrieval and explanation practice. They do not become fresh passage evidence because their display order changes. To judge transfer, eventually use an unfamiliar passage and new questions while preserving the conditions and your first responses. A correct answer with a poor explanation remains worth reviewing; a strong explanation developed after feedback remains a learning outcome, not a replacement first attempt.

## Guided practice

Read this short original passage:

> A fictional concert archive adds descriptions of audience reactions to its existing recordings. The editor says applause can document how a particular audience responded, but cannot alone establish which performance had the greatest artistic merit. The archive retains quiet recordings as well as enthusiastic ones and identifies the evidence supporting each description.

Write the main point, the editor's attitude toward reaction records, and one unsupported extension. Then make a ledger entry for the claim “The editor considers applause worthless.”

Check: reaction records can document a particular audience's response, while their use as an artistic ranking is limited. The editor accepts a use and restricts another. Calling applause worthless erases that accepted use; treating quiet recordings as proof of poor artistic quality adds a ranking the text does not establish. Your ledger should name the distinction between documenting a response and establishing artistic merit.

## Common mistakes

- Using a whole-passage impression when the question requires an exact detail.
- Defending a first impression after later paragraphs qualify it.
- Accepting an answer with one supported clause and one unsupported extension.
- Recording only the correct choice, without its evidence or the competing choice's error.
- Treating repeated passages or feedback-assisted corrections as fresh first-attempt results.

## Key points

- Map the passage, then select the operation required by each question.
- Match the complete answer to the passage's relationships and limits.
- Use an evidence ledger to identify a specific, repeatable review target.
- Keep first attempts, blind review, and feedback-assisted learning distinct.
- Seek transfer on unfamiliar text after understanding your errors on familiar text.

lessons.title: Reconstructing dense passage arguments
lessons.body:
Module 8 taught you to map passages and locate evidence. Dense argumentative reading requires a more detailed reconstruction. A paragraph may support a claim that becomes a reason for another claim. A sentence may accept an objection, limit its force, and defend a revised position. Your task is to recover those relationships without turning a qualified argument into a simpler but different one.

Work untimed while learning this method. The objective is a faithful account of what supports what, who accepts each claim, and how far the final position extends. Shorter notes help only when they preserve those distinctions.

## Recover the levels of support

An **[[argument hierarchy]]** organizes claims by their supporting roles: evidence supports a local conclusion, which may then support a broader conclusion. It is a structure of reasoning, not a ranking of interesting sentences. A vivid example can sit low in the hierarchy while a quiet qualification determines the reach of the whole argument.

Ask two questions of a claim: “What supports this?” and “What does this support?” A claim with answers to both may be an **[[intermediate conclusion]]**. The **[[main conclusion]]** is the position the argument ultimately supports within the passage. It need not appear last, and a sentence beginning with “therefore” can still express an intermediate step.

Do not force every sentence into a support chain. Some sentences identify a rival view, define a term, give background, or restrict a recommendation. Record those roles beside the relevant claim. A rival's conclusion can have its own supporting evidence without becoming the author's conclusion.

## Expand compressed reasoning carefully

A **[[compressed argument]]** leaves some relationships implicit or packs several reasoning steps into a small space. Reconstruct it by separating the stated claims and making their connections explicit. Distinguish an author's stated reason from an assumption you supply to explain how the reason would work.

For example, “Because the council's records omit rejected proposals, its files cannot establish the full range of proposals considered” contains an observation and a limitation. The observation concerns the records; the conclusion concerns what those records can establish. “No rejected proposals existed” is not an expansion of that reasoning. It reverses the point about incomplete evidence.

Read connectives in context. “Although” often marks a concession; “because” introduces a reason; “nevertheless” signals that an accepted consideration does not settle the issue. None guarantees a fixed argumentative role. Identify the actual claims before assigning labels.

### Example 1: Separate a useful procedure from a stronger claim

Read this original fictional account:

> (1) The Varo music panel requires judges to write preliminary evaluations before discussing applicants. Its chair claims that this procedure makes the final ranking accurate, because judges can no longer merely copy the first speaker's assessment.
>
> (2) Independent notes do remove that particular route of influence. Yet judges who all received the same mistaken description of an applicant's performance could independently repeat the same error. Agreement among the notes therefore cannot, by itself, establish that the shared assessment is accurate.
>
> (3) This limitation does not make preliminary notes pointless. Differences between them can reveal questions that discussion should investigate. The panel should retain the notes and examine the reasons behind agreement as well as disagreement, while treating the accuracy of a final ranking as requiring further support.

Step 1: Separate ownership. The chair claims that independent notes make the ranking accurate. The author accepts a narrower procedural benefit and challenges the stronger conclusion. Quoting the chair's reasoning does not endorse its full result.

Step 2: Reconstruct the local argument in paragraph (2). Judges might share mistaken information despite writing separately. Therefore, independence and agreement do not by themselves establish accuracy. The hypothetical explains a limit; it does not report an actual error in this panel's records.

Step 3: Locate the broader recommendation. Paragraph (3) recommends retaining notes while investigating the reasons behind the assessments. The limitation from paragraph (2) explains why agreement still needs examination. The usefulness of recorded differences supplies another reason to retain the procedure.

Step 4: Preserve the concession. Removing one route of influence is a real benefit in the passage. “Independent notes have no value” discards that benefit. “Independent notes guarantee accuracy” removes the author's limitation. Both distort the relationship between procedure and result.

Step 5: Match the requested level. A question about paragraph (2)'s conclusion needs the limit on what agreement establishes. A question about the passage's overall position needs the qualified recommendation. A true local conclusion can be an incomplete answer to the broader question.

## Restore every important qualification

A **[[qualification]]** restricts a claim's scope, strength, circumstances, or evidential basis. Preserve words such as “some,” “in these cases,” “on this evidence,” and “without additional information.” They are part of the claim, not decorative caution.

A **[[parenthetical qualification]]** places such a restriction inside an interruption, often marked by parentheses, commas, or dashes. When a sentence is difficult, first identify its main grammatical statement. Then restore the interruption and ask exactly what it modifies. Removing it is a temporary reading aid, not permission to delete it from your final interpretation.

Compare “The evidence does not establish that every design was copied” with “The evidence establishes that no design was copied.” The first limits a conclusion supported by the evidence. The second claims evidence for a contrary conclusion. Failure to establish a general claim does not establish its complete denial.

Also distinguish conditions on a recommendation from predictions of success. “Use the method where its assumptions can be checked” does not say those assumptions always hold, that the method must always succeed, or that every other method is worthless.

### Example 2: Keep the limitation attached to its target

Consider this invented passage:

> (1) Historian Eren compares patterns on the ceremonial coats of three fictional towns. Earlier commentators treated a shared border design as proof that one workshop controlled production in all three towns.
>
> (2) Eren finds that local workshop books contain different instructions for constructing that border. These differences do not rule out a common visual influence, but they undermine the claim that resemblance alone demonstrates centralized production.
>
> (3) Although the workshop books cannot settle the origin of every surviving coat, they justify distinguishing visual influence from production control. That distinction should guide future attributions, at least where a coat can be connected to the documented workshop practices. It should not become a claim that the towns developed in complete isolation.

Step 1: Extract the evidence. Different local construction instructions appear in the books. This supports a challenge to an inference from visual resemblance to centralized production. It does not establish that the towns never communicated.

Step 2: Recover the intermediate conclusion. Resemblance alone fails to demonstrate centralized production. The words “alone” and “demonstrate” matter: the passage criticizes the sufficiency of one kind of evidence without proving that centralized production was impossible.

Step 3: Identify the final position. Future attributions should distinguish influence from production control where the documented practices can be connected to a coat. The recommendation builds on the evidential distinction, rather than simply repeating that construction instructions differ.

Step 4: Attach each limit correctly. The books cannot settle every coat's origin; that restricts their coverage. “At least where” specifies cases for which the recommendation is defended, without deciding all other cases. The final warning excludes a stronger isolation claim. These are three different limits, not a general declaration that historical inference is impossible.

Step 5: Check a tempting paraphrase. “Eren proves that shared designs never indicate shared production” changes a criticism of resemblance alone into a universal prohibition. A faithful version says that the described resemblance does not, without further evidence, demonstrate production control.

## Test the reconstruction against the whole passage

Read your proposed account back through the passage. Can you identify the evidence for each step? Have you turned an objection into the author's view? Does the recommendation retain its conditions? Does your account explain why the author included a concession instead of treating it as irrelevant?

When comparing choices, check both the claim and its role. An answer can quote a true statement but call it the final conclusion when it supports a further recommendation. Another can correctly identify a recommendation but remove the condition under which it applies. Either error matters.

Keep a disputed connection visible. If the author relies on an unstated bridge, note the bridge as an assumption; do not silently convert it into passage evidence. Accurate reconstruction can reveal a weakness without requiring you to repair the author's argument.

## Guided practice

Read this original sentence:

> Because two different delivery schedules achieved the same reduction in late arrivals, the fictional guild cannot credit the reduction across both trials to just one of those schedules; nevertheless, since both trials also introduced advance notices, the notices deserve investigation rather than immediate adoption as a proven remedy.

Write the observation, the limited conclusion, and the recommendation. Then identify an unsupported stronger claim.

A supported response identifies equal reductions under different schedules as the observation. The guild cannot credit one schedule alone on that basis. The shared introduction of notices motivates further investigation, not certainty about their effect. “The schedules had no effect” goes beyond the passage; “the notices are a proven remedy” contradicts its stated caution.

## Common mistakes

- Treating a locally supported conclusion as the passage's final position.
- Preserving the topic of a sentence while deleting its conditions or degree of certainty.
- Turning evidence against one inference into proof of the opposite claim.
- Treating a hypothetical possibility as an observed event.
- Adding a reasonable bridge without identifying it as an assumption.

## Key points

- Track the support hierarchy and each claim's owner.
- Expand compressed relationships without inventing evidence.
- Restore qualifications after simplifying difficult grammar.
- Match the answer to the level and scope the question requests.

lessons.title: Reading technical language in context
lessons.body:
An unfamiliar term can make a passage feel less understandable than it is. Yet the author may supply the definition, comparison, or example needed to answer the question. Your task is to recover those relationships. The previous lesson reconstructed dense arguments; this lesson applies that care to technical descriptions, measurements, and explanations. You do not need to turn a short passage into a complete course in its subject.

## Build a usable meaning from the text

Start by identifying what kind of thing the unfamiliar expression names: an object, a procedure, a measured result, a proposed mechanism, or a category. Then look for a definition, contrast, example, or stated consequence. “In this study,” “we call,” and “defined as” often signal that the passage is specifying a local use. A familiar word can therefore demand as much attention as an unfamiliar one.

An **[[operational definition]]** specifies a procedure or observable rule used to identify or measure something. If a fictional inspection defines a “stable” display as one whose pointer remains within two marks for ten seconds, that is the reported test. It does not establish stability under every load or for every duration. The procedure makes a claim checkable while also setting its limits.

Preserve every part of that rule: the object tested, the operation, the threshold, and any duration or comparison condition. A shortened paraphrase should retain what decides membership or a result. “The pointer did not move much” loses both the stated boundary and the observation period.

## Follow references through changing descriptions

A **[[reference chain]]** connects the expressions used for the same person, object, claim, or process across a passage. An author might introduce “the revised counting rule,” later call it “this procedure,” and then discuss “its effect.” Resolve each link before combining the claims.

Grammar helps, but the nearest noun is not automatically the correct **[[referent]]**. The candidate must also fit the action or property being described. A rule can classify a record; a record does not itself become the classification procedure. When several candidates seem possible, replace the referring expression with each candidate and reread the whole sentence. Then check the preceding contrast or example. Do not manufacture certainty if the text still leaves a genuine ambiguity.

## Separate a measure from the broader target

A **[[proxy measure]]** is an observable measure used as an indicator of something else that interests the investigator. Counting completed visits may be used to investigate engagement, but completion and engagement are not identical merely because a report connects them. Ask what was actually recorded, what broader property is proposed, and what evidence links the two.

This distinction does not make indirect measures useless. A measure can describe its own recorded outcome accurately while supporting only a limited conclusion about the broader target. The link may require additional observations. Also distinguish a change in the measured object from a change in the rule used to score it. Recounting the same records under a new threshold can change a reported value without documenting a new event.

### Example 1: Read a gallery's engagement measure

Consider this original account:

> (1) The fictional Orin Gallery defines a “completed path” as a ticket whose number is scanned in all four exhibition rooms during one visit. Staff use completion counts as an indicator of engagement, by which they mean sustained attention to the exhibits.
>
> (2) A group guide can carry several tickets through the scanners while their owners remain in the entrance hall. The scanners record ticket numbers, not where their owners look. Moving the scanners beside each room's entrance increases the completion count. Staff do not record looking time or understanding of the exhibits.
>
> (3) The curator retains the counts for planning scanner maintenance but requests additional observations before describing the increase as greater engagement. The new arrangement may make scanning easier without changing attention to the displays.

Step 1: Recover the local definition. A completed path means that a ticket number receives four specified scans during one visit. It does not mean that its owner attentively viewed four rooms. The guide example shows why those descriptions can come apart.

Step 2: Identify the target and proxy. Sustained attention is the target. Completion count is the proposed indicator. Calling both “participation” in a paraphrase would conceal the distinction that drives the passage.

Step 3: Locate the observed change. More ticket numbers qualify after the scanners move. That is a result about scans under the arrangement described. The passage does not establish an increase in looking time, which staff never recorded.

Step 4: Explain the curator's position. She accepts a practical use for the counts while withholding a broader interpretation. “She rejects the records as inaccurate” lacks support: her stated concern is their interpretation as engagement. “She proves engagement did not increase” also goes too far: the increase remains unresolved, not disproved.

Step 5: Identify relevant further evidence. Observations connecting scans with sustained attention would address the proposed link. A second accurate count of the same scans could improve confidence in counting without establishing that link. Match the investigation to the uncertainty.

## Distinguish an observation from its explanation

Technical descriptions often move among a procedure, its result, and an account of why that result occurred. Label those roles mentally. A model that reproduces a pattern supplies a possible account under its assumptions. Reproducing the pattern does not, by itself, establish that the model describes the only process capable of producing it.

Conversely, an incomplete explanation does not erase the observation. Keep the author's actual degree of commitment: demonstrated, consistent with, suggested, or unresolved. A **[[qualification]]** may restrict the population, conditions, or proposed mechanism rather than reject the entire result. Trace the restriction to the claim it modifies.

### Example 2: Interpret technical support in an archive

Read another invented account:

> (1) An editor compares four copies of an invented ceremonial text. In her table, “support” for a reading means the number of copies containing it. A “witness” means one surviving copy, without implying that it was produced independently.
>
> (2) Copies Elm, Fir, and Pine omit the same line; Ash includes it. Records establish that Fir and Pine were copied directly from Elm. These derivative witnesses therefore add to the omission's numerical support without supplying independent instances of its origin.
>
> (3) The editor reports support of three for the omission. She does not conclude that the missing line was absent from the earliest text. Elm might have inherited the omission or introduced it. The table organizes surviving readings; it does not itself settle their history.

Step 1: Use the author's definition. Support here is a count of surviving copies. A score of three follows because Elm, Fir, and Pine each contain the omission. Substituting “three independent confirmations” changes the defined quantity.

Step 2: Follow the reference chain. “These derivative witnesses” refers to Fir and Pine, whose direct dependence on Elm has just been established. It does not include Ash, and it does not call every surviving copy derivative of Elm.

Step 3: Separate count from origin. Fir and Pine preserve an omission found in their source. Their existence increases the copy count but does not create two independently established origins for that omission. The editor can therefore accept the number while limiting what it proves.

Step 4: Preserve the unresolved alternative. Elm could have inherited or introduced the omission. Neither possibility is selected. “The editor proves that Elm altered the earliest text” turns an acknowledged possibility into a finding.

Step 5: Answer the requested task. For a detail about numerical support, use the counting rule. For a question about historical inference, combine the dependence records with the unresolved alternatives. A correct answer to one task is not automatically an answer to the other.

## Guided practice

An invented transport model defines a station as “covered” when the map contains at least one permitted route from the depot to that station. Its permitted routes use only roads marked open in the input file. The model records no journey times or vehicle capacities. An analyst corrects a road's input label from closed to open, and the model then lists an additional covered station. No vehicle has yet used the newly permitted route.

Before reading the check, state the operational definition, identify what changed, and explain whether the result establishes faster deliveries. Also name one question the model can answer as described.

Check: coverage means the existence of a permitted route under the input labels. Correcting a label changes which routes the model permits; it does not document an actual journey. The model can answer whether a station has such a route. Faster delivery is unsupported because neither journey times nor a delivery comparison was recorded. The result may guide further investigation without supplying that missing evidence.

## Common mistakes

- Importing an everyday meaning after the author defines a narrower technical use.
- Memorizing a technical label while dropping the procedure that gives it meaning.
- Treating a nearby noun as the referent without checking the sentence's relationship.
- Replacing a proxy with its target, or assuming an accurately counted proxy must be a valid indicator.
- Treating a scoring change as a demonstrated change in the underlying object.
- Calling a plausible explanation proven, or calling an unresolved outcome false.

## Key points

- Recover a term's meaning from definitions, contrasts, and examples in its context.
- Keep objects, procedures, measurements, and explanations distinct.
- Follow reference chains before joining claims across sentences.
- Ask what connects a proxy measure to its broader target.
- Preserve the author's conditions and degree of confidence in your answer.

lessons.title: Comparing agreement, disagreement, and silence
lessons.body:
Two passages can discuss the same subject without answering the same question. One writer may ask whether a result is reliable; another may ask whether acting on it would be desirable. They can share a recommendation for different reasons, or disagree about a narrow policy while accepting much of the same evidence. Comparing them requires more than assigning one a favorable attitude and the other an unfavorable one.

This lesson extends viewpoint tracking across two texts. Read each passage on its own terms, then compare specific commitments. A relationship you can explain with evidence from both passages is more dependable than a broad impression of similarity or conflict.

## Give the comparison an exact object

A **[[comparison proposition]]** is the particular claim whose treatment you check in each passage. It should identify the subject, asserted relationship, conditions, and strength. “Both discuss restoration” identifies a topic. “Both require new restoration material to remain identifiable” states a claim that each passage can support or fail to support.

Preserve the words that control **[[scope]]**. A claim about one pilot does not automatically concern every future program. “Can help” does not mean “always succeeds.” An author who approves collecting information may oppose using it for a particular decision. Changing any of those features can create a disagreement that the texts do not contain.

Before comparing, paraphrase each writer's central position and strongest reason. Then put a candidate proposition beside those summaries. Ask what the writer commits to about that proposition. Do not fill an empty space with what someone holding that profession, political outlook, or general preference would probably believe.

## Separate support, rejection, and an unresolved position

Agreement requires evidence that both writers accept the relevant claim. They need not use identical language or offer the same reason. Disagreement requires incompatible commitments about the same claim under the same conditions. One author's rejection of a universal claim can coexist with the other's acceptance of a limited instance.

**[[Textual silence]]** means that the passage does not establish the author's position on the particular claim being tested. The author may have a view outside the text. The reading task gives you no authority to supply it. Silence is therefore neither acceptance nor rejection.

An author can also expressly suspend judgment. “The evidence does not yet settle this question” is a stated assessment of the evidence; an omission provides no comparable assessment. Neither establishes that the underlying claim is false. Keep the difference between an undecided issue and a negative conclusion visible in your notes.

A compact table can expose the distinction:

| Evidence in a passage | Supported reading |
|---|---|
| The writer accepts the claim | Support |
| The writer accepts an incompatible claim | Rejection |
| The text establishes neither position | Undetermined |

“Undetermined” describes what you can attribute from the text. It is not a prediction that the writer would be undecided if asked directly.

### Example 1: Locate disagreement beneath shared concerns

Consider two original positions about an invented concert hall:

> Passage A: The hall should admit late arrivals between movements, while keeping the doors closed during each movement. Opening them during a movement can interrupt the quiet passages. Holding every late arrival until the entire concert ends imposes an avoidable cost, since the breaks provide an opportunity for entry without interrupting a movement.
>
> Passage B: Quiet passages deserve protection, and the doors should remain closed during each movement. Nevertheless, the hall should hold late arrivals until the concert ends. Even entry during breaks shifts attention toward the doors just before the next movement. Preserving continuity across the evening justifies that inconvenience.

Step 1: State the shared premise. Both writers want the doors closed during movements to protect the listening experience. Passage B does not reject that concern merely because it opposes Passage A's policy.

Step 2: State the exact policy question. Should late arrivals enter between movements? Passage A says yes; Passage B says no. The writers address the same people, interval, and proposed action, so this is a supported disagreement.

Step 3: Compare the reasons. Passage A treats breaks as an opportunity to avoid interrupting a movement. Passage B identifies an additional concern about attention and continuity across movements. Their disagreement need not imply that one thinks interruptions are harmless.

Step 4: Test an exaggerated answer. “They disagree about whether doors should ever be closed” fails: both support closing them during movements. “They disagree about whether late arrival should be punished” also fails. Neither describes inconvenience as deserved punishment.

Step 5: Mark the unanswered question. Neither passage establishes a view about ticket refunds. Passage A's concern for inconvenience does not prove support for refunds; Passage B's strict entry rule does not prove opposition to them. A new claim needs its own textual support.

## Compare the relationship between arguments

A **[[cross-passage relation]]** is the supported connection between the texts' claims, reasons, methods, or purposes. One passage may supply a mechanism for a pattern the other describes. It may limit an inference, challenge a decision criterion, add another consideration, or apply a shared principle to a new case.

Separate three questions: Do the authors accept the same finding? Do they draw the same conclusion from it? Do they support that conclusion for the same reason? An affirmative answer to one does not settle the others. Agreement about a recommendation can conceal a substantial difference about its justification.

Also distinguish an author from a reported opponent. If Passage A describes a critic before rejecting that critic's proposal, compare Passage B with the author's final position, unless the question explicitly names the critic. Carry speaker attribution across the passage boundary just as carefully as within one text.

### Example 2: Do not turn a necessary condition into approval

Consider two original discussions of an imagined apprenticeship program:

> Passage A: The program should not publicly rank apprentices by their one finished display. Tutors provided unequal amounts of help, so the displays do not support comparisons of independent performance. Any defensible comparison would have to include work completed without that assistance. This requirement alone does not settle how the program ought to use comparisons.
>
> Passage B: The program should abandon public rankings even if independent performance could be measured accurately. Public positions encourage apprentices to protect a rank instead of attempting unfamiliar techniques. Individual feedback can guide improvement without creating a public ordering.

Step 1: Identify common ground. Both oppose the current public ranking. Passage A rejects its evidential basis; Passage B objects to the educational effects of public ordering.

Step 2: Apply a proposed change. Suppose the program collects several independently completed tasks. That change addresses the unequal-assistance objection in Passage A. It does not answer Passage B's concern, which expressly survives accurate measurement.

Step 3: Stop at the supported conclusion. Passage A requires independent work for a defensible comparison. It does not say that independent work makes public ranking desirable. Treating the proposed change as automatic approval reverses the direction of the requirement and ignores the final sentence.

Step 4: Preserve the other boundary. Passage B opposes public ordering, not all assessment. Its support for individual feedback prevents the inference that the writer considers every evaluation harmful.

Step 5: Reject an invented disagreement. The passages do not establish that the authors disagree about the educational effects of public ranking. Passage A does not address those effects. You can identify different stated objections without inventing a rejection of either objection by the other writer.

## Predict a response from commitments, not personality

Some questions ask how one author would most likely respond to a claim in the other passage. Identify the relevant principle or reason first. Then ask what it supports in the new case, retaining any limits. A response can be warranted without appearing verbatim, but it must follow from a specific commitment rather than a guessed temperament.

In the concert example, Passage B's stated concern supports resisting entry during breaks even when no music is playing. It does not establish opposition to every change that makes attendance easier. In the apprenticeship example, accurate measurement would leave Passage B's stated objection intact. The same improvement would remove one objection in Passage A without establishing the author's final policy choice.

Check a proposed response clause by clause. An answer can begin with a supported reaction and end by assigning the writer a new factual belief. “This would address the measurement concern, so public ranking must be adopted” crosses that boundary.

## Guided practice

Read these invented statements:

> Passage A: A village workshop should offer an optional evening session. Several residents cannot attend the morning session, and the unused room is available then. The workshop should preserve its morning session as well.
>
> Passage B: The morning session should continue because its small groups allow careful feedback. The workshop should collect information about demand before deciding whether to expand its schedule. This discussion does not determine whether an evening session would attract enough participants.

Write one agreement, one proposed disagreement that lacks support, and one difference in the authors' approaches.

A reasoned response: both favor retaining the morning session. “They disagree about whether an evening session would attract enough participants” is unsupported: Passage B leaves that issue unresolved, while Passage A's proposal does not establish a forecast of sufficient participation. Passage A recommends an option using an access problem and available space; Passage B calls for information before a decision about expansion. That difference concerns their recommendations about the decision process, not opposite factual conclusions about turnout.

## Common mistakes

- Comparing whole topics instead of complete propositions with matching conditions.
- Treating criticism of one use of evidence as rejection of the evidence itself.
- Assuming a writer accepts the opposite of every position not endorsed.
- Confusing a shared conclusion with a shared justification.
- Treating removal of one objection as proof that an author now approves a proposal.

## Key points

- Establish each author's commitment before assigning a relationship.
- Check agreement and disagreement at the same scope and strength.
- Keep silence distinct from denial and explicit suspension of judgment.
- Predict responses through stated reasons and qualifications.
- Use evidence from both passages to justify every comparative answer.

lessons.title: Integrating advanced and comparative reading
lessons.body:
Paired passages add an attribution task: keeping each author's commitments separate while comparing them. You must understand each argument, then identify the particular relationship the question asks about. A shared subject does not guarantee a dispute, and a disagreement about a policy does not imply disagreement about every supporting fact. This lesson combines dense argument reconstruction, contextual reading, and precise comparison in untimed sets.

The aim is a defensible account of the pair. Keep enough structure to relocate evidence without memorizing every example. When a question becomes difficult, identify whether the missing step concerns one passage's meaning or the relationship between passages. Those are different repair tasks.

## Build two accounts before combining them

Read the first passage for its organizing question, central claim, important reasons, and limits. Then read the second with the same discipline. Treat its author as an independent thinker: do not assume that every statement is a direct response to the first author. A second passage can approach a related problem at a different stage or scale.

A **[[comparative map]]** records each passage's position and reasons alongside the precise relationships between them. It can be a few short notes rather than a diagram. Record a shared issue, each author's answer, and one or two relationships you can actually defend. Keep local uncertainty visible. If an author does not address a proposed claim, write that the evidence is insufficient instead of supplying an imagined opinion.

For dense prose, reconstruct the **[[argument hierarchy]]** within each account. A measurement may support an intermediate finding, which then supports a qualified recommendation. Compare recommendations with recommendations and findings with findings before claiming a conflict. Authors can share a finding while assigning it different importance in a decision.

## Match the scope of the comparison

Write a candidate agreement or disagreement as one complete proposition. Include the relevant subject, conditions, time period, and degree of certainty. “Both discuss access” identifies a topic. “Both accept that supervised access can reveal information missing from a catalogue” identifies a claim whose support can be checked separately.

Look for **[[asymmetric support]]**: the passages provide different amounts or kinds of support for a proposed comparison. One author may explicitly reject a policy while the other accepts only one premise used to defend it. That is not enough to assign the second author the opposite policy. A clear statement on one side cannot fill a gap on the other.

Do not force symmetry in the reasons either. Two authors might endorse the same action for different purposes. Conversely, identical vocabulary can conceal different standards. One author's “success” may mean reliable description; another's may mean an improvement in public use. Preserve those definitions before comparing results.

### Example 1: Separate a shared finding from a disputed choice

Read this original pair:

> Passage A: A fictional music archive holds a unique reed instrument. Playing it can reveal responses that measurements of its shape do not capture. Yet each playing session can change wear marks that researchers cannot fully record. Where a unique instrument would gain new wear, the archive should preserve those marks and study response through declared approximations, even if some information remains inaccessible.
>
> Passage B: The same archive should never play an instrument that is structurally fragile. For a stable instrument, however, a carefully limited session may be justified when its response bears directly on a serious research question. Existing wear should be documented, although documentation is incomplete. Losing some evidence of use can sometimes be justified by gaining otherwise unavailable evidence of response.

Step 1: State each recommendation with its condition. A gives priority to preserving unique wear when playing adds wear. B permits some limited playing of stable instruments when the research value justifies the evidentiary cost. B does not recommend unrestricted performance.

Step 2: Identify shared commitments. Both accept that response can supply information unavailable from a static record. Both acknowledge a loss of wear evidence. B's explicit warning about fragile instruments cannot automatically be attributed to A, whose passage discusses a different condition.

Step 3: Form the conflict precisely. Consider a stable, unique instrument for which playing would add wear but answer an important response question. A's preservation rule excludes playing; B's balancing approach can allow it. This is a conflict about how to weigh competing kinds of evidence, not a dispute about whether playing changes an instrument.

Step 4: Reject an overstatement. “B considers old wear scientifically worthless” contradicts B's acknowledgement of an evidentiary cost. “A believes performance teaches nothing” contradicts A's opening sentence. Each distractor erases the concession that makes the disagreement interesting.

Step 5: Check the strongest comparison. Both recognize a trade-off, but assign different decision weight to preserving unique wear. That account explains their shared premises and their different recommendations without inventing a motive.

## Use each question to choose an evidence path

A relationship question needs an account of both passages. A function question may be local even when it appears in a comparative set. An application question asks whether a new example preserves the relevant relationship. Do not gather more text simply because two passages are available; gather the text that establishes the requested connection.

For an author's likely response, start with the author's stated reasoning. Then ask what follows about the particular proposal in the question. An unfamiliar proposal may fit a stated rule, violate it, or fall outside its scope. Do not turn a prediction of response into a general personality judgment such as “this author always favors innovation.”

For a supported cross-passage inference, state what each passage contributes. If removing one passage leaves the proposed comparison unsupported, identify the missing contribution. This is a way to audit the relationship, not a rule that every correct answer must depend equally on both texts.

### Example 2: Combine complementary inquiries without inventing agreement

Consider another original pair:

> Passage A: A fictional reading room wants to know whether visitors can locate a requested document. Its trial records whether each visitor reaches the correct folder. A successful location does not show whether the document answers the visitor's historical question. The trial should be used to improve navigation, not to rate the historical adequacy of the collection.
>
> Passage B: The reading room also wants to know whether its collection supports several competing accounts of local history. Researchers compare the kinds of surviving records and identify gaps in coverage. They make no measurement of how easily a visitor can find a folder. A collection can contain useful evidence that its current index makes hard to locate.

Step 1: Identify the measured targets. A examines document location. B examines evidentiary coverage. The shared setting does not make the inquiries interchangeable.

Step 2: Explain their relationship. A separates navigation from historical adequacy; B studies adequacy while recognizing that navigation can be poor. The accounts distinguish two dimensions and could inform complementary improvements. Neither passage requires a trade-off between them.

Step 3: Draw a bounded inference. Success on A's navigation measure cannot alone establish success on B's coverage inquiry. The measure and inquiry concern different outcomes. This does not imply that navigation and coverage can never be related in practice.

Step 4: Evaluate a proposed response. B would have textual grounds to resist using folder-finding success as the complete test of historical coverage. B does not provide grounds for predicting which index design visitors would find easiest.

Step 5: Preserve silence. Neither author states the cost of redesigning the index. The claim that both prefer a cheaper system has no support, even if it sounds reasonable. A missing cost discussion is not a judgment that cost is irrelevant.

## Review the pair without rewriting the first attempt

Preserve your first choices and reasons before reading explanations. If you reconsider without solutions, save that blind-review work separately. After feedback, record the correction and its evidence without replacing either earlier record. Use answer content in your notes because displayed choice letters can change.

For each mistake, identify its level: misunderstanding one author, losing a qualification, connecting claims with different targets, or treating silence as agreement or denial. Then explain the smallest correction that repairs the answer. “Compare more carefully” is too broad to guide the next attempt.

Repeated questions about the same pair are not independent first readings. An explanation for one question can expose the structure needed for another. Keep that exposure visible when judging progress. Fresh transfer requires an unfamiliar pair and new questions, not merely a different order for familiar material.

## Guided practice

Invented editor A wants all historical photographs dated where evidence permits, because sequence can clarify change. Editor B also considers evidence-supported dates useful, but wants uncertain dates visibly marked because an unsupported exact date can mislead. A does not discuss how uncertainty should be displayed.

Write one supported agreement, one tempting but unsupported disagreement, and one question requiring more evidence. A defensible agreement is that evidence-supported dating can be useful: both authors explicitly accept that point. Claiming that A wants doubtful dates presented as certain invents A's policy. Whether both would endorse a particular uncertainty symbol remains unanswered.

## Common mistakes

- Comparing a broad topic instead of the same proposition under the same conditions.
- Treating a local concession as acceptance of an entire recommendation.
- Assuming the second passage must refute the first.
- Assigning a view from one author's clear statement and the other's silence.
- Letting outside knowledge supply an author's missing commitment.
- Treating feedback-assisted recognition of a familiar pair as fresh reading evidence.

## Key points

- Build an accurate account of each passage before combining them.
- Compare claims at matching levels, with their conditions and strength intact.
- Allow agreement, conflict, complementarity, and insufficient evidence to remain distinct.
- Anchor predicted responses in stated reasons, not imagined personalities.
- Preserve first attempts and exposure records when reviewing comparative sets.

lessons.title: Developing and revising an argumentative position
lessons.body:
Comparative reading asks what different authors claim and how their reasons relate. Argumentative writing asks you to enter that discussion with a position of your own. You need to answer the issue, explain why your reasons matter, and address a serious competing consideration. A polished summary of the perspectives cannot do that work by itself.

LSAC's [writing-task overview](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/about/lsat-argumentative-writing), checked November 3, 2026, describes developing a position while engaging with arguments from other perspectives. This lesson uses original, untimed instructional exercises. Its planning and revision quiz does not grade an essay or convert writing performance into an official score. Save your own drafts and review notes separately.

## Turn an issue into a position

A **[[thesis]]** is the central position an essay undertakes to defend. It should answer the question at the level actually posed. If the issue asks how a shared facility should allocate scarce time, “shared facilities are important” gives background rather than a decision. A useful thesis identifies a policy or principle and the reason it deserves priority.

A position can be qualified without becoming evasive. “Give each applicant an initial turn, then allocate remaining time according to documented project needs” makes a definite choice with conditions. “Every side has strengths and the situation is complicated” postpones the choice. Qualifications should explain where the recommendation applies or how it responds to a competing concern.

You need not choose the most extreme position or combine every proposal. A defensible alternative may modify one perspective, distinguish cases, or propose another rule. Its quality depends on the reasoning you supply, not on whether it sounds like a compromise.

## Explain why your reasons count

A **[[decision criterion]]** states a standard for evaluating the options: broad access, dependable completion, protection against irreversible loss, or another relevant objective. Explain why that standard matters in this case and how the recommended approach serves it. Listing several attractive values without resolving their conflict leaves the decision unsupported.

Separate an empirical premise from an evaluative judgement. “A fixed schedule lets participants plan ahead” proposes a practical effect. “Predictable access should receive priority over last-minute flexibility” assigns that effect decision weight. The effect alone does not establish the priority. Your essay should expose that connection so a reader can assess it.

Use the supplied facts accurately. A hypothetical example can test a principle, but identify it as hypothetical. Do not turn an imagined outcome into reported evidence. If an important result is uncertain, consider whether a trial, condition, or narrower recommendation addresses the uncertainty. Adding a safeguard still requires explaining how it bears on the actual concern.

### Example 1: Defend a scheduling rule with an explicit criterion

Consider this original issue:

> A fictional observatory shares one teaching telescope. How should it allocate evening sessions? Perspective 1 favors equal turns so newcomers can participate. Perspective 2 favors consecutive sessions for projects that need repeated observations. Perspective 3 emphasizes advance notice, because some participants can attend only after arranging transport. The observatory cannot satisfy every request on the same evening.

Step 1: Identify the competing considerations. Equal turns address distribution, consecutive sessions address project continuity, and notice addresses usable access. None is merely an objection to astronomy. A fair response should represent the strongest relevant concern behind each view.

Step 2: Choose a criterion and thesis. Suppose the writer prioritizes a meaningful first opportunity while allowing a limited amount of continuity. A thesis could be: “The observatory should reserve regularly announced introductory sessions, then allocate a capped share of remaining evenings to documented projects requiring continuity.” This is one defensible position, not the only acceptable policy.

Step 3: Build the reason. A nominal right to compete for every evening may yield little access if recurring projects consume the schedule. A protected introductory share responds to that risk. A limited continuity allocation recognizes that a single isolated turn may not accomplish some projects' stated purposes. The word “capped” signals that continuity does not receive unlimited priority.

Step 4: Address the strongest objection. A project leader might argue that the cap interrupts valuable work. The response should acknowledge that cost and defend the access priority, rather than accuse leaders of selfishness. Published criteria and schedules can also respond to the advance-notice concern without guaranteeing that every participant can attend.

Step 5: Draft the reasoning as connected prose. For example: “An evening is useful only if its allocation serves a workable opportunity. Regular introductory sessions would protect an entry point for newcomers, while a limited continuity allocation would let some projects do work an isolated turn cannot support. This arrangement sacrifices some project capacity. That cost is justified when preserving broad entry into a shared teaching facility is a central purpose, although the chosen allocation should be reviewed if introductory sessions repeatedly go unused.” The final condition gives relevant evidence a role without inventing an attendance result.

## Meet a serious competing argument

A **[[counterargument]]** supplies a reason against your position or against a step supporting it. It may challenge a premise, propose a different priority, or identify a consequence your argument neglected. Choose one with enough force that answering it clarifies your reasoning.

A **[[concession]]** accepts a point without necessarily accepting the opponent's final conclusion. A **[[rebuttal]]** gives a reason the objection does not defeat the position as defended. These can work together: accept a genuine cost, then explain why another consideration outweighs it, or narrow the policy to reduce the cost.

Avoid answering a weaker claim than the one presented. If a perspective worries that summaries can omit important context, saying “summaries are sometimes accurate” does not answer the possibility of selective omission. Address the actual risk and explain the proposed response's limits.

### Example 2: Revise a response that overclaims

Read this original issue and draft:

> A fictional oral-history centre is considering searchable summaries of its recordings. Perspective 1 values easier discovery. Perspective 2 worries that compressed summaries can distort a speaker's emphasis. Perspective 3 favors letting contributors review descriptions before publication. A draft argues: “All summaries should be published immediately. Searchability proves that they represent speakers fairly, and anyone who worries about distortion opposes access.”

Step 1: Find the unsupported connections. Searchability concerns finding material; fairness concerns how it is represented. One does not prove the other. The draft also turns a concern about distortion into a general opposition to access, misrepresenting Perspective 2.

Step 2: Preserve a defensible aim. The writer can still favor searchable descriptions. A stronger thesis might support publication after a process that checks descriptions against recordings, allows contributor review, and clearly links each summary to its source. Those are proposed safeguards, not facts already established by the prompt.

Step 3: State a **[[revision rationale]]**: an explanation of which argumentative problem a change repairs and why. Here the revision replaces an unsupported equivalence with separate reasons for discoverability and faithful representation. It also gives the competing concern a direct role in the proposed process.

Step 4: Draft a fair response. “Concern about compressed descriptions identifies a real cost of making recordings easier to find. A description should therefore be treated as an entry point, with a clear route to the full recording and a process for correcting misrepresentation. Contributor review could reveal omissions that an editor missed, although it would not guarantee that every description is complete or that publication would be immediate.” This response recognizes the objection and limits the safeguard's claimed effect.

Step 5: Check the revised position's cost. A review process may delay publication. The essay should explain why reducing misrepresentation justifies that delay, or describe a narrower review process it can defend. Ignoring the new trade-off would leave the revision unfinished.

## Draft, then revise at the right level

Plan a sequence of reasons, not a mandatory paragraph count. An opening should establish the issue and position. The body should develop the argument, including a serious competing consideration. A closing can clarify the defended judgement and its limits without adding a new unsupported premise.

Revise reasoning before polishing individual words. Ask whether the thesis answers the issue, each paragraph advances the argument, evidence is represented accurately, and a counterargument receives an actual response. Then improve transitions, ambiguous references, sentence clarity, and mechanics. Correct punctuation cannot repair an unsupported inference.

Keep the first draft, a later independent revision, and any revision made after feedback distinct. Record why significant changes were made. The reference sheet supplies two original prompts for full essays and a self-review checklist. Write one complete response before consulting examples again; then use the checklist to diagnose the reasoning. These notes are your manual study record, not an automated writing assessment in the app.

## Guided practice

A fictional gallery must decide whether to rotate a small display frequently. One perspective values breadth of exposure, another values time for careful study, and a third wants predictable dates for school visits. Write a thesis and one paragraph answering the strongest competing concern.

One defensible approach is a stable core with scheduled rotating works, supported by separate reasons for repeated study and breadth. Explain why that arrangement serves the chosen priorities, and acknowledge that it gives fewer spaces to rotation. A different policy can also succeed if its reasons address the issue and the competing concern. “Everyone benefits and there are no costs” would need evidence the prompt does not provide.

## Common mistakes

- Summarizing perspectives without taking a position.
- Treating a preference as a reason that needs no explanation.
- Inventing statistics or presenting a hypothetical outcome as observed evidence.
- Responding to a distorted or weaker version of a competing argument.
- Adding a safeguard without explaining its relevance or its limits.
- Revising style while leaving the argument's central gap intact.

## Key points

- State a thesis that answers the issue and identify the criteria supporting it.
- Explain the connection between premises, priorities, and recommendations.
- Represent competing arguments fairly and answer one with substance.
- Use qualifications to define a position, not to avoid choosing one.
- Preserve drafts and revision rationales so improvement remains traceable.

lessons.title: Choosing deliberate skips and planned returns
lessons.body:
## Give the next action a reason

Earlier modules developed argument analysis, evidence-based reading, and deliberate revision. Now put those skills inside a limited practice window. The objective is to direct attention where it can improve your answers while protecting the record of what you actually accomplished. Finishing quickly, reaching every item, and feeling certain are different outcomes. None alone establishes accurate reasoning.

A deliberate skip is a decision to leave an unresolved task after protecting your current response and identifying what remains. A planned return is a later attempt to repair a specific unresolved issue. Neither promises that every difficult item will eventually be solved. They help you avoid spending the remaining window without deciding what that spending is for.

The situations below use original instructional material. Any practice window is a learning condition, not a prescription for an LSAT administration. Consult the timing-and-format reference before choosing conditions for administration-matched practice.

## Compare what another attempt could accomplish

The **[[opportunity cost]]** of continuing is the useful work you give up elsewhere. Time already spent is gone whether you stay or move. The relevant comparison concerns the next action: what could it establish here, and what would it prevent you from checking elsewhere?

Useful persistence changes the problem. You may have located the conclusion, noticed a qualification, or identified a rule whose contrapositive distinguishes the remaining choices. That gives the next reread a target. Repeating the same sentences while alternating between the same reactions supplies no comparable reason to continue.

Ask three questions before another attempt:

- What exactly is unresolved: the task, a relationship in the source, or a difference between choices?
- What operation could resolve it: connect two rules, inspect a qualification, or test a proposed assumption?
- What result would count as progress or as a reason to stop?

These are reasoning questions, not a demand for precise numerical estimates of your chances. A familiar-looking item can conceal a difficult gap; an intimidating one can require a short, decisive check. Choose from identifiable work rather than its appearance.

## Set a stop rule around progress

A **[[stop rule]]** is a condition for ending an attempt when its further cost is no longer justified by the available next step. For example: after a targeted comparison, move if you still cannot explain the distinction and cannot name a different test. That rule can be observed during review. “Leave whenever I feel uncomfortable” cannot distinguish discomfort with progress from discomfort without progress.

No universal number of seconds determines the correct decision. Your chosen practice conditions, remaining work, and the scope of the available check matter. A concrete next step can justify continuing, but merely naming one does not make its cost worthwhile. Reconstructing an entire passage and checking a single limiting word are different commitments.

Before leaving, select or record the current best response if one is supported, preserve the uncertainty, and mark the unresolved item for possible return. If you have no reason to prefer a response, record that limitation honestly. Do not describe an unsupported provisional selection as a reasoned elimination. The record should distinguish what you understood from what remained unsettled.

### Example 1: Finish a newly identified check

Consider this original argument:

“A repair cooperative reports that the proportion of inspected tools needing replacement fell after a maintenance workshop. Therefore, fewer inspected tools needed replacement after the workshop than before it.”

A learner has narrowed a flaw question to two descriptions: the argument confuses a proportion with a number, or it assumes that workshop attendance was compulsory. The learner has spent longer than intended but now notices the shift from “proportion” to “fewer tools.” Should the learner immediately leave because of the earlier delay?

Step 1: Identify the live difference. The first description concerns the relationship between a part and its total. The other concerns who attended. The conclusion compares numbers of tools, so the newly noticed wording offers a targeted test.
