If the platform immediately shows feedback, preserve the timed record and label the later review according to what appeared.

Be precise about scope. If only an overall score appeared, record “review after aggregate feedback; individual keys unseen.” That differs from both feedback-free reconsideration and studying every explanation. If an explanation for one reading question reveals the author's central position, subsequent review of related questions may be affected even if their individual keys remain closed. Finish the intended independent work on a shared passage before opening any of its explanations when the workflow allows.

If an accidental reveal occurs, note it honestly and continue with an appropriately labeled learning activity. Closing the page or waiting several days does not establish that the information has stopped influencing you. The earlier frozen responses remain useful. The later assistance record explains why their revisions answer a different question.

## Pair responses before interpreting gains

A **[[response transition]]** compares one item's recorded status across two phases. After the planned independent work is complete and scoring information is available, distinguish right-to-right, right-to-wrong, wrong-to-right, and wrong-to-wrong transitions. Track blanks separately: a blank may become right, become wrong, or remain blank. A correct answer reached after feedback is another phase, not an independent-review success.

Keep the scoring basis fixed within a comparison. When working with authorized official practice, use the scoring instructions for that exact form to identify the items included in its reported result. Do not add an excluded practice section or silently remove omissions. You may retain an additional count across all assigned work for learning, provided its denominator and purpose are explicit. Original Erudior counts have no official scale conversion.

### Example 2: Four gains, one loss

In a fictional twenty-item learning set, the cutoff record has fourteen correct answers, four wrong answers, and two blanks. Before seeing feedback, the learner reconsiders the set. Thirteen original correct answers remain correct and one changes to a wrong answer. Three original wrong answers become correct and one stays wrong. One blank becomes correct and the other remains blank.

Count the later correct answers by origin: thirteen retained, three repaired, and one newly supplied, totaling seventeen. The remaining outcomes are two wrong and one blank. All twenty items are still represented. Relative to fourteen correct at cutoff, the net gain is three. Four items moved into the correct category, but one moved out. Reporting four improvements without the harmful change would conceal part of the review process.

Now inspect reasons, not only totals. Suppose the three successful repairs corrected reversed conditions, while the harmful change replaced a qualified inference with an absolute claim. Those are different mechanisms and may need different repairs. The answer added to the blank also deserves a reason: extra time, a better evidence search, and mere recognition are not interchangeable explanations.

If only selected items had been reconsidered, carry the untouched cutoff choices forward explicitly when computing a whole-set later total. A result based on six reviewed items and fourteen carried-forward choices is not evidence that all twenty were independently re-solved. Keep the review coverage visible alongside the score.

## Guided practice: Reconstruct a defensible summary

Open the simulation-record reference and create a blank record for the next planned practice session. Fill its source, form identity, exposure, conditions, and preservation method before opening questions. Decide how you will label later work if the interface reveals feedback sooner than planned. Do not test that workflow by previewing fresh questions reserved for the simulation.

Then analyze this fictional eight-item record. At cutoff, five responses are correct, two are wrong, and one is blank. During a separate second pass, one wrong response becomes correct, one correct response becomes wrong, and the blank becomes correct. All other responses stay unchanged. The learner had already seen the aggregate result, but no keys or explanations.

The later record contains six correct and two wrong, so the net gain is one. It should be labeled review after aggregate feedback, with the keys and explanations still unseen. Preserve the original five out of eight. Explain both successful changes and the harmful one. No official scaled score follows from this original exercise, and the higher later total does not establish improvement on unfamiliar material.

## Common mistakes

Keeping only the final answer sheet destroys the distinction between cutoff performance and later completion. Treating an unknown historical response as blank invents a fact. Comparing choice letters without form and item identities may compare different answers. Recording an interruption only as a smaller active-time total hides how the session actually unfolded.

Another mistake is calling every unassisted-looking correction blind review. A total score, a colored correctness mark, or a subtle hint is information worth recording. Finally, a review total can improve while introducing new errors. Preserve transitions and reasoning so the next lesson can turn the record into a specific, testable repair.

## Key points

- Freeze responses at each applicable cutoff and retain blanks, unknowns, and later versions distinctly.
- Identify exact forms, sections, items, and selected alternatives before comparing records.
- Record actual conditions and assistance at the scope where they occurred.
- Plan independent review around the real feedback behavior of the permitted workflow.
- Count gains, losses, omissions, and carried-forward responses before interpreting a later total.

lessons.title: Interpreting results and testing repairs
lessons.body:
## Make the next practice answer a useful question

A full simulation produces more evidence than one total can express. It records answers under a particular workload, alongside uncertainty, omissions, exposure, and interruptions. The previous lessons protected that evidence. This lesson uses it to choose a repair and specify what would count as progress. An attractive explanation for a disappointing result is only a proposal until the record supports it.

An **[[error mechanism]]** is the specific reasoning or execution process that could have produced an observed mistake. Reversing a conditional, losing a reported speaker, and repeatedly rereading without a return plan are different mechanisms. A broad label such as inference or reading identifies a task family, not the step that failed. Start with what the learner actually did, then connect that action to the unsupported answer.

## Read each result on its own terms

Keep three records distinct. Original Erudior work produces raw counts with stated denominators. Authorized official practice may supply a scaled practice result for its particular form and scoring configuration. An administered LSAT produces an official score through LSAC's process. Similar-looking numbers do not make these records interchangeable.

Use the official practice platform's report or the scoring instructions supplied for that exact form and version. Do not substitute a chart from a different form, add practice-only questions to a scored total, or invent a conversion for the course bank. LSAC's general scoring page explains raw-to-scaled scoring and that wrong answers receive no deduction; it does not supply a conversion for arbitrary original exercises. The linked repair reference includes that primary source.

Record the attempt conditions beside the reported result. An official practice report remains a practice report if the learner repeated the form, paused outside the declared rules, or consulted explanations. The displayed number does not erase those conditions. Retain useful learning evidence while narrowing the claim: a familiar paused attempt cannot establish the same thing as an unfamiliar uninterrupted attempt under the intended protocol.

For comparisons, show each attempt's identity, format, exposure, conditions, and result. A series can reveal a recurring concern without proving that the newest method caused every increase. Forms may differ, repeated items may be recognized, and the learner may have changed several habits. Missing information should remain missing instead of becoming an assumed zero or an invented clean attempt.

### Example 1: Two summaries of the same evidence

Nia completes two original teaching packets, each with twenty-four questions. In Packet A, six questions target conditional reasoning and eighteen target other skills. She answers three of the six conditional questions and fifteen of the other eighteen correctly. In Packet B, twelve questions target conditionals and twelve target other skills. She answers eight in each group correctly. Both packets are unfamiliar, but they were independently written and are not established equivalent forms.

First calculate the complete totals. Packet A gives eighteen correct out of twenty-four, or seventy-five percent. Packet B gives sixteen out of twenty-four, about sixty-seven percent. The overall raw percentage is lower on B. That observation is accurate and should remain in the record.

Next inspect the composition. Conditional accuracy changes from three out of six to eight out of twelve: fifty percent to about sixty-seven percent. Other-skill accuracy changes from fifteen out of eighteen to eight out of twelve: about eighty-three percent to about sixty-seven percent. The overall decrease does not establish that conditional performance declined; B contains a larger conditional share and a different collection of questions. Neither does the conditional increase prove a general improvement from two small, unequated samples.

Finally choose the next evidence. Nia inspects why the conditional answers failed. If she repeatedly treated a necessary condition as sufficient, that mechanism suggests a targeted repair. She does not multiply either packet percentage by a score range or report an LSAT score. The raw results guide learning while preserving the limits of the comparison.

## Reconstruct the point of failure

For each priority item, write the task, the relevant evidence, the cutoff choice, and the reason that choice seemed attractive. Compare the strongest competing answers. Identify the first unsupported step in the learner's reasoning. For a passage question, distinguish confusing a speaker from overlooking a qualification; both can produce a wrong inference, but they call for different changes.

Include correct answers marked uncertain and correct answers supported by faulty reasoning. They earn full raw credit. Their review flag records a learning concern rather than taking points away. Also examine a few confident correct answers: understanding why a reliable method worked can make the repair more precise. Do not manufacture a diagnosis merely because every row is supposed to have one.

Separate observations from explanations. "I reread the same paragraph three times and still attributed the scientist's objection to the author" describes evidence. "I was tired" proposes one explanation. A late-section cluster makes fatigue worth investigating, but differences in item demands and familiarity remain possible. A single self-report cannot establish a unique cause.

## Turn a mechanism into a testable repair

A **[[repair hypothesis]]** states that a specified change should reduce a particular error in a stated situation. Replace "be more careful" with an observable action: before choosing an inference answer, identify whose claim it is and underline the sentence that licenses its strength. Say what failure would look like too, such as selecting an answer that turns a qualified reported view into the author's universal claim.

A **[[verification task]]** is a subsequent task chosen to check whether a proposed repair works under declared conditions. Reworking the missed question can establish that the explanation is now understood. A new question or passage addresses transfer more directly. Neither result alone proves mastery. Record whether the action was used, what answer it produced, and whether it introduced another problem such as excessive time cost.

Choose a manageable priority from recurrence, consequence, and the available evidence. There is no universal formula requiring the most frequent topic to come first. Several errors sharing one mechanism may be repairable together; a single severe misunderstanding may also merit attention. Give a reason for the choice, define a small practice task, and reserve a later unfamiliar check. If several changes are introduced together, interpret them as a bundle rather than identifying one as the proven cause.

### Example 2: Repairing the reasoning behind a correct answer

An original argument says that every proposal approved for a roof garden has a drainage review. Sam selects the correct answer that a proposal without a drainage review was not approved. In his explanation, however, he writes that completing a drainage review always guarantees approval. His choice earns credit, but his stated reasoning reverses the condition and could fail on another question.

First identify the exact relationship. Approval requires review. The supplied rule permits a reviewed proposal that was rejected for another reason. It does not permit an approved proposal with no review. Sam's correct choice follows by contraposition, while his claimed guarantee does not follow.

Next propose a repair: translate the condition, state its contrapositive, and actively test whether the converse permits a counterexample. Rework the roof-garden example to make the distinction explicit. Then use an unfamiliar question about a different subject, without a cue announcing that it contains the same trap. Save the first answer and explanation before feedback.

Suppose Sam answers the new item correctly but again claims that the necessary condition guarantees the outcome. The answer alone does not verify the repair; the faulty mechanism remains. If he supplies the valid relationship but takes much longer, the conceptual repair may be developing while efficient use still needs work. The record should describe both observations instead of forcing a single pass-or-fail label for his ability.

## Guided practice: A repair cycle with an unfamiliar check

The separate repair-set reference contains eight original questions. Four are independent reasoning questions; four concern one new reading passage. The key identifies the evidence and each alternative's limitation. Record exposure and conditions before beginning. Finish and freeze all eight responses before opening the key, since its explanations can teach methods relevant to later items. A known skill focus may cue a method; note that this supported transfer exercise is not a fully uncued measurement.

Choose one missed or uncertain item after reviewing the whole set. Write the unsupported step, a concrete replacement action, and the kind of unfamiliar task that would test it. If all answers are secure, examine one explanation for an unwarranted assumption rather than inventing an error. Arrange the later unfamiliar check from appropriately authorized material; repeating this same eight-item set cannot become fresh evidence.

For a reasoning check, consider a learner with four late reading misses who reread two explanations before recording review answers. Can the learner conclude that stamina caused all four and that independent review repaired them? Neither conclusion follows. Section position suggests a question to investigate; feedback exposure makes the later answers assisted. A sound next step preserves those facts, reconstructs a specific failure, and tests a repair on new work.

## Common mistakes

Replacing a mechanism with a topic leaves the next action vague. Calling every timed miss a pacing problem skips the reasoning review. Counting only successful answer changes hides harmful changes. Removing uncertain correct answers from the raw numerator changes the scoring rule instead of improving diagnosis.

Another mistake is treating a high repeated-form score as proof that a method transfers. Familiar work can teach the repair, but unfamiliar work supplies different evidence. Finally, a lower fresh result does not automatically refute every improvement: inspect task mix, conditions, and the actual mechanism while retaining the lower result honestly.

## Key points

- Preserve the source, scoring configuration, exposure, and conditions behind each result.
- Use the scoring instructions for the exact official form; keep original-course counts raw.
- Diagnose an unsupported step, including when a correct answer has unreliable reasoning.
- Turn one priority into an observable repair and a declared verification task.
- Record both outcome and process, then look for recurring evidence across unfamiliar work.

lessons.title: Integrating writing and draft review
lessons.body:
## Give writing its own evidence record

A multiple-choice simulation and a writing session reveal different work. One records selections among supplied alternatives; the other requires the learner to construct and defend a position. Include both in the study plan, while preserving the conditions and outcome of each. Completing many multiple-choice forms does not demonstrate that an essay can develop a reasoned response within its own deadline.

Earlier writing lessons taught positions, perspectives, planning, and timed revision. This lesson follows an essay across versions and turns its weaknesses into a later writing task. A **[[draft lineage]]** is the ordered record of a draft and its revisions, including when each version was produced and what assistance preceded it. Keeping that lineage makes it possible to say which reasoning appeared within the original writing window.

## Plan a separate writing session

LSAC's guidance, checked November 3, 2026, describes Argumentative Writing as separately administered and unscored. Standard allocations are fifteen minutes for prewriting analysis and thirty-five minutes for essay writing; approved accommodations and current instructions govern individual conditions. The prewriting phase can be left after five minutes. Do not assume that leaving it early extends the writing phase. The linked timing reference supplies the primary sources.

Choose the session purpose before opening the prompt. An original Erudior prompt can support a timed rehearsal or an untimed repair. Authorized official practice can also familiarize the learner with the actual interface. State which purpose applies, the prompt identity, previous exposure, planning and drafting windows, and permitted aids. The course's manual worksheet records practice; it does not issue an official writing assessment.

Writing need not be appended to the end of every multiple-choice simulation. Schedule it deliberately as a separate activity, with enough time afterward to preserve the cutoff version and later review. If a learner chooses to practise writing after another demanding activity, record that context. Do not silently treat the combined custom session as a required official test sequence or evidence about an independent writing session.

Keep the prompt unopened until the intended start if the goal is a first encounter. Studying its perspectives beforehand changes the task, even when no model essay is seen. A topic can also be familiar without the exact prompt being familiar; record the known exposure accurately rather than declaring that any familiarity invalidates learning.

## Freeze the text before explaining it

At the drafting cutoff, save the text exactly as it stands, including unfinished sentences. Save planning notes separately when the practice setup permits. Do not paste an unwritten outline point into the essay and label it part of the timed draft. The point may show useful planning, but it was not yet communicated to the reader.

Record the actual planning and writing durations, pauses, prompt exposure, and assistance. If an automatic correction or external suggestion affects the text, describe the practice condition rather than pretending the writer independently produced it. Interface tools and permissions differ; a faithful rehearsal follows the applicable official guidance, while a learning exercise can declare its own aids honestly.

Then make a separate copy for independent revision if desired. Record when feedback arrives and create another version for changes influenced by it. A revision can incorporate both the learner's ideas and a reviewer's contribution; label that mixture. Copying an edited file into a new filename does not change how its reasoning was produced.

### Example 1: An argument that arrives after the cutoff

In an original prompt, a public audio archive is deciding whether to publish unverified recordings immediately with caution labels or delay publication until descriptions have been checked. At cutoff, Imani's draft supports immediate access because researchers might identify important material. It mentions a risk of mistaken attribution but gives no answer to that concern. Her outline includes the phrase "display uncertainty prominently," which has not been developed in the essay.

First preserve the cutoff text and notes separately. The essay contains a position and a reason, but its response to mistaken attribution remains incomplete. The outline records an intended move; it does not establish that a reader received a developed reply within the writing window.

Next Imani independently adds a paragraph explaining provisional labels and a correction channel. She acknowledges that researchers may still circulate an incorrect attribution and argues that restricted public claims plus access benefits justify the remaining risk. This version develops a defense rather than promising that labels prevent every misunderstanding. Its added reasoning belongs to the independent revision.

Finally a reviewer asks who would monitor corrections. Imani adds a proposed review responsibility and discusses its cost. The third version is feedback-assisted. Comparing all three identifies a useful next target: during a fresh prompt, bring one serious objection and a supported response into the cutoff draft. The later polished essay shows learning, while the original version identifies the work that was not yet completed on time.

## Review the argument, not just the surface

A **[[writing review]]** examines what the essay claims, how its reasons support that claim, how it engages other perspectives, and whether its structure makes those relationships understandable. This course uses descriptive review rather than an invented official numerical rubric. A smooth opening or a long essay can coexist with an unsupported conclusion.

Begin by stating the draft's actual position in one sentence. Find the reason carrying the main recommendation. Check whether the evidence supports the claim's strength and scope. Next identify a competing perspective that matters to this position. Describe it fairly, then inspect whether the essay answers its concern or merely repeats its own benefit.

Distinguish a proposed safeguard from an established result. A writer may recommend a pilot, eligibility rule, or review process, but should explain why it could help and what uncertainty remains. A hypothetical example illustrates a possibility; it is not a survey that happened. Precise percentages do not become factual merely because they make the recommendation sound decisive.

After reviewing the core reasoning, inspect paragraph order, transitions, sentence clarity, and mechanics. These features matter because the reader must be able to follow the argument. Prioritize the change that addresses the most consequential obstacle in this draft. There is no need to rewrite every sentence when a specific missing inference is the immediate learning target.

### Example 2: Choosing a revision that repairs the position

Leo's original essay favors reserving some evening rehearsal rooms for ensembles while keeping others available to individuals. He argues that group rehearsals require coordinated access and that individuals with unpredictable schedules still need flexible opportunities. His conclusion instead recommends that every room be reserved by ensembles a month in advance. A reviewer also notices a repeated adjective in the introduction.

First compare the conclusion with the defended policy. The reasons support a mixed arrangement. They do not justify eliminating individual access. The unsupported expansion is more consequential than the repeated adjective because it changes what the essay asks the reader to accept.

Next formulate the repair. Leo can align the conclusion with the mixed arrangement, explain how rooms might be allocated, and acknowledge that the exact division requires information about demand. He should not invent attendance figures to claim that one precise split is already proven best. If he truly wants the universal reservation policy, he would need a new argument that addresses the loss of individual access.

Finally specify the later check. On an unfamiliar issue, Leo will compare the conclusion's scope with the reasons before the cutoff. A successful observation would be a consistent defended position, with the comparison completed inside the declared writing window. Fixing this familiar essay establishes a repaired version; it does not yet establish that the same check will be remembered and used on a new prompt.

## Set one target for the next draft

A **[[revision target]]** is a specific change in argumentative performance to attempt in a later version or new essay. "Improve writing" gives no clear observation. "State and answer the strongest relevant competing concern before polishing the introduction" identifies an action whose result can be inspected in the cutoff text.

Keep the target narrow enough to evaluate, but do not force every prompt into the same argument. The next issue may require a different position, a different objection, or an explicit qualification. Compare the reasoning function rather than memorized sentences. If a target improves objection handling while leaving the conclusion unfinished, record both outcomes and adjust the plan.

## Guided practice: Preserve, review, transfer

The writing-record reference contains two original prompts, each with a key question and three perspectives. Read the shared practice instructions before opening the chosen prompt. Record exposure and separate planning and drafting conditions, then save the cutoff text. Conduct a descriptive review and, if useful, create independent and feedback-assisted revisions with their lineage intact.

Use the second prompt later only if it remains unfamiliar. If it was previewed while scrolling, record that fact and use another appropriately authorized unfamiliar prompt for a fresh check. Do not compare essay quality through word count alone. Ask whether the chosen target appears in the later cutoff version and whether the reasons actually support the new position.

For a check, suppose a learner's thirty-five-minute practice draft has no reply to an objection, but a tutor supplies one before the learner revises it. What belongs in the record? Preserve the original omission, the timing condition, the tutor's contribution, and the revised text. The revision may be excellent learning. It cannot establish that the reply was independently produced during the earlier writing window.

## Common mistakes

Merging notes and later revisions into the cutoff text hides the performance being studied. Counting every mention of a perspective as a response ignores whether its concern was addressed. Treating feedback-assisted changes as independent confuses their origin. Assigning an official-looking writing score to a personal checklist gives the numbers an authority the course has not established.

Another mistake is using the same improved essay repeatedly as fresh evidence. Retain familiar drafts for detailed practice, and use unfamiliar issues to examine transfer. A useful study plan preserves both kinds of work without making either do the other's job.

## Key points

- Schedule writing deliberately and record its own prompt, timing, aids, and exposure.
- Preserve the cutoff draft, notes, independent revisions, and assisted revisions separately.
- Review the thesis, support, competing concerns, and scope before choosing a target.
- Use descriptive evidence rather than an invented official writing score.
- Inspect the target in a later unfamiliar cutoff draft, including any remaining trade-offs.

lessons.title: Auditing rare errors and response decisions
lessons.body:
## Look closely when the total hides the problem

Module 11 connected practice records to repairs. As accuracy improves, a total can become less informative about what to change next. Two misses might come from one recurring scope error, two unrelated misunderstandings, or one reasoning error and one recording slip. A small count does not identify which explanation is true. Nor does a perfect small set establish that every method used was reliable.

A **[[rare-error audit]]** examines a small set of consequential mistakes and fragile successes in enough detail to identify what the available record supports. Its purpose is to choose a useful next action. It does not require an elaborate diagnosis for every miss. Sometimes the honest conclusion is that the process was not recorded well enough to distinguish competing explanations.

Include uncertain correct answers and correct answers reached through invalid reasoning. Preserve their raw credit. A review flag answers a different question: does the reasoning give the learner a method that can work on unfamiliar material? Keep reliable correct examples nearby as comparisons, especially when they involve similar wording or demands.

## Reconstruct a decision before naming its cause

For a priority item, retain the source, task, first choice, final choice at cutoff, confidence, and any reasoning written before feedback. Then identify the exact relationship the task required. A must-follow question requires support for every part of the answer. A passage question may depend on who expressed a view, what the author endorsed, or how strongly a claim was qualified.

**[[Mechanism evidence]]** is information about the reasoning or execution step that produced a response. A contemporaneous note reading "some means most here" directly supports a quantifier diagnosis. A wrong choice that could result from either a quantifier error or a speaker mix-up leaves both possibilities open. The choice is evidence about the outcome; it need not uniquely identify the process.

Separate three statements: what happened, what might explain it, and what would help distinguish the explanations. "The final answer says all" is observable. "I ignored the word usually" is a proposed account unless the record supports it. A new task that varies the qualification while holding the reasoning demand similar can help investigate the account. A story formed after reading the explanation should be labeled retrospective rather than presented as a preserved first-attempt thought.

### Example 1: A correct answer with an unreliable denominator

A committee invites forty-eight curators to state a preference between opening an exhibition now and delaying it. Thirty-six respond; twenty-four of the respondents prefer delay. The other twelve respondents prefer opening now. Nothing is reported about the preferences of the twelve people who did not respond. The question asks what must be true of the forty-eight invited curators.

Lena chooses "At least half of the invited curators prefer delay." That is correct: twenty-four known supporters divided by forty-eight invitees is one half. Additional supporters among the nonrespondents could raise the proportion, so "at least" is warranted. The result does not depend on guessing why anyone failed to respond.

Lena's note, however, says, "Twenty-four out of thirty-six is two thirds, so two thirds of everyone invited prefer delay." The calculation uses respondents as its denominator and then transfers the proportion to all invitees. Her selected answer earns credit, but that explanation exceeds the evidence. If none of the twelve nonrespondents prefers delay, exactly half of all invitees does. If all twelve prefer delay, three quarters do. Both situations fit the report.

Compare the tempting alternatives. "Exactly two thirds of invitees prefer delay" describes one possible allocation of the unknown preferences, not a required result. "Every nonrespondent opposes delay" supplies an unsupported view. "Fewer than half of respondents prefer delay" contradicts twenty-four out of thirty-six. The correct answer survives these comparisons for a narrower reason than Lena gave.

The audit records a correct outcome, a denominator substitution in the written reasoning, and unknown nonrespondent preferences. A precise repair is to name the population beside each fraction and test unknown cases before selecting a quantified claim. Repeating the curator question can clarify the method; an unfamiliar problem with a different response rate tests its use more directly. Correct raw credit and a serious repair target can coexist.

## Count opportunities as well as failures

Two mistakes among eight relevant opportunities and two among forty are different descriptions. State the denominator and define what counted as an opportunity. Do not divide a speaker-attribution error count by all questions and call that the accuracy on speaker-attribution questions. Also avoid assuming that two collections are equally demanding merely because they have the same topic label.

Small samples can suggest a priority without establishing a stable personal error rate. A recent absence of mistakes might reflect reliable execution, easier demands, favorable sampling, or unnoticed fragile reasoning. Retain the result and its limits. Review several relevant instances, including correct ones, before claiming that a mechanism has disappeared.

Broad task labels can also hide a useful pattern. Turning "sometimes" into "always" in reading and treating evidence that "may explain" a result as a necessary explanation in reasoning are different tasks with a related increase in claim strength. Conversely, two reading misses can require different repairs if one loses the speaker and the other misidentifies the author's purpose.

## Inspect changes in both directions

A **[[harmful change]]** is a recorded move from a correct response to an incorrect response on the same item under the same scoring basis. Its existence does not establish that retaining first answers is the best general policy. Helpful changes and wrong-to-wrong changes belong in the same record, together with revisits that leave an answer unchanged.

Evaluate the reason available when the decision was made. Finding a previously overlooked qualification can justify a change. Feeling that a longer answer sounds more sophisticated supplies no comparable textual support. A helpful outcome can still follow weak reasoning; a defensible process can still produce a mistake. Use outcomes to locate decisions, then inspect the reasoning rather than equating the two.

### Example 2: Changes that gain one answer overall

In an original twenty-four-question exercise, Omar revisits twelve items before cutoff and changes eight answers. The recorded transitions are complete; there are no blanks. The remaining twelve items are not revisited. Each row gives the item count and the correct totals before and after review.

| Response record | Items; correct before / after |
|---|---|
| Wrong to right | 3 items; correct: 0 before, 3 after |
| Right to wrong | 2 items; correct: 2 before, 0 after |
| Wrong to wrong | 3 items; correct: 0 before, 0 after |
| Revisited, retained | 4 items; correct: 3 before, 3 after |
| Not revisited | 12 items; correct: 11 before, 11 after |
| Total | 24 items; correct: 16 before, 17 after |

First calculate the observed effect of the changes: three gains minus two losses equals one additional correct answer. Saying that review "fixed three" is incomplete if it hides the two losses. Saying that changing answers "cost two" is equally incomplete if it hides the gains. The three wrong-to-wrong changes did not alter the correct total, although they used time and may reveal a shared misconception.

Next inspect a harmful change. A passage says that verbal resemblance alone cannot establish which of two letters was written first. Omar initially chooses the supported statement that resemblance by itself is insufficient to establish their order. He changes to the broader claim that textual comparison cannot contribute to dating letters because the wording feels more decisive. The problem is an unsupported expansion from "alone is insufficient" to "cannot contribute," not the physical act of changing an answer.

Finally inspect costs and alternatives. The record establishes a net gain of one from these changes. It does not establish that this was the best use of the available time: a different revisit selection might have produced a different result, which was not observed. Omar can test a more specific action on new work: before changing, identify the evidence that defeats the current answer and supports the replacement. He should record unsuccessful applications and time costs as well as successes.

## Guided practice: Keep a diagnosis provisional

An archive introduces a booking portal in the same month that it extends opening hours. Missed appointments decline. A question asks which fact most helps distinguish the effects of these two changes. Priya selects a comparison between visitors offered the portal and visitors without access, with opening hours held the same. Her answer is correct, but her saved note says, "The portal came first, so it caused the decline." On another item, she changes a correct qualified claim to a universal claim; no reason for the change is recorded.

What should the audit preserve, and what should it investigate? Keep full credit for the archive answer while flagging the unsupported causal explanation. The comparison is useful because it separates the portal difference from the hours difference; mere temporal order would not establish the causal effect. Test whether Priya can explain such a comparison on unfamiliar work without relying on that shortcut.

For the other item, record the harmful change and the increase in claim strength. Losing the qualification is a plausible mechanism, but the missing reasoning prevents a firm claim about why she changed. Ask for a prospective explanation on the next relevant task rather than reconstructing certainty from the answer key. The two records justify focused investigation, not a conclusion that every miss shares one cause.

## Common mistakes

Auditing only misses overlooks fragile correct reasoning. Subtracting credit for uncertainty confuses diagnosis with raw scoring. Naming a cause from the chosen distractor alone can conceal alternative paths to the same response.

Another mistake is presenting memorable failures without the relevant opportunities, or reporting only successful changes. Finally, an inflexible first-answer rule or mandatory-change rule can replace evidence-based decisions with a new source of errors. Judge the proposed repair by its use and consequences on unfamiliar work.

## Key points

- Preserve raw outcomes while separately flagging uncertain or weakly justified correct answers.
- Distinguish the observed response from evidence about the mechanism that produced it.
- Keep relevant opportunities, task demands, and small-sample limits visible.
- Record helpful, harmful, and neutral changes, plus revisits that retain an answer.
- Test a specific replacement action without treating one success as a readiness guarantee.

lessons.title: Choosing focused refinements
lessons.body:
## Choose the next change for a reason

Once errors become less frequent, every missed answer can seem to demand a new technique. That reaction can make a reliable approach harder to use. A learner adds extensive diagrams after one conditional miss, summarizes every paragraph after one attribution error, and checks every answer twice after one harmful change. Each addition may have a sensible purpose, yet their combined demands can crowd out useful work.

The rare-error audit supplies observations about what failed. This lesson decides which observation deserves the next limited practice period and how to evaluate a proposed change. The aim is a more dependable process under the learner's intended conditions. Collecting more procedures is not itself evidence of improvement.

## Compare mechanisms, opportunities, and consequences

A **[[refinement priority]]** is a reasoned choice of a specific performance issue to address next. State the mechanism, the evidence for it, the proposed action, and why it takes precedence now. "Reading needs work" names an area. "I twice treated a concession to one part of a reported view as endorsement of the whole view" identifies a process that a targeted check could address.

Consider recurrence together with opportunities. Three attribution errors among nine relevant tasks and one conditional error among four relevant tasks are different observations. The counts alone neither establish stable error rates nor prescribe a priority. Small samples, differing difficulty, and uncertain classifications limit the comparison. Keep the actual denominators instead of treating three misses as three times the risk.

Consequence also matters. A single basic misunderstanding may affect several later tasks. Conversely, many vocabulary flags may need little intervention if the learner consistently resolves the terms from context and answers with valid reasons. Correct answers with faulty reasoning remain correct in the raw total while providing legitimate evidence for a refinement.

Finally, consider what can be tested usefully now. A well-supported mechanism with a small observable repair may be a better immediate choice than an uncertain explanation requiring a broad overhaul. That is a planning judgment, not a universal ranking formula. Record why another concern was deferred so it can be reconsidered if new evidence changes the balance.

### Example 1: A repeated boundary error or a broad reading overhaul?

Lena has one short practice session available. Her unfamiliar mixed-work records contain three attribution errors among nine relevant tasks, one conditional reversal among four relevant tasks, and eight vocabulary flags. Her explanations for all eight vocabulary answers use the passages correctly. She wants to address a recurring, documented mechanism with an action small enough to test in this session.

Inspect one attribution miss. A passage reports Rell's claim that historical labels make visitors stay longer. The author accepts that the labels can answer visitors' questions but observes that the study did not measure visit duration. Lena selected an answer saying that the author endorses Rell's claim about longer visits.

The unsupported step is precise. Accepting a benefit involving visitors' questions does not endorse a separate claim about visit duration. Lena joined a speaker's position to a different concession by the author. The other two recorded misses show the same joining of claims. Merely rereading more slowly may leave that operation unchanged.

Her immediate priority is therefore to separate the speaker and the exact proposition whenever competing answers turn on endorsement. The replacement action is brief: name who holds the disputed claim, then identify how much of that claim the author actually accepts. She tests it on unfamiliar material and records both the answer and its support.

This choice fits Lena's stated purpose better than a broad vocabulary program, which the present records do not support, or a complete rewrite of her reading routine. The conditional reversal still deserves repair; deferring it is not declaring it harmless. Nor do three observed attribution misses prove that attribution is her permanent weakest skill. The priority is provisional and tied to the evidence and time available.

## Account for what a strategy consumes

A **[[strategy cost]]** is a demand or loss associated with using a proposed method, such as extra time, reduced coverage, or new errors introduced by the procedure. Record benefits and costs separately. A successful local check can still consume the period previously used to return to unfinished questions.

Track the action as well as its result. Did the learner actually name the speaker? Did the notation help distinguish the claims? Was it used only when needed or applied to every sentence? Without these observations, an improved result cannot establish that the proposed method was used, and a poor result cannot establish that the method failed.

Conditional use can make a refinement more practical. A diagram may help untangle a branching rule chain but add little to a direct one-step conditional. A brief attribution check may help distinguish two competing claims without requiring a written summary of every paragraph. The condition for using the method should follow the mechanism it is meant to repair. Familiarity with a technique does not make it beneficial everywhere.

## Bound the trial before inspecting its outcome

Specify the task, the change, the evidence to record, and a review point. Keep the practice format, exposure record, and timing conditions visible. Where practical, change one feature at a time; if several features change together, treat the result as evidence about that bundle. Different unfamiliar forms still vary, so a before-and-after comparison is not a controlled causal experiment.

A **[[trial stopping rule]]** is a predeclared condition for ending or reconsidering a strategy trial. It concerns the evaluation of a method across practice work. The earlier stop rule concerned when to leave an individual attempt. Neither requires a universal time limit. A trial may end at a planned review point, after a clear cost threshold, or because the materials no longer test the intended mechanism.

Set a rule that serves the particular decision. For example, a learner testing a detailed annotation method could decide to pause and redesign it if a trial leaves two or more blanks at cutoff. That is the learner's chosen boundary for this experiment, not an LSAT standard. Reaching the boundary triggers the promised review even if one selected statistic looks encouraging. Stopping a trial also does not prove that every version of the method is unusable.

### Example 2: A local gain with an unchanged total

Amir compares two unfamiliar thirty-question teaching blocks. Each contains eight attribution tasks and twenty-two other tasks. They are not established equivalent forms. In the earlier block, he answered five attribution tasks and nineteen other tasks correctly, with six wrong answers and no blanks overall. In the annotation trial, he answered seven attribution tasks and seventeen other tasks correctly, with four wrong answers and two blanks overall.

First retain all thirty opportunities in each denominator. Both totals are twenty-four correct out of thirty. The attribution group improves from five out of eight to seven out of eight, while the other group falls from nineteen out of twenty-two to seventeen out of twenty-two. Omitting the two blanks would disguise an important cost and change the comparison.

Next inspect the process. Amir's notes show that the annotations helped him separate two reported views. They also occupied the return period, leaving the final two tasks untouched. These observations support investigating a trade-off. The two different blocks do not prove how many answers the method caused him to gain or lose.

Before the trial, Amir adopted the two-blank stopping rule described above. It has now been met. He pauses this version, retains the complete results, and redesigns the action to mark only a disputed speaker and proposition. The next unfamiliar check will examine both that reasoning and its cost. Continuing unchanged because attribution accuracy rose would ignore his declared decision rule; abandoning every form of annotation would reach beyond the evidence.

## Guided practice: Choose an action and a decision point

Mara has two recent unfamiliar attempts with sound reasoning on most questions. In three recorded answer changes, she replaced a supported qualified claim with a broader claim because the broader wording felt more decisive. She also reports feeling slow, but has no timing record identifying where time was spent. She wants one observable change for her next practice block, with a review afterward.

Choose between a universal instruction never to change answers, a complete pacing overhaul, and a check that requires a textual or logical reason for any change in claim strength. Specify what evidence you would save, including possible costs. Then decide whether one successful block would justify making the technique permanent.

The claim-strength check is the best-supported initial trial. It addresses the recorded mechanism while leaving evidence-based changes available. Save the original and revised choices, the reason for changing or retaining the response, the relevant support, and any extra time or unfinished work. The broad pacing overhaul rests on a less specific diagnosis, and the no-change rule would also block justified corrections. One successful block warrants continued observation, not a permanent guarantee. Decide at the planned review whether to retain, narrow, revise, or suspend the method.

## Common mistakes

The largest topic count can hide different mechanisms and unequal opportunities. A single dramatic miss can attract more attention than repeated, repairable failures. Equally, rarity does not make a foundational misunderstanding unimportant. Explain the priority instead of substituting a ranking slogan.

Another mistake is assessing a method only where it was intended to help. Extra omissions, harmful changes, and displaced review time remain part of its record. Changing several habits together and crediting only the favorite habit overstates the evidence. Finally, extending every trial until it produces a pleasing result defeats the declared review point.

## Key points

- Choose a specific refinement from recurrence, opportunity, consequence, and the strength of the diagnosis.
- Preserve raw credit for correct answers while investigating unreliable reasoning.
- Record the proposed method's use, benefits, and costs across the full task.
- Set a trial stopping rule that serves the particular decision and honor it.
- Retain, narrow, revise, or suspend the method as new evidence warrants.

lessons.title: Evaluating readiness evidence
lessons.body:
## Ask what the recent record can establish

The preceding lessons identified rare errors and selected focused refinements. The next question is whether recent work supports the decisions you now face. A good readiness review describes what you can demonstrate, what remains uncertain, and which additional evidence could change the plan. Your highest result belongs in that review, alongside the other relevant attempts.

An **[[evidence window]]** is a stated span of records used to examine a question about current performance. You might review all full attempts since a particular strategy change or all practice completed during a chosen period. State the window and the inclusion conditions before selecting results. If you choose a window afterward, explain why and inspect whether another reasonable boundary changes the picture. A window chosen solely to remove disappointing results hides evidence.

## Build an inventory before a summary

List every relevant attempt in the window, including interrupted or incompletely recorded work. Give each row a date, form identity, version, exposure history, intended protocol, actual conditions, assistance, and available result. Identify repeated sections or passages even when the form label is new. If history is unknown, preserve that uncertainty.

Next explain which records address the particular comparison. To examine execution across an unfamiliar full workload, you need evidence of that workload and unfamiliarity. A short targeted exercise can answer a narrower question. An interrupted attempt can reveal a difficulty worth investigating without establishing uninterrupted execution. Individual approved conditions belong in the intended protocol; a departure means a departure from that learner's declared conditions, not a difference from someone else's standard timing.

Keep excluded records visible with their reasons. This prevents two opposite errors: silently treating unlike attempts as equivalent, and deleting useful learning evidence because it does not fit one comparison. Missing responses remain unknown. A missing file does not establish that every answer was wrong, correct, or typical of the attempts that survived.

## Preserve the meaning of each number

Original course exercises produce raw counts. Authorized official practice can produce a scaled practice report using its exact form and scoring configuration. An administered LSAT produces its own official score. Record which kind of result you have. A course percentage and a scaled practice score cannot be averaged into a meaningful LSAT estimate.

Even among original exercises, equal percentages do not establish equal difficulty or coverage. Pooling correct answers over all assigned questions can accurately describe those observed responses, provided blanks remain in the denominator and the tasks' differences remain visible. That arithmetic does not equate the exercises or turn their aggregate into a score prediction. Averaging percentages without considering denominators can answer a different question from pooling responses.

### Example 1: A complete inventory with incomplete evidence

Ravi reserves four original twenty-four-question packets for a two-week review. His declared comparison concerns unfamiliar complete attempts under one specified practice protocol. None of the packets is an official form or an established equivalent of another. His inventory contains these records:

| Attempt | Raw result | Record status |
|---|---|---|
| A, first attempt | 22/24 | Complete; unfamiliar; protocol followed |
| B, first attempt | 21/24 | Complete; unfamiliar; protocol followed |
| A, repeat | 24/24 | Previously answered and reviewed |
| C | Not saved | Stopped early; responses were not saved |

First select the records that meet Ravi's declared comparison conditions. A and B qualify. Finishing the working period with blanks still supplies a complete cutoff record: twenty-one correct, one wrong, and two blank responses for B. The repeat and the interrupted attempt remain in the inventory with their different evidentiary roles. The fourth reserved packet has not yet been attempted and supplies no performance record.

Next calculate the observed aggregate for A and B: twenty-two plus twenty-one gives forty-three correct out of forty-eight assigned questions, about ninety percent. Dropping B's blanks would change the denominator to forty-six and overstate accuracy under the stated scoring rule. Adding the reviewed repeat would combine different exposure histories. Assigning C zero correct would invent unavailable responses.

Finally identify what the aggregate leaves open. It describes two small original packets under the recorded conditions. It does not show an official scaled score, establish an upward trend, or explain why B was lower. Ravi can inspect B's omissions and reasoning, preserve the missing-data problem for C, and use the remaining unfamiliar packet for a declared follow-up purpose. He cannot reconstruct C's lost answers from the other results.

## Read variation without manufacturing a forecast

A highest result demonstrates an observed success under its recorded conditions. A lowest result identifies another observed outcome. An observed range is the distance between those extremes in the selected records. It is sensitive to which attempts were retained and does not set guaranteed boundaries for future performance. Similar totals can also conceal different reasoning weaknesses, omissions, or costs.

LSAC explains that an administered score is an imperfect proficiency estimate and that its official score band is based on the standard error of measurement. A personal practice range is not that official band. This distinction is based on [LSAC's score-band guidance](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/lsat-scoring/lsat-score-bands), checked November 4, 2026. The course does not estimate an official band from a handful of practice results.

Read repeated evidence for both stability and uncertainty. Several unfamiliar attempts showing a repaired mechanism provide more opportunities to inspect transfer than one repeated success. They still leave questions about item demands, conditions, and whether the method will hold up elsewhere. A recent increase after several simultaneous changes does not isolate which change caused it. A recent decrease deserves examination without becoming a verdict that all progress has disappeared.

### Example 2: Strong outcomes with a specific unresolved issue

Clara has three unfamiliar full official-practice attempts in her chosen window. Each used the intended format and her declared protocol. For this fictional example, the exact forms' own reports show 172, 176, and 173. These are supplied practice reports, not conversions calculated from course questions. Clara's personal goal is 175.

First describe the results accurately. One reported result exceeds her goal; two fall below it. The observed span is 172 through 176, four points from lowest to highest. Neither the highest result nor the span promises her next outcome. The three reports do show that she completed the planned workload under the recorded conditions.

Next inspect the reasoning record. Across two attempts, Clara selected answers that attributed a quoted critic's objection to the passage author. A later targeted exercise produced correct choices, but the exercise announced that every question involved viewpoint attribution. That success supports learning with a cue; it leaves less direct evidence about noticing the distinction in mixed work. Her separate writing record also shows that a substantial objection was answered only during later revision.

Finally frame a decision. Clara can retain the successful parts of her approach and investigate the remaining viewpoint issue on unfamiliar mixed reading tasks. She can inspect whether a new writing draft addresses an objection within its declared drafting window. Another full simulation is useful if it addresses a remaining whole-session question and fits her available time. Its value depends on that purpose, alongside the cost of losing focused review time. No course rule requires a fixed number of additional simulations before she may decide how to proceed.

## Write a judgment that can be revised

A **[[readiness judgment]]** is a reasoned, revisable assessment of how the available evidence bears on a learner's stated goal and next decision. Include demonstrated performance, remaining concerns, uncertainty, and relevant practical constraints. Distinguish observation from interpretation: "two unfamiliar attempts included the same attribution error" is evidence; "this repair will eliminate it" remains a prediction.

Specify what new information would matter. A successful unfamiliar mixed check may support keeping a refinement. Repeated costs may justify changing it. An unresolved administration requirement calls for checking the applicable instructions rather than inferring compliance from practice success. Course completion records what was completed in this learning workflow; it is not an official readiness determination.

## Guided practice: Which claim survives the record?

Elena's declared review includes unfamiliar full attempts under her chosen protocol. She has one such attempt with a supplied official-practice report of 174, a reviewed repeat reporting 178, an unfamiliar attempt reporting 171 after an unscheduled pause outside her protocol, and a new original exercise with seven correct answers out of eight. What can her summary say, and what question should guide another activity?

The 174 result is the only attempt meeting all her stated comparison conditions. The other records retain learning value with their exposure, pause, or raw-result labels. They cannot be averaged together into one estimate, and the repeat does not establish unfamiliar performance at 178. One qualifying record gives limited evidence of consistency. Elena should identify whether another full attempt would address consistency across the workload, or whether a specific reasoning concern first warrants targeted work. The next activity should answer that identified question.

## Common mistakes

Selecting only the best recent attempts conceals variation. Treating missing results as failures invents information; ignoring that results are missing conceals uncertainty. Removing blanks changes raw scoring. Treating a personal range as an official score band creates unsupported precision.

Another mistake is declaring readiness solely from a high total while ignoring recurring invalid reasoning or unresolved requirements. The opposite mistake is demanding certainty before making any decision. A useful judgment preserves uncertainty and explains the learner's chosen next step in light of it.

## Key points

- Define the evidence window and comparison conditions, then show the complete inventory.
- Keep form identity, exposure, assistance, conditions, and missing information beside results.
- Preserve raw denominators and exact-form practice reports without inventing conversions.
- Treat observed variation as evidence about those attempts, without guaranteed future bounds.
- Make readiness judgments explicit, limited, and open to revision when relevant evidence changes.

lessons.title: Checking administration and writing requirements
lessons.body:
## Make the intended administration concrete

Recent practice can show how you reason under recorded conditions. It cannot establish that your appointment is scheduled, that an identification document meets the current rules, or that a writing sample has been approved. These are different questions with different evidence. A readiness decision should connect them without letting success in one area substitute for another.

An **[[administration record]]** is a dated account of the intended test, the requirements that apply to it, and the evidence supporting each item's status. It is a working record, not permission to test. Begin with the intended administration, location or region, testing modality, and any individual approved conditions. Then record where the applicable instructions came from and when you checked them. If a date or modality changes, revisit the affected entries.

Keep sensitive account details in the appropriate private account or secure personal record. A study worksheet can say that the confirmation was checked without copying passwords, identification numbers, or medical documentation. The useful evidence is that the relevant requirement has been verified, not that unnecessary private information has been spread across study files.

## Check applicability before copying a rule

A search result may summarize an older cycle. A general FAQ may describe several possibilities while a specific page explains a change for your intended administration. Compare the source's scope, effective date, and the component it concerns. An authoritative page can still be inapplicable to a different date or component.

The source check for this lesson was November 4, 2026. LSAC's [format transition guidance](https://www.lsac.org/lsat-will-look-little-different-starting-august-2027) distinguishes practice for administrations through June 2027 from the announced format beginning August 2027. The new-format practice release is announced for February 2027; that future announcement does not establish availability on the date of this lesson. Use the linked timing reference for the detailed structures, then recheck the applicable official guidance before relying on them.

LSAC's current [Getting Ready page](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/taking-lsat) describes a move toward test-center delivery for most candidates in the 2026–2027 cycle, with limited remote exceptions. Do not infer that an older description of remote choice grants an exception. Separately, [LSAT Argumentative Writing](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/about/lsat-argumentative-writing) has its own remote administration and preparation requirements. A multiple-choice location does not determine the writing location or equipment.

Individual approved conditions also matter. A generic timing table describes standard conditions; it does not override an approval that applies to the learner's session. Conversely, a requested adjustment is not established as approved merely because it would help. Preserve the exact decision and its scope. Resolve unclear or conflicting instructions through the official channel before treating the issue as settled.

## Record what is known and what remains open

A **[[requirement status]]** describes whether a specific requirement is confirmed, pending, unresolved, or inapplicable, together with the evidence for that description. These are worksheet labels, not LSAC account labels. Use whichever wording accurately describes what you can establish.

Confirmed means you have relevant current evidence, such as a recorded confirmation matching the intended date and time zone. Pending means an action or official processing step remains. Unresolved means information is missing or conflicts. Inapplicable needs a reason: it should not mean merely inconvenient or unfamiliar. A completed action may leave a requirement pending; uploading a document, for example, does not by itself establish acceptance.

For each open item, identify the next action, the responsible person or organization, and the applicable deadline from the current instructions. Avoid inventing a deadline because another candidate remembers one. When time zones matter, record the zone supplied with the date. If the instructions change, retain the earlier record as history and identify which conclusion must be updated.

### Example 1: A date change affects particular checks

Suppose Mina planned a June 2027 administration and built a study record around the then-applicable four-section structure. She now intends an administration after the announced August transition. Her folder contains a confirmed appointment for the earlier date, an older timing checklist, and several completed reading lessons. She has not yet checked the new appointment or future-format practice availability.

First identify the change: the target administration is different. The earlier confirmation establishes an earlier booking, not a booking for the new target. The timing checklist needs a scope check against the transition guidance and any approved conditions. A new-format practice announcement needs a current availability check before Mina reserves an actual form.

Next preserve what the change does not erase. Her reading lessons and error records still document learning; they do not become nonexistent because the session structure changes. Her old full-session results remain labeled with their actual format. She can use them for relevant skill review while recognizing that they do not reproduce the later whole-session workload.

Finally write actions that close the actual gaps: verify the new appointment and time zone, refresh the applicable instructions, and identify available authorized practice for the intended structure. Repeating every lesson would not confirm an appointment. Relabeling the old practice would not recreate a different test experience. Each action should answer the uncertainty that prompted it.

## Give writing its own completion trail

Writing preparation includes argumentative practice, but administrative completion depends on the required sample and its status. LSAC's [scoring guidance](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/lsat-scoring) states that score release requires an approved writing sample and no account holds. Check whether a prior sample remains acceptable in your file under the current guidance. Do not assume either that every earlier sample is sufficient or that every repeat test taker must create another one.

Submission, processing, and approval are distinct. An uploaded or completed writing session may still await review. The current official page describes processing time and availability; use those instructions to plan an appropriate margin instead of assuming that an attempt made just before score release will be approved immediately. A home practice essay is useful preparation, but it is not the required administered sample.

The [writing FAQ](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/frequently-asked-questions-about-lsat/frequently-asked-questions-about-lsat-argumentative) also describes current equipment, software, workspace, and permitted-item requirements. Check these separately from multiple-choice arrangements and test the relevant setup using the official preparation guidance. Do not infer that a tool permitted during ordinary study is permitted in the administered writing session. Preserve individual approvals where they apply, and ask the official service to resolve uncertainty rather than improvising a substitute procedure.

### Example 2: Three kinds of writing evidence

Jon has a polished essay from an Erudior prompt, a screenshot saying that an administered writing session was submitted, and an account entry showing that review is pending. He wants to mark the writing requirement complete because he has already written twice. Assume the current applicable instructions require an approved sample, and no other accepted sample is recorded.

The practice essay supports a descriptive review of his writing skills. It does not establish completion of the administered requirement. The submission record establishes that a session was sent for processing. The pending entry establishes that the available evidence does not yet show approval. These records answer separate questions even though all concern writing.

Jon should keep the practice essay in his learning record and the submitted session in his administration record. The requirement remains pending until the relevant status changes or the official service clarifies it. If a stated processing period passes or a deadline creates a concern, the next action is to consult the official instructions or support channel. Rewriting a practice essay cannot change the official account status. Calling the submission approved would conceal the very issue the checklist is supposed to reveal.

## Guided practice

A fictional candidate has verified the intended test date and location. Her appointment message supplies a time but the copied study calendar omits its time zone. She has also requested an adjustment and received an acknowledgment of the request, but no decision. A previous writing sample appears in her account, and she has not checked whether it satisfies the current requirement. Which entries can be closed now?

The verified date and location can be recorded as confirmed within their scope. The appointment time needs its stated zone restored and checked. The acknowledgment supports receipt of the adjustment request, not approval. The earlier writing sample requires an applicability and status check before it closes the current requirement. Do not reset every verified item to unknown, and do not treat a mostly complete checklist as evidence for the remaining entries. Assign a specific next action to each open item.

## Common mistakes

Treating registration, appointment scheduling, and writing approval as one event hides separate dependencies. Treating an old screenshot as current ignores later changes. Copying generic conditions over an individual approval can misstate the actual target. Treating a pending request as granted makes practice records inaccurate and leaves the administrative issue unresolved.

A final mistake is allowing a strong practice result to settle logistics. Confidence in reasoning does not verify a document, appointment, or sample status. Similarly, perfect administrative records do not establish a particular future score. Keep each conclusion tied to evidence capable of supporting it.

## Key points

- Identify the intended administration and component before applying instructions.
- Keep dated sources, individual approvals, status evidence, and open actions together.
- Recheck the entries affected by a changed date, modality, or official instruction.
- Track writing preparation, submission, and approval as distinct evidence.
- Use current official instructions to resolve actual requirements; course completion is not administrative confirmation.

lessons.title: Maintaining and adapting readiness
lessons.body:
## Turn the evidence into a workable next period

Finishing the instructional sequence leaves a practical question: what should your next period of preparation contain? The answer depends on current evidence, remaining uncertainties, available time, and the intended administration. Completing every lesson documents completed study. It does not eliminate the need to inspect recent unfamiliar performance, writing, or administrative requirements.

A **[[maintenance plan]]** is a deliberately limited schedule that preserves useful skills, addresses selected unresolved problems, and gathers enough new evidence to reconsider the plan. It should identify what each activity is for. Reviewing a known question may help reconstruct a valid inference. An unfamiliar task may check whether that inference transfers. A full simulation may examine a whole-session approach. A writing rehearsal may test whether an objection is answered within the declared drafting window. Their purposes should not disappear inside a single total of study hours.

The plan is a proposal to be revised, not a reward for achieving a particular practice number. You can use a maintenance structure while an important weakness remains, provided the plan includes a proportionate repair. You can also decide that a larger instructional return is warranted. Neither label determines a test-day result.

## Allocate time by function and actual capacity

Begin with the time that is realistically available for the next planning period. Then choose a small number of priorities supported by the rare-error audit and readiness record. Preserve room to review new work: collecting another result without examining it may leave the same uncertainty unresolved. Keep administrative actions visible, and allocate writing deliberately when it is relevant to the current plan.

Useful functions include retaining established reasoning habits, repairing a selected mechanism, testing that repair on unfamiliar material, reviewing the evidence, and resolving preparation logistics. An activity can serve more than one function, but record why it was chosen. Do not count the same hour twice simply because it has two purposes.

When capacity falls, reduce scope before silently abandoning the review that gives practice its meaning. A shortened week might use a smaller unfamiliar set plus careful review. That is a legitimate learning session when labeled accurately. It does not become a full simulation because the learner originally intended a full form. Reserve whole-session evidence for an occasion that actually supports the declared protocol.

### Example 1: Rebuild a smaller week

Nora expected twelve study hours but now has six. Her recent records show a recurring reversal of a necessary condition, mostly stable reading decisions, and an unfinished writing reply to a competing perspective. Her intended full-simulation slot is no longer available. She proposes the following custom six-hour plan; these durations are her allocation, not official test timing.

| Activity and time | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Conditional reasoning reconstruction — 60 minutes | Explain the rule and a valid counterexample |
| Unfamiliar short reasoning sets — 75 minutes | Observe whether the repair transfers |
| Review of those first attempts — 75 minutes | Inspect reasoning and unintended costs |
| Reading maintenance and review — 60 minutes | Retain passage-based answer support |
| Writing practice and draft review — 60 minutes | Develop and inspect the competing reply |
| Administration check — 30 minutes | Resolve the specific open preparation items |

The allocation totals 360 minutes, or six hours. It does not include a full simulation, and Nora should record that missing evidence rather than manufacture a whole-session result from the short sets. Each slot answers a stated need. Reading remains present without consuming the time intended for the recurring conditional problem. Writing remains a separate activity with its own draft record.

Nora should also specify what happens if a set takes longer than expected. She might shorten the remaining planned set while retaining review, or move an activity to a later day. She should record the actual changes. The plan succeeds as a usable schedule when it guides evidence-producing work within her constraints, not when every original estimate remains untouched.

## Decide in advance what would change the plan

A **[[revision trigger]]** is an observable event or finding that prompts reconsideration of a particular part of the plan. It does not dictate an automatic conclusion. Examples include another well-documented occurrence of the same error mechanism, a strategy that creates repeated omissions, an unresolved administration item approaching its applicable deadline, or a substantial change in available time.

Define the evidence and the response separately. “A second recorded reversal in unfamiliar work will prompt another mechanism review” is actionable. “Any wrong answer means I am unprepared” turns every ordinary variation into a global verdict. A trigger should also identify what information is needed before changing course. If exposure history is uncertain, clarify it before treating the result as evidence of fresh transfer.

Some triggers concern implementation rather than reasoning. If a planned activity cannot fit the actual week, revise its scope. If a format change alters the target simulation, update that protocol. If a previously useful tactic now consumes time without resolving uncertainty, examine its conditions and cost. The conclusion may be to retain, narrow, modify, or suspend the tactic; the observation alone need not choose among all four.

### Example 2: A change that helps and harms

Eli trials an extra check of every conditional statement. In his first unfamiliar short set, it catches one reversal, but he leaves three later questions blank at cutoff. His earlier set had no blanks, although the two sets are not established as equivalent. His notes show that he applied the extra check even when he had already stated the relationship correctly.
