First preserve the whole result. The caught reversal is useful evidence; the omissions and time observations also matter. Do not erase the blanks to report accuracy only among completed questions as if it were the complete-set result. Do not attribute every difference to the tactic when the forms and contexts also differ.

Next narrow the hypothesis. Perhaps a full second pass is useful when the wording actually creates uncertainty, while a brief direction check is sufficient after a clear reconstruction. That is a candidate refinement, not a demonstrated universal rule. Eli can practise recognizing that distinction and then test the revised action on unfamiliar work under declared conditions.

Finally define the next review. He will examine whether the identified reversal recurs, whether the action is used where intended, and whether omissions or other errors appear. If the record shows that he cannot apply the narrower action reliably, further instruction may be appropriate. If the action fits and the evidence is favorable, he can retain it provisionally. One encouraging set cannot establish a perfect-score method; one costly trial cannot establish that every form of checking is harmful.

## Keep stable parts stable for a reason

Changing several methods at once makes later evidence harder to interpret. When possible, test one focused adjustment while preserving established routines. This is a practical way to clarify observations, not a claim that personal study becomes a controlled experiment. New questions, context, and ordinary variation still matter.

Before adding a tactic close to an intended test, ask what specific problem it addresses and what evidence shows that you can execute it under relevant conditions. A remembered success on reviewed material is weaker evidence of transfer than an unfamiliar application. An appealing explanation is not the same as a practised action. If time is insufficient to evaluate a large change, a narrower repair or a return to a supported routine may be more defensible. The choice depends on the actual cost of leaving the problem unresolved as well as the cost of change.

Keep a small record of retained strengths too. Otherwise the plan can become an ever-growing catalog of errors with no account of what is functioning. Record the tasks and conditions under which a skill appears dependable, and identify the limits of that evidence. Retention work should preserve those functions without making every session a repeat of the same memorized examples.

## Guided practice

A learner has four hours available. She schedules ninety minutes of unfamiliar work, ninety minutes reviewing it, thirty minutes of writing practice, and thirty minutes checking an unresolved appointment detail. A friend suggests adding another two-hour set because more questions must produce better readiness. The learner would have to remove the review and the appointment check to fit it.

The proposed addition does not fit the current purposes or capacity without replacing activities that answer known needs. The existing plan totals 240 minutes. The learner can retain it, reduce the new set to preserve review, or deliberately reprioritize with a stated reason. More items alone do not establish greater learning or close the appointment issue. If she chooses a smaller unfamiliar set, its result should retain the actual denominator and conditions. If a whole-session question remains unanswered, keep that uncertainty visible.

## Common mistakes

An inflexible schedule can hide changes in capacity. A schedule based only on total hours can hide missing review or writing. Repeating familiar forms can create impressive numbers while leaving transfer uncertain. Removing inconvenient results from a readiness record can make the plan appear stronger without improving the underlying evidence.

Another error is treating a revision trigger as a verdict. A new mistake calls for examination of its mechanism and context. It does not necessarily require rebuilding every habit, postponing every plan, or intensifying every activity. Choose an action proportionate to the evidence and the decision it needs to inform.

## Key points

- Give each planned activity a purpose and fit the total to actual capacity.
- Retain first attempts, review time, writing evidence, and open administration items.
- State observable triggers for reconsideration without treating them as automatic verdicts.
- Inspect a strategy's gains and costs before retaining or revising it.
- Course completion closes the teaching sequence; readiness remains a reasoned judgment with visible uncertainty.

questions.stem: AB01 — During a four-week trial, a repair café opened on Wednesday evenings. Every evening session filled, and most attendees said they could not attend during daytime hours. Therefore, the café should retain its Wednesday-evening sessions. Which statement is the main conclusion?
choices: The café tested Wednesday-evening sessions for four weeks.
Every evening session offered during the trial was full.
The café should retain its Wednesday-evening sessions.
Most trial attendees could not attend during daytime hours.
Wednesday was the only evening on which attendance was tested.
questions.explanation:
“The café tested Wednesday-evening sessions for four weeks.” — This gives the setting and duration of the trial; it is not the recommendation being supported.

“Every evening session offered during the trial was full.” — This is evidence offered in support of keeping the sessions, not the main conclusion.

“The café should retain its Wednesday-evening sessions.” — The attendance and access observations are offered as reasons to accept this recommendation. Identifying it does not establish that every possible objection has been answered.

“Most trial attendees could not attend during daytime hours.” — This is a supporting observation about access. It helps explain the recommendation but is not itself the recommended action.

“Wednesday was the only evening on which attendance was tested.” — The passage does not say whether any other evenings were tested, and this would not state the recommendation anyway.

questions.stem: AB02 — Every application that received an interview included a writing sample. Lena’s application did not include a writing sample. Which conclusion must follow from these statements?
choices: Lena’s application did not receive an interview.
Lena’s application was rejected without being read.
Lena would have received an interview with a writing sample.
Every application with a writing sample received an interview.
No application besides Lena’s omitted a writing sample.
questions.explanation:
“Lena’s application did not receive an interview.” — The rule requires a writing sample for any interviewed application. If Lena’s had received an interview, it would have included a sample, contrary to the second statement.

“Lena’s application was rejected without being read.” — The statements settle interview status, not whether reviewers read the application or made a rejection decision.

“Lena would have received an interview with a writing sample.” — A required condition need not be sufficient. The passage supplies no guarantee about what would happen if she supplied a sample.

“Every application with a writing sample received an interview.” — This reverses the rule. Including a sample may coexist with other reasons for not receiving an interview.

“No application besides Lena’s omitted a writing sample.” — Nothing describes the number of other applications without samples. Lena’s case is not stated to be unique.

questions.stem: AB03 — A library increased its loan period from two weeks to three. The share of loans returned late fell during the following month. The director concludes that the longer loan period caused the decline. Which additional fact most weakens that causal explanation?
choices: The same categories of books could be borrowed in both months.
The library kept the same opening hours throughout both months.
The longer loan period applied to every ordinary book loan.
Several readers had requested longer loan periods before the change.
Automatic return-date reminders also began when the policy changed.
questions.explanation:
“The same categories of books could be borrowed in both months.” — Stable book categories do not supply a competing cause for the decline.

“The library kept the same opening hours throughout both months.” — Stable opening hours remove one possible change rather than explain the decline independently of the loan policy.

“The longer loan period applied to every ordinary book loan.” — The policy’s broad application is consistent with the proposed explanation; it does not identify an alternative cause.

“Several readers had requested longer loan periods before the change.” — Earlier requests show a preference, not a separate change that could account for fewer late returns.

“Automatic return-date reminders also began when the policy changed.” — Reminders could also reduce late returns. Their simultaneous introduction prevents the before-and-after comparison from isolating the longer loan period. This weakens the causal claim without proving the policy had no effect.

questions.stem: AB04 — Every proposal reviewed by Panel R was publicly archived. Some proposals were reviewed by both Panel R and Panel S. Which conclusion follows?
choices: Every proposal reviewed by Panel S was publicly archived.
Some proposals reviewed by Panel S were publicly archived.
Every archived proposal was reviewed by both panels.
Some proposals reviewed by Panel R were not publicly archived.
No proposal was reviewed by a panel other than R or S.
questions.explanation:
“Every proposal reviewed by Panel S was publicly archived.” — Only the proposals shared with Panel R are guaranteed to be archived. Panel S may have reviewed others.

“Some proposals reviewed by Panel S were publicly archived.” — At least one proposal belongs to both reviewed groups. Because it was reviewed by R, it was archived; therefore at least one S-reviewed proposal was archived.

“Every archived proposal was reviewed by both panels.” — The archive rule runs from R review to archiving, not from archiving to review by both panels.

“Some proposals reviewed by Panel R were not publicly archived.” — This contradicts the statement that every R-reviewed proposal was archived.

“No proposal was reviewed by a panel other than R or S.” — The statements do not describe other panels or prohibit them from reviewing proposals.

questions.stem: AB05 — A swimming pool recorded fewer visitors this month than last month but more locker rentals. A visitor can rent at most one locker per visit. Which fact, if true, best helps reconcile these observations?
choices: The pool continued to offer the same number of lockers.
The pool charged the same admission price in both months.
Several lockers were repainted shortly before the new month.
Many visitors switched from cars to buses and brought bags inside.
The pool continued to record each visitor and each locker rental.
questions.explanation:
“The pool continued to offer the same number of lockers.” — Unchanged capacity does not explain why more of the smaller group rented lockers.

“The pool charged the same admission price in both months.” — A stable admission price supplies no reason for an increased share of visitors to rent lockers.

“Several lockers were repainted shortly before the new month.” — Repainting alone does not establish a reason for increased rentals; no relevant change in usability or demand is given.

“Many visitors switched from cars to buses and brought bags inside.” — People switching from cars to buses may bring bags they previously left in cars and may then need lockers. A sufficiently larger rental share can produce more rentals despite fewer visitors. The fact helps reconcile the observations without claiming to prove this happened.

“The pool continued to record each visitor and each locker rental.” — Consistent recording supports treating the figures as comparable, but does not explain their opposite movements.

questions.stem: AB06 — A shop installed a new outdoor sign, and its customer count increased the next week. The owner argues: “The sign was the only change I deliberately made to the business, so it must have caused the entire increase.” What is the principal flaw?
choices: It ignores changes outside the owner’s deliberate business decisions.
It assumes that the customer count increased before the sign appeared.
It concludes that a new sign can never affect customer behavior.
It treats the sign’s installation cost as the shop’s total revenue.
It infers that every other shop must have installed a similar sign.
questions.explanation:
“It ignores changes outside the owner’s deliberate business decisions.” — External events, such as changed pedestrian traffic, could contribute even if the owner made no other deliberate change. The premise does not establish the sign as the sole cause.

“It assumes that the customer count increased before the sign appeared.” — The passage places the increase after installation, not before it. The flaw is causal overconfidence rather than a reversed timeline.

“It concludes that a new sign can never affect customer behavior.” — The owner attributes an effect to the sign. The argument does not deny that signs can affect behavior.

“It treats the sign’s installation cost as the shop’s total revenue.” — Neither installation cost nor revenue figures appear in the reasoning.

“It infers that every other shop must have installed a similar sign.” — The argument makes a claim about this shop’s increase, not other shops’ actions.

questions.stem:
AB07 — A historian proposes mapping complaints about factory noise to identify the loudest districts of a nineteenth-century town. Surviving written complaints are concentrated in two districts, so the historian initially treats those districts as the loudest. The proposal assumes that the number of preserved complaints closely tracks the amount of noise residents experienced.

A later archive review complicates that assumption. The two districts had neighborhood associations whose secretaries regularly submitted written petitions and retained copies. Residents of several other districts often brought concerns to officials orally, and few records of those conversations survive. Thus, differences in documentation could affect the map even if noise levels were similar.

The complaints should not be discarded. They can reveal residents’ priorities and how organized groups sought a response. But using their distribution to rank noise levels requires evidence beyond the complaints themselves. A map of surviving complaints is first a map of documented protest, not automatically a map of sound.

Which statement best expresses the passage’s main point?
choices: Written complaints have no value for the study of industrial towns.
Complaint maps are informative but need other evidence to rank noise levels.
Neighborhood associations created the factory noise they protested.
All districts of the town experienced exactly the same noise levels.
Oral complaints were more accurate than written petitions in every case.
questions.explanation:
“Written complaints have no value for the study of industrial towns.” — The final paragraph expressly identifies useful information in the complaints.

“Complaint maps are informative but need other evidence to rank noise levels.” — This preserves both parts of the author’s position: the documents are useful, but unequal documentation limits the proposed noise ranking.

“Neighborhood associations created the factory noise they protested.” — The associations are described as producing and preserving records, not producing factory noise.

“All districts of the town experienced exactly the same noise levels.” — Similar noise is offered as a possibility that exposes the inference gap, not an established finding of equality.

“Oral complaints were more accurate than written petitions in every case.” — The passage discusses whether records survive, not a universal accuracy advantage for oral complaints.

questions.stem:
AB08 — A historian proposes mapping complaints about factory noise to identify the loudest districts of a nineteenth-century town. Surviving written complaints are concentrated in two districts, so the historian initially treats those districts as the loudest. The proposal assumes that the number of preserved complaints closely tracks the amount of noise residents experienced.

A later archive review complicates that assumption. The two districts had neighborhood associations whose secretaries regularly submitted written petitions and retained copies. Residents of several other districts often brought concerns to officials orally, and few records of those conversations survive. Thus, differences in documentation could affect the map even if noise levels were similar.

The complaints should not be discarded. They can reveal residents’ priorities and how organized groups sought a response. But using their distribution to rank noise levels requires evidence beyond the complaints themselves. A map of surviving complaints is first a map of documented protest, not automatically a map of sound.

What is the main function of the second paragraph?
choices: It proves that factory noise was absent outside the two districts.
It supplies a new numerical ranking of every district’s noise level.
It rejects the use of all archival evidence in historical research.
It identifies a documentation difference that could distort the proposed map.
It demonstrates that the historian intentionally concealed contradictory data.
questions.explanation:
“It proves that factory noise was absent outside the two districts.” — The paragraph gives no evidence of an absence of noise. Sparse records and absent noise are different claims.

“It supplies a new numerical ranking of every district’s noise level.” — It provides no numerical measurements or replacement ranking.

“It rejects the use of all archival evidence in historical research.” — Its criticism targets one inference from the surviving records, not all archival research.

“It identifies a documentation difference that could distort the proposed map.” — Different petition and preservation practices offer an alternative reason for the unequal record counts, weakening the initial interpretation.

“It demonstrates that the historian intentionally concealed contradictory data.” — No claim about the historian’s intentions appears. A methodological problem is not evidence of deliberate concealment.

questions.stem:
AB09 — A historian proposes mapping complaints about factory noise to identify the loudest districts of a nineteenth-century town. Surviving written complaints are concentrated in two districts, so the historian initially treats those districts as the loudest. The proposal assumes that the number of preserved complaints closely tracks the amount of noise residents experienced.

A later archive review complicates that assumption. The two districts had neighborhood associations whose secretaries regularly submitted written petitions and retained copies. Residents of several other districts often brought concerns to officials orally, and few records of those conversations survive. Thus, differences in documentation could affect the map even if noise levels were similar.

The complaints should not be discarded. They can reveal residents’ priorities and how organized groups sought a response. But using their distribution to rank noise levels requires evidence beyond the complaints themselves. A map of surviving complaints is first a map of documented protest, not automatically a map of sound.

Which inference is best supported?
choices: Districts without neighborhood associations never complained about noise.
Preserved complaints always exaggerate the disturbance residents experienced.
Officials responded more effectively to oral complaints than to petitions.
Written petition counts can establish noise rankings without further evidence.
Few surviving complaints do not establish that a district had little noise.
questions.explanation:
“Districts without neighborhood associations never complained about noise.” — The passage says residents elsewhere raised concerns orally, so the absence of an association does not establish silence.

“Preserved complaints always exaggerate the disturbance residents experienced.” — Nothing establishes exaggeration, let alone in every preserved complaint.

“Officials responded more effectively to oral complaints than to petitions.” — The effectiveness of officials’ responses is not compared.

“Written petition counts can establish noise rankings without further evidence.” — This is the inference the author warns against: documentation differences require additional evidence for a noise ranking.

“Few surviving complaints do not establish that a district had little noise.” — Few records may reflect how concerns were expressed and preserved. The text therefore supports withholding a conclusion of little noise from that fact alone.

questions.stem:
AB10 — Passage A: Natural-history museums should expand digital access to their collections. Detailed images let distant readers inspect features of specimens that would otherwise remain unavailable to them, and reducing repeated handling can help protect fragile objects. Images nevertheless omit some properties, including weight and texture. Funding digital access alongside physical collections can broaden use without treating photographs as complete replacements for objects.

Passage B: Digital museum resources can help students arrive at a visit with better questions. Their educational value depends partly on explaining their limits. A student who sees a color image may mistakenly believe that it also establishes an object’s texture or weight. Teaching materials should identify what a representation leaves out and, where feasible, provide other evidence for those properties. Digital resources can therefore prepare and extend encounters with objects without making every physical encounter unnecessary.

The authors would most clearly agree with which statement?
choices: Physical museum collections should receive no further funding.
Digital images are unsuitable for any serious educational purpose.
Digital images do not preserve every property of the objects represented.
Distant readers benefit less from images than local visitors do.
Every physical museum encounter becomes unnecessary after digitization.
questions.explanation:
“Physical museum collections should receive no further funding.” — Passage A expressly supports funding digital access alongside physical collections; B does not call for ending funding.

“Digital images are unsuitable for any serious educational purpose.” — Both authors identify educational or access benefits from digital resources.

“Digital images do not preserve every property of the objects represented.” — A names omitted weight and texture; B warns students not to infer these properties from a color image. This is their clear shared position.

“Distant readers benefit less from images than local visitors do.” — Neither passage compares the amount of benefit received by distant and local users.

“Every physical museum encounter becomes unnecessary after digitization.” — A rejects complete replacement, and B expressly denies that every physical encounter becomes unnecessary.

questions.stem:
AB11 — Passage A: Natural-history museums should expand digital access to their collections. Detailed images let distant readers inspect features of specimens that would otherwise remain unavailable to them, and reducing repeated handling can help protect fragile objects. Images nevertheless omit some properties, including weight and texture. Funding digital access alongside physical collections can broaden use without treating photographs as complete replacements for objects.

Passage B: Digital museum resources can help students arrive at a visit with better questions. Their educational value depends partly on explaining their limits. A student who sees a color image may mistakenly believe that it also establishes an object’s texture or weight. Teaching materials should identify what a representation leaves out and, where feasible, provide other evidence for those properties. Digital resources can therefore prepare and extend encounters with objects without making every physical encounter unnecessary.

How does Passage B relate to Passage A?
choices: It develops an educational implication of a limitation that Passage A acknowledges.
It denies that digital images can broaden access to museum collections.
It establishes that protecting fragile objects conflicts with all student learning.
It supplies measurements proving that weight can be read directly from color images.
It criticizes Passage A for claiming that images capture every physical property.
questions.explanation:
“It develops an educational implication of a limitation that Passage A acknowledges.” — A acknowledges omitted physical properties. B develops how educators should address those omissions so students use representations appropriately.

“It denies that digital images can broaden access to museum collections.” — B does not deny broader access and describes a useful role for digital materials.

“It establishes that protecting fragile objects conflicts with all student learning.” — B does not claim a conflict between preservation and all learning; no such general result is established.

“It supplies measurements proving that weight can be read directly from color images.” — B gives the opposite warning and presents no measurement data.

“It criticizes Passage A for claiming that images capture every physical property.” — A never makes that claim. Describing B this way misattributes to A a position it explicitly avoids.

questions.stem:
AB12 — Passage A: Natural-history museums should expand digital access to their collections. Detailed images let distant readers inspect features of specimens that would otherwise remain unavailable to them, and reducing repeated handling can help protect fragile objects. Images nevertheless omit some properties, including weight and texture. Funding digital access alongside physical collections can broaden use without treating photographs as complete replacements for objects.

Passage B: Digital museum resources can help students arrive at a visit with better questions. Their educational value depends partly on explaining their limits. A student who sees a color image may mistakenly believe that it also establishes an object’s texture or weight. Teaching materials should identify what a representation leaves out and, where feasible, provide other evidence for those properties. Digital resources can therefore prepare and extend encounters with objects without making every physical encounter unnecessary.

A teacher gives students color photographs of specimens and asks them to determine each specimen’s exact weight from the photographs alone. Which revision would best follow Passage B’s advice?
choices: Tell students that a sharper image necessarily reveals exact weight.
Identify the image’s limits and provide separate evidence of weight.
Require students to guess weight without acknowledging any uncertainty.
Replace every question about specimens with unrelated vocabulary drills.
State that viewing a photograph makes examination of objects pointless.
questions.explanation:
“Tell students that a sharper image necessarily reveals exact weight.” — Greater sharpness does not establish that a photograph records weight, and B cautions against assuming it does.

“Identify the image’s limits and provide separate evidence of weight.” — B recommends naming omitted properties and, where feasible, supplying other evidence. This directly addresses the unsupported task.

“Require students to guess weight without acknowledging any uncertainty.” — Unacknowledged guessing leaves the representation’s limitation unaddressed.

“Replace every question about specimens with unrelated vocabulary drills.” — B supports using digital resources to improve inquiry, not abandoning questions about specimens.

“State that viewing a photograph makes examination of objects pointless.” — B says digital resources can prepare and extend physical encounters, not make them pointless.

questions.stem: A learner completes an authorized official LSAT practice form and uses that form’s official conversion. How should the resulting scaled number be labeled?
choices: An official LSAT score issued for an administered examination
A scale that can also convert percentages from original Erudior sets
A scaled official-practice result, with its practice conditions recorded
A verified prediction of the learner’s next administered examination result
questions.explanation: The form-specific conversion supports a scaled official-practice result. It does not turn practice into an administered examination, so calling it an official LSAT score mislabels the result. Applying it to original Erudior sets transfers a conversion to questions it was not designed for. Predicting the next examination result adds an unsupported guarantee; future performance and conditions may differ.

questions.stem: A learner selects the keyed answer but cannot explain why the strongest alternative fails. Which record best preserves the useful evidence?
choices: Record the question as mastered because the selected answer was correct
Keep the answer correct and mark its reasoning as uncertain correct
Change the answer to incorrect because its justification was incomplete
Label the question a timing error without checking the session conditions
questions.explanation: Uncertain correct preserves both facts: the selection earned credit, but its justification needs work. Mastery is not established by one correct selection with weak reasoning. Changing the raw result to incorrect destroys the answer record rather than adding the needed interpretation. A timing label requires evidence about the process; incomplete justification alone does not identify time pressure as the cause.

questions.stem: A learner repeatedly answers the opposite task after overlooking EXCEPT in question stems. Which follow-up most directly addresses the observed error?
choices: Restate the requested task in several fresh stems before selecting an answer
Memorize the keyed choices from the missed items without reviewing their stems
Shorten the time allowance on every section before identifying the task
Study unrelated legal vocabulary instead of examining the missed wording
questions.explanation: Restating fresh stems practices the specific task-reading step that failed. Memorizing choices does not show that the learner can interpret a new task. Less time may increase pressure without correcting the misread. Unrelated legal vocabulary does not address overlooking EXCEPT; the evidence supports a wording-focused intervention.

questions.stem: Which plan supplies the most useful evidence about whether time pressure contributes to a learner’s errors, while recognizing that it cannot perfectly isolate the cause?
choices: Compare a memorized timed test with an unfamiliar untimed test and ignore exposure
Compare a timed reading set with an untimed arithmetic set and ignore the skills
Compare scaled scores from unrelated sources and ignore their question formats
Compare several fresh timed and untimed sets with similar skill coverage and recorded conditions
questions.explanation: Several fresh timed and untimed sets with similar coverage and recorded conditions provide more interpretable evidence, though difficulty and other differences can still matter. A memorized test confounds the comparison with prior exposure. Reading versus arithmetic changes the skill being measured. Unrelated scoring sources may use incompatible measures, so their numbers alone do not identify a timing effect.

questions.stem: Which error-log entry best supports a specific improvement task after a learner chooses an answer broader than the passage supports?
choices: I missed this question; I must become a more capable test taker
The key was C; I will memorize C before opening the same item again
I changed two observed branches into every branch; I will check scope on fresh items
I felt rushed; I will assume time explains this and every other mistake
questions.explanation: Identifying the change from two branches to every branch gives a specific scope failure and a task that can test its correction. The broad self-judgment identifies no reasoning step. Memorizing C rehearses a key rather than the method. Feeling rushed is relevant context, but assuming it explains all mistakes replaces investigation with an unsupported causal claim.

questions.stem: After reviewing a scope error and explaining the original item correctly, which next observation offers the best evidence of transfer?
choices: Selecting the remembered key on the same item immediately after review
Independently rejecting an overbroad answer on an unfamiliar item
Copying the explanation accurately into the error log without applying it
Recognizing the same stimulus while skipping its question and alternatives
questions.explanation: Applying the scope distinction independently to an unfamiliar item is transfer. Recalling the same key may reflect memory. Copying an explanation can help organize study but does not demonstrate application. Recognizing a stimulus shows familiarity, not the ability to evaluate its alternatives or solve a new problem.

questions.stem: A passage reports results for two schools. A learner chooses an answer asserting the same result for every school, and no further evidence is supplied. Which error hypothesis most directly matches the record?
choices: Scope: the chosen population exceeds the population supported
Timing: every unsupported generalization is caused by rushing
Arithmetic: choosing a broader population is always a calculation error
Transcription: the learner must have selected a different answer accidentally
questions.explanation: The move from two observed schools to every school is directly a scope expansion. Time pressure may contribute, but the record does not establish that cause. No calculation appears, so an arithmetic label lacks support. An accidental selection is possible in general, but nothing here makes it a better explanation than the visible reasoning mismatch.

questions.stem: A learner obtains 10/16 on the original Erudior baseline. Which conclusion is justified by that result alone?
choices: The learner’s future official LSAT score can be calculated from this percentage
The learner’s current limitations are permanent and need no further measurement
The same result will occur on every fresh set covering the same broad skills
The attempt provides a recorded starting point for inspecting current learning needs
questions.explanation: The attempt is a starting point whose mistakes and conditions can guide study. The original set supplies no LSAT conversion. One result does not establish a permanent limit. Fresh sets can differ in content and difficulty, and performance can change, so identical future results are not implied.

questions.stem: A learner gets 11 questions correct, selects wrong answers on three, and leaves two unanswered in the 16-item baseline. What is the full-set first-attempt report?
choices: 11/16, with three wrong selections and two unanswered recorded separately
11/14, with unanswered items omitted from the headline denominator
13/16, counting unanswered items as correct because no wrong choice was made
14/16, counting every attempted question as correct regardless of its answer
questions.explanation: All 16 offered items belong in the full-set denominator, and only the 11 correct selections earn credit. The fraction 11/14 describes attempted-item accuracy and needs that separate label. Unanswered items do not earn credit, so 13/16 is inflated. Attempts are not the same as correct answers, so 14/16 also overstates performance.

questions.stem: Before seeing the key, a learner revisits an uncertain answer and changes it. Which recording method preserves the distinction between first attempt and blind review?
choices: Overwrite the first answer so the sheet contains only the latest response
Check the explanation first and then label the copied correction blind review
Keep the original answer and confidence, and record the reviewed answer separately
Raise the original confidence after the key confirms the reviewed answer
questions.explanation: Separate columns preserve what the learner initially chose and what changed before feedback. Overwriting loses the first-attempt evidence. Reading the explanation first makes the correction post-feedback rather than blind review. Raising the original confidence afterward rewrites what the learner knew at the time and conceals potentially useful overconfidence or uncertainty.

questions.stem: A learner completes the untimed baseline using their usual accessibility supports, after already reading the arguments lesson. What is the most informative record?
choices: Untouched baseline under standard conditions, because only the final total matters
Invalid attempt, because any accessibility support prevents useful learning
Official timed result, because the questions involve LSAT-related reasoning
Original untimed practice, with the prior lesson exposure and supports recorded
questions.explanation: Recording prior instruction and supports makes the result interpretable without pretending that conditions were different. Calling it untouched ignores known exposure. Accessibility supports do not make a learning attempt useless; describing the conditions is what matters. Original untimed questions do not become an official timed test simply by practicing related reasoning skills.

questions.stem: During blind review, one originally wrong answer becomes correct and one originally correct answer becomes wrong. The total remains 12/16. What should the learner conclude?
choices: No reasoning changed because the original and reviewed totals are identical
The totals hide two changed decisions that both need investigation
Both original answers should be replaced so no disagreement remains
The unchanged total proves that time pressure had no influence on any answer
questions.explanation: One gain and one loss cancel numerically, but both decisions provide evidence worth investigating. Equal totals do not imply unchanged reasoning. Replacing the originals would erase the history needed to understand the changes. The total alone does not establish or rule out a timing effect on particular answers.

questions.stem: A passage first presents the hypothesis that a new gallery layout alone increased visits. It then reports that free admission began at the same time. It concludes that the available evidence cannot separate the layout's effect from the admission policy's effect. Which description best captures its structure?
choices: It rejects one observation and replaces it with an unrelated observation.
It supplies two independent proofs of the original hypothesis.
It presents an explanation, introduces a complication, and limits the conclusion.
It describes two policies without assessing any claim about their effects.
questions.explanation: The initial explanation is challenged by a change occurring at the same time, so the conclusion limits what the evidence establishes. No observation is rejected: increased visits and free admission are both accepted. The two changes are not independent proofs of the layout's effect. The final sentence does assess the causal claim, so this is more than a description of policies.

questions.stem: A writer states, 'The proposal has merit, but its costs are underestimated.' Which statement best captures the writer's position?
choices: The proposal has strengths and a problem in how its costs have been assessed.
The proposal lacks merit because any underestimated cost makes it worthless.
The proposal should be adopted because its merits settle the cost question.
The proposal is financially impossible regardless of its possible benefits.
questions.explanation: The writer acknowledges merit while criticizing the cost assessment. Calling the proposal worthless contradicts that acknowledgment and adds a rule about any cost underestimate. Adoption is not recommended, and the costs are expressly still a concern. Financial impossibility is also stronger than an underestimated cost; the writer does not say the project cannot be funded.

questions.stem: After describing a theory that every local bird of one species nests near water, a paragraph reports observations of local birds of that species nesting far from water. Which paragraph note best captures its function?
choices: Birds, water, nests, local observations.
Explains why water attracts every bird.
Confirms the original universal theory.
Presents cases challenging the theory.
questions.explanation: The cases conflict with the theory's claim about every local bird, so the paragraph challenges that theory. A noun list names the topic but loses the relationship to the earlier claim. The paragraph offers no explanation of attraction to water, and the far-from-water nests undermine rather than confirm the universal theory.

questions.stem: A passage reports that a scholar attributes a theater's closure entirely to declining attendance. The author then observes that attendance was stable during the final year and argues that the scholar has overlooked a steep rent increase. Which interpretation is best supported?
choices: The author endorses the scholar's complete explanation of the closure.
The author challenges the reported explanation as overlooking relevant information.
The author proves that attendance can never affect a theater's survival.
The author describes both explanations without evaluating either one.
questions.explanation: The stable attendance and overlooked rent increase are objections to the scholar's complete explanation. Reporting the scholar's view is not endorsement. A claim about this theater's final year does not establish that attendance never matters anywhere. The explicit charge that the scholar overlooks a factor is an evaluation, not a neutral presentation of two views.

questions.stem: A critic claims, 'Every mural commissioned by this town remains undamaged throughout its first year.' A report documents one town-commissioned mural that was damaged after six months. What does this case establish about the critic's claim?
choices: Every mural commissioned by the town is damaged within its first year.
The critic's claim about every such mural is false.
No mural can remain undamaged for as long as six months.
The town should stop commissioning murals immediately.
questions.explanation: One mural within the claimed category that fails the stated condition is enough to refute 'every.' The single case does not establish that all murals are damaged or that none can last six months; those are new universal claims. A policy recommendation to stop commissioning murals requires further reasons that the report does not provide.

questions.stem: A passage states only, 'The policy worked on some of the occasions studied.' Treat 'some' as at least one, without assuming it means 'some but not all.' Which statement must be true?
choices: The policy worked on every occasion studied.
The policy failed on at least one occasion studied.
The policy worked on most occasions studied.
The policy worked on at least one occasion studied.
questions.explanation: 'Some' establishes at least one successful occasion. It supplies neither the universal success required by 'every' nor the proportion required by 'most.' It also does not establish a failure: all occasions could have been successful without contradicting the statement. Thus neither 'always' nor 'not always' follows from 'sometimes' alone.

questions.stem: Your passage map says, 'Second paragraph: presents two studies that complicate the theory.' A question asks which participants were excluded from the second study. What is the best next step?
choices: Return to the second study and inspect the stated exclusion criteria.
Choose whichever answer most strongly criticizes the theory.
Assume the two studies excluded the same participants.
Answer from the main point without returning to the study.
questions.explanation: The map locates the relevant material; the question requires its exact detail. The strongest criticism need not identify an exclusion criterion. The fact that two studies share a paragraph does not establish identical participant rules. A main-point summary is too general to answer this specific question reliably without checking the wording.

questions.stem: A historian writes, 'Changing trade routes and rising harbor costs both contributed to the port's decline. The trade-route changes began affecting commerce decades before the harbor costs rose.' Which claim is supported by these statements?
choices: Trade-route changes were the only cause of the port's decline.
Harbor costs had a greater total effect than trade-route changes.
Both factors contributed, and the effects of the route changes began earlier.
The earlier factor necessarily had the greater total effect.
questions.explanation: The historian assigns a role to both factors and places the route changes earlier. Naming only the trade routes contradicts the contribution attributed to harbor costs. Nothing measures either factor's total effect, so the claim favoring harbor costs is unsupported. Earlier onset likewise does not establish a greater total effect.

questions.stem: A passage argues that translating a museum's labels can help visitors understand unfamiliar objects. It adds that counting visitors alone cannot show whether that understanding improved. Which statement best expresses the passage's main point?
choices: The passage concerns museums, translated labels, and visitor counts.
Translated labels can aid understanding, but visitor totals alone do not measure that benefit.
Translation invariably increases both visitor numbers and understanding.
Visitor numbers are useless for every decision a museum makes.
questions.explanation: The central claim combines a possible benefit with a limit on one way of measuring it. Naming museums and labels states the topic rather than the claim. 'Invariably increases' adds certainty and a claim about visitor numbers that the passage does not make. A limit on measuring understanding does not make visitor numbers useless for every other decision.

questions.stem: A researcher writes, 'Our survey of this year's festival volunteers found that some wanted training before their first shift. The survey did not ask volunteers at other festivals.' Which inference stays within the evidence?
choices: At least one volunteer surveyed at this festival wanted training before a first shift.
Most volunteers at other festivals wanted the same training.
Every volunteer at this festival wanted training before a first shift.
At least one surveyed volunteer opposed training before a first shift.
questions.explanation: The stated 'some' supports at least one person within the surveyed group. The survey provides no results for other festivals and gives no basis for 'most' there. It does not establish universal support at this festival. Nor does 'some wanted training' establish that anyone opposed it; some does not by itself mean some but not all.

questions.stem:
Passage A: 'Digitizing archives provides valuable remote access. Remote-user counts should be one measure of success, although not the only measure.'

Passage B: 'Remote access is valuable. Evaluators should also inspect which collections are searchable, since scanning only familiar documents may leave neglected collections difficult to find.'

Which statement best describes the relationship between the passages?
choices: B denies the access benefit that A endorses.
A rejects the collection-coverage measure that B recommends.
B develops an additional evaluation concern while sharing A's view of remote access.
Both treat remote-user counts as a sufficient measure of success.
questions.explanation: Both call remote access valuable, and B adds a concern about searchable collection coverage. B therefore does not deny the benefit. A does not discuss collection coverage, so silence cannot be treated as rejection. A explicitly says user counts are not the only measure, while B asks for coverage too; neither treats user counts as sufficient.

questions.stem: A review concludes, 'The available records do not show whether longer opening hours increased attendance. Attendance totals were recorded only after the hours changed.' Which response best respects that conclusion?
choices: Longer hours certainly increased attendance.
Longer hours certainly did not increase attendance.
Attendance must have declined because earlier totals are missing.
The effect remains unsettled by these records.
questions.explanation: Without the needed earlier totals, these records do not settle the effect. A definite increase and a definite absence of increase each go beyond that stated uncertainty. Missing earlier records likewise do not establish a decline. Failure to establish an effect is different from establishing that the effect did not occur.

questions.stem: Roof rooms cannot open until they pass inspection. Their inspection will not occur until next month. Thus, those rooms will be closed for this week's tour. Since the tour requires access to the roof rooms, the museum should postpone it. Which claim functions as an intermediate conclusion?
choices: Roof rooms cannot open until they pass inspection.
The inspection will not occur until next month.
The tour requires access to the roof rooms.
The museum should postpone this week's tour.
The roof rooms will be closed for this week's tour.
questions.explanation: The claim that the roof rooms will be closed for the tour has two roles. The inspection requirement and inspection date support it; it then combines with the tour's need for those rooms to support postponement. That makes it an intermediate conclusion. The inspection requirement is a starting premise, and the inspection date is another starting premise. The statement that the tour requires roof-room access supplies an additional premise for the recommendation. The recommendation to postpone is the main conclusion, not an intermediate step. Trace what supports each claim and what that claim supports in turn. A word such as “thus” helps locate one inference, but the complete passage reveals which conclusion is the final objective.

questions.stem: The council should replace the underground pipes before repaving Cedar Lane. Replacing the pipes requires digging through the lane's surface. If the lane were repaved first, that new surface would have to be broken up for the pipe work. Which statement expresses the main conclusion?
choices: The council should replace the pipes before repaving Cedar Lane.
Replacing the underground pipes requires digging through the lane's surface.
Repaving first would leave a new surface that the pipe work would damage.
The council has already replaced the pipes beneath most of Cedar Lane.
Any lane with underground pipes should remain unpaved for its entire lifetime.
questions.explanation: The opening recommendation sets out the action the author wants the council to take: replace the pipes before repaving. The remaining statements support that order. The need to dig through the surface is an offered reason. The consequence of repaving first explains why the proposed order would avoid destroying a newly laid surface; it supports the recommendation rather than replacing it as the main conclusion. The passage never says the pipes have already been replaced. It also does not argue that lanes should remain unpaved forever. Its recommendation concerns the sequence of two projects on Cedar Lane. The main conclusion can appear first even when the explanation of its support follows afterward.

questions.stem: “Since April, the station has recorded the number of bicycles parked outside each weekday. Its records show that the racks are often full.” What role does “Since April” play in this passage?
choices: It introduces a reason that explains why every bicycle rack became full.
It identifies the conclusion that the station needs additional bicycle racks.
It specifies when the recording period began.
It attributes the station's records to a different speaker's disputed opinion.
It establishes that April's observations prove what will happen in every later month.
questions.explanation: “Since April” specifies the start of the period during which the station has kept records. Here “since” is a time expression. It does not give a reason why the racks became full, and the passage makes no recommendation to add racks. The phrase does not introduce another speaker or a disagreement about the records. It also does not guarantee that future months will repeat April's pattern. Words that sometimes signal logical support can serve ordinary grammatical functions in a different sentence. Read the relationship the words express in context. The records may support a further argument someone could make, but that possible argument should not be inserted into the passage.

questions.stem: A critic says, “The archive project is expensive, so it should be canceled.” The editor responds, “A grant covers its full cost, and the project will preserve records that are deteriorating. We should proceed with it.” Which claim is the editor's conclusion?
choices: The archive project is expensive and should therefore be canceled.
The project will preserve records that are deteriorating.
A grant covers the archive project's full cost.
The critic believes cost is a reason to cancel the project.
The archive project should proceed.
questions.explanation: The editor argues that the project should proceed. The grant and preservation benefit are the reasons the editor offers for that position. The grant statement is therefore a premise, as is the claim about preserving deteriorating records. Cancellation is the critic's conclusion, which the editor opposes. Describing the critic's view about cost correctly identifies part of the exchange, but it does not state what the editor is trying to establish. Keep a speaker label beside each claim when a stimulus includes competing voices. A conclusion indicator inside a quotation identifies that quoted speaker's reasoning; it does not make the quoted conclusion the position endorsed by a later speaker.

questions.stem: A report states, “Some classrooms with exterior shades remained cooler during the afternoon measurements.” Which paraphrase preserves the scope of that statement?
choices: Every classroom with exterior shades was cooler throughout the school year.
At least some shaded classrooms stayed cooler during those afternoon measurements.
Every classroom that remained cooler had exterior shades installed.
Shaded classrooms were cooler during every measurement taken in the study.
Exterior shades alone caused the temperature difference in every classroom.
questions.explanation: “At least some shaded classrooms” preserves the limited group, and “during those afternoon measurements” preserves the observation period. It does not promise that all shaded rooms behaved that way. The school-year paraphrase expands both the number of rooms and the time period. The statement that every cooler classroom had shades reverses the relationship and excludes other kinds of cooler room without support. The every-measurement version extends the claim beyond the specified afternoon measurements. The last choice adds a claim that shades alone caused the difference, as well as extending it to every classroom. A faithful paraphrase must preserve limits and must not turn an observation into proof of a cause.

questions.stem: Two engineers agree that a reservoir emptied overnight. One asks how that happened. The other replies, “The outlet gate remained open because its closing mechanism failed, so water continued to escape.” In this context, what is the reply's primary purpose?
choices: To establish that the reservoir emptied, which the first engineer denies.
To recommend replacing every outlet gate in the region immediately.
To prove that all failures of a closing mechanism empty a reservoir.
To explain an event both engineers already accept.
To report unrelated events without proposing a connection between them.
questions.explanation: Both engineers already accept that the reservoir emptied. The reply proposes a causal account of that event, so its primary purpose is explanation. It is not trying to overcome a denial that the reservoir emptied; the stem explicitly says they agree. It makes no recommendation about replacing gates. It also does not state a universal rule about every closing-mechanism failure. Finally, the events are linked: mechanism failure leaves a gate open, allowing water to escape. They are not presented as unrelated observations. The explanation itself could later require supporting evidence. Classifying its conversational purpose does not mean that its proposed cause has already been verified.

questions.stem: A workshop organizer says, “Attendance increased after we distributed flyers, so the flyers caused the increase.” Even if both events occurred as stated, which question raises a possible gap between the evidence and the causal conclusion?
choices: Did a change in the class schedule also attract additional attendees?
Are you sure attendance increased after the flyers were distributed?
Could attendance actually have declined after the flyers were distributed?
Is it possible that no flyers were distributed before attendance increased?
Is it possible that all the extra attendees arrived before any flyer distribution?
questions.explanation: Asking about a schedule change allows the reported sequence to remain true while testing a possible alternative contributor to the increase. It examines the step from “after the flyers” to “because of the flyers.” Asking whether attendance increased after distribution directly challenges the reported observation. Suggesting that attendance declined disputes the increase. Suggesting that no flyers preceded it disputes the timing of distribution. Suggesting that all extra attendees arrived before any distribution also challenges the stated sequence. The correct response does not establish that flyers had no effect. It identifies information needed before treating timing alone as adequate evidence of the claimed cause.

questions.stem: The museum should retain the entrance ramp. It provides step-free access to the collection. In addition, maintaining the ramp costs less than removing it would. How are the last two statements used in the argument?
choices: The access statement is offered as evidence that maintaining the ramp costs less.
The cost statement is offered as evidence that the ramp provides step-free access.
They provide separate reasons for retaining the ramp.
They describe two objections that the author accepts against retaining the ramp.
They provide background while leaving the recommendation without any offered support.
questions.explanation: The access benefit and the cost comparison each supply a reason to retain the ramp. Neither is presented as a reason to believe the other, so the structure is two lines of support rather than a chain of intermediate conclusions. The first choice incorrectly makes access evidence of cost. The second makes cost evidence of access. Calling the statements objections reverses how the author uses them: they favor retaining the ramp. Calling them mere background misses their connection to the recommendation. This question asks about the relationship among claims, not whether they settle every possible practical consideration. Reasons can be identifiable even when the author has not supplied a complete decision analysis.

questions.stem: On a twelve-item baseline, a learner has five correct answers with clear justifications, two correct guesses, four incorrect answers, and one unanswered item. Which report preserves both raw credit and uncertainty?
choices: 5/12 correct, with the two correct guesses recorded as incorrect
7/11 correct, with the unanswered item removed from the total
7/12 correct, with the two correct guesses flagged for review
9/12 correct, with uncertainty counted as two additional points
5/10 correct, with the two correct guesses removed entirely
questions.explanation: "7/12 correct, with the two correct guesses flagged for review" counts five justified correct selections plus two correct guesses and retains every item in the denominator. "5/12 correct, with the two correct guesses recorded as incorrect" removes two earned points. "7/11 correct, with the unanswered item removed from the total" changes the twelve-item denominator. "9/12 correct, with uncertainty counted as two additional points" counts the correct guesses twice. "5/10 correct, with the two correct guesses removed entirely" excludes answered questions because of confidence, producing a different and misleading measure. The uncertain selections belong in the review queue, but their raw points remain.

questions.stem: A learner scores 7/12 on a first attempt, 11/12 on the same set after review, and 8/12 on a fresh set with a similar skill mix. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The repeated gain proves that four additional skills are now mastered
The fresh score proves that review raised general ability by one point
The repeated score should replace the first result in the baseline record
The lower fresh score proves that the review produced no useful learning
Familiar-item performance improved, while transfer still needs more evidence
questions.explanation: "Familiar-item performance improved, while transfer still needs more evidence" reports the observed repeated improvement without assuming its cause or permanence; the fresh result is relevant but limited evidence. "The repeated gain proves that four additional skills are now mastered" treats four additional correct answers as four mastered skills and ignores answer memory. "The fresh score proves that review raised general ability by one point" ignores set difficulty and other conditions. "The repeated score should replace the first result in the baseline record" erases the starting measurement. "The lower fresh score proves that the review produced no useful learning" overstates the opposite conclusion: unfamiliar items can be harder even when learning occurred.

questions.stem: A learner took the first untimed set after a long workday and a higher-scoring fresh set after resting. Why should fatigue be recorded when interpreting the difference?
choices: It is another changed condition that complicates attributing the gain to study
It proves that fatigue alone caused every incorrect answer on the first set
It allows the first score to be adjusted upward by the number of tired misses
It makes the two sets identical in difficulty once their percentages are known
It means the rested result can be converted directly into an official score
questions.explanation: "It is another changed condition that complicates attributing the gain to study" identifies fatigue as a possible confound, not an established cause. "It proves that fatigue alone caused every incorrect answer on the first set" claims more than the observations show. "It allows the first score to be adjusted upward by the number of tired misses" invents unearned credit and assumes which answers fatigue affected. "It makes the two sets identical in difficulty once their percentages are known" cannot follow from recording a condition; different sets may still vary. "It means the rested result can be converted directly into an official score" supplies no valid calibration for an original set.

questions.stem: A learner has not yet opened the explanations for a missed item. Which sequence best preserves diagnostic information while supporting learning?
choices: Read the explanation, overwrite the first answer, then report a revised baseline
Save the first answer, reason again, compare explanations, log a correction, try fresh practice
Memorize the keyed choice, repeat the same item, then record the skill as mastered
Discard unfinished items, calculate a higher percentage, then reduce the next time limit
Read every explanation, clear the uncertainty flags, then count all reviewed answers as fresh
questions.explanation: "Save the first answer, reason again, compare explanations, log a correction, try fresh practice" is the sound sequence. Saving the first answer preserves the initial evidence. Reasoning again before consulting the explanation supports review; record any correctness or answer feedback already seen. Logging the correction and trying fresh practice then checks transfer. "Read the explanation, overwrite the first answer, then report a revised baseline" loses the original measurement. "Memorize the keyed choice, repeat the same item, then record the skill as mastered" substitutes recall for demonstrated understanding. "Discard unfinished items, calculate a higher percentage, then reduce the next time limit" distorts accuracy and adds pressure without investigating the error. "Read every explanation, clear the uncertainty flags, then count all reviewed answers as fresh" erases useful confidence information and mislabels exposed material.

questions.stem:
Read this original passage.

A regional seed exchange counts its success by the number of seed varieties deposited each year. More deposits can preserve useful options for growers, but the total alone says little about whether growers can actually obtain the seeds. A variety may appear in the catalog even when only a small sample remains, and a deposit may lack reliable instructions for cultivation.

The exchange's staff recently began recording how many requested varieties could be supplied and whether recipients could use the accompanying growing information. These records do not replace the deposit count: preserving diversity remains an important goal. They do, however, reveal practical limitations that a rising catalog total can conceal. The exchange should therefore evaluate its work using both preservation and usable access, rather than treating additional catalog entries as a complete measure of success.

Which statement best expresses the passage's main point?
choices: Preserving seed diversity matters less than supplying familiar varieties.
Cultivation instructions determine whether seed varieties should be preserved.
A rising deposit total shows that most growers can obtain needed seeds.
The staff's new records make the deposit count unnecessary for evaluation.
Evaluation should consider both preserved diversity and usable seed access.
questions.explanation: The answer combining preserved diversity and usable access captures the final recommendation and both paragraphs' reasoning. The passage retains preservation as important while showing why a deposit count is incomplete. Giving familiar varieties priority invents a ranking the author does not make. Treating instructions as the condition for preservation changes a problem with usability into an admission rule. A rising total does not establish that most growers obtain seeds; that is precisely the limitation under discussion. Making deposit counts unnecessary contradicts the explicit statement that the new records do not replace them. The main point must preserve the author's combined standard, not select only one of its parts.

questions.stem:
Read this original passage.

Researchers tested a new method of displaying bus-arrival information at two stops. During the first week, surveyed passengers estimated their waits more accurately than passengers had in an earlier survey. The researchers described this finding as promising, but noted that the first survey occurred during regular service and the later one during a week with unusually few delays. They have scheduled a longer comparison that will record actual delays as well as passengers' estimates. Until that comparison is complete, the researchers regard the finding as provisional. They continue collecting data rather than recommending immediate use of the display across the entire network.

As used in the passage, 'provisional' most nearly means:
choices: Established independently of the conditions under which it was observed.
Tentative and subject to revision when further evidence becomes available.
Rejected because the researchers have shown the opposite result to be true.
Restricted by agreement to people who took part in the initial survey.
Scheduled to become certain once a predetermined amount of time passes.
questions.explanation: 'Tentative and subject to revision' fits the researchers' decision to obtain a longer comparison before relying on the promising result. The study conditions may explain part of the difference, so the finding is not established independently of those conditions. The opposite result has not been proved, and the initial finding has not been rejected. Nothing suggests a confidentiality restriction on participants. Certainty will not arrive merely because time passes; the additional evidence must be assessed. The surrounding contrast between a promising early observation and a pending comparison determines the contextual meaning.

questions.stem:
Read this original passage.

An early museum catalog lists each painting displayed in the main gallery, and a historian initially treated the list as a complete account of the museum's exhibition that year. Letters from two visitors describe small sculptures displayed in an adjoining room. Both visitors give detailed descriptions that match objects the museum already owned at the time. No sculptures appear in the catalog. The historian now regards the catalog as useful evidence about the main gallery but insufficient by itself to describe the entire exhibition. The letters do not establish how many visitors entered the adjoining room, how long its display remained open, or whether still other rooms contained exhibits.

Which inference is best supported by the passage?
choices: The catalog's omission shows that its list of paintings is inaccurate.
The letters establish the total number of objects shown that year.
A useful record of one gallery can omit displays elsewhere in the museum.
Most museum visitors preferred the sculpture room to the main gallery.
The historian can determine how long the sculpture display remained open.
questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes useful evidence about one gallery from a complete account of the exhibition. That supports the inference that a useful gallery record can omit displays elsewhere. The omission of sculptures does not show that the listed paintings are wrong. The letters do not count every exhibit and expressly leave possible additional rooms unresolved. Descriptions from two visitors establish no preference among most visitors. The display's duration is specifically left unknown. The correct inference combines the record's limited scope with its continuing value, rather than treating an incomplete source as either wholly unreliable or complete.

questions.stem:
Read this original passage.

A town restored vegetation along a stream, and its volunteers subsequently counted more fish in the restored stretch. The project report attributed the increase to the restoration and recommended using the same approach on every stream in the district. The report compared the restored stretch only with its own count from the previous year.

During the same period, several unrestored streams also showed higher fish counts following a season of unusually favorable water levels. These increases do not establish that the restoration had no benefit. They indicate that a year-to-year increase can occur without restoration, so the town's comparison does not by itself show how much of its increase the project caused. Further comparisons are needed before treating the project's apparent success as sufficient grounds for a district-wide policy.

What is the primary function of the second paragraph?
choices: To establish that the restoration necessarily reduced fish populations.
To explain how volunteers should count fish during unfavorable conditions.
To identify a limitation in the evidence supporting the report's recommendation.
To demonstrate that every stream in the district responds identically to water levels.
To show that the report recommended restoration before gathering any observations.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph identifies a limitation: other streams improved without restoration, so the project's before-and-after comparison does not isolate its contribution. That qualifies the evidence supporting the broad recommendation. It does not establish a harmful effect; it explicitly leaves a benefit possible. Counting techniques are not discussed. Several unrestored streams do not establish identical responses in every stream. The report did use observations from two years, so the absence-of-observations answer is false. The paragraph challenges what the evidence can justify, rather than proving the project failed or proposing a method for counting fish.

questions.stem: The city planted trees on three blocks. Those blocks were cooler in July than nearby blocks without new trees. Therefore, planting trees can help reduce summer street temperatures. Which statement is the conclusion?
choices: The city planted trees on three blocks.
The three blocks were cooler in July.
Planting trees can help reduce summer street temperatures.
Nearby blocks had no newly planted trees.
questions.explanation: The claim that planting trees can reduce temperatures is what the author uses the comparison to support. The planting on three blocks describes the intervention, their cooler temperatures describe the observation, and the absence of new trees describes the comparison group; those three claims supply premises. Identifying the conclusion does not establish that trees were the only cause of the difference.

questions.stem: Which passage most clearly presents an argument rather than merely reporting observations?
choices: The library opens at nine and closes at six.
The library should extend its hours because evening demand exceeds available seating.
The library installed new lights last Tuesday.
The library has two entrances and a reading room.
questions.explanation: The recommendation to extend hours is supported by a reason about evening demand, so this passage presents an argument. The opening-hours passage reports a schedule, the lighting passage reports an event, and the entrances passage describes facilities. None of those other passages, as written, offers one claim as a reason for accepting another.

questions.stem: Every member of the debate team studies rhetoric. Maya studies rhetoric. Therefore, Maya is on the debate team. What is the flaw?
choices: It treats studying rhetoric as proof of debate-team membership.
It denies that debate-team members study rhetoric.
It assumes Maya does not study rhetoric.
It treats Maya's membership as a stated premise rather than a conclusion.
questions.explanation: The rule runs from membership to studying rhetoric, so studying rhetoric alone does not establish membership. Maya could study rhetoric without joining the team. The argument affirms, rather than denies, that members study rhetoric; it expressly says Maya studies rhetoric; and it presents Maya's membership after "therefore" as its conclusion, not as a stated premise. The flaw shows that membership is not established, not that Maya is definitely a nonmember.

questions.stem: Which statement is offered as a premise in this argument: "We should add a second train because the morning service is routinely overcrowded"?
choices: A second train has already been added.
Overcrowding is impossible to address.
Train service should be reduced.
The morning service is routinely overcrowded.
questions.explanation: Routine overcrowding is the reason offered for adding a train. The passage does not say a second train already exists, does not claim overcrowding is impossible to address, and recommends adding service rather than reducing it. Those three alternatives are not stated support for the recommendation.

questions.stem: An organizer argues: "The hall's only exit is blocked, so the hall cannot safely host tonight's event. Therefore, we should move the event." What role does the claim that the hall cannot safely host the event play?
choices: It is supported by the blocked-exit claim and supports moving the event.
It is the final recommendation, with no further claim depending on it.
It is an unrelated description of the hall's usual appearance.
It is an objection the organizer reports and then rejects.
questions.explanation: The claim is an intermediate conclusion: the blocked exit supports the safety judgment, which supports moving the event. Moving the event is the final recommendation, so the safety judgment is not the last step. The claim concerns safety and connects the argument's two steps, rather than describing appearance. The organizer endorses it; no rejected speaker or objection appears.

questions.stem: Two offices installed new lamps. Their employees subsequently reported fewer headaches than employees in two offices without new lamps. A manager concludes that the lamps reduced headaches. Which question most directly investigates a gap in this comparison?
choices: Did every employee prefer the lamps' color to the old color?
Did workload or other working conditions also differ between the offices?
Was the lamp manufacturer's name longer than its competitors' names?
Were the offices listed alphabetically in the staff directory?
questions.explanation: Differences in workload or other working conditions could help explain the headache difference, so investigating them addresses whether the comparison isolates the lamps' effect. Color preference alone does not establish the cause of headaches; the passage supplies no link that makes unanimous preference the central issue. Manufacturer-name length and alphabetical listing do not address a relevant alternative cause. The comparison may offer evidence even though it does not by itself prove the causal conclusion.

questions.stem: Everyone at a meeting accepts that the gallery closed early. A curator says, "It closed early because a water pipe burst." What is the curator primarily doing in this context?
choices: Arguing that the already accepted closure never occurred.
Offering a reason to believe that the gallery should close tomorrow.
Explaining an accepted event by identifying its proposed cause.
Describing the gallery without relating any events to each other.
questions.explanation: The curator supplies a proposed cause of an event the audience already accepts. The curator does not deny the closure, make a recommendation about tomorrow, or merely list unrelated features. The context establishes that the closure is accepted, making explanation the primary function; the word "because" alone would not settle that function in every context.

questions.stem: A notice states only: "Since the museum renovated its entrance, monthly attendance has increased." Which reading adds the fewest unsupported claims?
choices: The renovation must be the only cause of the increase.
The increase proves that the renovation was unnecessary.
The museum is recommending another entrance renovation.
Attendance increased during the period after the renovation.
