If A and B are both true, the original, converse, and inverse are all true. A true with B false violates the original, so it cannot serve as a permitted counterexample. If both are false, the original, converse, and inverse are again all true.

questions.stem:
A clerk reasons: "If an order carries a priority label, it is placed in a blue folder. This order does not carry a priority label. Therefore, it is not placed in a blue folder."

Given only the stated rule and fact, which description best identifies the reasoning error?
choices: The clerk has drawn the valid contrapositive from the absence of a blue folder.
The clerk has used the converse to infer a priority label from a blue folder.
The clerk has treated the inverse as though it followed from the original rule.
The clerk has assumed that a priority label and a blue folder cannot occur together.
questions.explanation: The inference has the inverse form: not priority, therefore not blue. The rule allows a nonpriority order to be placed in a blue folder, so the conclusion is not established. A valid contrapositive would begin with not blue and conclude not priority; that is not the clerk's starting fact. The converse would begin with blue and conclude priority, also a different inference. The clerk does not claim that priority and blue are incompatible; the original rule allows and requires blue when priority occurs.

questions.stem:
A shelf's number of sealed boxes is a whole number, zero or greater.

Which statement is the precise negation of "The shelf contains at least six sealed boxes"?
choices: The shelf contains at most six sealed boxes.
The shelf contains no sealed boxes.
The shelf contains fewer than six sealed boxes.
The shelf contains more than six sealed boxes.
questions.explanation: The original permits six or more; its complement is zero through five, expressed as fewer than six. At most six wrongly includes six, a count that satisfies the original. No sealed boxes selects only zero and omits one through five. More than six is a narrower version of the original claim rather than its negation, and it excludes the required zero-through-five range.

questions.stem:
In a fictional tile exercise, each tile has exactly one of three colors: red, blue, or green.

Which statement is equivalent to the negation of "Tile V is red"?
choices: Tile V is blue or green.
Tile V is blue.
It is not known whether Tile V is red.
Tile V has no color.
questions.explanation: Blue or green covers the entire nonred part of the stated domain. Blue alone is too narrow because a green tile also makes the original claim false. Uncertainty about whether the tile is red concerns knowledge and could coexist with an actually red tile. Having no color is excluded by the setup and does not express the two remaining color possibilities.

questions.stem:
A fictional machine has this rule: "If the machine is not in standby mode, its fan is running."

Which statement is logically equivalent to the rule?
choices: If the machine is in standby mode, its fan is not running.
If the fan is running, the machine is not in standby mode.
If the fan is not running, the machine is not in standby mode.
If the fan is not running, the machine is in standby mode.
questions.explanation: Reverse and negate the sides: not running implies not (not in standby). Double negation makes the consequent in standby. Standby implying not running is the inverse; a standby machine with its fan running is allowed by the original. Running implying not standby is the converse, defeated by that same allowed case. Not running implying not standby fails to negate the whole original antecedent; a standby machine with its fan stopped satisfies the original but falsifies that alternative.

questions.stem:
Which statement is the precise negation of "The seal is intact and the label is legible"?

Read "or" inclusively, allowing both alternatives to hold.
choices: The seal is not intact and the label is not legible.
The seal is not intact or the label is not legible, possibly both.
Exactly one of these is true: the seal is not intact; the label is not legible.
The seal is intact or the label is legible, possibly both.
questions.explanation: Negating the conjunction requires at least one component to fail, including the possibility that both fail. Requiring both failures is too strong: an intact seal with an illegible label already makes the original false. Requiring exactly one failure is too narrow because a broken seal with an illegible label also negates the original. Intact or legible is not the complement: it is true when both are true, which also makes the original true.

questions.stem:
A fictional dispatch system follows this rule: "If a package is coded urgent and sent overnight, it receives a tracking code or a seal scan, or both."

Which rule is logically equivalent? Every "or" in the choices is inclusive.
choices: If a package receives no tracking code and no seal scan, it is not coded urgent or is not sent overnight.
If a package receives no tracking code and no seal scan, it is not coded urgent and is not sent overnight.
If a package receives no tracking code or no seal scan, it is not coded urgent or is not sent overnight.
If a package is not coded urgent or is not sent overnight, it receives no tracking code and no seal scan.
questions.explanation: The original has form (U and N) → (T or S). Its contrapositive is (not T and not S) → (not U or not N). Requiring both not U and not N is too strong: a nonurgent overnight package could lack both outputs without violating the original. Using no tracking code or no scan as the trigger is also too strong: an urgent overnight package could have a tracking code but no scan. Inferring no tracking code and no seal scan from not being coded urgent or not being sent overnight is the inverse; a nonurgent package could still receive a tracking code and a scan.

questions.stem:
In a fictional permit registry, if a form is marked urgent or signed by the director, or both, it receives a date stamp and a registry code. Form V receives no registry code.

Assuming the rule and fact are true, which conclusion must follow?
choices: Form V is marked urgent.
Form V receives no date stamp.
Form V is neither marked urgent nor signed by the director.
Form V is signed by the director.
questions.explanation: Let U mean urgent, S signed, D date stamp, and C registry code. The contrapositive of (U or S) → (D and C) is (not D or not C) → (not U and not S). Missing the code satisfies that antecedent, establishing both not urgent and not signed. Either urgent status or the director's signature would require a code, so those individual claims conflict with the rule and fact. No date stamp is not established: the compound output already fails because the code is missing, whether or not a stamp exists.

questions.stem:
A fictional equipment register uses this rule: "If a device is registered and inspected, it is recorded as eligible for the service pool." Device D is not registered.

Given only the rule and that fact, which statement correctly describes what follows?
choices: Device D must not be recorded as eligible for the service pool.
Device D could be recorded as eligible or not recorded as eligible without violating the stated rule.
Device D must be recorded as eligible for the service pool.
Device D cannot have been inspected.
questions.explanation: Because D is not registered, the compound antecedent registered and inspected is false. The rule imposes no eligibility conclusion for that case; either truth value for recorded as eligible is compatible with it. Concluding that no eligibility record can exist treats failure of a sufficient condition as failure of the necessary condition. Concluding eligibility is equally unsupported because the sufficient condition has not been established. Inspection remains undetermined: D could have been inspected without being registered.

questions.stem:
For a museum's current storage arrangement, if a crate is fragile and stored in the loft, it has a foam insert or a rigid divider, or both. Crate W is fragile and currently has neither protective feature.

Assuming the rule and facts are true, which conclusion must follow?
choices: Crate W is not fragile.
Crate W has never been stored in the loft.
Crate W is currently stored in the loft.
Crate W is not currently stored in the loft.
questions.explanation: Missing both protective features establishes that W is not fragile or is not currently in the loft. Fragility is given, so the not-fragile alternative is false; not currently in the loft must therefore hold. Claiming that W is not fragile contradicts the stated fact. Claiming it has never been in the loft improperly extends a current restriction into an entire history. Claiming it is currently in the loft would make both sufficient conditions true while neither required protective alternative holds, violating the rule.

questions.stem: A fictional display follows this rule: 'A red ring appears if the inserted token is verified.' Which sentence expresses the same conditional relationship?
choices: If a red ring appears, the inserted token is verified.
If the inserted token is verified, a red ring appears.
If the inserted token is not verified, a red ring appears.
If the inserted token is verified, no red ring appears.
questions.explanation: The clause introduced by 'if' supplies the sufficient condition: verification guarantees a red ring under this rule. Inferring verification from a red ring reverses the relationship. Guaranteeing a ring for an unverified token changes the triggering condition; the original rule leaves that case open. Claiming that verification guarantees no ring contradicts the result the rule gives for a verified token.

questions.stem: In a fictional classifier, a sample receives a green label only if its archive entry is complete. The rule always holds. Which statement follows?
choices: Every sample with a complete entry receives a green label.
Every sample without a green label has an incomplete entry.
Every sample receives a green label, regardless of its entry.
No sample with an incomplete entry receives a green label.
questions.explanation: A complete entry is necessary for receiving the label. An incomplete entry therefore rules out a green label. Making a complete entry guarantee a label reverses the condition. A sample without a green label can still have a complete entry, so the label's absence does not establish an incomplete entry. The rule neither labels every sample nor permits a label regardless of whether the necessary condition is met.

questions.stem:
Consider two descriptions of the same fictional token system:

Description 1: 'Only amber tokens enter the upper tray.'

Description 2: 'The only tokens that enter the upper tray are amber tokens.'

Read each as a general classification restriction, without assuming that any token enters the tray. Which comparison is correct?
choices: Both descriptions make being amber necessary for entering the upper tray.
Both descriptions make being amber sufficient for entering the upper tray.
Description 1 makes amber necessary; Description 2 makes amber sufficient.
Description 1 makes amber sufficient; Description 2 makes amber necessary.
questions.explanation: Both descriptions restrict upper-tray entrants to amber tokens: entering implies being amber. Neither says that every amber token enters. Making amber sufficient in both descriptions reverses both restrictions. The two mixed comparisons each reverse one of them without any change in the restricted group. The position of 'the only' does not replace reading the complete claim, and neither restriction establishes that an entrant exists.

questions.stem: A fictional labeling rule states, 'A crate is striped if and only if its lid is latched.' Which pair of conditionals, taken together, is equivalent to the complete rule?
choices: Striped implies latched; not latched implies not striped.
Latched implies striped; not striped implies not latched.
Striped implies latched; latched implies striped.
Striped implies not latched; latched implies not striped.
questions.explanation: 'If and only if' gives both directions: striping requires a latched lid, and a latched lid guarantees striping. Pairing 'striped implies latched' with 'not latched implies not striped' repeats one direction and omits its reverse. Pairing 'latched implies striped' with 'not striped implies not latched' repeats the opposite direction and also omits part of the biconditional. The pair with negative results prevents striping and latching from occurring together, whereas the stated rule permits both and requires them to agree.

questions.stem: A fictional status system follows the rule, 'The lamp lights unless flag T is active.' Use the inclusive conditional reading of 'unless,' which allows lighting and an active flag to occur together. Which conditional directly translates the rule?
choices: If flag T is active, the lamp does not light.
If the lamp lights, flag T is inactive.
If flag T is inactive, the lamp lights.
If the lamp does not light, flag T is inactive.
questions.explanation: Under the stated reading, absence of the exception condition guarantees the other condition: an inactive flag guarantees lighting. Making an active flag cancel the light adds an unsupported cancellation rule. Inferring an inactive flag from lighting also wrongly excludes the allowed overlap. Inferring an inactive flag from no lighting has the wrong sign: if the lamp does not light, the equivalent contrapositive requires the flag to be active.

questions.stem: A fictional sorter follows this rule on every cycle: 'The sorter sends a notice unless switch R is active.' Use the inclusive conditional reading, allowing an active switch and a sent notice together. On the present cycle, no notice is sent. What must be true?
choices: Switch R is active on the present cycle.
Switch R is inactive on the present cycle.
The stated rule has necessarily been broken on the present cycle.
Whether switch R is active remains undetermined on the present cycle.
questions.explanation: An inactive switch would require a notice. Since no notice is sent, the switch must be active. Calling it inactive would produce the exact combination the rule excludes. A cycle with an active switch and no sent notice is consistent with the rule, so the given fact does not mean that the rule was broken. The switch's state is determined by contraposition. Saying that it remains undetermined overlooks information supplied by the rule.

questions.stem: A fictional monitor follows the rule, 'A log is printed unless the blue flag is active.' Use the inclusive conditional reading of 'unless,' so printing and an active flag may occur together. The blue flag is active, and no other information is supplied. What does the rule establish about printing?
choices: A log must be printed because the blue flag is active.
A log cannot be printed because the blue flag is active.
An active blue flag is impossible if the rule is obeyed.
Whether a log is printed is not determined by the given information.
questions.explanation: The rule guarantees printing when the flag is inactive. With an active flag, both printing and not printing are consistent with it. Requiring printing from an active flag invents an additional trigger. Forbidding printing with an active flag turns the exception condition into a guarantee of cancellation. Neither follows. Saying that an active flag is impossible also prohibits a state that the rule permits.

questions.stem: A fictional device obeys this operating rule: 'Its screen never lights without a charged cell.' Which statement expresses the same requirement?
choices: A charged cell guarantees that the screen lights.
The screen lighting requires a charged cell.
The screen remaining dark requires the absence of a charged cell.
A charged cell requires the screen to remain dark.
questions.explanation: Without a charged cell there is no lighting, equivalently lighting implies a charged cell. Treating the cell as a guarantee of lighting reverses the requirement: it is necessary, not stated to be sufficient. A screen may remain dark despite having a charged cell, so darkness does not require the cell's absence. Requiring darkness whenever a charged cell is present incorrectly makes the cell incompatible with lighting; the original rule permits both and requires the cell whenever lighting occurs.

questions.stem: A test printer follows this rule: 'While inspection mode is active, a tag prints only if both the code is valid and the tray is loaded.' This statement supplies no rule outside inspection mode. Which restatement preserves its full conditional scope?
choices: If inspection mode is active and a tag prints, the code is valid and the tray is loaded.
If inspection mode is active, a tag prints regardless of the code and tray.
If the code is valid and the tray is loaded, inspection mode is active.
If a tag prints, the code is valid and the tray is loaded regardless of the mode.
questions.explanation: The outer condition limits the requirement to inspection mode. Within that mode, printing requires both a valid code and a loaded tray. Making the mode sufficient to produce printing adds a guarantee of an outcome. Inferring the mode from code validity and a loaded tray invents a relationship the rule does not give. Requiring both properties whenever a tag prints removes the outer condition and extends the restriction to occasions about which the statement supplies no rule.

questions.stem: A fictional file system obeys this rule: 'A file is marked ready only if it has been checked by Irena or Sol, or both.' Which situation violates the rule?
choices: A file is marked ready after both Irena and Sol checked it.
A file is marked ready after Irena checked it and Sol did not.
A file is marked ready although neither Irena nor Sol checked it.
A file is not marked ready, and neither Irena nor Sol checked it.
questions.explanation: Marking a file ready requires at least one of the two checks. A ready file with neither check fails that requirement. Both checks satisfy the inclusive alternative, so readiness after both checks is allowed. Irena's check alone also satisfies the requirement. A file with neither a ready mark nor a check is allowed because the rule does not require a check or a ready mark for every file. Satisfying the requirement need not itself guarantee readiness.

questions.stem: A fictional console follows this rule at every check: 'Without an amber card in its reader, the console displays a circle.' At the current check, the console does not display a circle. Which conclusion follows?
choices: There is no amber card in the reader at the current check.
There is an amber card in the reader at the current check.
The console displays a circle at the current check.
Whether an amber card is in the reader cannot be determined.
questions.explanation: The rule translates as no amber card implies a displayed circle. Its contrapositive is no displayed circle implies an amber card. Claiming that there is no amber card would require the circle that is absent. Claiming that a circle is displayed contradicts the given observation. Saying that the card's presence remains undetermined misses the conclusion supplied by contraposition. 'Without' negates the card condition, not the displayed result.

questions.stem: An unseen inventory is governed by this classification rule: 'Each box is gold-marked if and only if it is in row K.' No observation establishes that any boxes exist or that either property occurs. Which statement must follow?
choices: At least one box is gold-marked.
Every box is in row K.
No box is gold-marked.
Any box outside row K is not gold-marked.
questions.explanation: The biconditional includes gold-marked implies in row K, whose contrapositive establishes that any box outside row K is not gold-marked. The rule does not establish a gold-marked box's existence. An unmarked box outside row K would satisfy the rule, so not every box need be in row K. A gold-marked box in row K would also satisfy it, so the absence of gold-marked boxes is not required either. This relationship does not establish whether any gold-marked boxes exist.

questions.stem: An inventory rule states that all digitized journals are indexed. No other information about the collection is given. Which statement must be true?
choices: Some indexed journals are digitized.
All indexed journals are digitized.
No digitized journal is unindexed.
Every journal in the collection is indexed.
questions.explanation: The rule excludes a digitized journal that is not indexed. The answer denying any digitized, unindexed journal therefore preserves the universal restriction. Claiming some indexed journals are digitized adds existence; the rule permits an empty digitized group. Claiming all indexed journals are digitized reverses the direction. Claiming every journal is indexed expands the starting group beyond digitized journals. A rule governing every member of a group does not itself populate that group or restrict other journals.

questions.stem: Some painters in a fictional society are musicians. Which conclusion follows from that statement alone?
choices: Some musicians in the society are painters.
Some painters in the society are not musicians.
All painters in the society are musicians.
Most musicians in the society are painters.
questions.explanation: The premise supplies at least one person who is both a painter and a musician. That same witness establishes that some musicians are painters. Claiming some painters are not musicians reads some as some but not all. Claiming all painters are musicians strengthens an existential statement into a universal one. Claiming most musicians are painters adds a majority measured against an unspecified musician population. Reversing the order of the two properties of an existing shared member does not change the witness.

questions.stem: Some booklets in an archive are not indexed. Which statement must be true?
choices: Some indexed items in the archive are not booklets.
No booklet in the archive is indexed.
Every unindexed item in the archive is a booklet.
Some unindexed items in the archive are booklets.
questions.explanation: At least one item is both a booklet and unindexed, so some unindexed items are booklets. The claim about indexed items that are not booklets changes both properties of the witness. Saying no booklet is indexed unnecessarily excludes other booklets that could be indexed. Saying every unindexed item is a booklet extends one shared member into a universal claim. Preserve the complete properties of the original witness, including the negative property.

questions.stem: Which statement is the precise logical negation of 'Every reviewed file is archived'?
choices: Every reviewed file is unarchived.
At least one reviewed file is unarchived.
At least one archived file is unreviewed.
Every archived file is reviewed.
questions.explanation: At least one reviewed, unarchived file is exactly the counterexample that makes the original all claim false. Saying every reviewed file is unarchived demands more than needed; if the reviewed group were empty, it would not even supply a counterexample. An archived, unreviewed file lies outside the group the original rule restricts. Saying every archived file is reviewed reverses the relationship rather than negating it, and both universal statements could hold together. Negation requires a reviewed file lacking the asserted archival property.

questions.stem: Which statement is the precise logical negation of 'No restored map has a watermark'?
choices: Some restored maps have watermarks.
All restored maps have watermarks.
Some maps with watermarks are not restored.
All maps without watermarks are restored.
questions.explanation: Some restored maps having watermarks supplies a shared member that defeats the original no-overlap claim. Requiring all restored maps to have watermarks is stronger than necessary and supplies no counterexample when no restored map exists. A watermarked map that is not restored lies outside the restricted group and is compatible with the original statement. The claim that every unwatermarked map is restored does not establish the forbidden overlap. One restored, watermarked map is enough to negate the claim.

questions.stem: Every trial record in a collection is stored. Some stored records are bilingual. What do these statements establish about bilingual trial records?
choices: At least one trial record must be bilingual.
No trial record can be bilingual.
Every bilingual record must be a trial record.
Whether any trial record is bilingual remains undetermined.
questions.explanation: Whether a bilingual trial record exists remains undetermined. The bilingual stored witness has not been located inside the trial-record group. It could be a trial record, but it could instead be a different kind of stored record. Thus asserting at least one bilingual trial record adds an unproved overlap, while asserting none excludes a permitted overlap. Assigning every bilingual record to the trial group is also unsupported. Even a nonempty trial group could be separate from the bilingual stored records.

questions.stem: Every engraved token in a collection is dated. Some engraved tokens are silver. Which conclusion must be true?
choices: Every silver token is dated.
Some dated tokens are silver.
Some dated tokens are not engraved.
Every dated token is silver.
questions.explanation: The existential premise supplies an engraved silver token. The universal rule makes that same token dated, establishing that some dated tokens are silver. The claim that every silver token is dated extends the rule to silver tokens that might not be engraved. The claim about a dated token that is not engraved invents a member outside the engraved group. The claim that every dated token is silver extends one witness's property to an entire group. The valid inference preserves one existing object's properties without changing some into all.

questions.stem: No mural in a collection is portable. Which statement is logically equivalent, without assuming that either group has members?
choices: Every nonportable object in the collection is a mural.
Some murals in the collection are nonportable.
No portable object in the collection is a mural.
Some portable objects in the collection are murals.
questions.explanation: No portable object being a mural expresses the same absence of overlap from the other direction. The claim that every nonportable object is a mural reverses an inclusion and unnecessarily restricts objects outside the mural group. The claim that some murals are nonportable adds existence, which a no statement alone does not supply. The claim that some portable objects are murals asserts exactly the overlap the premise forbids. Symmetry of disjointness does not establish that either group has members.

questions.stem: A team has exactly ten gardeners. Six are trained in first aid, and seven know the evacuation route. Which statement must be true?
choices: Exactly three gardeners have both properties.
At most two gardeners have both properties.
At least six gardeners have both properties.
At least three gardeners have both properties.
questions.explanation: The counts require thirteen memberships across two groups drawn from ten people. At least three are second memberships, so at least three gardeners belong to both groups. Exactly three is not guaranteed; an overlap of four, five, or six also fits. At most two shared gardeners permits at most twelve memberships, which cannot reach thirteen. At least six shared gardeners is not required: three shared, three first-aid-only, and four route-only gardeners satisfy both counts. Training and route knowledge do not establish actual emergency performance.

questions.stem: In a finite office, most editors are proofreaders, and most proofreaders are illustrators. Here most means more than half. Which conclusion must follow?
choices: Some editors are illustrators.
Some proofreaders are editors.
Most editors are illustrators.
All illustrators are proofreaders.
questions.explanation: The first strict-majority claim supplies at least one person who is both an editor and a proofreader, so some proofreaders are editors. The claims that some or most editors illustrate improperly chain majorities measured against different groups. All proofreading editors could be among the proofreaders who do not illustrate, while other proofreaders supply the illustrating majority. Saying all illustrators are proofreaders reverses a relationship and strengthens it to all. The passage does not place every illustrator in the proofreading group.

questions.stem: A group contains exactly twelve reviewers. Which statement is the precise negation of 'Most of these reviewers approve the proposal,' where most means more than half?
choices: None of the twelve reviewers approves the proposal.
More than six reviewers do not approve the proposal.
At most six reviewers approve the proposal.
Exactly six reviewers approve the proposal.
questions.explanation: The original claim requires at least seven approving reviewers. Its negation permits zero through six, so at most six approve. None approve is unnecessarily strong. More than six do not approve excludes the six-approve, six-do-not-approve case, which also negates the original majority claim. Exactly six approve permits only an even split and excludes other valid negating cases. Negating more than half produces at most half, not necessarily a majority on the other side.

questions.stem: A report says, 'Many of the association's records were reviewed.' It supplies no count, percentage, or special definition of many. Which interpretation respects that limitation?
choices: The word many alone supplies no exact fraction of the records.
The word many guarantees that more than half the records were reviewed.
The word many guarantees that fewer than half the records were reviewed.
The word many establishes that every record was reviewed.
questions.explanation: The word many alone supplies no exact fraction. It may suggest a substantial number in context, but no count or threshold is specified here. More than half replaces that unspecified quantity with a strict majority. Fewer than half imposes the opposite unsupported bound. Every record was reviewed strengthens the description to a universal claim. Retain the report's actual limitation instead of assigning many a private numerical definition.

questions.stem: Which description best identifies a necessary assumption of a particular argument?
choices: An unstated commitment required by the reasoning offered for its conclusion.
Any unstated claim strong enough to establish the conclusion by itself.
A claim required by every imaginable argument for the same conclusion.
Any plausible fact that would make the conclusion more attractive.
questions.explanation: The relevant dependence is between an unstated commitment and the particular reasoning being evaluated. A claim strong enough to establish the conclusion by itself may be much stronger than the argument needs. Requiring the claim in every imaginable argument changes the task: a different argument could use entirely different evidence. A plausible fact that makes the conclusion attractive may merely help or concern a different consideration. Necessity requires explaining what the offered reasoning loses if the commitment is false, rather than identifying any useful support.

questions.stem: A collection's rule states that any record that is both authenticated and indexed is eligible for display. Record Vale is authenticated. An archivist concludes that this rule establishes Vale's eligibility for display. Which unstated claim is required to apply the rule to Vale?
choices: Every authenticated record in the collection is indexed.
Every display-eligible record in the collection is authenticated.
Vale is indexed.
Every indexed record in the collection is display-eligible.
questions.explanation: Vale's indexing supplies the other input needed to apply the stated joint-condition rule. If Vale is not indexed, authentication alone does not activate that rule. Claiming that every authenticated record is indexed would supply Vale's indexing, but is stronger than necessary: other authenticated records could be unindexed while Vale is indexed. Requiring authentication of every display-eligible record reverses a relationship and does not supply the missing input. Making indexing alone sufficient for display adds a different rule that this argument does not require.

questions.stem: Several attendees of yesterday's writing clinic submitted usable notes. An organizer uses those note-submitting attendees as the witnesses for the conclusion that at least one North Club member submitted usable notes. Which assumption does this witness-based reasoning require?
choices: Every attendee of the writing clinic belongs to North Club.
At least one of the note-submitting attendees belongs to North Club.
Every North Club member attended the writing clinic.
Only North Club members are capable of producing usable notes.
questions.explanation: At least one of the note-submitting attendees must belong to North Club for those attendees to supply a club member with usable notes. If none belongs, this evidence supplies no such witness, even if a club member elsewhere submitted notes. Membership of every clinic attendee demands more overlap than the conclusion needs. Attendance by every club member is also unnecessary when a single relevant attendee suffices. Restricting the ability to produce usable notes to club members is an excessive generalization about capability; nonmembers may produce usable notes without harming the inference.

questions.stem: A cooperative is choosing between proposals R and S. Both meet its stated safety requirements. R costs thirty tokens and S costs fifty. A member argues that the cost difference gives the cooperative a reason to prefer R. Which assumption is required by that argument?
choices: Lower cost always outweighs every noncost advantage in any decision.
Every proposal the cooperative could consider has identical safety features.
R costs less than every other proposal the cooperative could ever receive.
A lower cost can count in favor of a proposal in this decision.
questions.explanation: The argument treats lower cost as a reason favoring R, so cost must be capable of counting in a proposal's favor in this decision. This is a claim about one reason, not a guarantee that R is best overall. Making lower cost override every other advantage in any decision is far stronger than needed. Identical safety features across every possible proposal are unnecessary; the passage supplies the relevant safety facts about R and S. R need not be cheapest among every proposal ever received to have a cost advantage over S.

questions.stem: A theater sold 240 tickets for Tuesday's performance. Each ticket admits at most one distinct person. A manager relies exclusively on those ticket sales to infer that more than 200 different people attended. Which unstated condition must hold for the sold tickets to supply that many different attendees?
choices: All 240 sold tickets were used by different people who attended.
Every sold ticket was purchased at the same price.
At least 201 sold tickets were used by 201 different people who attended.
No one attended the performance without buying a ticket.
questions.explanation: More than 200 different attendees requires at least 201 different people. For the sold tickets to supply that evidence, at least 201 must have been used by different attendees. Requiring all 240 to have been used by different people is stronger than necessary: some tickets could go unused or be held by repeat entrants. Equal purchase prices do not establish attendance or distinct people. Excluding attendance without a purchased ticket is unnecessary; extra attendees would not undermine the count supplied by used tickets. The question concerns the manager's ticket-based route, not independent evidence of other attendees.

questions.stem: Every shortlisted design in a contest is waterproof, and Neris is shortlisted. An analyst concludes that Neris is waterproof. A reader proposes the additional assumption that every waterproof design is shortlisted. Is that assumption required?
choices: No; the stated rule and Neris's shortlist status already establish the conclusion.
Yes; a rule relating two groups always needs its converse before it can be applied.
Yes; the stated facts leave open whether any shortlisted design exists.
No; the conclusion is false unless a separate field test is reported.
questions.explanation: The original forward rule applies directly to the given fact that Neris is shortlisted, so waterproofing follows without the proposed converse. A conditional does not need to be reversible before it can be applied in its stated direction. The claim that existence is unestablished overlooks the named shortlisted design. The field-test objection rejects the conclusion despite the accepted premises; the exercise supplies an exact rule, and no additional test premise is needed. Do not invent a missing assumption when the given premises already complete the inference.

questions.stem: A writer predicts that a hall will become quieter because new panels have been installed. The reasoning relies on those panels reducing incoming noise. Suppose the panels do not reduce noise, but the hall nevertheless becomes quieter because of an unrelated road closure. What does this case illustrate?
choices: A true conclusion proves that every commitment used to support it was correct.
A commitment cannot be necessary to reasoning if its conclusion might be true without it.
The road closure automatically becomes a premise of the writer's original argument.
A conclusion can be true even though the offered route to it loses a required connection.
questions.explanation: The road closure can make the prediction come true while the panel-based justification fails. Necessity concerns the presented reasoning, not every possible cause of a true conclusion. A true conclusion does not verify all commitments used in an argument for it. Saying that any independently possible conclusion eliminates the need for assumptions confuses truth with justification. The road closure also does not retroactively become a premise of the original argument; adding that reason would supply a different basis for the prediction.

questions.stem: For exactly forty batches, Method A uses five liters of production water per batch and Method B uses three. These figures exclude cleanup. An analyst concludes that switching from A to B reduces the combined production-and-cleanup water for these batches. Which cleanup condition is required for that reduction?
choices: Neither method uses any water for cleanup.
Method B's cleanup water is less than Method A's cleanup water plus eighty liters.
Method B uses at least eighty liters more cleanup water than Method A.
Method A uses more cleanup water than Method B.
questions.explanation: Production under A uses 200 liters and under B uses 120, a saving of eighty. The combined total falls only if B's additional cleanup use is less than eighty liters relative to A. Exactly eighty extra would erase the saving, and more would reverse it. No cleanup water under either method would be sufficient, but is not required. At least eighty extra liters for B prevents a reduction. Less cleanup water under B would also be sufficient, but is unnecessary because a smaller increase can leave part of the production saving.

questions.stem: A fictional archive's policy permits release exactly when the author has consented and the archive has approved the report. Report K is queued for release tomorrow. A coordinator infers that K satisfies the release policy. Which unstated claim is necessary for that inference, even though it does not fill every gap?
choices: Every report queued for release has its author's consent.
Report K has its author's consent.
The archive approves every report submitted to it.
Report K is the only report queued for release tomorrow.
questions.explanation: K must have its author's consent to satisfy the policy, so the coordinator relies on that commitment. Consent alone does not finish the argument: approval of K is also required and has not been established. Consent for every queued report is broader than necessary; other queued reports could lack it while K satisfies the policy. Approval of every submitted report is similarly excessive compared with the need for K's approval. K's being the only queued report does not supply either required authorization. One necessary assumption can be correct while another missing commitment remains.

questions.stem: A student finds an unstated claim that, when added to an argument's premises, guarantees its conclusion. Before calling the claim a necessary assumption, what additional issue should the student examine?
choices: Whether the claim repeats every noun that appears in the premises.
Whether the claim is stronger than every other possible supporting statement.
Whether the claim sounds plausible in ordinary life, regardless of the stated reasoning.
Whether the offered reasoning could retain its required support while the claim is false.
questions.explanation: A sufficient addition can go beyond what the reasoning requires. Checking whether the offered support can survive the claim's falsity distinguishes necessity from mere sufficiency. Repeating nouns is a verbal similarity test, not an assessment of dependence. Being stronger than other possible support does not establish necessity and often introduces unnecessary scope. Ordinary plausibility also does not show whether this particular argument relies on the claim. The evaluation must remain tied to the actual premises, conclusion, and level of support under examination.

questions.stem: A lab authorizes use of a device when either its calibration is current or it passes a substitute check; either allows both. Device P passed the substitute check. A technician concludes that P is authorized for use and also suggests that P's calibration is probably current. Is current calibration a necessary assumption for establishing the authorization conclusion?
choices: No; the substitute-check route establishes authorization even if the calibration is not current.
Yes; losing any proposed supporting route always defeats every other route.
Yes; the stated either-or condition requires both current calibration and a passed substitute check.
No; merely being a device in the lab establishes authorization without either condition.
questions.explanation: The passed substitute check independently satisfies one sufficient route supplied by the rule. Outdated calibration would remove the suggested calibration route but would not remove the established substitute-check route. Losing one proposed reason does not always defeat another independent reason. Requiring both current calibration and a passed substitute check changes the inclusive-or condition into an and requirement. Being a device in the lab is not stated to guarantee authorization; the successful inference uses the substitute-check result. Identify which support remains before treating an assumption for one branch as necessary to the entire justification.

questions.stem: A workshop has six participants, each assigned a different kit. All six assigned kits are complete. Under the stated supply plan, each participant can receive equipment only through that person's assigned kit. An organizer concludes that every participant will have a complete kit available at the start of the workshop. Which unstated commitment does this plan-based reasoning require?
choices: All six participants have attended an earlier workshop.
Every kit the organization has ever owned is complete.
Every assigned kit will be available to its assigned participant at the start.
The organization will buy additional unassigned kits before the workshop.
questions.explanation: The conclusion covers every participant, and the plan supplies each person exclusively through the assigned kit. Each assigned kit therefore must be available to that person at the start. Attendance at an earlier workshop is unrelated to this availability and is not required. Completeness of every kit ever owned extends far beyond the six relevant kits, whose completeness is already given. Buying unassigned kits is not required and does not supply an assigned kit under the stipulated plan. Universal wording can be appropriate when the required commitment genuinely covers the entire relevant group.

questions.stem:
A proposed assumption says, "Every trial included in the report was conducted at 20 degrees."

Which statement is its precise negation?
choices: At least one trial included in the report was conducted at a temperature other than 20 degrees.
No trial included in the report was conducted at 20 degrees.
Every trial excluded from the report was conducted at a temperature other than 20 degrees.
It is not known whether every trial included in the report was conducted at 20 degrees.
questions.explanation: The universal claim fails exactly when at least one included trial was not conducted at 20 degrees. Saying that no included trial used 20 degrees is too strong: one exception is enough, even if many other trials used that temperature. A claim about excluded trials changes the population and can be true or false independently of the candidate. Uncertainty about the temperatures concerns what is known; the original claim could still be true despite that uncertainty. A negation check assumes the candidate is false, not merely unverified.

questions.stem:
Consider the proposed assumption, "Some invited residents can attend the meeting at the proposed time."

Which statement should replace it during a precise negation check?
choices: Some invited residents cannot attend the meeting at the proposed time.
Every invited resident can attend the meeting at the proposed time.
No invited resident can attend the meeting at the proposed time.
Some uninvited residents cannot attend the meeting at the proposed time.
questions.explanation: Some means at least one. Its negation denies every qualifying instance: no invited resident can attend at that time. Some invited residents being unable to attend can coexist with others being able to attend, so it need not falsify the original. Every invited resident being able to attend does not deny the original and, if invitees exist, entails it. A statement about uninvited residents changes the group and does not determine whether any invited resident can attend. Keep both the invitation status and the proposed time fixed.

questions.stem:
A device's added running cost is a nonnegative amount measured in credits per day. A candidate assumption states that this cost is less than 12 credits per day.

Which statement is the candidate's precise negation?
choices: The added running cost is at most 12 credits per day.
The added running cost is at least 12 credits per day.
The added running cost is more than 12 credits per day.
The added running cost is zero credits per day.
questions.explanation: Negating a strict less-than boundary includes the boundary itself: the cost must be at least 12. At most 12 includes costs such as 5, which satisfy the original claim, so it is not the complement. More than 12 wrongly excludes exactly 12, a value that already makes the original false. Zero is permitted by the nonnegative range and satisfies the original less-than-12 statement. It is one possible original case, not a negation. Retaining the daily accounting period also matters; none of these claims should be converted into a monthly figure.

questions.stem:
"The design can meet the deadline under the currently permitted schedules" means that at least one currently permitted schedule meets the deadline.

Which statement is the precise negation of that claim?
choices: Every currently permitted schedule meets the deadline.
At least one currently permitted schedule misses the deadline.
No future change to the scheduling rules could make the deadline achievable.
No currently permitted schedule meets the deadline.
questions.explanation: Denying the existence of any permitted successful schedule gives no currently permitted schedule meeting the deadline. Every permitted schedule meeting it strengthens the success claim rather than denying it when such schedules exist. One permitted failure can coexist with a different permitted success, so a failure alone does not negate possibility. A claim about every possible future rule change extends far beyond the current rules: the current design might be unable to meet the deadline even though a later rule change would help. Negate the specified possibility within its fixed conditions.

questions.stem:
An exact rule states that every project with both a verified inventory and a staff roster qualifies for dispatch. Project Birch has a verified inventory. An author applies this rule to infer that Birch qualifies for dispatch.

Which unstated input is required for this particular application, as shown by considering its negation?
choices: Every project with a verified inventory qualifies for dispatch.
Project Birch has a staff roster.
Every project has a verified inventory.
No qualifying project is delayed after qualification.
questions.explanation: Birch's staff roster supplies the missing part of the joint condition. If Birch lacks a roster, the author cannot activate this stated rule for Birch, although qualification might still be possible through another route. Requiring every verified project to qualify is broader than needed; another verified project could lack a roster and fail to qualify while Birch's application works. Requiring every project to have a verified inventory is also unnecessary because Birch's inventory is already given. Delays after qualification concern a later outcome that the argument neither uses nor establishes.

questions.stem:
Two footbridges stand at a site. An author concludes that a person can cross there on foot today. A candidate assumption says, "Both footbridges are usable today." A learner replaces that candidate with "Neither footbridge is usable today" and treats the resulting failure of the bridge route as proving that both bridges must be usable.

What is the error in that test?
choices: The replacement is too strong; the precise negation allows one unusable bridge while the other remains usable.
The replacement is too weak; a proper negation must also eliminate every possible crossing at other sites.
The replacement is exact, so both bridges being usable is necessary for any bridge crossing at this site.
The stated existence of two bridges already establishes that both are usable, so no unstated connection is involved.
questions.explanation: Not both usable means at least one is unusable, possibly both. It allows one usable bridge, which can preserve the proposed bridge route. Replacing both with neither therefore tests a stronger condition and can falsely make the original candidate appear required. Eliminating crossings at other sites would further change the scope rather than repair the negation. Calling the replacement exact confuses not both with neither. The bridges' stated existence does not establish their present usability. The candidate demands more than the availability of one usable bridge requires.

questions.stem:
A club's rule says that any proposal with both a sponsor and a completed review is listed on Friday's agenda. Proposal Elm has completed its review. The rule is the author's only offered justification for concluding that Elm will be listed. The candidate assumption is that Elm has a sponsor.

A learner rejects the candidate because Elm might still be listed through some other authorization even if it had no sponsor. Which assessment is correct?
choices: The rejection is justified because a necessary input to this rule must be required by every imaginable listing procedure.
The rejection is justified because missing a sponsor proves that Elm cannot be listed by any procedure.
The candidate is unnecessary because completing a review alone satisfies the stated two-part condition.
The rejection confuses possible independent truth with justification; a sponsor is still needed to activate the stated rule for Elm.
questions.explanation: A sponsor is required for this application of the joint-condition rule. Another authorization could make the conclusion true without supplying the missing input to the justification actually offered. Requiring this input to be necessary for every imaginable listing procedure conflates one route with all possible routes. Inferring that Elm cannot be listed from the absence of a sponsor improperly treats a sufficient listing condition as the only possible condition. Treating review completion alone as sufficient drops the sponsor part of the explicitly stated conjunction. The check diagnoses the offered reasoning, not every possible way the conclusion could be true.

questions.stem:
An argument uses a recurring observed pattern to support a qualified forecast. A learner correctly negates a candidate assumption while keeping the stated observations fixed. Under that negation, the observations remain relevant and reasonably persuasive, although the forecast receives slightly less support. The learner declares the candidate necessary solely because support decreased.

Which assessment best evaluates that declaration?
choices: Any decrease in support establishes that the candidate was required by the argument.
A qualified forecast cannot depend on any unstated assumption because it allows uncertainty.
A slight decrease alone does not establish dependence; the learner must identify something the offered reasoning actually requires.
Because support remains, the original observations must deductively guarantee the forecast.
questions.explanation: A necessary assumption is a dependency, not every claim that would improve the argument. The stipulated small reduction, with relevant and reasonably persuasive evidence remaining, does not by itself demonstrate that the reasoning requires the candidate. Calling any decrease decisive confuses helpful support with necessity. A qualified forecast can still rely on unstated connections, so uncertainty does not eliminate assumptions. Remaining inductive support also does not become a deductive guarantee; the forecast may be reasonably supported while failure remains possible. A correct test must connect the negation to the specific dependency being claimed.

questions.stem:
In a particular workshop, a candidate assumption states, "If a participant submits a survey, that participant has read the guide."

Treat this as a rule covering every participant in that workshop. Which statement precisely negates it?
choices: Any participant who has not read the guide does not submit a survey.
Any participant who has read the guide submits a survey.
At least one participant submits a survey without having read the guide.
No participant submits a survey.
questions.explanation: A universal conditional is false when a relevant instance has its antecedent true and consequent false: a participant submits without having read the guide. Nonreading implying nonsubmission is the contrapositive, which preserves the original rule rather than negating it. Reading implying submission is the converse and does not deny the original; both could hold together. No participant submitting satisfies the original rule without any activating instance, so it cannot be its negation. The required exception must concern a participant in this workshop, with the original survey and guide relationship intact.

questions.stem:
A passage states that 40 of 50 survey respondents favor evening opening hours. A candidate assumption says that the respondents do not all belong to one club. During a negation check, a learner imagines all 50 belonging to one club and also changes the reported result so that only 10 favor evening hours.

Which correction properly isolates the candidate's negation, without yet deciding whether the candidate is necessary?
choices: Change the proposed conclusion to a claim about morning hours instead of evening hours.
Add a new premise that every club exactly represents the wider population.
Negate the reported count instead and leave club membership undecided.
Keep the stated 40-of-50 result true and test the case in which all 50 belong to one club.
questions.explanation: The negation of not all belonging to one club is all belonging to one club. That membership pattern can coexist with the stated 40-of-50 result, which should remain fixed. Changing the target to morning hours tests a different conclusion. Adding exact population representativeness supplies new support not stated in the passage. Negating the reported count challenges a premise rather than the candidate assumption. Isolating the membership claim is the correct procedure, but it does not by itself settle whether membership diversity is necessary; that still depends on the complete argument and its offered inference.

questions.stem:
A question asks which additional statement would guarantee the conclusion when combined with the stated premises. A learner rejects a candidate solely because its precise negation still allows the conclusion to be true through a different route.

What should the learner do instead?
choices: Reject every candidate whose negation permits even one case with a true conclusion.
Test whether the premises together with the candidate guarantee the conclusion; a sufficient addition need not be necessary.
Accept the candidate whenever the conclusion is possible, even if it could also be false with the candidate true.
Require the candidate to be both necessary and sufficient even though only sufficiency was requested.
questions.explanation: The task asks for sufficiency, so the relevant test adds the candidate to the premises and asks whether a false conclusion remains possible. A statement can complete one guaranteed route while other routes remain available when that statement is false. Rejecting every candidate whose negation permits a true conclusion improperly imposes necessity. Mere possibility of the conclusion is too weak for a guarantee because a counterexample could remain. Requiring both necessity and sufficiency similarly adds a demand the question did not make. Match the operation to the requested logical relationship.

questions.stem:
A fictional service eliminates an expense of 90 credits per month and charges a subscription fee of 35 credits per month. Other new monthly charges, if any, are nonnegative. These amounts account for every cost change. A manager concludes that total monthly cost will decrease by a positive amount.

Which candidate identifies the required restriction, whose precise negation defeats that conclusion under the stated complete model?
choices: The other new monthly charges are less than 55 credits.
The other new monthly charges are exactly zero credits.
The other new monthly charges are less than 20 credits.
The other new monthly charges are at least 55 credits.
questions.explanation: Let the other new charges be x. The monthly saving is 90 minus 35 minus x, or 55 minus x, so a positive decrease requires x below 55. Its negation, x at least 55, leaves zero saving or an increase. Exactly zero is too strong: negating it allows 10 credits of extra charges and still a positive saving. Below 20 is also too strong: 25 credits of extra charges falsifies that candidate while leaving a saving of 30. At least 55 directly opposes the required restriction; its negation permits the positive saving instead of defeating it.

questions.stem: Every device meeting standard K is field-safe. Device N meets standard K. An analyst concludes that N can be used in humid rooms. Which additional rule supplies a sufficient bridge to that exact conclusion?
choices: Every field-safe device can be used in humid rooms.
Every device that can be used in humid rooms is field-safe.
Device N's compliance with standard K was verified twice.
No field-safe device can be used in humid rooms.
questions.explanation: The field-safe-to-humid-use rule connects the property established for N to the claimed capability. The rule from humid use to field safety runs in the reverse direction and permits field-safe devices that cannot be used in humid rooms. Verifying N's compliance twice adds support for an already accepted premise without supplying the missing relationship. Excluding every field-safe device from humid use contradicts the proposed conclusion when applied to N. A bridge must connect the established property to the property actually concluded.

questions.stem: An analyst relies solely on a reservoir gauge's displayed number as a measurement of the reservoir's present level. She uses that number as evidence that the level is low. Which assumption does this particular reading-as-measurement route require?
choices: Every gauge ever installed at the reservoir has always been exact.
All reservoirs in the region currently have the same level.
Rainfall is the only influence on reservoir levels.
This display is not fixed at a demonstration number independently of the reservoir's level.
questions.explanation: Excluding a fixed demonstration number protects the reading-as-measurement route. If the display were generated independently of the level, it would supply no measurement of that level through the proposed route. Requiring every gauge ever installed to be exact extends far beyond the current display. Requiring regional levels to match is irrelevant to measuring this reservoir. Making rainfall the only influence concerns the cause of a level, not whether this display measures it. The defender does not by itself rule out every other measurement failure.

questions.stem: A reader says, “This answer connects the premise's concept to the conclusion's concept, so it must be a necessary assumption.” Which response best identifies the problem?
choices: A connecting statement can never be a necessary assumption.
A bridge describes a function; its exact strength must still be tested for the task.
Every bridge is both necessary and sufficient for every argument.
Any answer using the conclusion's vocabulary is automatically correct.
questions.explanation: A bridge describes the connection supplied, not whether that precise claim is required or sufficient. A universal bridge may guarantee a conclusion about one object while being broader than the reasoning needs. Saying a connecting statement can never be necessary is equally mistaken; a required connection can have a bridge role. Calling every bridge necessary and sufficient confuses function with two distinct logical relationships. Choosing vocabulary alone ignores direction, subject, and scope. The reader must evaluate the specific candidate against the specific question.

questions.stem: The matte cover produces less glare than the glossy cover under the exhibition lights. Therefore, the curator should choose the matte cover. No selection rule is stated. Which gap best describes the argument?
choices: It has not shown that the glossy cover produces any glare at all.
It has not shown that every curator has previously used matte covers.
It has not connected the stated glare advantage to what the curator should choose.
It has not shown that choosing a cover will change the exhibition lights.
questions.explanation: The conclusion recommends a choice, whereas the premise establishes a comparative property. A selection standard connecting the glare advantage to what should be chosen is missing. The argument need not prove a separate absolute amount of glossy-cover glare to identify its recommendation gap. Other curators' past choices are not required by this reasoning. Changing the lights is not the claimed effect or the selection criterion. The relevant missing connection is normative: how the established fact supports the recommended action.

questions.stem: Object Cam has been restored. Therefore, Cam is ready for exhibition. Consider adding “Every restored object is ready for exhibition.” Which assessment is best?
choices: The added rule is sufficient, but the universal claim is broader than a required connection about Cam alone.
The added rule is necessary merely because it contains both key terms.
The added rule is insufficient because Cam's restoration is not established.
The added rule proves that no unrestored object is ready for exhibition.
questions.explanation: The universal rule applies to the given restoration of Cam and yields readiness, so it is sufficient. A narrower connection could support Cam's readiness while some other restored object remained unready; the universal claim is not required in that form. Shared terms alone do not establish necessity. Cam's restoration is explicitly supplied, so the proposed insufficiency objection misreads the premise. Excluding all unrestored objects would reverse and negate the stated sufficient relationship without justification. Broad strength can be useful for sufficiency without proving necessity.

questions.stem: Current members may enter an event, and anyone with a valid signed invitation may also enter. A screen labels Uma a member. Separately, the passage states that Uma has a valid signed invitation. An advocate concludes that Uma may enter. Suppose the screen is in demonstration mode and supplies no membership information. What follows about the support?
choices: Both entry routes fail because the screen controls every rule.
Uma must be denied entry because membership is now disproved.
The valid signed invitation can be ignored because it was stated second.
The screen-based route fails, but the valid invitation independently establishes entry permission.
questions.explanation: The valid invitation satisfies its own sufficient rule, so permission remains established even when the screen supplies no evidence of membership. The screen's failure does not change the separately stated invitation fact or rule. Claiming both routes fail invents a shared dependency. Claiming Uma must be denied entry treats unestablished membership as disproved and overlooks the invitation route. Sentence order does not reduce the invitation's logical role. A defender of one branch is not automatically necessary to a conclusion independently established by another branch.

questions.stem: An inspector uses a package's label to infer its contents. A candidate assumption says that the label has not been transferred from a different package. Why does the candidate's defender role alone fail to establish that it is sufficient for the inference?
choices: A defender can never bear on a package's contents.
The original label might still be inaccurate, so excluding transfer leaves another possible failure.
Excluding transfer proves that the package has no contents.
An unstated claim cannot be considered in a sufficient-assumption task.
questions.explanation: A label could remain on its original package while misstating what is inside. Excluding transfer removes one failure without guaranteeing accurate contents information. Saying a defender can never bear on contents denies the evident relevance of attachment to the correct package. Saying the package must be empty invents a conclusion. Sufficient-assumption tasks specifically ask what adding an unstated claim would establish. The candidate's function is relevant, but completing a proof requires checking every remaining route to a true premise and false conclusion.

questions.stem: Some workshop participants are designers. Every designer is a trained reviewer. An organizer concludes that some workshop participants can assess entries. Which addition connects the existing witness to the missing property?
choices: Some people outside the workshop can assess entries.
Every person who can assess entries is a trained reviewer.
Every trained reviewer can assess entries.
Every workshop participant is a designer.
questions.explanation: The existing participant who is a designer is a trained reviewer; the reviewer-to-assessment rule makes that same person able to assess entries. An assessor outside the workshop supplies a different witness and does not connect the required groups. The assessment-to-reviewer rule runs backward and allows trained reviewers who cannot assess. Making every workshop participant a designer extends a known property without supplying the missing assessment capability. The correct bridge carries one existing person's properties through the full chain.

questions.stem: A passage states that a proposed schedule reduces overtime and concludes that it should be adopted. A student inserts only “This schedule should be adopted” and calls that an explanation of the missing connection. What is the best assessment?
choices: Repeating the conclusion establishes a general rule about every schedule.
The repetition shows that overtime reduction is always necessary for adoption.
Restating a conclusion changes it into independent evidence for itself.
The conclusion is then explicitly assumed, but its connection to the overtime premise remains unexplained.
questions.explanation: Adding the conclusion makes that claim available directly, but does not explain why overtime reduction supports the recommendation. This is circular as a justification of the disputed claim. It supplies no general rule about schedules and no necessary overtime condition for adoption. A conclusion does not become independent evidence merely through repetition. Distinguish the trivial fact that an added conclusion entails itself from the useful task of supplying a noncircular connection between the original reasons and that conclusion.

questions.stem: An analyst cites two dashboards as separate measurements of tank pressure. Both dashboards copy the output of the same sensor. The analyst's conclusion relies only on those measurements. Which consideration most directly challenges treating the two readings as independent protection against sensor failure?
choices: The dashboards use different colors for their numbers.
A disconnected source sensor could make both dashboards report numbers unrelated to tank pressure.
The dashboards were manufactured in different years.
The tank's location has a short name.
questions.explanation: Both readings depend on the same sensor, so a failure at that shared source can remove both evidential connections. Two displayed outputs do not supply independent protection against that specific failure. Different colors affect presentation rather than the common data source. Different manufacture years do not remove the stated shared input. The location's name has no bearing on measurement support. A defender excluding the source failure could protect both branches, unlike a candidate addressing only one dashboard's separate display fault.

questions.stem: A rule says that any proposal that improves access and meets the cost limit should be selected. Proposal Birch improves access. The advocate concludes that Birch should be selected by this rule. Which candidate fills the specific missing input?
choices: Another proposal meets the cost limit.
Every selected proposal improves access.
Birch meets the cost limit.
Every proposal that improves access exceeds the cost limit.
questions.explanation: Birch must supply both inputs for this stated sufficient rule: improved access and compliance with the cost limit. Its cost compliance is the missing input. Another proposal's cost status cannot combine with Birch's access improvement. The rule from selection to access does not establish either Birch's cost compliance or selection. Claiming every access-improving proposal exceeds the limit would block this route rather than fill it. The candidate completes the stated rule application; that does not make the rule the only imaginable reason for selecting Birch.

questions.stem: An argument treats a report about Station East as evidence for a claim about Station West. A candidate says the report's measurements also apply to Station West under the stated conditions. How should its role be assessed?
choices: It can bridge the subjects while also excluding the failure that the measurements are irrelevant to West.
It must be irrelevant because a candidate can have only one role.
It automatically proves every conclusion about both stations.
It can be evaluated without reading the report's scope or the proposed conclusion.
questions.explanation: Applying the measurements to West connects the evidence to the subject of the conclusion and protects against the wrong-subject failure. Bridge and defender roles can therefore overlap. Requiring a single exclusive label misunderstands these functional teaching descriptions. Applicability does not guarantee every possible conclusion; the report's content, strength, and conditions still matter. Ignoring scope or the actual conclusion prevents judging whether the candidate supplies the needed relationship. Describe what the claim does before deciding whether its exact strength satisfies the question.

questions.stem: A club has exactly eighty members. Exactly thirteen of the twenty members in a pilot prefer a new schedule, and the other seven do not. What is the smallest number of supporters among the sixty members outside the pilot that would guarantee that more than half of the entire club prefer the schedule?
choices: Twenty-seven.
Twenty-one.
Twenty-eight.
Thirteen.
questions.explanation: More than half of eighty requires at least forty-one supporters. Thirteen are known, so at least twenty-eight outside supporters are needed: thirteen plus twenty-eight is forty-one. Twenty-seven would yield forty, exactly half. Twenty-one would yield thirty-four, and thirteen would yield twenty-six. The pilot denominator of twenty cannot replace the target denominator of eighty. This exact counting exercise identifies the minimum addition that guarantees the stated whole-club majority; it does not infer unobserved preferences from the pilot result alone.

questions.stem: Every inspected generator is usable today. Generator H was inspected. An engineer concludes that H will run at noon tomorrow. Which rule, if added, is sufficient for that exact conclusion?
choices: Every generator usable today will run at noon tomorrow.
Every generator that runs at noon tomorrow is usable today.
Every generator usable today will remain usable tomorrow.
Some generator will run at noon tomorrow.
questions.explanation: H is usable today under the given rule. A rule from that capability to actual operation at noon tomorrow supplies both the time connection and the change from usable to running. The reverse rule permits usable generators that do not run. Continuing usability still does not establish actual operation. The existence of some running generator does not identify H as that generator. The correct addition matches the exact subject, time, and force of the conclusion.

questions.stem: An argument establishes that Lio completed a course and then concludes that Lio may use a workshop. A proposed sufficient bridge is “Everyone who completed the course may use the workshop.” Why should a reader avoid automatically treating this same universal bridge as a required assumption?
choices: Universal statements are never sufficient for conclusions about one person.
Required assumptions must always be unrelated to the conclusion.
Lio's completion is disproved whenever any other graduate lacks permission.
A narrower rule could support Lio's permission while another course graduate lacked permission.
questions.explanation: A rule applying to Lio's relevant category could provide the needed connection while excluding some other graduate. That would make the universal bridge false without removing this narrower route. Universal rules can certainly be sufficient for a named case, so denying their sufficiency is wrong. Required assumptions concern the reasoning rather than unrelated matters. Another graduate's lack of permission does not contradict Lio's course completion. Breadth must be evaluated against the task rather than accepted or rejected automatically.

questions.stem: Most of the museum's twenty volunteer guides who replied to a survey favor later opening hours. The director concludes that most residents of the city favor later opening hours. Which unestablished connection is most directly relevant?
choices: Whether later opening hours occur later in the day than earlier hours.
Whether these respondents' preferences justify the claimed result about the city's residents.
Whether every volunteer guide has visited every other museum.
Whether the city has exactly twenty buildings.
questions.explanation: The evidence concerns responding volunteer guides, while the conclusion concerns the city's residents. The argument needs support for that population transfer at the stated majority strength. The meaning of later versus earlier does not address the inferential gap. Universal experience at other museums is not required to connect these preferences to the target group. The city's building count is unrelated to the group of residents whose preferences are claimed. A result about respondents does not by itself establish the target population result.

questions.stem: Every job approved on Monday is cleared on Monday. Job L was approved on Monday. The conclusion is that L is cleared on Tuesday. Which addition is sufficient without supplying any further unstated rule?
choices: Every job cleared on Tuesday was cleared on Monday.
Some job approved on Monday is cleared on Tuesday.
Every job cleared on Monday is also cleared on Tuesday.
Every job cleared on Monday was approved on Monday.
questions.explanation: The premises establish Monday clearance for L. Carrying every Monday-cleared job to Tuesday clearance applies directly to L. The Tuesday-to-Monday rule runs backward and leaves L's Tuesday status open. Some Monday-approved job could be cleared Tuesday while L is not. The Monday-clearance-to-Monday-approval rule adds a same-day converse without connecting to Tuesday. The time label belongs to the condition and cannot be silently carried forward.

questions.stem: Plan Juniper reduces packaging waste and fits the stated budget. Therefore, Juniper should be adopted. Which candidate is sufficient for this recommendation when added to the premises?
choices: Every plan that reduces packaging waste and fits the stated budget should be adopted.
Every plan that should be adopted reduces packaging waste.
Some plan that fits the stated budget should be adopted.
Every plan that reduces packaging waste has been discussed at a meeting.
questions.explanation: The rule making the two established properties sufficient for adoption applies to Juniper and yields the exact recommendation. The rule from adoption to waste reduction gives a necessary feature of recommended plans, not a reason to recommend Juniper. The existential recommendation could concern a different plan. Discussion at a meeting supplies neither a decision criterion nor an adoption rule. The sufficient candidate is broad, but broad scope is not disqualifying when it establishes the requested narrower conclusion.

questions.stem: Everyone who receives a permit may enter the studio on Saturday. Suri received a permit. An argument concludes that Suri will enter the studio on Saturday. A candidate merely repeats that Suri is permitted to enter then. Why is that candidate insufficient?
