choices: Saturday is outside the time scope of the given permission rule.
Suri's receipt of a permit is not stated.
A permission rule can never apply to a named person.
Permission does not establish that Suri will actually enter.
questions.explanation: The rule and permit establish permission. Suri could choose not to enter, so actual attendance remains unproved even after the candidate is added. Saturday is explicitly the rule's time scope. Permit receipt is an explicit fact. A universal rule does apply to a named person who meets its condition. The error is a modal shift from what Suri may do to what Suri will do, not a problem with the time, the named subject, or the stated permit.

questions.stem: Some editors are translators. Every editor is careful. A writer concludes that every translator is careful. Which addition makes that universal conclusion follow?
choices: Some translators are careful.
Every translator is an editor.
Every careful person is a translator.
Some careful people are not editors.
questions.explanation: If every translator is an editor, the existing editor-to-careful rule covers every translator. Merely asserting some careful translators supplies an overlap already established by the premises but does not cover all translators. The careful-to-translator rule runs in the wrong direction and permits careless translators. A careful person outside the editor group supplies an unrelated witness. The correct addition expands the supplied carefulness rule to the entire group in the universal conclusion.

questions.stem: Option Alder costs seventy units and available option Birch costs ninety units. An analyst concludes that Alder is cheaper than every other available option. Which addition is sufficient?
choices: Every available option other than Alder costs at least ninety units.
Birch is more popular than every other available option.
Alder cost more than seventy units last year.
Some available option other than Birch costs eighty units.
questions.explanation: The universal ninety-unit lower bound puts every competing available option above Alder's seventy-unit price. Birch's popularity concerns a different measure. Alder's past price changes the time of comparison without limiting current competitors. An eighty-unit competitor would also cost more than Alder, but another option could still cost less than seventy. The premise compares Alder with Birch alone; the conclusion expands the comparison base to every other available option.

questions.stem: Process New uses exactly five energy units per item, while Process Old uses exactly six. These per-item amounts account for all energy use. An analyst concludes that New's total energy use in its run is lower than Old's in its run. Which additional statement guarantees the conclusion?
choices: New produces twice as many items as Old.
New and Old produce items of the same color.
Both runs produce the same positive number of items.
Old's run produces at least one item.
questions.explanation: With the same positive output n, New uses 5n and Old uses 6n, so New's total is lower. Positivity prevents the equal-zero case. Twice as much New output would make its total 10n against Old's 6n for positive Old output, so it does not guarantee a reduction. Item color gives no output comparison. Positive Old output alone leaves New's output unrestricted. A lower rate establishes a lower total only with a sufficient connection between the counting bases.

questions.stem: A reviewer cites only Cedar's approved, nondigitized record as a counterexample to “Every approved record in Register R is digitized.” Which assumption does this particular counterexample route require?
choices: Every approved record is nondigitized.
Cedar's cited record belongs to Register R.
Cedar's record is the only approved record anywhere.
No record in Register R is digitized.
questions.explanation: The cited record must belong to Register R to refute a universal claim restricted to that register. Its approval and lack of digitization are given, but its register membership is not. If it lies outside R, this particular example does not refute the scoped claim, even though another counterexample might exist. Requiring every approved record to be nondigitized, making Cedar's record unique, or excluding all digitized records from R extends far beyond what one valid counterexample needs. Match the witness to the exact domain.

questions.stem: Every certified exhibitor is registered on Tuesday, and every exhibitor registered on Tuesday is eligible to enter on Tuesday. The conclusion is: if an exhibitor is certified, that exhibitor will enter on Wednesday. Which additional rule is sufficient?
choices: Every exhibitor eligible to enter on Wednesday is eligible to enter on Tuesday.
Every exhibitor registered on Tuesday is eligible to enter on Wednesday.
Every exhibitor who enters on Wednesday is certified.
Every exhibitor eligible to enter on Tuesday will enter on Wednesday.
questions.explanation: A certified exhibitor is registered Tuesday and therefore eligible Tuesday. The rule from Tuesday eligibility to actual Wednesday entry completes the chain for any certified exhibitor. The Wednesday-to-Tuesday eligibility rule runs backward and does not establish entry. Extending registration to Wednesday eligibility supplies permission without actual attendance. The Wednesday-entry-to-certification rule reverses the desired conclusion. The correct addition preserves the person while supplying both the time connection and the change from eligibility to an event. No exhibitor's existence must be invented to prove this conditional conclusion.

questions.stem: In one collection, every submitted record is catalogued and every indexed record is searchable. Record Vale was submitted. Which added statement is sufficient to establish that Vale is searchable?
choices: Every catalogued record in this collection is indexed.
Every indexed record in this collection is catalogued.
Some catalogued records in this collection are indexed.
Every searchable record in this collection was submitted.
questions.explanation: Making every catalogued record indexed completes the forward route: Vale is submitted, so it is catalogued; the addition makes it indexed; the existing rule then makes it searchable. Making indexed records catalogued reverses the missing relationship and leaves Vale's indexing unsettled. Some catalogued records being indexed could concern records other than Vale. Making searchable records submitted describes a requirement on searchable records; it does not make Vale's submission sufficient for searchability. Those alternatives permit Vale to be catalogued but neither indexed nor searchable.

questions.stem: Under a workshop's exact rule, any volunteer who is both trained and cleared can supervise a session. Neri is a trained volunteer. Which added statement is sufficient to establish that Neri can supervise?
choices: Every volunteer who can supervise is cleared.
Some trained volunteers are cleared.
Every trained volunteer is cleared.
Every cleared volunteer is trained.
questions.explanation: Clearing every trained volunteer supplies Neri's missing clearance. Neri then has both inputs to the supervision rule. Requiring clearance of those who can supervise gives a necessary condition without establishing it for Neri. Some trained volunteers being cleared could identify someone else, so it need not establish Neri's permission to supervise. Making every cleared volunteer trained runs from clearance to training, while Neri's known property is training. That reversed rule also permits Neri to be uncleared and unable to supervise. The successful addition is broader than Neri alone, but it is sufficient.

questions.stem: Some editors are reviewers, and every reviewer is registered. Which added statement is sufficient to establish that some editors are trained?
choices: Some registered people are trained.
Every registered person is trained.
Every trained person is registered.
Every trained person is an editor.
questions.explanation: If every registered person is trained, the existing editor-reviewer witness is registered and then trained. That same person establishes that some editors are trained. Some registered people being trained could concern people who are not editors. Making trained people registered reverses the useful rule and allows the editor-reviewer witness to be untrained. Making trained people editors would connect the groups if a trained person were established, but the premises do not establish any trained person. All of the universal statements must be applied in the usable direction, and existence cannot be supplied by a universal rule alone.

questions.stem: Every approved group is permitted to use the east room during one scheduled session. Group Reed is approved. A planner concludes that Reed actually uses the east room during that session. Which added statement is sufficient to establish the conclusion?
choices: Every group that actually uses the east room during the session is approved.
Some approved groups actually use the east room during the session.
Every approved group is also permitted to use the west room during the session.
Every group permitted to use the east room during the session actually uses it then.
questions.explanation: Making permitted east-room use sufficient for actual use connects Reed's established permission to the claimed action at the same session. Requiring approval of actual east-room users runs backward from action to approval and leaves Reed free not to use the room. Some approved groups using the room could concern groups other than Reed. Permission to use the west room is another permission, not evidence of actual east-room use. The successful candidate is a strong fictional rule, but the task asks whether adding it guarantees the conclusion, not whether such a rule is realistic.

questions.stem: For every proposal in a program, nomination implies screening, and approval implies funding. Which added rule is sufficient to establish that every nominated proposal receives funding?
choices: Every funded proposal is nominated.
Every approved proposal is screened.
Every screened proposal is approved.
Every screened proposal is nominated.
questions.explanation: Making screening sufficient for approval joins nomination to screening, screening to approval, and approval to funding. Any nominated proposal therefore receives funding. Making funded proposals nominated reverses the desired overall relation. Making approved proposals screened reverses the missing middle link. Making screened proposals nominated makes the first relationship reversible but still never reaches approval or funding. Each unsuccessful addition permits a nominated, screened proposal to be unapproved and unfunded. No particular nominated proposal has to be asserted to prove the universal conditional relationship.

questions.stem: Every orchard sapling is fenced, and Cedar is an orchard sapling. To establish that Cedar is watered, a learner adds the rule that every fenced plant is watered. The learner worries that this rule also covers fenced plants outside the orchard. Which assessment is correct?
choices: The rule is sufficient because its breadth does not prevent it from applying to Cedar.
The rule is insufficient unless every watered plant is also a fenced orchard sapling.
The rule must be necessary because any statement completing this proof is necessary.
The rule is insufficient because sufficient assumptions may mention only named individuals.
questions.explanation: Cedar's orchard status establishes fencing, and the proposed rule then establishes watering. Covering additional fenced plants does not interfere with that proof. Requiring every watered plant to be a fenced orchard sapling adds a reverse restriction that the proof does not need. Calling every successful completion necessary confuses enough with required: a narrower addition about Cedar could also establish its watering without the broad rule. Restricting sufficient assumptions to named individuals is unfounded; a universal rule can complete a proof about one individual.

questions.stem: Every editor is a reviewer, and Ina is an editor. Someone adds that some reviewers are certified and concludes that Ina is certified. Which possible case shows that the addition is insufficient while preserving every stated premise and the addition?
choices: Ina is not an editor but is a certified reviewer.
Ina is an editor, a reviewer, and certified.
Ina is an editor and reviewer, but no reviewer is certified.
Ina is an uncertified editor and reviewer; Oren is a certified reviewer.
questions.explanation: Ina can be an uncertified editor-reviewer while Oren supplies the certified reviewer required by the addition. That case preserves every accepted statement and makes the conclusion false. Making Ina a noneditor contradicts an explicit premise. Making Ina certified leaves the conclusion true, so it does not demonstrate insufficiency. Making every reviewer uncertified contradicts the added existential statement. A counterexample must preserve all accepted statements and defeat the conclusion; merely describing a different situation is not enough.

questions.stem: A proposed addition is compatible with an argument's premises. With the addition accepted, the exact conclusion must follow. With its negation accepted instead, the conclusion could be true or false. What is the correct assessment of the addition?
choices: It fails as a sufficient assumption because its negation does not force the conclusion false.
It meets the sufficiency test because accepting it with the premises guarantees the conclusion.
It meets the sufficiency test only if no different addition could establish the conclusion.
It merely strengthens the argument because the conclusion can also be true without it.
questions.explanation: The addition meets the sufficiency test: the premises plus that addition guarantee the exact conclusion. A conclusion's possible truth when the addition is false does not undo that forward guarantee. Requiring the negation to force the conclusion false imposes a different condition. Requiring a unique possible addition is also mistaken; multiple statements can complete a proof, though a question should supply only one successful choice. Calling the addition merely strengthening overlooks the stated guarantee. A sufficient route need not be the only route by which the conclusion could be true.

questions.stem: Every selected record is logged, and every searchable record is public. Record Lark is selected and digitized. Which added statement is sufficient to establish that Lark is public?
choices: Every logged record that is searchable is digitized.
Every logged record that is digitized is searchable.
Every public record that is digitized is logged.
Some digitized records are searchable.
questions.explanation: Lark's selection establishes logging, and its digitization is given. The rule making logged, digitized records searchable therefore applies to Lark; searchability then establishes its public status. Making logged, searchable records digitized requires searchability as an input and cannot establish it from Lark's known properties. Making public, digitized records logged requires the very public status still to be proved. Some digitized records being searchable could concern other records. The successful rule uses both of Lark's established properties and reaches the missing middle condition in the correct direction.

questions.stem: Every copper badge in an inventory is numbered. Which added statement is sufficient to establish that every copper badge in the inventory is red?
choices: Some numbered badges in the inventory are red.
Every red badge in the inventory is numbered.
At least one badge in the inventory is copper.
Every numbered badge in the inventory is red.
questions.explanation: Making every numbered badge red takes any copper badge from copper to numbered and then red, so the universal conclusion follows. Some numbered badges being red can leave a copper badge outside the red group. Making red badges numbered reverses the useful relationship and allows numbered copper badges to be nonred. Establishing a copper badge's existence does not establish its color. The conclusion is a universal restriction; it does not separately claim that copper badges exist.

questions.stem: A committee notes that Plan Birch reduces waiting time without increasing cost. It concludes that it should adopt Plan Birch. Which added decision rule is sufficient to establish that conclusion?
choices: The committee should adopt any plan that reduces waiting time without increasing cost.
Every plan the committee should adopt reduces waiting time without increasing cost.
The committee may consider any plan that reduces waiting time without increasing cost.
Some plans that reduce waiting time without increasing cost should be adopted.
questions.explanation: The rule directing adoption of any plan with Birch's established properties supplies a complete bridge to the recommendation. Requiring those properties of plans that should be adopted runs in the reverse direction; it does not make the properties sufficient. Permission to consider a plan is weaker than a recommendation to adopt it. Some qualifying plans deserving adoption need not include Birch. The successful rule is assumed for this reasoning exercise; the proof does not separately establish that it is an appropriate real-world decision policy.

questions.stem: Every booking active in April is indexed in April. Every booking indexed in May receives a permit in May. Booking Vela is active in April. Which added statement is sufficient to establish that Vela receives a permit in May?
choices: Every booking indexed in April receives a permit in April.
Every booking indexed in May was indexed in April.
Every booking indexed in April is indexed in May.
Some bookings indexed in April are indexed in May.
questions.explanation: April activity makes Vela indexed in April. Carrying every April-indexed booking into May indexing supplies the condition needed for the May-permit rule. An April permit does not establish a May permit. Requiring May-indexed bookings to have been indexed in April reverses the needed time connection and leaves Vela's May status open. Some April-indexed bookings also being May-indexed could concern other bookings. The complete proof preserves both the named booking and the month attached to each condition.

questions.stem: Weekend markets that hired musicians had higher average stall sales than markets without musicians. An analyst concludes that hiring musicians increased sales. Which additional fact most weakens the causal inference from this comparison?
choices: At the markets with musicians, performances began before the first customer purchases.
Markets with musicians had much larger promotion budgets, which funded both musician hiring and advertising that independently boosted stall sales.
The musicians played instruments that had been used at other kinds of public events.
Most stall owners said they enjoyed listening to the musicians while working.
questions.explanation: Larger promotion budgets fund the musicians and a separate advertising influence on sales. That common factor can help explain the association without the comparison isolating a musician effect. Beginning performances before purchases supplies temporal order but does not identify the cause of the sales difference. The instruments' use at other events does not bear on these markets' sales. Owners' enjoyment concerns a different outcome and does not establish that music increased customer purchases. The budget fact weakens the attribution without proving that musicians contributed nothing.

questions.stem: Parks reporting recent increases in litter also introduced extra volunteer patrols. A commentator concludes that the extra patrols initiated those increases. Which fact most directly undermines that proposed direction of influence?
choices: Volunteers recorded litter using the same counting procedure as the earlier park staff.
Patrol members began each route at the entrance used by regular visitors.
The association between extra patrols and more litter appears in every park in the report.
Dated records show that each park added the patrols only after its litter count had risen, specifically in response to that rise.
questions.explanation: The dated response shows the increase preceding and prompting the extra patrols, undermining the claim that those patrols initiated that earlier increase. Consistent counting procedures support comparability rather than the claimed reversed chronology. A patrol's starting location does not explain the direction of influence. Repeating the association across the parks still does not establish which factor came first. The temporal evidence addresses the initiation claim; it does not settle whether the patrols later changed litter levels in some other way.

questions.stem: A lending library began sending reminder postcards in September, and its late-return rate then fell. Its director concludes that the postcards helped reduce late returns. Which additional fact most strengthens that explanation?
choices: Otherwise comparable branches without postcards had stable late-return rates over the same period; due-date policies, borrower mix, and opening hours remained matched.
The library lengthened every loan period when it introduced the postcards, and longer loan periods tend to reduce late returns.
Recipients often complimented the postcards' artwork without commenting on their borrowing behavior.
The postcards were printed by the same company that printed the library's posters several years earlier.
questions.explanation: Stable rates at comparable branches without postcards make a general period-wide change less convincing as the explanation for the treated library's decline. The stated matching also reduces several concrete comparison concerns. Lengthening loan periods supplies an additional plausible cause and weakens the attribution to postcards. Compliments about artwork do not establish changed return behavior. The printer's past work does not connect the reminders to timely returns. The comparison strengthens the proposed contribution without guaranteeing the same result at every library.

questions.stem: Employees using a structured request template omitted fewer required details than employees writing free-form requests. A manager concludes that the template reduces omissions. Which fact most strengthens the inference that the template, rather than differences between the employees, explains the result?
choices: Employees were allowed to choose their format, and the most experienced employees all chose the template.
Template documents occupied less storage space than free-form documents containing the same information.
Within each experience level, employees were assigned formats by chance, completed comparable requests, and were scored by the same omission rules; the template advantage recurred.
Employees who used the template preferred its colors to the colors of the organization's previous form.
questions.explanation: Chance assignment within experience levels, comparable tasks, common scoring, and a repeated advantage reduce the specific concern that different employees or measurements created the result. Concentrating experienced employees in the template group leaves an alternative explanation for fewer omissions. Storage size is a different outcome and does not isolate an omission effect. Color preferences likewise do not establish better completeness. The design strengthens the causal inference; random assignment does not guarantee perfect equality or eliminate every possible limitation.

questions.stem: After a sorting room added pads to its work trays, fewer fragile pieces were damaged. The supervisor proposes that the pads helped by preventing pieces from sliding into tray edges during sorting. Which fact most directly supports that proposed mechanism?
choices: Replacing a worn pad takes less time than replacing a worn tray.
The room's staff prefer the pads' appearance to that of the uncovered trays.
The supplier sells the same pads to offices that use them beneath display stands.
Recordings of matched sorting runs show less sliding on padded trays, and the avoided edge collisions were a frequent source of damage in unpadded runs.
questions.explanation: The recordings connect pads to reduced sliding and link the prevented collisions to the relevant damage. They provide evidence that the proposed process operated, rather than merely describing a conceivable benefit. Replacement time concerns maintenance convenience. Staff preference concerns appearance. Use beneath display stands in other offices does not show what caused damage during these sorting runs. Evidence for the mechanism strengthens the explanation but does not show that pads prevent every kind of damage or determine the exact size of their contribution.

questions.stem: An office replaced its chairs and installed a new search interface in the same week. Average file-lookup time then fell. A manager credits the chairs for the improvement. Which additional finding most weakens that attribution?
choices: The new chairs allow users to adjust their seat height.
Comparable groups using the new interface with old chairs improved equally, while groups using new chairs with the old interface did not improve.
The old chairs remain available in a storage room that employees rarely visit.
The new interface uses fewer colors than the old interface, without any reported difference in legibility.
questions.explanation: The comparison varies the chairs and interface separately: improvement accompanies the interface change even without new chairs, while changing chairs alone does not produce the reported improvement. That pattern weakens the chair attribution and supports the simultaneous interface change as an alternative. Height adjustment describes a possible chair feature without showing its effect on lookup time. Storage availability does not compare employees' performance. An unconnected color difference does not establish the cause of the time change. The result is evidence about the tested settings, not a proof that chairs can never affect work.

questions.stem: A technician claims that a diffuser can help reduce echo in rooms with bare walls. A critic notes that some carpeted rooms have little echo without a diffuser and therefore declares the technician's claim disproved. Which assessment is best?
choices: The critic proves that a diffuser always increases echo in bare-walled rooms.
A contributing cause must be present whenever the outcome occurs, so the critic's test is decisive.
Another route to little echo does not by itself refute a possible diffuser contribution under the stated conditions.
The technician's claim is established merely because the critic's observation is insufficient to disprove it.
questions.explanation: The technician claims a possible contribution in bare-walled rooms, not that a diffuser is necessary for low echo everywhere. Carpeted rooms provide another possible route under different conditions. Their low echo neither proves that diffusers increase echo nor shows that contributing causes must be universally necessary. The critic's unsuccessful objection also does not establish the technician's claim; positive support still needs assessment. Match the proposed counterexample to both the strength and the conditions of the causal statement.

questions.stem: In a fictional packaging line, a supervisor claims that a new feeder, when operated correctly within its stated load range, always prevents the line from stopping. Which finding most directly challenges that guarantee?
choices: A verified run within the stated load range stopped while the new feeder was operating correctly.
Several runs before the feeder was installed stopped while packages were being loaded.
A correctly operated run within the stated load range finished without stopping.
Operators require training before they can learn the feeder's controls.
questions.explanation: A stopped run satisfying every stated condition is a counterexample to the universal guarantee. Stops before installation do not test what the feeder guarantees when present and correctly operated. A successful run is consistent with the claim, but one success does not establish every run's success. Training requirements do not contradict a guarantee explicitly restricted to correct operation. This counterexample rejects the always-prevents claim; it does not by itself show that the feeder never reduces the frequency of stops.

questions.stem: A researcher claims that playing a one-minute reminder substantially increases the number of records volunteers complete during a forty-five-minute session. Which result most weakens that claim for the tested sessions?
choices: The reminder's written transcript can be displayed in several different fonts.
Most volunteers say the reminder sounds pleasant.
Across repeated comparable sessions with balanced task difficulty and the same counting procedure, completion totals with the reminder are consistently no higher than totals without it.
Some volunteers complete few records during sessions in which no reminder is played.
questions.explanation: The repeated, relevant comparison fails to show the claimed increase while preserving task difficulty, session length, and the outcome measure. It therefore weakens the substantial-effect claim for these conditions. Available fonts do not measure completed records. Pleasantness is a different outcome. Low completion by some volunteers without a reminder supplies no comparison showing what a reminder changes for comparable volunteers. Do not invent an unreported benefit to dismiss the stated result, but do not expand the result into proof that no reminder could ever help in another setting.

questions.stem: In a fictional materials comparison, a coated outdoor storage box stays cooler than an otherwise similar uncoated box. An analyst attributes the difference to the coating. A critic suggests that extra shade over the coated box explains the result. Which fact most directly strengthens the analyst's case against that particular alternative?
choices: During every measurement period, both boxes received the same direct sunlight and neither was shaded.
The coated box was under a tree for most measurements while the uncoated box was in direct sunlight.
Workers preferred the coated box's color even before temperature measurements began.
The coating cost less than a replacement storage box.
questions.explanation: Equal direct sunlight with neither box shaded removes the specified shade difference as the explanation for the measured temperature contrast. Greater shade over the coated box would support the critic's alternative instead. Color preference does not measure heat effects, and replacement cost concerns a different comparison. Excluding shade strengthens the attribution relative to that challenge without eliminating every possible explanation or proving that the coating works under every condition.

questions.stem: On the same day, a theater installed entrance posters and extended its ticket-pickup hours. Pickup totals increased. The director claims that the posters alone caused the entire increase. Which added fact most directly weakens this exclusive attribution while remaining compatible with the posters having helped?
choices: Some audience members had picked up tickets before either change occurred.
The posters used a typeface that appeared on earlier theater programs.
The extended hours began on the same day that the posters were installed, as the director already knew.
Separate comparisons establish that the extra hours made a positive contribution to the increase during the period in question.
questions.explanation: An established positive contribution from extended hours contradicts the claim that posters alone account for the entire increase, while allowing the posters to have contributed too. Earlier ticket pickups establish a baseline activity, not a cause of the later increase. Reused typography does not identify the source of changed pickup totals. Merely repeating the known timing of both changes adds no new evidence isolating their effects. The force of the added comparison depends on the director's exclusive wording; another contributor would not by itself disprove a modest poster-contribution claim.

questions.stem: A print shop reports fewer misplaced jobs after adding color-coded tray markers. A manager proposes that the markers reduce misplacement. Which additional result most strengthens that causal explanation?
choices: The markers are more expensive than the shop's previous labels.
Across matched batches and operators, removing the markers raises misplacement again and restoring them lowers it; the order of these conditions is balanced and other procedures remain fixed.
Operators who already made the fewest mistakes were the only ones initially given marked trays.
The markers remain readable when viewed from the shop's front entrance, but jobs are sorted elsewhere.
questions.explanation: The repeated change with removal and restoration, under matched conditions and balanced ordering, ties the outcome more closely to the markers than a single before-and-after observation does. It reduces selection, practice-order, and simultaneous-procedure concerns without guaranteeing a universal effect. Higher price does not establish effectiveness. Giving markers only to the most accurate operators creates an alternative explanation for the initial difference. Readability from an irrelevant location does not show that operators used the markers during sorting. The matched reversal pattern directly strengthens the proposed contribution.

questions.stem: A wall tile muffled sound in a particular frequency range during a laboratory test. An engineer therefore expects the tile to reduce the troublesome machinery noise in Workshop R. Which additional fact, if true, most strengthens that expectation?
choices: The tile's color matches a color already used on Workshop R's walls.
Most machinery noise in Workshop R lies outside the range used in the test.
Most of Workshop R's troublesome machinery noise falls within the range the tile muffled.
The laboratory also sells protective equipment unrelated to the tile.
questions.explanation: Matching the workshop's troublesome noise to the tested range connects the observed performance to the target setting. It strengthens the expectation without establishing that every source of workshop noise will disappear. Matching wall colors does not bear on noise reduction through any supplied relationship. Placing most machinery noise outside the tested range raises a transfer concern instead of supporting the inference. The laboratory's unrelated equipment sales do not establish the tile's performance in Workshop R. The useful addition supplies a specific relevance connection, not merely a shared topic.

questions.stem: A library's lending log has no March entries for the novel River Glass. A librarian concludes that no one borrowed the novel during March. Which additional fact, if true, most weakens that reasoning?
choices: The log omits classroom loans, and copies of River Glass were available for classroom borrowing during March.
The novel's author also published a collection of essays under a different title.
Every loan of the novel had to be entered in this log, and the March entries were checked for omissions.
The illustration on the novel's cover matches the illustration shown in its catalogue entry.
questions.explanation: The omitted classroom channel makes the absence of log entries less informative about all borrowing. The log can remain exactly as described even if classroom loans occurred. This weakens the inference without proving that a classroom loan actually occurred. The author's other book does not determine March loans of this novel. Requiring and checking entries for every loan supports the completeness connection and therefore strengthens the argument. A matching cover illustration concerns identification, but no supplied issue makes it evidence of borrowing or the absence of borrowing. Keep the target month, title, and loan claim fixed.

questions.stem: During a test, a conservator heard a chime just after a restored bell was struck. She concludes that the bell's sound-producing mechanism is probably working. Which additional fact, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
choices: A nearby loudspeaker was playing recorded bell chimes throughout the test.
A website repeats the conservator's description of the test without adding any observation.
The workshop's brochure uses a drawing of the bell on its cover.
An independent test isolated the bell from other sound sources and recorded a clear chime each time it was struck.
questions.explanation: The independent test supplies an additional observation of this bell producing a chime while other sound sources are excluded. That corroborates the working-mechanism conclusion without requiring that the bell be free of every possible remaining defect. A loudspeaker playing chimes supplies a competing source for what was originally heard and weakens the sound-based inference. A website that merely copies the conservator's account does not provide an independent observation. The brochure's drawing concerns presentation rather than the bell's current function. Genuine corroboration contributes information beyond a second publication of the same claim.

questions.stem: Supplier A quotes a production price of 45 credits for an order, while Supplier B quotes 60 credits for the identical order. A coordinator concludes that choosing A will minimize the order's total cost. Which additional fact, if true, most weakens that conclusion?
choices: A and B print their quotes on paper of different colors.
A requires a further handling fee of 40 credits, while B's quoted price covers every cost of the order.
Both production quotes have stayed at the stated amounts for the past month.
A offers an optional decorative insert that the coordinator does not need and would not order.
questions.explanation: A's mandatory fee makes its known total at least 85 credits, exceeding B's complete 60-credit total. The production quotes remain true, but they no longer support choosing A to minimize total cost. Quote-paper colors supply no cost relationship. Stable quoted production prices do not settle additional charges. An optional insert that will not be ordered adds no cost to this order. The useful weakener connects directly to the difference between the stated price component and the total the conclusion compares.

questions.stem: A checklist has a checkmark beside Gauge M and yesterday's date beside that mark. A supervisor concludes that M was inspected yesterday. Which additional fact, if true, most strengthens the inference?
choices: An identical copy of the checklist was posted in a second room.
On this checklist, a checkmark is entered only after inspection, and the adjacent date records that inspection's completion.
Gauge M also appears on an inventory of equipment owned by the workshop.
Staff sometimes enter checkmarks and planned dates before carrying out the inspections.
questions.explanation: The stated recording convention connects both features of the entry to a completed inspection on the dated day. It directly supports the supervisor's interpretation. A second posting of the same checklist does not supply a second inspection record. Inventory membership establishes that the gauge is equipment in the workshop, not when it was inspected. Advance checkmarks and planned dates would undermine the inference from this entry to a completed inspection. The relevance of the marking procedure comes from how it changes the meaning of the accepted observation.

questions.stem: Ten boxes arrived at an office, each containing twenty forms. From those counts, a clerk concludes that the delivery supplies two hundred usable forms. Which additional fact, if true, most weakens that inference?
choices: The boxes carry consecutive identification numbers from one through ten.
The forms use the office's standard readable typeface.
The delivery driver also delivered an unrelated parcel to the office last month.
A leak left five forms in each of the ten boxes unusable for the office's intended purpose.
questions.explanation: The unusable forms still count among the twenty in each box, so the original counts remain true. But at least fifty of the two hundred forms are unusable, leaving at most one hundred fifty usable forms from this delivery. Consecutive box numbers do not establish usability. A readable typeface supports a relevant aspect of usability rather than weakening it. The driver's earlier unrelated delivery does not bear on these forms' condition. The weakener exposes the missing connection between counting objects and counting objects fit for the stated purpose.

questions.stem: A gallery's sensor recorded 100 activations during one opening period and 150 during the next, after the sensor was moved. The curator concludes that more visitors came during the second period. Which additional fact, if true, most weakens the comparison?
choices: Only visitors activated the sensor: each visitor activated it once in the old position and twice in the new position.
The two opening periods lasted the same number of hours.
A visitor map shows the new sensor position more clearly than it showed the old position.
The sensor reliably recorded every activation at both positions.
questions.explanation: The count-to-person relationship changed. Under the stated patterns, 100 activations represent 100 visitors in the first period, while 150 represent 75 in the second. More activations therefore do not support more visitors here. Equal period lengths do not undermine the comparison. A clearer map gives no relationship between activations and distinct visitors. Reliable activation recording protects the accuracy of the raw counts but does not show that an activation means the same number of people at both locations. A measurement can be accurately recorded yet misinterpreted.

questions.stem: A committee recommends the North site for a service center because it gives most households a shorter journey than the South site. Which additional fact, if true, most strengthens the recommendation?
choices: The North site's name appears before the South site's name in an alphabetical list.
The South site can accommodate many residents whom the North site cannot accommodate.
Both sites equally satisfy every nontravel requirement, and the committee's agreed selection rule then favors shorter journeys for most households.
Both site names appear on a map printed several years before the service center was proposed.
questions.explanation: Equal satisfaction of the other requirements, combined with the agreed selection rule, connects the stated travel advantage to choosing North. This is relevant support for the recommendation, not merely another fact about the sites. Alphabetical order has no supplied role in the selection standard. South's accommodation advantage raises a relevant concern about choosing North and therefore points against the requested strengthening. Appearance on an old map establishes no decision criterion. Evaluate the added fact against the actual recommendation and the reasons offered for it.

questions.stem: Three trade newsletters report that a new coating lasts longer than the old coating. A buyer treats their agreement as three independent confirmations of the new coating's superiority. Which additional fact, if true, most weakens that evidential claim?
choices: The newsletters use different typefaces in their printed editions.
Each newsletter reports a separate test conducted by a different independent laboratory.
All three newsletters copied the same unverified manufacturer announcement without obtaining further observations.
The newsletters are all written for people who purchase coating materials.
questions.explanation: Copying one unverified announcement provides one underlying source repeated three times, not three independent confirmations. The new coating might still last longer, but the claimed multiplication of independent evidence fails. Different typefaces do not establish independent observation. Separate tests by independent laboratories would support the buyer's independence claim and strengthen the evidential case. A shared readership explains the newsletters' subject matter without establishing whether their sources are independent. Count underlying information, not merely the number of places where a claim appears.

questions.stem: A researcher finds opened seed capsules near a nesting ledge and concludes that at least some birds on that ledge can open that type of capsule. Which additional fact, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
choices: The ledge and the capsules have similar brown coloring.
A clear recording shows one of those birds opening an intact capsule of the same type without help.
Another animal that visits the ledge is known to open those capsules at night.
Three observers independently measured the height of the nesting ledge.
questions.explanation: The recording directly demonstrates the claimed capability in at least one bird from the specified group. It supplies additional support beyond the mere proximity of opened capsules to a nest. Similar colors establish no opening capability. Another animal that opens the capsules gives an alternative source for the original observation and weakens that observation's attribution to birds. Repeated measurements of ledge height may corroborate the height, but the passage supplies no connection between height and capsule opening. Independent observations matter only when their content bears on the target claim.

questions.stem: A reader accepts that a proposed fact supplies a relevant additional reason for a forecast, but rejects it as a strengthening answer solely because the forecast could still fail. Which correction best addresses the reader's mistake?
choices: A fact strengthens only if it makes every possible future outcome certain.
Any remaining possibility of failure makes new evidence irrelevant.
Any true statement strengthens a forecast, even without a relevant connection.
A fact can increase support for a forecast without eliminating all uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Strengthening concerns an increase in support relative to the supplied argument. The accepted relevant reason can provide that increase even when failure remains possible. Requiring certainty imposes a sufficient-proof standard that the question did not ask for. Remaining uncertainty does not make a relevant reason irrelevant. Truth alone is also insufficient: a true statement about an unrelated matter need not change support for the forecast. Keep the direction and relevance of the change separate from the argument's final level of certainty.

questions.stem: A writer cites a word in a published transcription of a village diary as evidence that the diarist used that word. New information establishes that the word was inserted by the modern editor and was absent from the diary at that location. Which assessment best describes the effect on the writer's argument?
choices: The cited entry no longer supports the claimed usage, though the diarist might have used the word elsewhere.
The new information proves that the diarist never used the word in any setting.
The editor's insertion independently confirms that the diarist used the word in the original entry.
The information is irrelevant because the conclusion might still be true for another reason.
questions.explanation: The new information removes the connection between the word in the published transcription and the diarist's original language at that location. The fact that the transcription contains the word remains true, but that fact no longer supplies the offered usage evidence. Excluding the word from every setting would go beyond the new information. An editor's insertion does not confirm original use. The possibility of independent usage elsewhere does not make the damage to this particular justification irrelevant. A weakener can defeat a cited reason without establishing the conclusion's universal negation.

questions.stem: A warehouse records twenty errors before introducing a procedure and eight afterward, with exactly one thousand items processed in each period. The manager concludes that the procedure reduced the error rate. Which question would most help evaluate the comparison supporting that conclusion?
choices: Does the procedure's printed title contain an even number of words?
Did the warehouse process one thousand items in each period?
Does the manager prefer the color of the new record sheet?
Were categories counted as errors before the change excluded from the later error count?
questions.explanation: Excluding formerly counted error categories could create a lower recorded rate without a comparable reduction in actual errors. A yes therefore weakens the comparison, while no removes that specific measurement concern without proving causation. Title length and color preference have no stated relationship to the error result. Equal processing totals are already given; imagining that they differed would change a premise rather than investigate an unresolved issue. The useful question checks whether the two recorded numerators represent the same relevant outcome.

questions.stem: A fictional club will eliminate eighty-four credits of expense during the first year of a service and pay thirty credits in first-year service charges. The only other possible expense change is a nonnegative setup fee. The club predicts a positive first-year saving. Which question most directly resolves the remaining cost issue?
choices: Is the setup fee below one hundred credits?
Is the setup fee below fifty-four credits?
Is the service's name shorter than the club's name?
Will the service charge anything in the fifth year?
questions.explanation: The first-year saving is eighty-four minus thirty minus the setup fee, or fifty-four minus that fee. A fee below fifty-four leaves a positive saving; at least fifty-four leaves no saving or an increase. The hundred-credit boundary is less direct because a fee of ten and a fee of seventy both fall below it but produce opposite first-year results. Name length is irrelevant to the complete cost model. Fifth-year charges address a different period. The correct boundary distinguishes the outcomes the stated conclusion treats differently.

questions.stem: Seventy percent of respondents to a town survey favor a proposed festival. An advocate concludes that most town residents favor it. Which question would most help evaluate the transfer from respondents to residents?
choices: Does the survey's heading use the town's official font?
Have organizers held festivals in other towns with different populations?
Were residents opposing the festival substantially less likely to respond than residents favoring it?
Was seventy percent the proportion favoring it among the respondents?
questions.explanation: Unequal response related to the measured opinion could inflate support among respondents relative to all residents. Yes weakens the population inference; no removes that particular response-bias explanation while leaving other sampling issues open. The font has no stated connection to responses or opinions. Festivals in different towns do not establish how this town's respondents relate to its residents. The seventy-percent respondent result is already a premise, so repeating it does not investigate the unresolved population connection.

questions.stem: Sorting errors fell at a depot after new bin labels were installed. The director attributes the decrease to the labels. Which question would most help evaluate that attribution?
choices: Did otherwise comparable depots without new labels show a similar decrease during the same period using the same error definitions?
Are the new labels stored alphabetically in the supplier's catalog?
Does the depot's name begin with the same letter as the supplier's name?
Have employees ever worked at an unrelated business outside the industry?
questions.explanation: A similar decrease without the labels would suggest a background change that could account for the depot's trend. No comparable decrease would make this particular alternative less supported, improving the relative case for the labels without proving their effect. Catalog order and matching name initials have no stated connection to sorting. Unspecified work at unrelated businesses does not identify a relevant difference or explanation. The useful question compares the outcome when the proposed factor differs under relevant shared conditions.

questions.stem: Residents who work afternoons cannot attend a club's afternoon repair session. The organizer expects a new morning session to attract those residents. Which question would most help evaluate the proposed availability link?
choices: Do current afternoon participants prefer the club's older poster design?
Does the word morning appear in the club's oldest newsletter?
Is the repair room's door painted the organizer's favorite color?
Are the intended residents free to attend at the proposed morning time?
questions.explanation: If the intended residents are available in the morning, the new time addresses their scheduling obstacle, though interest and actual attendance still need support. If they are unavailable then too, the plan does not solve that group's availability problem. Poster preferences among current users, a historical word occurrence, and door color have no supplied connection to the target residents' schedules. The useful question can have different support effects even when its favorable answer does not guarantee the plan's success.

questions.stem: A scanner's recorded errors fell from forty in one period to thirty in the next. The same error definition was used, but the positive number of items scanned in each period is unknown. An analyst concludes that the error rate fell. Which question most directly distinguishes a lower rate from a rate that stayed the same or increased?
choices: Did the later period have more sunny days outside the building?
Was the later number of scanned items more than three-quarters of the earlier number?
Did the scanner's casing have the same number of screws in both periods?
Were fewer than forty errors recorded in the later period?
questions.explanation: Write earlier workload as M and later workload as N, both positive. The later rate is lower exactly when 30/N is below 40/M, equivalent to N being more than three-quarters of M. Yes establishes a lower rate; no gives equality at the boundary or a higher rate below it. Sunny days and casing screws have no stated relationship to the relevant totals. Fewer than forty later errors is already established by the given thirty and cannot resolve the denominator. The question targets the exact comparison threshold.

questions.stem: A plan needs qualified staff to run a new workshop. Asking whether enough qualified staff are available has two effects: no blocks the proposed operation, while yes removes the staffing obstacle but does not guarantee customer attendance. A student dismisses the question because yes does not prove the entire plan will succeed. Which assessment is best?
choices: The question remains useful because its answers change the assessment of a relevant implementation condition.
The student is right because an evaluation question must prove the whole conclusion with either answer.
The question is useful only if both answers have exactly equal effects in opposite directions.
The student should assume staff are available and ignore the other answer.
questions.explanation: The answers distinguish an unavailable essential input from removal of that particular obstacle, so they materially affect evaluation even though attendance remains unresolved. Requiring either answer to prove the whole conclusion imposes too strong a standard. Equally large opposite effects are also unnecessary; a serious objection and its absence can form a useful contrast. Assuming a favorable answer prevents evaluating the question's informational role. Test what each answer would establish about the actual reasoning rather than demanding a complete verdict from one fact.

questions.stem: Cabinet Alder has a lower purchase price than Cabinet Birch. A manager recommends Alder on the ground that it will have the lower total ownership cost over five years. Which question most directly examines the gap in that cost comparison?
choices: Do both cabinet names contain the same number of letters?
Is Alder's purchase price below Birch's purchase price?
Would Alder's required replacement and maintenance expenses exceed Birch's by more than its purchase-price advantage over the five years?
Do the manufacturer's promotional photographs have identical backgrounds?
questions.explanation: Additional later expenses relative to Birch can reverse Alder's purchase-price advantage over the stated horizon. Yes means this comparative offset exceeds the initial saving and weakens the lower-total-cost justification. No removes that particular offset as a reason to reject it, without necessarily settling every other expense. Equal name lengths and photograph backgrounds have no stated cost link. The initial price comparison is already given and does not answer the broader ownership-cost question. Compare both products' relevant expenses over the same five years rather than considering Alder's later expenses in isolation.

questions.stem: Each of two rooms can hold forty participants, so an organizer concludes that the event can accommodate eighty participants at the proposed time. Which question most directly evaluates the unstated connection between the two capacities and the event's capacity?
choices: Does one room have older decorative pictures than the other?
Do the rooms' names have different initials?
Can both rooms be used for this event simultaneously at the proposed time?
Can each room individually hold forty participants?
questions.explanation: Simultaneous availability permits combining the two stated capacities for this event; lack of it blocks that particular eighty-person route. A yes does not prove every possible event requirement is satisfied, but it addresses the missing connection. Picture age and name initials have no given relation to availability or capacity. Each room's individual capacity is already a premise. Adding capacities without checking that the resources can be used together can overstate what the plan can accomplish at the required time.

questions.stem: A fictional machine saves twelve operating credits for each full week it runs and has an eighteen-credit setup cost. It can run for zero to six full weeks during the first six-week period; these are all expense changes. A planner predicts a positive saving during that period. Which question most directly resolves whether the stated cost criterion is met?
choices: Will the machine run for at least two full weeks during that first six-week period?
Will the machine's name appear on an internal sign?
Will the machine remain in the building after the first year?
Is the setup cost less than sixty credits?
questions.explanation: Two operating weeks yield twenty-four saved credits against eighteen of setup, leaving a positive six; additional weeks increase that saving. Zero or one full week cannot cover the setup cost. Thus yes and no fall on opposite sides of the relevant boundary. A name on a sign has no cost role in the complete model. Presence after a year concerns a different horizon. The setup cost is already known to be eighteen, so asking whether it is below sixty leaves the unresolved operating duration untouched.

questions.stem: An unattributed essay repeatedly uses a phrase that writer Mira also repeats in her published work. An editor takes that similarity as evidence that Mira wrote the essay. Which question would most help evaluate the identifying value of the phrase?
choices: Does the editor prefer longer essays to shorter ones?
Did many other writers in the same setting and period routinely use the same phrase?
Does Mira's name have the same number of letters as the editor's name?
Is the essay currently stored on the editor's top shelf?
questions.explanation: Widespread use by other relevant writers would reduce the phrase's value in distinguishing Mira from alternatives. Lack of such widespread use would make that particular similarity more informative, without proving authorship or excluding every other explanation. The editor's length preference, name length, and shelf choice have no supplied connection to who wrote the essay. The evaluation concerns how well the cited feature separates the proposed attribution from competing possibilities, not whether the feature merely occurs in both texts.

questions.stem: Two neighborhood newsletters report that a public garden has reopened. A reader treats the reports as two independent confirmations and concludes that the garden is open. Which question would most help assess the claimed independence of the support?
choices: Are the newsletters printed on different colors of paper?
Do both newsletters discuss unrelated community events?
Do their titles have the same number of words?
Were both reports copied from the same notice without any independent check of its accuracy?
questions.explanation: A yes reveals a shared unchecked source, weakening the claim that the reports provide two independent confirmations. A no rules out that exact shared, unchecked route but does not by itself establish independent reliable support. Other source relationships could still need examination. Paper color, unrelated coverage, and title length do not establish how the reopening reports were obtained. The reader must examine the evidence's actual source relationship rather than infer independence from the existence of two publications. The answers affect the weight of the offered corroboration without necessarily settling the garden's actual status.

questions.stem: A garden center's booking trial shortened each user's pickup queue by six minutes. The manager predicts that the system reduces users' total time arranging and completing a pickup, including advance booking. Which added finding most weakens that prediction?
choices: The booking screen uses the same colors as the center's signs.
Each user spent nine extra minutes booking, with every other time component unchanged.
Each user spent only one extra minute booking, with every other time component unchanged.
The booking system's subscription costs the center less than a competing system.
questions.explanation: Nine additional booking minutes offset the six-minute queue reduction and increase the specified total by three minutes. This accepts the reported queue improvement while defeating the broader total-time prediction for those users. Matching sign colors supplies no relevant time connection. One extra booking minute would leave a five-minute total saving and therefore support the prediction. A cheaper subscription concerns the center's expense, not users' time, without a further link supplied in the passage. Match the added evidence to the complete measure in the conclusion.

questions.stem: A lending center proposes text reminders to reduce forgotten pickups. The proposal relies on forgetful borrowers seeing the reminders before their pickup deadlines. Which finding most strengthens that proposed route?
choices: The reminder software's logo contains the center's initials.
The messages in a comparable pilot usually arrived after the pickup deadline.
Borrowers already remembering every pickup preferred a different font.
In a comparable pilot, borrowers who often forgot read timely reminders and missed fewer pickups, with other procedures unchanged.
questions.explanation: The pilot connects timely exposure among the intended borrowers to fewer missed pickups under comparable procedures. It supports uptake and the intended behavioral result without guaranteeing that every future borrower will respond. The logo does not establish any relevant link. Messages arriving after deadlines undermine the timely-reminder mechanism. A font preference among borrowers who already remember every pickup neither addresses the target group nor shows an effect on forgotten pickups. Evidence should concern the people and behavior through which the plan is expected to work.

questions.stem: A workshop currently dispatches forty parcels daily. It plans to double label-printing capacity from forty to eighty parcels per day and predicts more completed dispatches. Demand exceeds eighty daily. Which fact most weakens the output prediction?
choices: Every parcel must be packed on its dispatch day, and packing is already at its unchanged limit of forty parcels daily.
Packaging supplies are sufficient for eighty parcels daily.
The replacement printer uses the workshop's existing label format.
The printing staff can operate the new printer without additional training.
questions.explanation: Mandatory same-day packing capped at forty prevents completed dispatches from exceeding the current forty, even if labels become faster. Same-day packing excludes drawing on previously packed inventory. This identifies the bottleneck relevant to the claimed output. Supplies for eighty remove a possible obstacle rather than establish an unchanged forty-parcel ceiling. Compatible labels and trained operators support implementation of the printing improvement; neither shows that final dispatch output is limited. Faster printing could have another benefit, but this question concerns completed parcels per day.

questions.stem: A gallery predicts that adding evening hours will increase the number of distinct people visiting each week. It cites strong attendance during a trial's added hours. Which trial finding most weakens the use of that attendance as evidence of additional weekly visitors?
choices: Several visitors preferred evening lighting to afternoon lighting.
The gallery remained open during all its previously offered hours.
Every evening visitor had shifted a visit from the original hours, and the number of distinct weekly visitors was unchanged.
The gallery used the same entrance for evening and afternoon visits.
questions.explanation: Complete shifting with an unchanged distinct-person count shows displacement rather than additional weekly users. Strong evening attendance can coexist with no increase in the stated objective. A lighting preference may explain why existing visitors prefer evenings but does not establish a larger weekly population. Keeping the original opening hours does not establish that additional people attended them or the evenings. Using the same entrance has no stated connection to distinct-person counts. The finding challenges the inference from activity in the new period to growth in the whole-week result.

questions.stem: A publisher predicts that a replacement sorting line will reduce handling time during the first month after the purchase order. Once operational, the line sorts the relevant material faster. Which fact most weakens that first-month prediction?
choices: The line will remain available for several years after installation.
The operating instructions use familiar terminology.
The line can handle every material type currently processed.
Delivery and required installation cannot finish until twelve weeks after the order.
questions.explanation: A twelve-week delay prevents the faster line from operating in the claimed first month, removing the route to that period's handling-time reduction. Its later availability could matter to a longer horizon but cannot produce the specified early benefit. Familiar instructions and material compatibility address implementation obstacles favorably rather than block the first-month result. The finding does not deny that the line may save handling time once operational. It targets the period explicitly promised by the conclusion.

questions.stem: A community workshop expects a new cutting station to reduce a documented equipment queue next week. The station's demonstrated capacity is adequate, but its launch depends on obtaining a required fitting and a trained operator. Which fact most strengthens the implementation link?
choices: Another workshop has painted its cutting station yellow.
The correct fitting is installed and a qualified operator is scheduled for every planned opening period next week.
The workshop has printed posters advertising a launch date, without checking staffing.
The required fitting will be unavailable until the following month.
questions.explanation: Installed equipment and scheduled qualified coverage satisfy the two identified practical conditions for next week's launch. This strengthens implementation while leaving the final result subject to other relevant circumstances. Another workshop's paint color supplies no connection. Advertising a date without checking a requirement does not establish that the requirement can be met. An unavailable fitting directly obstructs the planned launch and weakens the route. Removing a concrete obstacle is relevant support even though it need not prove every claim about future queues.

questions.stem: A fictional archive recommends a sorter because it eliminates 120 operating credits each month and has an 80-credit monthly subscription, so monthly operating cost will fall. The only possible additional cost change is a service fee. Which fact most weakens the stated cost justification?
choices: The sorter and its replacement have the same exterior dimensions.
The service fee is ten credits per month.
A mandatory service fee adds fifty credits per month.
The subscription can be paid on either of two dates without any price difference.
questions.explanation: A fifty-credit fee produces 130 new monthly credits against 120 eliminated, an increase of ten. It defeats the stated lower-cost justification under this complete cost model. A ten-credit fee leaves a thirty-credit saving and supports rather than undermines that justification. Exterior dimensions supply no cost effect in the given model. A choice of payment date with no price difference also leaves the totals unchanged. The recommendation might have other possible reasons, but the question concerns the reason actually offered.

questions.stem: A manager predicts that a voluntary reservation tool will shorten queues by moving most users' check-in work to an advance online step. Which finding most weakens that prediction, rather than merely raising a separate concern about whether to buy the tool?
choices: Most intended users cannot complete the online step and must still do all their check-in work at the queue.
The software subscription costs more than the manager initially expected.
The software company's office is farther away than a competitor's office.
The tool's name is unpopular with the committee selecting it.
questions.explanation: If most intended users cannot complete the advance step, the plan loses its proposed way of moving their check-in work out of the queue. The higher subscription price can affect a purchase recommendation without itself showing that check-in work will stay in the queue. The company's office location has no stated connection to how the tool operates. Disliking its name likewise does not establish an effect on user check-in. A negative fact must connect to the exact prediction, not merely make the proposal less attractive on another dimension.

questions.stem: A wash station's replacement uses exactly four liters per cycle rather than six, and cycles account for all its water use. The manager predicts lower total weekly water use. Which added fact most weakens that prediction?
choices: Weekly use rises from one hundred cycles on the old station to two hundred on the replacement.
Weekly cycle counts remain fixed at one hundred.
The replacement's instruction panel uses larger lettering.
The old station and replacement fit in the same floor area.
questions.explanation: One hundred old cycles use six hundred liters, while two hundred replacement cycles use eight hundred. The increase in use more than offsets the lower per-cycle rate and undermines the total-water prediction. Keeping one hundred cycles would reduce the total from six hundred to four hundred, supporting the prediction. Larger lettering and equal floor area have no stated effect on the total cycle count or water rate. A lower rate does not settle the total without an appropriate connection between activity levels.

questions.stem: A repair studio's current sessions are fully booked. It predicts that adding two evening sessions will increase the number of distinct customers completing repairs each week. Which finding most strengthens the step from added capacity to additional customers?
choices: Existing customers say the studio's current sign is readable.
Every evening reservation was made by someone canceling a daytime reservation in the same week.
Previously unserved customers filled the pilot's new sessions and completed repairs while existing customers' weekly completions remained unchanged.
The proposed sessions have the same length as the studio's oldest sessions.
questions.explanation: The pilot shows added capacity used by previously unserved customers who actually complete the target activity, without losing existing completions. It strengthens both uptake and the distinct-customer objective. A readable sign does not connect new capacity to new customers. Customers merely replacing daytime reservations indicate displacement, not additional people. Equal session length alone does not show that anyone new will attend or complete a repair. The pilot supports a forecast under comparable conditions without guaranteeing all future weeks.

questions.stem: A studio predicts that an easier booking form will increase completed appointments. It cites a pilot in which one hundred appointments were booked, compared with eighty in the earlier comparable period. Which finding most weakens that use of the booking increase?
choices: The new form asks for fewer characters in an address field.
The studio's booking staff found the new screen easier to read.
Both periods used the same definition of a completed appointment.
Only sixty pilot appointments were completed, compared with seventy in the earlier period.
questions.explanation: The completed-appointment count falls from seventy to sixty despite the increase in bookings. This directly challenges treating more bookings as evidence of more completed appointments in the pilot. Fewer typed characters and easier screen reading concern intermediate convenience and do not establish the final outcome. A common completion definition supports comparability rather than supply an adverse result. The relevant distinction is between an initial action and the objective the plan is supposed to improve.

questions.stem: A club's stated decision rule is to adopt a storage change if it reduces retrieval time without increasing annual expense or damaging the stored materials. A trial establishes reduced retrieval time. Which finding most strengthens the recommendation under that rule?
choices: The storage units come in three decorative finishes.
A complete annual-cost check finds no increase, and a relevant materials trial finds no damage under the proposed conditions.
Club members disagree about the storage change's name.
The change requires an annual fee that exceeds all identified annual savings.
questions.explanation: The cost check and relevant materials trial address the two remaining stated decision conditions, adding support for adoption alongside the retrieval-time benefit. Decorative choices and disagreement about the name do not bear on the specified criterion. A fee exceeding all identified savings counts against the no-increase condition and therefore weakens the stated recommendation. The materials evidence supports the relevant condition without claiming that one trial proves the absence of every imaginable future risk. Use the decision rule the passage supplies rather than invent a different priority.

questions.stem: In a poll of 700 people on a cycling club's mailing list, 560 favored adding bicycle parking in the city center. A planner concludes that approximately 80 percent of the city's residents favor the addition. Which finding, if true, most weakens that conclusion?
choices: All 700 responses were entered into the poll's database without transcription errors.
The cycling club plans to publish the same results in its next newsletter.
A random sample from the complete city-resident register, with responses from everyone selected, found only 24 percent in favor.
The poll's charts accurately display 560 as 80 percent of 700.
questions.explanation: The separately selected resident sample addresses the target population and gives a sharply different result, weakening the extension from the cycling mailing list to all residents. It does not require denying that 560 original respondents favored the addition. Accurate transcription and a correctly drawn chart support the reporting of the original observations but do not establish their representativeness. Publishing the same result again supplies no new population evidence. The central issue is which people the original sample represents, not whether its arithmetic or presentation is accurate.

questions.stem: A cooperative invited every member to answer a website survey. Seventy percent of those who replied preferred a digital guide to a printed guide. The organizer infers that most members prefer the digital guide. Which finding, if true, most strengthens that inference?
choices: A random sample of the initial nonrespondents answered the same question by telephone, with everyone selected responding, and 71 percent preferred the digital guide.
The designers of the digital guide own recently manufactured phones.
Most initial nonrespondents said that they strongly preferred printed guides when contacted later.
The original survey results were reprinted in a larger typeface.
questions.explanation: The follow-up reaches a randomly selected part of the initially missing group and finds a similar preference, reducing concern that website respondents were unusual in the relevant respect. This strengthens the population inference without guaranteeing every unobserved member's preference. The designers' phone ownership does not establish members' preferences. A strong printed-guide preference among most initial nonrespondents would challenge the generalization rather than strengthen it. Reprinting the same observations changes their display without supplying new evidence about the people who did not answer.

questions.stem: A studio rejected 8 percent of submitted designs last year and 4 percent this year. Its director treats the lower rejection rate as evidence that this year's submitted designs were generally of higher quality. Which finding, if true, most weakens that use of the rates?
choices: Both percentages cover all submissions received during the same calendar quarter of their respective years.
The page numbers in the studio's published report were changed before printing.
Both percentages were calculated correctly from the recorded rejection counts and submission totals.
