This year the studio relaxed its standards and accepted several kinds of defect that required rejection last year.
questions.explanation: Relaxed standards provide a reason for the rejection rate to fall without improved submitted quality. The new information changes what the accepted rates can establish rather than denying that they were recorded. Matching calendar periods helps the comparison instead of undermining it. Changed page numbers do not affect design quality or rejection standards. Correct arithmetic supports the reported rates but cannot ensure that the same quality threshold produced them. A comparison of recorded outcomes needs a sufficiently consistent measurement rule for the inference being drawn.

questions.stem: In a trial, Sorter T misclassified 2 percent of its items and Sorter U misclassified 6 percent. An analyst infers that T's design is more reliable for the ordinary sorting work the trial was intended to represent. Which finding, if true, most strengthens that inference?
choices: Both sorters were painted the same color before testing, and neither was repainted during the trial.
Both sorters received equally difficult, randomly allocated batches of ordinary work under the same conditions and error criterion.
Sorter T received substantially easier batches than Sorter U, despite both batches being described as ordinary work.
Sorter T's brochure contains more pages and photographs of its casing than Sorter U's brochure does.
questions.explanation: Comparable workloads, conditions, and error criteria reduce important alternative reasons for the observed reliability difference. Random allocation further supports treating the batches as a fair comparison; it does not make the trial an infallible proof. Matching paint colors does not address a stated source of classification error. Easier work for T would weaken the inference that its design explains the better result. Brochure length and casing photographs provide no evidence about ordinary sorting performance. The relevant similarities concern the tasks and the measurement of success.

questions.stem: A courier delivered 60 shipments late in one month and 45 late the following month. These are complete counts under the same lateness definition. A manager concludes that a shipment was less likely to be late in the second month. Which finding, if true, most weakens that conclusion?
choices: The courier delivered 900 shipments in each month.
The courier delivered 1,200 shipments in the first month and 450 in the second.
The courier changed the color of its logo between the two months.
Both monthly counts were checked against the complete shipment records without finding errors.
questions.explanation: With 1,200 and 450 shipments, the late rates are 60/1,200 = 5 percent and 45/450 = 10 percent. The smaller late count therefore accompanies a higher late share, defeating the proposed observed-rate comparison. Equal totals of 900 would instead make 45 a smaller share than 60. A logo-color change does not establish anything about lateness. Verifying the counts supports the accepted observations without supplying their denominators. The manager's claim concerns the proportion of shipments, so raw event counts alone are insufficient.

questions.stem: Inspectors recorded 12 flawed items from Method A and 18 from Method B. An auditor concludes that Method A produced a smaller proportion of flawed items in these runs. Which finding, if true, most strengthens that comparison?
choices: Method A produced 300 items, while Method B produced 900, with every item inspected.
Method A's run began on a Monday, while Method B's report was filed on a Thursday.
Method B's report contains more pages describing the inspection procedure.
Each method produced 600 items, and every item was inspected using the same flaw criterion.
questions.explanation: Equal totals of 600 and complete inspection under one criterion make the flawed shares directly comparable: 12/600 = 2 percent for A and 18/600 = 3 percent for B. Totals of 300 and 900 would reverse the comparison, producing 4 percent for A and 2 percent for B. The named weekdays do not supply a relevant output or inspection comparison. Report length does not establish either a denominator or a consistent criterion. The added equal totals support the exact claim about these runs, not every possible future use of the methods.

questions.stem: A museum received 2,500 survey responses from people who had recently bought tickets through its website. Ninety percent favored selling tickets only online next year. The director concludes that most current attendees favor that policy. Which finding, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
choices: Seventy percent of current attendees buy tickets only in person, and a complete survey of that group found that all opposed online-only sales.
All 2,500 website-survey responses were entered into the database without transcription errors.
Recounting the same responses confirmed that 90 percent of those respondents favored online-only sales.
The museum's current tickets display its logo above the admission date.
questions.explanation: The newly described in-person group makes up a majority of the target population and opposes the policy, directly undermining the conclusion. The large website response count cannot override this evidence about a group excluded by the purchase-based selection. Accurate transcription and a confirming recount preserve the website respondents' result but do not expand its population coverage. Logo placement is unrelated to attendees' preferences. A large selected sample can still misrepresent the broader population when the selection mechanism is linked to the policy being evaluated.

questions.stem: Thirty incoming trainees tested a new assembly manual and made fewer errors than comparable trainees using the old manual. An instructor predicts that the new manual will reduce similar errors among next term's incoming trainees. Which finding, if true, most strengthens the extension to that group?
choices: The new manual has a different cover color from the old manual.
Next term's tasks will require techniques that were absent from the trial.
The trial participants were randomly selected from next term's incoming class, whose training will use the same tasks and error definitions.
The storage shelves in next term's classroom will be repainted before instruction begins.
questions.explanation: Selection from the target class and continuity of tasks and scoring make the trial more informative about the specified future group. They support the extension without guaranteeing that every trainee will improve. A different cover color has no stated connection to assembly errors. Techniques absent from the trial would make transfer to next term less secure rather than stronger. Repainting shelves does not address trainee characteristics, task demands, or measurement. A result in observed cases needs relevant support before it is extended to a broader group or later setting.

questions.stem: Team Aspen completed a smaller percentage of its tasks late than Team Birch did. A reviewer infers that Aspen performs better than Birch on comparable tasks. Which finding, if true, most weakens that inference?
choices: Both teams used the same definition of late completion when recording their results.
Both teams completed the same total number of tasks during the period being compared.
The teams' names are printed in identical typefaces in the report.
In each of the only two task categories, Birch's late rate was lower; Aspen handled a much larger share of the easier category.
questions.explanation: The category-specific results favor Birch on comparable work, while the different task mixture explains how Aspen can still have a better overall rate. The aggregate advantage therefore does not establish superior performance on comparable tasks. A common lateness definition supports measurement consistency. Equal total task counts do not ensure equal proportions of easy and difficult tasks. Identical typography has no bearing on performance. Group composition can change an overall percentage even when the within-category comparisons point in the other direction.

questions.stem: In the second of two annual town surveys, residents reported more park visits than in the first. A council member takes the difference as evidence that residents made more park visits in the second year's survey period. Which finding, if true, most strengthens that comparison?
choices: The second survey counted walking past a park as a visit, while the first required entering the park.
The same randomly selected residents answered both rounds using the same question wording, visit definition, season, and length of reporting period.
Printed copies of both survey reports were stored in the same filing cabinet.
The park names were placed in alphabetical order in the second report's appendix.
questions.explanation: Keeping respondents and relevant measurement conditions consistent makes the reported change better evidence of a change in visits rather than a change in who answered or what counted. It does not eliminate every possible reporting error. Counting passersby only in the second round would weaken the comparison by broadening the measure. Shared storage and alphabetical ordering change neither the underlying visits nor the survey's comparability. The useful added information concerns the meaning and scope of the observations, not the arrangement of the resulting documents.

questions.stem: Complete annual member polls found that 60 percent supported repairing a club's hall last year, compared with 40 percent this year. The secretary concludes that fewer members now support repair. Which finding, if true, most weakens that conclusion?
choices: The club had exactly 1,000 members in each year.
Both polls used the same preference question and the same answer choices.
The club had 1,000 members last year and 2,000 members this year.
This year's report was printed on paper of a different color.
questions.explanation: The changing membership totals give 600 repair supporters last year and 800 this year. The proportion fell while the number rose, defeating the secretary's count conclusion without disputing either percentage. Equal totals of 1,000 would support a fall from 600 to 400 supporters. Matching question wording and choices helps comparability but does not determine the membership totals. Paper color is irrelevant to preference counts. Read whether the conclusion concerns a number or a share before deciding what a percentage change establishes.

questions.stem: A service surveyed every person who subscribed at the year's start and renewed at its end. Eighty percent were satisfied with the service. Only renewers were surveyed, but the company concludes that most people who subscribed at the year's start were satisfied. Which finding, if true, most strengthens that conclusion?
choices: An independent random sample of the start-of-year subscribers who canceled answered the same question, with everyone selected responding, and 81 percent were satisfied.
Many start-of-year subscribers who canceled identified dissatisfaction with the service as their main reason.
The service had already operated for five years before the survey year began.
The company changed its logo after the survey results were collected.
questions.explanation: The independent follow-up supplies relevant evidence about the missing former subscribers and finds satisfaction similar to that of renewers. It reduces the survivorship concern without guaranteeing the preferences of every unsurveyed canceler. Dissatisfaction as a frequent cancellation reason would challenge the extension from renewers instead. The service's age alone does not establish this group's satisfaction during the target year. A later logo change does not address their reported experience. When the target includes former participants, observations limited to those who remain need support for the omitted group.

questions.stem:
A fictional archive follows this exact rule today: every request approved for digitization has a tracking number. Request Tern has a tracking number today. An analyst concludes that Tern is approved for digitization today.

Which description most precisely identifies the reasoning error?
choices: It treats a condition required for approval as though that condition guarantees approval.
It treats a sufficient condition for approval as though that condition cannot occur without approval.
It infers that the request lacks approval because a required tracking number is absent.
It infers that a tracking number cannot be assigned because approval is absent.
questions.explanation: Approval implies a tracking number, but a tracking number does not imply approval. Tern could be numbered while awaiting approval; that case preserves both premises and defeats the conclusion. The tracking number is not established as sufficient for approval, so describing an established sufficient condition misstates the given rule. No tracking number is said to be absent, and the argument does not infer a lack of approval. Approval is also not said to be absent, and the argument does not conclude that numbering is impossible. The mistake is the unsupported converse, not a valid inference from a missing necessary condition.

questions.stem:
A fictional service desk guarantees that any request marked urgent receives a same-day response. Request Lumen is not marked urgent. A clerk concludes that Lumen will not receive a same-day response.

Which possibility demonstrates why the conclusion does not follow?
choices: Lumen is marked urgent and receives a same-day response.
Lumen is not marked urgent and receives no same-day response.
Lumen is not marked urgent and nevertheless receives a same-day response.
Lumen is marked urgent and receives no same-day response.
questions.explanation: A nonurgent request with a same-day response obeys the guarantee, preserves Lumen's stated nonurgent status, and makes the clerk's conclusion false. The guarantee supplies one sufficient condition for that response, not the only route to it. A nonurgent request without a same-day response makes the conclusion true, so it does not refute the inference. An urgent request with a same-day response fits the general rule but contradicts Lumen's stated status. An urgent request without that response contradicts both the rule and the stated status. The clerk has used the unsupported inverse.

questions.stem:
In a fictional permit system, a proposal receives expedited review whenever it is complete and endorsed by a supervisor. Proposal Alba is complete. An official therefore concludes that Alba receives expedited review.

Which description best identifies the gap?
choices: The official infers completeness from expedited review rather than applying the rule forward.
The official uses one part of a joint sufficient condition without establishing the other part.
The official infers a lack of expedited review from a lack of completeness.
The official fails to rule out proposals that are both complete and endorsed.
questions.explanation: The rule requires completeness and endorsement together to guarantee expedited review. Endorsement has not been established. Alba could be complete, unendorsed, and not expedited without breaking the rule. The argument does not reason backward from expedited review to completeness. It does not assert a lack of completeness or conclude a lack of review. Complete and endorsed proposals are precisely the cases to which the rule applies; they need not be ruled out. The defect is a dropped input, not a converse or inverse inference.

questions.stem:
A fictional inventory follows this exact rule today: if a device is tagged for loan or reserved for display, or both, it has both an inspection record and a custody record. Device Oriole has no custody record today. An auditor concludes that Oriole is neither tagged for loan nor reserved for display today.

Which assessment of the auditor's reasoning is correct?
choices: It is flawed because a missing custody record establishes only that the inspection record is also missing.
It is flawed because the rule permits a loan tag without either required record.
It is flawed because an either-or input allows exactly one of the two input conditions to survive.
It is valid because the absence of one required output excludes each independently sufficient input.
questions.explanation: The rule is (loan tag or display reservation) → (inspection record and custody record). A missing custody record makes the whole required output false. Its contrapositive establishes neither loan tag nor display reservation. The inspection record could still exist, so its absence is not established. A loan tag without both required records would violate the rule. The inclusive input means either condition alone would require the custody record; with that record missing, neither input can hold. Calling every reversed inference a flaw would miss valid contraposition here.

questions.stem:
A fictional studio stipulates that every approved shipment travels in a rigid case or receives a foam lining, or both. Shipment Sable has no foam lining. A coordinator concludes that Sable is not approved.

Which description most precisely identifies the flaw?
choices: The coordinator treats one alternative way to satisfy a requirement as though it were individually necessary.
The coordinator assumes that a shipment with both protective features must violate the requirement.
The coordinator attributes the studio's overall shipping capacity to each individual shipment.
The coordinator infers approval from the presence of one protective feature.
questions.explanation: An approved Sable could travel in a rigid case without foam lining. That case satisfies the rule and the missing-foam premise while making the conclusion false. Either protective feature can satisfy the stated output, so foam alone is not required. Although excluding shipments with both features would misread inclusive or, the coordinator does not make that claim. No property of the studio as a whole is transferred to a shipment. The conclusion denies approval; it does not infer approval from a protective feature. The actual error concerns treating one disjunct as necessary.

questions.stem:
A fictional registry follows this rule: if an application is signed and dated, it is entered in the ledger. Application Rowan is not entered in the ledger. A reviewer concludes that Rowan is neither signed nor dated.

Which assessment is correct?
choices: The rule establishes that Rowan is signed, although it leaves the date unknown.
The reviewer correctly negates the joint input by requiring both parts to be false.
The rule establishes that at least one input is absent, but the reviewer concludes that both are absent.
The reviewer wrongly treats ledger entry as enough to establish both a signature and a date.
questions.explanation: Contraposition gives not entered → not (signed and dated), equivalent to not signed or not dated. Rowan could be signed but undated and not entered, or dated but unsigned and not entered. Either case refutes the stronger neither-nor conclusion. No signature is established by the rule and missing entry alone. Requiring both inputs to fail confuses not both with neither. The reviewer is reasoning from a missing ledger entry, not from its presence, so a description of inferring signature and date from ledger entry identifies a different error.

questions.stem:
A fictional tour consists of exactly four stages traveled consecutively with no overlap. Each stage takes less than an hour. A guide concludes that the entire tour, including any waits between stages, takes less than an hour.

Which description most precisely identifies the flaw?
choices: The guide assumes that any difference between the four stages prevents their durations from being compared.
The guide treats the duration of the whole tour as a guarantee about each stage's exact duration.
The guide mistakes a necessary condition for a sufficient condition in an explicit if-then rule.
The guide transfers a duration bound on every part to the whole without accounting for combined time.
questions.explanation: Four twenty-minute stages already total eighty minutes, even if there are no waits. This countermodel preserves the bound on every stage but defeats the bound on the whole. Consecutive durations accumulate, so the part-level bound does not transfer unchanged. The guide does not reject comparisons because stages differ. The reasoning moves from stage durations to total duration, not from the whole to each part. No explicit conditional relating a necessary and sufficient condition is being reversed. The exact problem is the unsupported part-to-whole transfer.

questions.stem:
A fictional help team consists of three specialists. Collectively, the team can provide assistance in all six languages on its service list: for each listed language, at least one team member speaks it. A manager concludes that every team member speaks all six languages.

Which description best identifies the error?
choices: The manager assumes that exactly one specialist speaks each listed language.
The manager assigns the team's collective range of abilities to each member without support.
The manager infers the team's collective range solely from a universal claim about its members.
The manager rejects a comparison because the specialists have different job titles.
questions.explanation: Each specialist could speak a different pair of the six languages. The team would cover all six collectively while no member covered all six individually. The premise permits this division of abilities, so it does not establish the manager's conclusion. Exactly one speaker per language is neither asserted nor needed for collective coverage; the manager instead concludes that all three specialists speak every listed language. The argument begins with a collective claim, not with a universal claim that every member speaks all six. No comparison is rejected and no difference in job titles is supplied. The flaw is an unsupported group-to-member transfer.

questions.stem:
A fictional inspection team has this property: every current member holds a current access permit. Iona is a current member of the team. A coordinator concludes that Iona holds a current access permit.

Which assessment is correct?
choices: It commits a division flaw because any inference from a team-related premise to a member is invalid.
It commits a composition flaw because Iona's membership is used to establish a property of the team.
It validly applies a property expressly attributed to every member to a person known to be a member.
It uses the converse because permit possession is treated as proof of team membership.
questions.explanation: The premise expressly states that every current member has a current permit, and Iona is such a member. The conclusion therefore follows. This is not an unsupported transfer of a collective property: the property was already attributed to each individual member. No inference is made from Iona's property to a property of the whole team. The argument also does not infer membership from permit possession; it starts with membership and applies the given universal rule. Labels about parts and wholes must fit the actual quantifier and support direction.

questions.stem:
In a fictional district, Cedar Archive reduced its document-retrieval delays after adopting a new training course. Birch Archive has the same number of employees and uses filing cabinets of the same color. A consultant concludes that adopting the course will probably reduce Birch's retrieval delays as well. The argument provides no information about whether the archives face similar retrieval tasks or sources of delay.

Which criticism most directly addresses the reasoning?
choices: The argument relies on shared features without establishing similarities relevant to how the course might reduce delays.
The argument is defective because two archives must be identical in every respect before comparison can support a forecast.
The argument is defective because a conclusion about a probable result requires premises that guarantee that result.
The argument treats every employee's individual retrieval speed as equal to the archive's total retrieval speed.
questions.explanation: The projected training benefit depends on whether the course addresses comparable tasks or causes of delay. Equal staffing and cabinet color do not establish that connection. The relevant criticism identifies the missing basis for transferring the result. An analogy does not require identity in every respect; irrelevant differences need not matter. A probabilistic conclusion can have support without a deductive guarantee. No individual speed is equated with total archive speed, so a part-whole description does not match the passage. The criticism also need not prove that Birch will receive no benefit.

questions.stem:
Two fictional heater prototypes have the same heating mechanism, container size, insulation, and liquid volume. A test of Prototype A, starting at 20 degrees, reaches 40 degrees after ten minutes. An engineer predicts that B, tested under the same conditions, will probably take about the same time, while acknowledging that a direct test could reveal a difference. The prototypes have different display fonts, which are stipulated to have no effect on heating.

Which assessment best fits the engineer's comparison?
choices: The different display fonts defeat the inference because any difference makes an analogy unusable.
The shared features prove that both prototypes must perform identically under every possible condition.
The prediction follows by contraposition from a rule requiring every heated liquid to reach 40 degrees.
The comparison offers relevant support for a limited prediction, and the stipulated font difference does not itself undermine it.
questions.explanation: Matching features that bear on heating, with matching starting and testing conditions, supports the modest prediction. The passage expressly makes the font difference irrelevant to heating, so that difference alone is no reason to reject the analogy. The engineer does not claim identical performance under every possible condition, and the stated similarities do not establish that universal guarantee. No conditional with the alleged temperature requirement is given, so contraposition does not describe the reasoning. Relevant similarities can support a forecast without eliminating all uncertainty.

questions.stem:
A fictional association requires every certified project to have an audit record. Project Vireo has an audit record. An author concludes that Vireo is certified. A critic correctly notes that the author has reversed the stated conditional, then concludes that Vireo must therefore be uncertified.

Which assessment of the critic is correct?
choices: Identifying the reversed conditional establishes that the audit-record premise must be false.
The critic identifies a support failure but wrongly treats that failure as proof that the author's conclusion is false.
The critic's final conclusion follows because the original rule guarantees that audited projects are uncertified.
The critic should reject the original rule because its converse is always false whenever the original is true.
questions.explanation: The rule and audit record allow Vireo to be certified or uncertified. The author's conclusion is not established, but it could still be true. The critic therefore adds an unwarranted claim when declaring Vireo uncertified. Identifying a reasoning error does not refute the accepted audit-record premise. The rule requires an audit record for certified projects; it does not prohibit certification for audited ones. A converse can happen to be true in a particular setting even though the original conditional does not establish it, so it is not always false. Both evaluations must distinguish unsupported from disproved.

questions.stem: The new cabinets at Wren Archive prevent rainwater from reaching the documents inside them. The archivist concludes that documents stored in these cabinets cannot be damaged. Which description most accurately identifies the flaw?
choices: It treats evidence about possible future damage as proof that the documents have already been damaged.
It assumes that rainwater must damage every document that is not stored in one of the new cabinets.
It treats protection against one possible cause of damage as establishing protection against every possible cause.
It concludes that protection from rainwater is unnecessary because other possible causes of damage might remain.
questions.explanation: Preventing rainwater exposure addresses one possible cause of damage. The conclusion excludes damage from any cause, without addressing other possibilities such as mishandling. The argument makes no claim that damage has already occurred, so the description involving past damage misstates the conclusion. It also does not say that rainwater damages every document outside the new cabinets; that accusation adds a claim about unprotected documents. Finally, the archivist treats rainwater protection as enough, rather than declaring it unnecessary. The cabinets may be useful even though the stated guarantee exceeds the support offered.

questions.stem: No surviving record mentions repairs to the clock in Alder Pavilion. A historian therefore concludes that the clock has never been repaired. The historian's reasoning is most vulnerable because it does what?
choices: Treats the absence of surviving documentation of an event as establishing that the event never occurred.
Rejects the contents of surviving records merely because their authors might have wanted the clock repaired.
Treats evidence that the clock currently works as establishing that every earlier repair was successful.
Assumes that a repair mentioned in one historical record must also be mentioned in every other record.
questions.explanation: A repair could have occurred without its documentation surviving. Nothing establishes that every repair would necessarily appear in the surviving records, so their silence does not justify the definite historical conclusion. The historian does not reject any record because of its author's wishes. The clock's current functioning is not offered as evidence, and the argument reaches no judgment about repair quality. Nor does it assume that one recorded repair must appear in all other records: no recorded repair is identified. Absence of documentation can matter when record completeness is established, but that connection is missing here.

questions.stem: Mara proposes one additional ferry crossing on Friday evenings during the summer. A critic replies, "Mara wants the ferry to run continuously every night throughout the year, regardless of demand. That would waste resources, so her proposal should be rejected." What is the central flaw in the critic's response?
choices: It rejects Mara's proposal solely because she would personally benefit from the additional summer crossing.
It infers that Friday demand is high from information about demand on other days of the week.
It treats the current ferry schedule as evidence that the proposed additional crossing would save resources.
It substitutes a substantially broader proposal for Mara's actual proposal and then attacks that substitute.
questions.explanation: One extra crossing on summer Fridays differs from continuous service every night all year. The critic's resource objection targets the expanded substitute, so it does not establish the stated objection to Mara's actual proposal. Nothing says Mara would benefit personally; the response does not attack her interests. No information about demand on other days is used to infer Friday demand. The critic also does not use the current schedule to predict savings, instead predicting waste from the exaggerated proposal. Mara's proposal might have other weaknesses, but this response has not identified them.

questions.stem: Rena recommends extending a gallery's opening hours, citing independently maintained entrance records showing people arriving after closing. An opponent responds, "Rena is applying to manage evening shifts and would benefit from longer hours. Therefore, the entrance records she cites must be inaccurate." Which criticism most precisely addresses the opponent's reasoning?
choices: It concludes that longer hours cannot help visitors merely because Rena has not proved that they would help.
It treats Rena's possible personal interest as sufficient reason to reject the independently maintained records she cites.
It relies on the entrance records to settle whether Rena would perform competently as an evening manager.
It assumes that independently maintained records establish that anyone citing them has no personal financial interest.
questions.explanation: Rena's interest may motivate scrutiny of her recommendation, but it does not establish that the independently maintained records are inaccurate. The opponent needs a connection between that interest and a defect in the records. The conclusion concerns the records' accuracy, not whether longer hours could ever help visitors, so the description of a rejected benefit prediction targets a different claim. The opponent does not use the records to assess Rena's managerial competence. It also explicitly recognizes her possible interest, rather than inferring that citing independent records eliminates such an interest. The source concern must match the evidence's actual provenance.

questions.stem: Orin is an acclaimed architect with no experience studying grammar or designing language instruction. Orin endorses a new grammar workbook. A committee argues, "Orin's architectural judgment is outstanding, so this workbook must teach grammar accurately." Which description best captures the committee's error?
choices: It treats demonstrated competence in one field as sufficient authority for a claim requiring knowledge of another field.
It infers that the workbook is widely popular merely from evidence that the workbook teaches grammar accurately.
It dismisses Orin's recommendation because an architect could receive personal benefits from endorsing a workbook.
It concludes that grammar instruction must follow the same design principles as the construction of a building.
questions.explanation: The offered support is Orin's architectural competence, which supplies no established expertise about grammar accuracy. Relying on a relevant expert can provide evidence; the problem is the unsupported transfer of authority between these fields. The committee makes no popularity claim, and workbook accuracy is its conclusion rather than an accepted premise. It endorses Orin's recommendation instead of dismissing it because of personal benefit. It also does not claim that grammar and buildings obey identical design principles; that description invents a specific theory the argument never presents. The workbook could be accurate, but the offered credential does not establish that.

questions.stem: A sealed crate has arrived at the Lantern Guild. No member has inspected it or received information about its contents, but most members believe that it contains ceramic bowls. The chair concludes that it contains ceramic bowls because that belief is so widely shared. What is the flaw?
choices: It assumes that a claim cannot be true unless every member of the guild accepts the claim.
It treats an inspection of the crate's contents as evidence of what most members previously believed.
It treats the prevalence of an uninformed belief as sufficient evidence that the believed claim is true.
It infers that members want ceramic bowls from evidence that they know the crate contains ceramic bowls.
questions.explanation: The members' shared belief establishes something about their opinions, but the passage supplies no informed basis linking those opinions to the crate's actual contents. The chair uses agreement as a substitute for such evidence. The chair does not require unanimous belief for truth; the stated premise concerns most members. No inspection took place, so an inspection cannot be the offered evidence about earlier opinions. The argument also draws no conclusion about what the members want and does not establish that they know the contents. The criticism concerns the use of opinion to establish the external fact, not the existence of the opinion itself.

questions.stem: A librarian says, "Our catalog classifications are accurate because our checking system approves them. We know the checking system is reliable because its judgments agree with our catalog classifications." These are the only grounds offered for either assessment. Which flaw is present?
choices: It assumes that a classification becomes inaccurate whenever a checking system changes an earlier judgment.
It uses each of two assessments to justify the other without providing an independent basis for either.
It rejects an outside assessment of the catalog on the ground that outside assessors lack library experience.
It moves from the reliability of this particular checking system to the reliability of every checking system.
questions.explanation: Catalog accuracy is supported by system approval, while system reliability is supported by agreement with that same catalog. Without an independent reason to trust either, the assessments circle back to one another. No changed judgment is described, so the argument does not identify changes as a cause of inaccuracy. No outside assessment is introduced or rejected on expertise grounds. The conclusion also remains about this catalog and its checking system; it does not generalize to every checking system. The error is the dependence of each offered justification on the other unestablished assessment, regardless of whether both assessments happen to be true.

questions.stem: A coordinator says that a festival's attendance forecast is too optimistic. The chair replies, "Accepting that assessment would discourage several volunteers. Therefore, the attendance forecast is accurate." Which description most accurately identifies the chair's flaw?
choices: It uses evidence about attendance at an earlier festival to infer that volunteers will remain enthusiastic this year.
It rejects the coordinator's assessment because the coordinator lacks experience managing volunteers at this festival.
It treats the usefulness of an accurate forecast as evidence that the volunteers want to prepare a new forecast.
It treats an undesirable consequence of accepting a criticism as establishing that the criticized forecast is accurate.
questions.explanation: A belief's effect on volunteer enthusiasm does not establish whether the forecast accurately predicts attendance. Even if the stated discouragement would occur, the forecast could still be too optimistic. No earlier attendance evidence supports a prediction about enthusiasm. The chair does not challenge the coordinator's experience, so an attack on qualifications is not the stated reasoning. Nor does the chair infer that volunteers want to prepare another forecast from the usefulness of accuracy. The specific move is from a consequence of accepting criticism to a factual conclusion about the forecast.

questions.stem: An attendance register identifies every participant in today's workshop. There is one completed feedback form from each participant, and every form requests a longer break. The organizer concludes that every participant in today's workshop requested a longer break. A critic rejects that conclusion because people who did not attend today's workshop were not surveyed. What is wrong with the critic's objection?
choices: It assumes that the register excludes some attendees despite an explicit statement that the register identifies them all.
It assumes that a request for a longer break establishes that every participant disliked the workshop as a whole.
It treats the opinions of nonattendees as sufficient evidence that today's attendees submitted different feedback forms.
It objects to the failure to support a conclusion about a broader group than the organizer's conclusion concerns.
questions.explanation: The organizer's conclusion concerns only today's participants, all of whom are covered by the given forms. Failure to survey nonattendees does not undermine that limited conclusion. The critic never challenges the register's coverage of actual attendees; the objection concerns people outside that group. It also does not infer overall dissatisfaction from a request for a longer break. No nonattendee opinions are actually supplied, and the critic does not use them to show that different forms were submitted. The flaw is the mismatch between the population the criticism demands and the population the organizer actually addresses.

questions.stem: Ada is assessing two courtyard designs specifically for how well they support quiet reading. The East design uses locally made tiles, while the West design does not. Offering only this difference as her reason, Ada concludes that East is the better design for quiet reading. Which criticism identifies the unsupported step?
choices: Ada has not established that locally made tiles could be included in either of the two courtyard designs.
Ada has not connected the tiles' place of manufacture to the criterion used to judge the courtyard designs.
Ada treats her preference for East as evidence that the builders themselves also prefer the East design.
Ada assumes that the two designs are identical in every respect because both are intended as courtyards.
questions.explanation: The stated criterion is suitability for quiet reading. A difference in tile origins needs a connection to that criterion before it supports the comparative conclusion. It is already given that East uses locally made tiles, so questioning whether either design could include them overlooks a premise. Ada reaches no conclusion about the builders' preferences. She also expressly cites a difference, rather than treating the designs as identical. The flaw is not that local production can never matter to a decision; it is that its relevance to this decision's specified criterion has not been established.

questions.stem: Established records date the opening of Bell Tower to twenty years before Pavo was born. Pavo nevertheless claims to remember personally seeing a blue tower at that opening. A historian relies solely on Pavo's claimed eyewitness memory to conclude that the tower was blue when it opened. Which criticism is warranted?
choices: The historian treats disagreement among several eyewitnesses as sufficient reason to accept whichever account was recorded last.
The historian assumes that a witness's preference for blue buildings establishes the actual color of Bell Tower.
The historian relies on claimed firsthand knowledge that the established chronology shows the source could not have acquired.
The historian rejects a source's account merely because the source has no professional training in architectural history.
questions.explanation: Someone born twenty years after an opening could not have personally witnessed that opening. This chronological conflict directly undermines the claimed firsthand basis on which the historian relies. Accepting that Pavo made the statement does not require accepting its content as true. No disagreement among multiple eyewitnesses or rule favoring the latest account is given. Pavo's color preferences are not stated. The historian accepts the account rather than rejecting it for lack of professional training. This is a relevant source criticism because it challenges the specific opportunity to observe, not an unrelated personal characteristic. The actual opening color remains unsettled by this testimony.

questions.stem: For a small exhibition, completing the incoming loan inventory means confirming that every expected loan object has arrived and been logged. The records confirm that every such object has arrived and been logged. The organizer reasons, "Our loan inventory is therefore complete. Consequently, the exhibition is ready to open." Which description locates the flaw in this chain?
choices: It treats completion of the loan inventory as sufficient to establish that the exhibition's other required preparations are complete.
It treats the exhibition's readiness as the evidence for the claim that every expected loan object has arrived.
It applies a requirement about every expected loan object even though the stated inventory standard concerns only some loan objects.
It assumes that an incomplete inventory establishes that opening the exhibition at any future time will be impossible.
questions.explanation: The records satisfy the supplied definition of a completed loan inventory, so that intermediate step is supported. Moving from completed inventory to readiness to open leaves other preparation, such as arranging displays, unaddressed. The description using readiness as evidence for arrived objects reverses the argument's direction: readiness is the final conclusion. The inventory standard expressly concerns every expected loan object, so the accusation involving a standard about only some objects contradicts the premise. The organizer also asserts that inventory is complete, not that an incomplete inventory makes every future opening impossible. A correct diagnosis identifies the unsupported final step without attacking the supported intermediate step.

questions.stem: Paint peeled from all tested boards that used varnish V and stood in direct light. One hypothesis says varnish V causes peeling in either tested lighting condition and varnish W does not. Another says direct light causes peeling with either varnish, while shade does not. Which test best distinguishes these stated accounts?
choices: Observe more boards coated with varnish V in the same direct light.
Compare both varnishes under direct light and shade while holding other relevant conditions fixed.
Confirm again that the original boards had both varnish V and direct light.
Ask whether observers found the original peeling surprising.
questions.explanation: Crossing varnish type with light condition separates the two proposed factors. V in shade and W in direct light generate different expectations under the stated hypotheses. More V boards in direct light or another confirmation of the initial pairing repeats conditions both accounts predict will produce peeling. Observer surprise supplies no evidence about which proposed process caused the pattern. The useful comparison changes one proposed factor while retaining control over the other and over relevant background conditions.

questions.stem: Two explanations for stains in a storeroom both predict that the room was damp. One says dampness alone produced the stains; the other says dampness combined with a particular coating did. A new record confirms that the room was damp. What is the best assessment of that record?
choices: It proves that the coating played no role.
It proves that the coating was necessary for every stain.
It has no possible relevance to any investigation of the stains.
It supports a condition shared by both accounts but does little by itself to distinguish them.
questions.explanation: Dampness is expected under both stated explanations, so confirming it does not settle whether the coating also mattered. The record proves neither that coating had no role nor that it was necessary for all stains. Calling it irrelevant to every investigation goes too far: it could bear on a third account that denies dampness. Evidence can support a shared condition without strongly discriminating between the two rivals currently being compared.

questions.stem: Two shop directories contain the same obsolete room number. One explanation says both compilers copied room information from an outdated list; a rival says they independently verified all room numbers on site. Production logs show that both used the outdated list and neither conducted on-site checks. What is most directly supported?
choices: The common-source explanation is favored over the stated independent-verification explanation for the shared room error.
Every entry and every sentence in both directories must have been copied.
Both compilers knowingly intended to mislead readers.
Any repeated error always proves copying, even without production records.
questions.explanation: The logs directly identify a common source for room information and rule out the rival verification process as stated. That supports an explanation of this shared error. It does not establish that all wording was copied, that either compiler intended deception, or that a repeated error by itself always proves copying. Those alternatives extend the conclusion beyond the specific process and evidence given. Preserve both the scope of the explanatory target and the stronger evidence supplied by the logs.

questions.stem: A proposed process predicts that a visible ring will appear after at least forty minutes under the stated conditions. All required conditions are present, but inspection stops after ten minutes and finds no ring. An investigator rejects the process solely on that basis. What is the main problem?
choices: A missing observation can never count against any proposed explanation.
The absence of a ring proves that a different process caused the result.
The inspection ended before the stated prediction required the ring to appear.
Any process that mentions time is impossible to test.
questions.explanation: The prediction concerns a ring after at least forty minutes, so a ten-minute absence does not conflict with it. Missing observations can count against a hypothesis when its relevant conditions, timing, and detection requirements are satisfied. The early absence does not establish a rival cause. Time-dependent processes can be tested by observing for an appropriate duration. The error lies in treating an inadequately timed check as a failed prediction, not in the general idea of testing explanations.

questions.stem: A machine buzzes. One account says a loose panel vibrates; a rival says an internal motor alone produces the buzz regardless of the panel. With motor operation and all other relevant conditions fixed, repeatedly fastening the panel stops the buzz and loosening it restores the buzz. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: No internal motor can ever produce a buzz in any machine.
Every noise this machine has made must have come from the panel.
The two stated accounts receive exactly equal support from the result.
The panel account is favored over the stated motor-only account in this test.
questions.explanation: Repeatedly changing the panel condition while holding motor operation and other relevant conditions fixed makes the result fit the panel account and conflict with a motor-only account that predicts independence from the panel. That supports a relative conclusion for this test. It does not establish a universal claim about motors or explain every noise across the machine’s history. Equal support ignores the accounts’ different predictions. Evidence that distinguishes two specified explanations need not settle every imaginable alternative or interaction.

questions.stem: A hypothesis predicts a test strip will turn blue after thirty minutes if a sample is neutral in acidity. After thirty minutes the strip has not changed, but the sample’s acidity is unknown. An analyst declares the hypothesis false. Which unresolved issue most directly matters?
choices: Whether the hypothesis uses fewer words than competing descriptions.
Whether the sample was neutral in acidity, as required for the prediction.
Whether a competing account predicts no color change in acidic samples.
Whether every imaginable explanation has already been listed.
questions.explanation: Neutral acidity is an auxiliary condition needed for the stated color prediction. Without knowing whether it held, the missing color does not by itself establish a failed prediction under the hypothesis’s required circumstances. Wording length does not address that condition. A rival prediction about acidic samples does not establish whether this sample was neutral, so it does not settle whether the original hypothesis received a valid test. Exhaustively listing all imaginable explanations is unnecessary to see this specific gap. The task is to check whether the test satisfied the prediction’s conditions before rejecting the hypothesis on the basis of the absent result.

questions.stem: A factory records fewer leaks but greater total fluid loss. One proposed explanation says corrosion enlarged the remaining leak openings, increasing average fluid loss per leak enough to outweigh the lower count. An analyst says that because this explanation could reconcile the observations, it must be the actual and sole cause of the result. Which criticism is most appropriate?
choices: Any explanation involving fluid volume contradicts a statement about leak counts.
An explanation is useful only if it establishes that both observations are false.
The analyst treats an account’s ability to fit the observations as proof that it actually occurred and excludes all alternatives.
The analyst should reject any explanation that introduces a mechanism not directly mentioned in the original observations.
questions.explanation: The proposed corrosion process could raise average loss per leak enough to reconcile the lower count and higher total. Compatibility does not establish that corrosion actually occurred or that no other influence contributed. Fluid volume is relevant to the count-total relationship, so its mention is no contradiction. Denying both observations abandons reconciliation. A proposed mechanism can be a useful explanation even when the original observations do not directly mention it; that possibility still needs evidence before being accepted as the actual and sole cause. The mistake is the jump from explanatory possibility to exclusive causal proof.

questions.stem: Two explanations fit an initial observation. The shorter explanation predicts that objects in a specified comparison group will also change color; the longer explanation predicts that they will not. A reliable check under the stated conditions finds no color change in that group. A student chooses the shorter explanation solely because it is shorter. What is the best assessment?
choices: Length alone does not overcome the observation that conflicts with the shorter explanation’s stated prediction.
The longer explanation must explain every observation in every setting because it fits this one result.
The comparison result has no bearing on explanations once they fit an initial observation.
The shorter explanation is always correct regardless of any contrary test result.
questions.explanation: The comparison observation matters because the accounts make different predictions, and it conflicts with the shorter account under the specified conditions. Brevity does not automatically defeat that evidential difference. The result favors the longer account in this comparison without proving universal explanatory success. Ignoring later tests freezes the judgment at the initial observation. Automatically preferring a shorter explanation regardless of contrary evidence substitutes a superficial rule for assessing fit and predictions.

questions.stem: An account originally predicted that every tested tile from batch K would crack in either of two temperature conditions. Cool K tiles remain intact. Its defender now says K tiles crack only in the warmer condition and claims the original account predicted this outcome all along. Which response is most accurate?
choices: The account has been revised; its new prediction should be acknowledged and assessed with appropriate evidence.
Any revision after new evidence is forbidden, so the revised account must be false.
The intact cool tiles directly confirm the original prediction that they would crack.
Calling the new statement an explanation makes further testing unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The original prediction included cracking in the cool condition, whereas the revision excludes it. Changing an account can be reasonable, but the changed claim cannot be credited as an unchanged successful prediction of the earlier result. The revision is not automatically false merely because it is a revision. Intact tiles conflict with, rather than confirm, the original cracking prediction. A new label or account does not eliminate the need for evidence bearing on its distinguishing expectations.

questions.stem: A delivery delay could have resulted from late sorting or from slow label printing. An audit shows that sorting finished at its usual time, while a documented printer stoppage added an hour before departure; all subsequent steps took their usual time. Which inference is best supported?
choices: Sorting speed can never affect departure times on any day.
The two explanations fit the audited sequence equally well.
The audit favors the printing explanation over an explanation locating this delay entirely in late sorting.
Every departure delay throughout the delivery company has the same cause.
questions.explanation: The audit places an added hour at label printing and finds no delay in sorting or subsequent steps. That distinguishes the explanations for this recorded departure. It does not show that sorting is irrelevant on other days or that every company delay has a printer cause. Equal support ignores the timing evidence that the late-sorting account fails to match. The justified conclusion is comparative and specific to the audited sequence, not universal across all future or historical departures.

questions.stem: For a particular late dispatch, records show that sorting ended twenty minutes late and a printer stoppage then added another thirty minutes. An investigator insists that only one of those two stages can have contributed to the delay. What is the best assessment?
choices: Neither stage can contribute because two changes occurred.
The recorded stages can both contribute; the evidence does not require an exclusive choice between them.
The first delayed stage must account for every later minute, whatever the records show.
The last delayed stage proves that sorting finished on time.
questions.explanation: The sequence explicitly contains twenty minutes of sorting delay followed by thirty additional minutes at printing. Both can contribute to the late dispatch, so an exclusive either-or is unwarranted. Multiple changes do not prevent causal contribution. Treating the first stage as accounting for all later delay ignores the additional recorded stoppage. Treating the last stage as proof of timely sorting contradicts the stated sorting record. Competing accounts need not be mutually exclusive unless their actual claims or the evidence make them so.

questions.stem: A narrow hypothesis guarantees that a marker will turn red within five minutes whenever conditions C hold. In a stipulated reliable test, all conditions C hold for ten minutes, the marker remains observable throughout, and it never turns red. Which conclusion follows about the stated hypothesis?
choices: It is confirmed because any observation can be fitted to an explanation.
It survives unchanged if the five-minute limit is silently changed to twenty minutes.
Every other possible explanation is now proved true.
Its guaranteed prediction fails under the stipulated test, so the hypothesis as stated is refuted by that result.
questions.explanation: The hypothesis guarantees red within five minutes under C; the reliable observation supplies C and no red even over ten minutes. Those stipulations directly conflict with the guarantee. Treating every outcome as confirmation ignores the content of the prediction. Changing the time limit produces a revised hypothesis and does not preserve the original guarantee. Refuting one stated hypothesis does not prove all rivals, which may conflict with one another or face their own problems. Here the timing, required conditions, and reliable detection are expressly fixed.

questions.stem: A theater sold 300 tickets one month and 400 the next, yet its total ticket revenue fell. Each ticket has one purchaser and there are no refunds or other ticket charges. Which additional fact most directly explains the result?
choices: The theater had enough seats to admit every ticket holder in both months.
More performances were offered during the second month.
Every ticket cost ten credits in the first month and six credits in the second.
Every ticket cost the same positive amount in both months.
questions.explanation: At ten credits each, 300 tickets produce 3,000 credits; at six credits each, 400 produce 2,400. The lower price therefore explains falling revenue alongside rising unit sales. Having sufficient seats says nothing about revenue per ticket. Additional performances can help explain more tickets but supply no reason for lower total revenue. A fixed positive price, with the stated complete accounting, would make revenue rise with ticket sales and would deepen the conflict rather than resolve it.

questions.stem: A factory used the same complete defect checks in two months. The proportion of its products found defective fell from two percent to one percent, but the number found defective increased. Which additional fact reconciles those observations?
choices: The factory produced three times as many products in the second month as in the first.
The factory produced the same positive number of products in both months.
The second month used a less sensitive defect check than the first.
No products were found defective in the second month.
questions.explanation: If the first positive production total is N, the defect counts are 0.02N and 0.01 times 3N, or 0.03N. The proportion halves while the count rises by half. Equal production totals would make the defect count fall when its proportion halves. A less sensitive check contradicts the stated unchanged checks rather than explaining the data under them. No later defects conflicts with both the one-percent finding and the increase in their number. Keep the stated measurement method and both observations fixed.

questions.stem: A club recorded more workshop attendances this year than last year, yet fewer distinct people attended. Each attendance records one person at one workshop, and a person can attend several workshops. Which fact best explains how both results occurred?
choices: Every person attended exactly one workshop in both years.
The club replaced some afternoon workshops with morning workshops.
The total number of workshop attendances actually fell this year.
The smaller group of attendees returned for enough additional workshops per person to raise the attendance total.
questions.explanation: Repeated participation allows a smaller number of people to generate more attendance events. The added fact explicitly supplies enough additional participation to produce the larger total. Exactly one workshop per person would make attendance events and distinct people equal in each year, so the reported opposite trends could not follow. Moving workshop times does not by itself explain how often people returned. Saying that total attendances fell denies an accepted observation. The useful distinction is between people and the events those people generate.

questions.stem: A pump moved more water per operating hour after an adjustment, but moved less water in total per day. It moved 240 liters per hour before the adjustment and 300 afterward. Which added fact most directly resolves the apparent discrepancy?
choices: The pump operated for ten hours per day before and afterward.
Its daily operating time fell from ten hours to six hours.
Its daily operating time increased from six hours to ten hours.
The adjustment increased the amount of water moved per operating hour.
questions.explanation: Ten hours at 240 liters per hour yields 2,400 liters; six hours at 300 yields 1,800. The reduction in operating time outweighs the increase in hourly throughput. Ten hours in both periods would instead produce more daily water afterward. Increasing operating time while increasing hourly throughput would also raise the total. Repeating the hourly improvement does not supply the missing duration needed to understand the lower daily output. The reconciliation preserves both the improved rate and the reduced total.

questions.stem: Beginners completed an activity successfully at rates of twenty percent last year and thirty percent this year. Experienced participants improved from eighty percent to ninety percent. Nevertheless, the overall success rate fell. The two groups include all participants without overlap. Which fact can explain the overall decline?
choices: The two groups had equal numbers of participants in each year.
Experienced participants made up ninety percent of last year’s participants but only ten percent of this year’s.
Experienced participants made up ten percent of last year’s participants but ninety percent of this year’s.
The overall success rate is always the simple average of the two group rates, regardless of group sizes.
questions.explanation: With ninety percent experienced participants initially, the overall rate is 0.9 times 80 plus 0.1 times 20, or seventy-four percent. With only ten percent experienced later, it is 0.1 times 90 plus 0.9 times 30, or thirty-six percent. The shift toward the lower-success group outweighs improvements within both groups. Equal group sizes would produce an increase from fifty to sixty percent. Shifting toward the higher-success group would reinforce improvement. An unweighted average ignores the stated possibility of unequal group sizes.

questions.stem: Independent observers found fewer dangerous incidents in a workshop this year, using the same observation method as last year. Yet workers filed more reports about such incidents. Which additional fact most helps reconcile the two trends?
choices: Workers filed the same number of reports in both years.
This year’s observers reclassified harmless events as dangerous incidents.
Workers were less willing to report incidents this year than last year.
A new confidential reporting process led workers to report a much larger share of the incidents they experienced.
questions.explanation: A much larger reporting share can produce more reports even when the underlying incidents become less frequent. It connects workers’ reporting behavior to the apparent discrepancy while preserving the independent observation trend. Equal report totals deny the given increase. Reclassifying harmless events changes the stated observation method and would not directly explain why worker reports rose despite the measured decline. Lower reporting willingness pushes reports in the same downward direction as fewer incidents and therefore deepens the tension unless another explanation is invented.

questions.stem: A studio used fewer units of heating energy during the second of two months but paid more for those units. Its bill in each month consisted only of the number of units used multiplied by that month’s positive unit price. Which fact best helps explain the result?
choices: The unit price doubled while the number of units used fell by one quarter.
The unit price and number of units used both fell by one quarter.
The unit price remained fixed while the number of units used fell.
The studio used more units of heating energy in the second month.
questions.explanation: Writing the original positive price and usage as P and U, the later bill is 2P times 0.75U, or 1.5PU. The bill rises by half despite lower use. Lowering both price and use would lower the bill under the complete stated model. A fixed price with reduced use would also lower it. Claiming more units were used denies the accepted reduction. The correct fact changes the relevant price by enough to offset the reduced quantity without adding an unmentioned billing component.

questions.stem: For the same commuters, average driving time fell after a new bridge opened, but average time from leaving home to arriving at work increased. Each commute includes driving and a ferry crossing. Which fact most directly explains the two results together?
choices: The bridge shortened the driving portion of the journey.
The ferry crossing took the same time and had the same waiting time in both periods.
A reduced ferry schedule increased average waiting time by more than the bridge reduced driving time, with all other portions unchanged.
The commuters’ driving time was longer after the bridge opened.
questions.explanation: The added ferry waiting time exceeds the driving time saved, so total home-to-work time rises while driving time falls. Repeating the bridge’s driving benefit leaves the longer total unexplained. Unchanged ferry travel and waiting do not supply an offset to the driving reduction. Longer driving denies the first observation. The correct statement distinguishes one component of a journey from its complete duration and explicitly supplies the size relationship needed for the reported total change.

questions.stem: Two statements use exactly the same definition and measurement: one says a particular sealed jar contained exactly ten marbles at noon, and the other says that same jar did not contain exactly ten marbles at that same noon. Both are stipulated to concern the identical contents at the identical instant. Which assessment is best?
choices: A change in the jar’s contents after noon makes both statements true at noon.
An average of ten marbles across several other jars makes both statements true.
A different definition of marble resolves the conflict while retaining the stipulated definition.
The statements are contradictory under the stipulations; an ordinary added fact cannot make both true.
questions.explanation: Exactly ten and not exactly ten deny one another when jar, instant, contents, and definition are fixed. A later change concerns a different time. Other jars and their average concern different objects and measures. Changing the definition abandons an explicit stipulation. Reconciliation works on an apparent conflict created by missing context; it does not make a proposition and its direct negation jointly true under the same fixed interpretation. This item tests the limit of the reconciliation task.

questions.stem: Every returning volunteer is one year older this year than last year, yet the average age of all current volunteers is lower. Which additional fact most directly explains how that is possible?
choices: All last year’s volunteers returned and no new volunteers joined.
Many much younger volunteers joined, lowering the combined average enough to offset the aging of returning volunteers.
The age of each returning volunteer actually decreased.
The returning volunteers all have different birthdays.
questions.explanation: New younger members can lower the average for the full current group while every returning individual ages. The choice explicitly supplies enough new participation to account for the direction of the average change. If precisely the same people returned with no newcomers, adding one year to each would raise the mean by one year. Decreased ages contradict the given observation. Different birthdays do not explain the lower overall average when every returning person’s stated year-to-year age change is fixed. Distinguish individual change from group composition.

questions.stem: After a library introduced better humidity control, newly stored folders deteriorated more slowly. Yet most folders removed from storage this month were badly deteriorated. Which additional fact most helps explain why these observations can coexist?
choices: No folders removed this month were deteriorated.
The new humidity system made recently stored folders deteriorate faster.
Most folders removed this month had already suffered serious damage during many years of storage before the new system was installed.
All folders in the library were made of the same material.
questions.explanation: Preexisting damage in older folders explains why a removal group can remain badly deteriorated even though newly stored folders now deteriorate more slowly. The observations concern different histories; the improvement need not reverse damage already sustained. Denying deterioration among removed folders contradicts the second observation. Faster deterioration of new folders contradicts the first. Shared material does not explain the different storage periods or accumulated damage. The useful addition connects timing and accumulated prior damage to the apparently surprising outcome.

questions.stem: A machine produced more units per operating hour than before, but its total output for the month fell. Which question identifies the most relevant missing connection before evaluating proposed explanations?
choices: Did the machine’s operating hours or time spent stopped change enough to offset its higher hourly output rate?
Can the statement about a higher hourly output rate simply be rejected?
Does a higher hourly output rate by definition guarantee more monthly output, whatever the operating hours?
Should monthly output be replaced with the selling price of each item?
questions.explanation: Monthly output depends on production rate while operating and the duration of operation, so a reduction in operating time can reconcile the two observations. Rejecting the hourly output statement violates the task of accepting both observations. Treating a higher hourly rate as a guarantee of total output repeats the hidden assumption that duration cannot offset it. Selling price concerns revenue rather than the stated output count and substitutes another measure. The useful question exposes the background expectation without pretending the actual offset has already been established.

questions.stem: A theater donated 45 percent of its 200 subscription seats last season and 30 percent of its 400 subscription seats this season. Both figures cover all subscription seats, and donation is defined identically in both seasons. The director concludes that the theater donated fewer subscription seats this season. Which description most accurately identifies the reasoning error?
choices: It infers a smaller donated count from a smaller donated share despite the increase in the total number of seats.
It infers that donating seats caused subscriptions to increase merely because the two changes occurred together.
It treats the proportion of donated seats that were used as the proportion of used seats that were donated.
It describes a decline of fifteen percentage points as a relative decline of fifteen percent.
questions.explanation: The donated counts are $0.45(200)=90$ and $0.30(400)=120$. The lower share accompanies a larger count because the total doubled, so the count-from-share description identifies the error. The director proposes no cause of subscription growth. No premise concerns seat use, so reversing proportions involving used seats is not the reasoning employed. The share falls by fifteen percentage points, but the director never calls that a relative fifteen-percent decline; the claim being assessed concerns fewer donated seats.

questions.stem: A design exhibition accepted 30 percent of its 200 entries last year and 45 percent of its 200 entries this year. A report concludes: "The accepted share increased by 15 percent relative to last year's accepted share." Which flaw does that conclusion contain?
choices: It combines the two years by giving their percentages equal weight despite their unequal numbers of entries.
It substitutes a difference of fifteen percentage points for the relative change from the starting percentage.
It reverses the proportion of accepted entries that were submitted into the proportion of submissions accepted.
It assumes an unchanged entry total although the premises establish that the number of entries increased.
questions.explanation: The percentages differ by fifteen percentage points, but the relative increase is $(45-30)/30=50\%$. The counts confirm the same relative change: 60 accepted entries became 90. Substituting the percentage-point difference for relative growth is the error. Equal weighting across unequal entry totals is not involved; both totals are 200 and the report does not compute a combined share. No proportion of accepted entries being submitted is reversed. The entry total is explicitly unchanged, so the criticism claiming that the premises establish an increased total misstates them.

questions.stem: Workshop Alder had 24 completers among its 40 trainees. Workshop Birch had 36 completers among its 90 trainees. The records include every trainee, with the same completion criterion. An administrator concludes that Birch had the higher completion rate because 36 is greater than 24. What is the error?
choices: The administrator adds the same trainee to both workshop totals when combining the records.
The administrator infers that each Birch trainee had a greater chance of completing than each Alder trainee from workshop-wide results.
The administrator treats a larger number of completers as sufficient to establish a larger share of trainees completing.
The administrator assumes that completion counts are equal merely because the two workshops use one criterion.
questions.explanation: Alder's completion rate is $24/40=60\%$, whereas Birch's is $36/90=40\%$. A larger completion count does not establish a larger completion share when the trainee totals differ. The administrator neither combines records nor counts anyone twice. The administrator compares observed workshop-wide rates and makes no claim about each individual trainee's chance, so an inference from group results to every individual is not its move. It explicitly compares different completion counts rather than assuming equal counts from a shared criterion. The shared criterion makes the counts comparable in meaning but does not eliminate their different denominators.

questions.stem: Gallery Cedar received 200 entries before a 20 percent increase in entries. Gallery Elm received 1,000 entries before a 10 percent increase. A commentator concludes that Cedar gained more entries because its percentage increase was twice Elm's. Which description best identifies the flaw?
choices: It treats a difference between two percentage values as the relative increase in either gallery's share of all entries.
It averages the two galleries' growth percentages without weighting them by their final entry totals.
It assumes that a percentage increase and a subsequent percentage decrease cancel despite different bases.
It infers a larger numerical gain from larger relative growth without accounting for different starting totals.
questions.explanation: Cedar gains $0.20(200)=40$ entries, while Elm gains $0.10(1000)=100$. Cedar has the greater relative increase but the smaller numerical gain. Different starting totals therefore defeat the stated inference. The commentator does not describe either gallery's share of the combined entries or use a percentage-point difference as relative growth. No average of the growth percentages is calculated. No subsequent decrease occurs, so cancellation of successive changes is not the error. The missing connection is between each growth percentage and the count to which it applies.
