questions.stem: A maker room's invented principle permits any member who has completed orientation and holds a current badge to reserve a bench. Mira and Leo are members. Mira completed orientation, and Leo holds a current badge. Mira's badge status and Leo's orientation status are unknown. Whose permission to reserve a bench is established by this principle and these facts?
choices: Mira's permission is established, but Leo's is not.
Leo's permission is established, but Mira's is not.
Both Mira's and Leo's permissions are established.
Neither Mira's nor Leo's permission is established.
questions.explanation: To use this sufficient route, establish orientation and a current badge in the same member. Mira has established orientation but unknown badge status; Leo has an established badge but unknown orientation status. Neither complete input is established. Granting permission to Mira ignores her missing badge information, while granting it to Leo ignores his missing orientation information. Granting both combines different people's properties as if they belonged to each person. Unknown inputs also do not establish that either person is prohibited from reserving.

questions.stem: A center's invented rule says: During winter sessions, every pottery demonstration with at least eight paid reservations must have an assistant. Demonstration D takes place in an autumn session and has ten paid reservations. No other staffing rule is given. Which assessment is best?
choices: The winter rule does not establish an assistant requirement for demonstration D.
The ten reservations establish the assistant requirement regardless of the season.
The autumn date establishes that having an assistant at demonstration D is prohibited.
The winter rule establishes that an assistant has already been assigned to demonstration D.
questions.explanation: The rule's scope is winter sessions, whereas demonstration D is in autumn. Ten paid reservations satisfy the numerical condition but cannot replace the seasonal condition. Ignoring the season improperly extends the rule. Inferring a prohibition in autumn invents an opposite result for an uncovered case. Inferring an actual assignment both ignores the seasonal restriction and turns a requirement into a report of compliance. The given rule leaves this autumn demonstration's staffing requirement unresolved.

questions.stem: An invented application system normally assigns complete applications to the ordinary lane and assigns urgent applications to the priority lane. Its explicit priority instruction says that the urgent rule overrides the ordinary rule: applications satisfying both conditions are assigned only to the priority lane. Application T is complete and urgent. Where is T assigned under the full instructions?
choices: Only to the ordinary lane because it is complete.
To both lanes because each general rule must apply without qualification.
Only to the priority lane because the stated override governs the overlap.
To neither lane because the overlapping conditions prevent a decision.
questions.explanation: T satisfies both conditions, and the explicit override assigns overlapping cases only to the priority lane. Assigning T only to the ordinary lane ignores that priority. Assigning both lanes treats the general rules as unqualified after the instructions have supplied a qualification. Assigning neither mistakes a resolved overlap for an unresolved conflict. The conclusion relies on the stated override, not on an assumption that urgency always takes priority in actual organizations.

questions.stem: An invented classification rule says that every instrument calibrated this month and passing its load check qualifies for a trial. It provides no other qualification restrictions. Which described case violates that rule?
choices: An instrument was calibrated this month, failed its load check, and qualifies for a trial.
An instrument was last calibrated a month ago, passed its load check, and qualifies for a trial.
An instrument was calibrated this month, failed its load check, and does not qualify for a trial.
An instrument was calibrated this month, passed its load check, and does not qualify for a trial.
questions.explanation: Calibration this month together with a passed load check guarantees qualification. The case with both features but no qualification therefore violates the rule. A failed load check leaves the joint condition false, so either qualification or nonqualification is compatible with this rule alone. Calibration only a month ago also fails to establish the current-month input; qualifying despite that does not violate the stated sufficient route. The rule does not make its two conditions necessary for every qualification.

questions.stem: Every printed trial guide contains a page index. Guide Fir is a printed trial guide. Its editor concludes that Fir should be retained for evaluation. Which additional principle is sufficient to justify that conclusion?
choices: A guide should be retained for evaluation only if it contains a page index.
An editor is permitted to retain for evaluation any guide containing a page index.
Every guide containing a page index should be retained for evaluation.
A guide containing a page index should be retained for evaluation if it cost less than fifty units to produce.
questions.explanation: Fir's status as a printed trial guide establishes that it contains a page index. The principle recommending retention for every guide with an index then establishes the exact conclusion. Requiring an index for retention runs in the other direction and does not recommend retention for Fir. Permission to retain is weaker than the conclusion that Fir should be retained. The cost-qualified principle would need a production-cost fact that is not supplied. A sufficient principle must complete the route using the facts actually given.

questions.stem: A question provides an argument and asks which general principle, if accepted, is sufficient to justify its conclusion. Which method directly answers that task?
choices: Accept the conclusion first and choose a principle that would follow from that conclusion alone.
Add each candidate principle to the stated premises and test whether the exact conclusion follows.
Choose a statement the argument needs even if that statement leaves other gaps in its support.
Choose the most appealing real-world policy without checking its connection to the stated premises.
questions.explanation: A justification question asking for sufficiency requires the candidate plus the premises to establish the conclusion. Starting from the conclusion reverses the support task and can select a consequence that offers no justification. A necessary statement can leave other gaps open, so necessity alone does not satisfy the question. Personal policy appeal is not a test of whether the hypothetical rule connects these premises to this conclusion. This differs from an application question in which the general principle is already supplied and the cases must be tested against it.

questions.stem: Every selected prototype report uses the common format, and report Cedar is a selected prototype report. The conclusion is that Cedar should be archived. Consider the added principle: Every report using the common format should be archived. Which assessment is correct?
choices: The principle justifies the conclusion with the premises, but that success does not show the principle is necessary.
The principle cannot justify the conclusion because it covers more reports than the conclusion mentions.
The principle must be necessary because any principle that justifies a conclusion is necessary.
Replacing it with "Only reports using the common format should be archived" would also establish the conclusion.
questions.explanation: Cedar is selected, so it uses the common format; the added principle then establishes that Cedar should be archived. A broad rule can have a valid consequence about one report, so its breadth does not defeat sufficiency. Sufficiency also does not establish necessity: a narrower rule recommending archiving every selected prototype report would complete the argument without the proposed rule's reach over all other common-format reports. The only-reports replacement makes the format necessary for the recommendation but does not establish that Cedar should be archived. Direction remains essential even when the same subject matter appears in both rules.

questions.stem:
(1) In an invented ceramics study, technicians made twenty-four test tiles. Twelve received code H and spent their final drying period in a heated room; the other twelve received code C and dried in a cool room. Codes were assigned before inspection and identified the drying room, not a tile's condition. All tiles were inspected for visible cracks under a lamp after seven days.

(2) A later notebook shows that the H tiles came from Batch North and the C tiles from Batch South. Two H tiles and five C tiles had visible cracks at inspection. The study did not measure later wear, water absorption, or strength. The same inspection method was used for both groups, but the records do not establish that room temperature was their only relevant difference.

(3) The curator accepts the counts as descriptions of the inspected tiles but calls the temperature explanation provisional. She proposes repeating only the visible-crack inspection after the same seven-day period, this time using tiles from one batch divided between the two rooms. The current counts do not distinguish a temperature effect from possible batch differences. Her proposed comparison addresses that uncertainty rather than identifying the best tile for every use.

Question: According to paragraph (1), what was code H intended to identify when it was assigned?
choices: A tile that already showed visible cracks before inspection.
A tile assigned to the heated room for its final drying period.
A tile made from Batch South for a water-absorption test.
A tile that had passed a later test of strength and wear.
questions.explanation: Paragraph (1) explicitly says that the codes identified drying rooms and were assigned before inspection, so H identifies assignment to the heated room. A visible-crack result is not what the code records; H tiles included both cracked and uncracked tiles. Batch South supplied the C group in paragraph (2), and no water-absorption test was conducted. Passing strength or wear tests is also unsupported because those outcomes were not measured.

questions.stem:
(1) Accounts of the fictional traveler Mira Yel's journey survive in nine handwritten copies of her letters. Her sister Lena made the copies after the journey, preserving place names but omitting greetings and arrival dates. The originals are missing. The account does not establish that Lena copied every original letter, and the surviving texts do not identify the duration of travel between towns.

(2) One copy says that Mira reached Bren after leaving Dale. A second refers to that same single visit to Bren and places it before her arrival in Kest. Researcher Oris uses these links to place the three visits in relative order. He does not assign calendar dates to them, and he leaves other visits unordered when their relationships are not stated.

(3) A critic argues that the absence of arrival dates makes the copies useless for reconstructing the journey's sequence. Oris agrees that the copies cannot supply those dates, but rejects that broader assessment. A partial sequence can be established from the stated before-and-after relationships even when its calendar positions remain unknown. He presents the result as a limited reconstruction, without claiming that it includes every stop Mira made.

Question: What surviving material is described in paragraph (1)?
choices: Nine original envelopes bearing the traveler's arrival dates.
Nine dated diary entries written during the journey.
Nine copies of the traveler's letters, made by her sister after the journey.
Nine travel letters authored by the sister while visiting the towns.
questions.explanation: Paragraph (1) identifies nine handwritten copies of Mira's letters, made by Lena after the journey. The original letters are missing, and the account supplies no surviving envelopes with dates. The texts are copied letters, not dated diary entries; arrival dates were omitted. Lena performed the copying, but Mira was the traveler whose letters she copied, so treating Lena as the author traveling between towns reverses their roles.

questions.stem:
(1) The fictional borough of Nerin published a bench directory under a new inspection protocol. Surveyors recorded benches they could reach through an open public entrance during their visit. They did not enter locked gardens or grounds marked private, even when benches were visible through a fence. Entrance status was recorded for the inspection day; the directory makes no promise about future opening hours.

(2) An older directory had counted only benches visible from the street. The new survey added several benches inside open courtyards that could not be seen from the street. Surveyors noted each included bench's location and seat count. They did not assess its condition, test continuous public access, or record its installation date. The two directories therefore describe observations made under different procedures.

(3) The authors describe the new method as providing expanded coverage. They mean that the inspection now reaches some locations the earlier street-based method left out. They do not describe the directory as a census of every bench in the borough: locked gardens and private grounds remain outside the survey. Nor do they use the directory's additional entries to calculate how many benches were newly installed between the two publications.

Question: Under the new protocol, which circumstance would exclude a bench from inspection even if it could be seen through a fence?
choices: The bench was inside a garden whose entrance was locked during the visit.
The bench was inside a courtyard reached through an open public entrance.
The bench was absent from the older street-based directory.
The bench's installation date had not been recorded.
questions.explanation: Paragraph (1) expressly excludes locked gardens even when a bench is visible through a fence. An open public entrance instead provides the kind of access the new protocol permits. Paragraph (2) says the survey added benches missing from the older street-based account, so earlier absence is not an exclusion rule. Installation dates were not recorded for included benches; lacking one therefore does not itself disqualify a bench from this survey.

questions.stem:
(1) A fictional translation festival plans to display six English versions of a poem by the invented writer Eris Vale, then award a prize to the version deemed most faithful. Critic Taren objects that the announcement never says what fidelity requires. A reader might prize repeated sounds, another the ease of following the speaker's thought, and another the preservation of an unsettled image. These priorities can conflict. Taren's objection is well taken: a prize claiming to recognize fidelity needs a clearer standard than an unexplained preference. That need does not imply that every translation is equally defensible or that readers are incapable of judging particular choices.

(2) In the committee's pilot display, version L uses the same English verb at three points where the source repeats one word. Version M uses three different verbs to make the English sound more fluid. L preserves a visible repetition; M gives up that feature in pursuit of smoother phrasing. The accompanying note supplies these facts without declaring which goal should control the award. Readers divide over the versions. Their preferences reveal different priorities, but the vote alone does not tell the committee why one priority should define fidelity for the entire poem. A favorite version and the best version under a specified criterion are different judgments.

(3) Interpretive differences also need to be distinguished from errors against clear textual constraints. The source explicitly places a boat's arrival before a storm; a separate trial version reverses that sequence. Calling the reversal a different aesthetic priority does not make it accurate on that point. By contrast, the source leaves the referent of one pronoun unsettled. A translator who chooses one possible speaker makes an interpretive decision that should be identified and explained. The translator need not preserve every ambiguity unchanged, but should not present a chosen resolution as something the source states unambiguously. The display can acknowledge legitimate alternatives while still correcting the reversed event order.

(4) The festival should therefore ask entrants to state their principal aims and provide brief commentaries explaining consequential choices and trade-offs. Readers could inspect how a version serves its declared aims and where it departs from other defensible aims, while checking clear source constraints. An audience-favorite prize could still report what that audience preferred; it should not silently become proof of greatest fidelity. Such a display would make translation choices accountable, not eliminate disagreement by decree. Its value would lie partly in showing why informed readers disagree and partly in making particular claims answerable to textual evidence. Transparent comparison offers more than an unexplained single ranking.

Question: Which statement best expresses the passage's main point?
choices: The festival should privilege repeated wording because fluency is generally an unreliable guide to a poem's meaning.
Readers should define fidelity individually without enforcing shared constraints supplied by the source text.
Displaying all versions before voting would make popularity a sufficient measure of the most faithful translation.
Translations should be compared against clear aims and textual constraints, with commentary exposing consequential interpretive choices.
questions.explanation: Paragraph (1) identifies an unspecified standard; paragraphs (2) and (3) distinguish competing priorities from clear errors; paragraph (4) recommends declared aims, commentary, and textual accountability. The complete main point joins those elements. Privileging repeated wording selects one of the priorities the passage leaves open rather than establishing it as the governing standard. Individual preferences without shared constraints ignore paragraph (3), where reversing a clear event order remains an error. Showing all versions may inform a vote, but paragraphs (2) and (4) expressly distinguish audience preference from a justified fidelity judgment.

questions.stem:
(1) Engineers studying the fictional Reachshore coast use a small wind chamber to investigate where sand first gathers behind reed barriers. Critics dismiss the model because it contains neither tides nor seasonal changes in wind. Those omissions matter for a forecast of long-term coastal protection, but that is not the chamber's immediate question. Lead researcher Nari wants to isolate how barrier arrangement affects the position of an early sand deposit under specified conditions. A model can answer that limited question without recreating the entire coast. Whether its result will justify a particular protection project remains a separate matter requiring a broader investigation.

(2) The team runs six pairs of twenty-minute trials, comparing a straight row of barriers with a staggered arrangement. Grain mixture, fan speed, barrier height, and trial duration are the same within each pair; the starting sand bed is reset to the same condition before each trial. In every pair, the main deposit band at the end of the trial lies farther downwind with the staggered arrangement. The recorded outcome is the band's position, not the total amount of retained sand. No trial continues beyond twenty minutes. These controlled comparisons challenge the claim that arrangement cannot affect early deposit position under the tested conditions, while leaving other outcomes unmeasured.

(3) A field crew also photographs a site with staggered barriers at the beginning and end of a two-week interval. Small ridges are visible at the second visit in locations broadly consistent with the chamber pattern. Yet waves crossed the site during that interval, wind conditions varied, and no matched straight-row site was observed. The photographs therefore do not isolate the barriers' effect or show what would have happened under the other arrangement. The resemblance is a reason to investigate further, not a controlled demonstration that the model explains everything occurring at the site. The crew records no estimate of long-term shoreline loss or total sand retained over a season.

(4) Nari proposes longer observations, appropriate comparison sites, and measurements of retained volume and erosion before recommending a protection project. The bridge between a plausible first-stage mechanism and a coastal-protection claim must be built with additional evidence, rather than assumed from a shared ridge shape. This requirement does not erase what the chamber comparison has already distinguished. Rejecting it solely because it omits tides would confuse a limited experiment with an attempted reproduction of every coastal process. Its proper use is to refine a specific explanation and guide subsequent tests, while allowing those later tests to reveal where the explanation ceases to be useful.

Question: Which statement best expresses the passage's main point?
choices: A model that omits tides should be rejected when planning subsequent coastal observations.
The field photographs establish that staggered barriers already provide the stronger long-term protection.
A limited model can inform a specific explanation, while broader protection claims require additional relevant evidence.
Differences in deposit position are sufficient to determine how much sand a coast will retain over a season.
questions.explanation: Paragraph (1) defends the chamber's limited question, paragraph (2) describes its result, paragraph (3) limits the field resemblance, and paragraph (4) calls for further evidence before recommending protection. Its main point preserves both the model's explanatory value and the boundary on broader claims. Omitting tides limits its use but does not justify rejecting it as a guide to further tests. The field photographs lack a matched comparison and long-term protection measures. Deposit position is also a different outcome from retained volume, so it cannot by itself settle seasonal retention.

questions.stem:
(1) Editors of a new edition of Nera's cooking notebooks propose replacing expressions such as "a handful" and "until it yields" with fixed quantities and cooking times. Their spokesperson describes the original directions as "chaos on the page." A usable recipe, the editors argue, should guide a cook toward a repeatable result.

(2) Repeatability is a worthwhile goal. Yet the notebooks also record Nera changing a quantity when fruit was unusually dry and shortening a cooking time when a mixture thickened early. Some variations therefore document deliberate adjustments rather than failures to record a single correct procedure. Replacing those directions silently would erase precisely the evidence that reveals this aspect of Nera's practice. This does not establish that every unclear instruction can now be reconstructed.

(3) Tested recipes with measured quantities would be a welcome addition to the edition. They should appear alongside transcriptions of the original directions, with editorial substitutions identified. Readers could then prepare a workable version while examining the judgments from which it was developed. Such a double presentation would serve practical use without disguising editorial decisions as Nera's own instructions.

Question: Which statement most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The edition should replace variable directions with tested quantities while retaining the full range of dishes in Nera's notebooks.
Some variations in Nera's notebooks record deliberate responses to ingredients rather than failures to preserve a single correct procedure.
The edition should preserve original directions and distinguish tested adaptations so readers can both cook and examine Nera's practice.
The notebooks should serve as a historical record, with practical cooking instructions reserved for a separate publication for modern readers.
questions.explanation: The proposal to preserve original directions while distinguishing tested adaptations captures the response to the editors' concern in paragraph (1), the historical reason in paragraph (2), and the combined presentation recommended in paragraph (3). The observation that some variations were deliberate is supported by paragraph (2), but it is a reason for the recommendation and is too narrow to express the whole passage's main point. Replacing variable directions with tested quantities conflicts with keeping transcriptions alongside adaptations; retaining the range of dishes would not preserve the directions themselves. Reserving practical instructions for a separate publication also conflicts with the proposed double presentation within this edition.

questions.explanation: Welcoming conditional approval is supported by the "welcome addition" in paragraph (3) together with the requirement to identify substitutions and preserve transcriptions. Doubt about culinary usefulness misreads paragraph (2)'s acceptance of repeatability as worthwhile and paragraph (3)'s description of a workable version. Appreciation of historical accuracy assigns the adaptations a status the passage carefully distinguishes from Nera's original directions; difficulty repeating measured quantities is also not the concern stated. Approval of replacement, even with a note about lost detail, contradicts paragraph (3)'s requirement that adaptations appear alongside the source directions.

questions.stem:
(1) Editors of a new edition of Nera's cooking notebooks propose replacing expressions such as "a handful" and "until it yields" with fixed quantities and cooking times. Their spokesperson describes the original directions as "chaos on the page." A usable recipe, the editors argue, should guide a cook toward a repeatable result.

(2) Repeatability is a worthwhile goal. Yet the notebooks also record Nera changing a quantity when fruit was unusually dry and shortening a cooking time when a mixture thickened early. Some variations therefore document deliberate adjustments rather than failures to record a single correct procedure. Replacing those directions silently would erase precisely the evidence that reveals this aspect of Nera's practice. This does not establish that every unclear instruction can now be reconstructed.

(3) Tested recipes with measured quantities would be a welcome addition to the edition. They should appear alongside transcriptions of the original directions, with editorial substitutions identified. Readers could then prepare a workable version while examining the judgments from which it was developed. Such a double presentation would serve practical use without disguising editorial decisions as Nera's own instructions.

Question: The passage is primarily intended to do which of the following?
choices: Explain how variations in Nera's ingredients led her to depart from a single procedure on particular cooking occasions.
Compare the numerical accuracy of the editors' proposed quantities with measurements recovered from Nera's original cooking equipment.
Defend the original directions as a sufficient practical manual for modern readers who lack the editors' cooking experience.
Argue for an edition that combines usable adaptations with a transparent record of the directions on which they are based.
questions.explanation: Arguing for a combined, transparent edition captures the text's principal activity: paragraph (1) introduces a proposed replacement, paragraph (2) supplies a reason to preserve source directions, and paragraph (3) recommends an arrangement serving both aims. Explaining Nera's adjustments describes evidence in paragraph (2), but omits the editorial proposal that evidence supports. Comparing numerical accuracy is unsupported: no recovered equipment or measurement comparison appears. Defending the source as a sufficient manual also misstates the position; paragraph (2) leaves some reconstruction unresolved, and paragraph (3) welcomes tested versions for practical use.

choices: The spokesperson and the author both dismiss the uncertainty as disorder, but disagree over how thoroughly to remove it.
The spokesperson dismisses the uncertainty as disorder, while the author regards some of it as evidence worth retaining.
The spokesperson admires the directions' flexibility, while the author regards their uncertainty as an obstacle to historical understanding.
The spokesperson tolerates the uncertainty for practical reasons, while the author criticizes the notebooks more severely for it.
questions.explanation: The contrast between dismissing disorder and retaining evidence is supported by paragraph (1)'s attribution of "chaos" to the spokesperson and paragraph (2)'s explanation of deliberate adjustments. questions.stem:
(1) Pattern cards from the fictional Rellan weaving guild use two naming systems. A sequence name identifies the opening arrangement of thread crossings; an appearance name identifies a feature of the finished cloth. The same cloth can consequently appear under different names in the guild's records. The surviving cards show both systems in use during the same period, rather than a uniform change from one to the other.

(2) Sequence names helped apprentices retrieve instructions for beginning a pattern. Two designs could share that beginning and diverge later, so the name alone did not specify every subsequent step. An accompanying diagram supplied the remaining instructions. A clerk searching for a familiar opening could thus find several patterns that produced different finished motifs.

(3) Appearance names helped merchants locate cloth bearing a requested motif. Patterns made through different sequences could receive the same appearance name when they produced similar visible features. Here, accompanying samples distinguished versions that the name grouped together. The paired records preserve a distinction between information used to begin making cloth and information used to recognize its finished appearance. Each naming system organized a different task, and each relied on further material for details.

Question: Which description most accurately identifies the primary purpose of the passage?
choices: To explain why merchants gradually replaced an earlier naming system that had been designed mainly for apprentices.
To explain how two naming systems organized different activities and supplied different information within one weaving community.
To recommend replacing separate naming systems with a combined vocabulary usable by apprentices and merchants alike.
To assess errors in surviving pattern names by comparing their technical accuracy with accompanying diagrams and samples.
questions.explanation: Explaining the different activities and information captures the whole account: paragraph (1) introduces coexisting systems, paragraph (2) connects sequence names to beginnings, and paragraph (3) connects appearance names to finished motifs. Gradual replacement conflicts with paragraph (1)'s express rejection of a uniform change between systems. Recommending a combined vocabulary imports a reform that the author does not propose. Assessing naming errors also misidentifies the task: shared names group patterns by particular features, and accompanying materials supply details; the passage does not treat that grouping as inaccurate naming.

choices: Nostalgic about the shared craft traditions that the two systems once helped sustain.
Skeptical about the practical value of systems that both depend on supplementary material.
Mildly critical of sequence names for conveying less about finished cloth than appearance names.
Analytical and evenhanded in explaining the distinct functions and limits of both systems.
questions.explanation: An analytical, evenhanded tone fits the parallel treatment: paragraph (2) identifies a use and a limit of sequence names, and paragraph (3) does the same for appearance names. Skepticism mistakes reliance on diagrams or samples for a judgment that the names lack value; both are described as helping their users. questions.explanation: Coexistence, different tasks, and supplementary detail unite all three paragraphs: paragraph (1) establishes simultaneous use, while paragraphs (2) and (3) explain the respective functions and limits. questions.stem:
(1) A new staging of Merin's puppet play The Empty Chair is advertised as a faithful reproduction of the script. Its director has added a narrator who explains the action during two long silences, promising to "rescue audiences from dead time." The published stage directions, however, specify both silences and prescribe movements that continue through them.

(2) During the first silence, figures approach the empty chair and retreat. During the second, they repeat the approach but remain beside it. Merin's accompanying note asks that viewers be left to decide what changed. The absence of speech is therefore part of the script's design, not an omission awaiting repair.

(3) Calling the added explanations a faithful reproduction is untenable. The narration supplies answers where the script expressly withholds them. An adaptation may invent such answers and may even produce an artistically effective result; that possibility does not make the invention a reproduction of the original directions.

(4) The performers' energetic movements are an achievement. The objection concerns the production's claim to fidelity, rather than the legitimacy of adaptation. Its publicity should identify the interpretive change instead of presenting explanation as preservation.

Question: Which statement best captures the main point of the passage?
choices: The production's added narration preserves Merin's intention by making changes in the figures' behavior clearer to present-day audiences.
The production's energetic performers deserve recognition because their movements preserve the uncertainty that Merin wanted viewers to experience.
The production should describe itself as a revival, while continuing to advertise its explanatory narration as a faithful reproduction.
The production may have artistic value, but its added answers to deliberate silences make its claim of faithful reproduction unsustainable.
questions.explanation: Possible artistic value combined with rejection of the fidelity claim captures paragraphs (2) through (4): the silence is deliberate, narration supplies answers it withheld, and adaptation is distinguished from reproduction. Making behavior clearer does not preserve the stated intention to leave the change for viewers to decide, so the clarity claim reverses paragraph (2)'s significance. The performers' energy is praised, but the passage does not say it preserves uncertainty despite the narration; that causal explanation is added. Changing the label to revival while retaining the fidelity claim fails to address the express objection in paragraphs (3) and (4).

Defend a director's interpretive freedom by showing that an explicit narrator can preserve the original function of scripted silence.

questions.stem:
(1) The fictional Orin stencil workshop keeps two records of every design. A print sheet shows the finished pattern at the size it will have on paper. A cutting ledger lists the separate openings made in the stencil. These records answer different questions even when they describe the same object.

(2) On a print sheet, each mark stays where it appears in the finished impression. A maker can compare the sheet with a new print to spot a missing or misplaced mark. However, the sheet does not show the order in which the stencil's openings were cut.

(3) The cutting ledger groups openings by the tools and cutting sequence used to make them. Several marks that appear far apart on the print sheet can therefore correspond to one ledger entry. This arrangement helps another cutter reconstruct the work, although it makes the visual pattern harder to inspect at a glance.

(4) When the workshop reissues a design, staff begin with the print sheet to identify the desired appearance, then consult the ledger to recreate the openings. Neither record replaces the other: their different arrangements preserve information needed at different stages.

Question: Which description best captures the organization of the passage?
choices: It introduces two complementary records, explains what each makes accessible, and then describes how they are used together.
It traces the replacement of an early recording system by a later system that preserves the same information more efficiently.
It compares the expense of maintaining two records and recommends keeping the record that is simpler to produce.
It introduces an apparent difference between two records and then shows that the difference disappears when a design is reissued.
questions.explanation:
Introducing complementary records, explaining their uses, and describing joint use matches the whole development. Paragraph 1 introduces the two records; paragraphs 2 and 3 distinguish their arrangements and uses; paragraph 4 combines them in a workflow.

The account of replacement does not fit: paragraph 4 expressly says neither record replaces the other, and the passage gives no history of successive systems. The comparison of expense imports a criterion the passage never evaluates; the visual difficulty in paragraph 3 is not a production-cost comparison. The account of a disappearing difference reverses paragraph 4's point. Reissuing a design uses the records together because their different arrangements preserve different information, not because the distinction has vanished.

Question: What is the primary function of paragraph 2?
choices: To describe the placement of each mark on a print sheet in relation to its position in the finished impression.
To explain the sequence of cuts that a maker should follow when reconstructing the original stencil.
To explain how a print sheet supports a visual check while identifying information that the sheet does not preserve.
To challenge the need for a cutting ledger by showing that a print sheet can preserve the entire production process.
questions.explanation:

Challenging the ledger's necessity also reverses the limitation: a print sheet does not preserve the entire production process, and paragraph 4 describes the records as complementary.

choices: It presents evidence that the workshop has made mistakes in transferring the finished design to its ledger.
It identifies a reason that a print sheet cannot reveal the positions of marks in a finished impression.
It supports a recommendation that cutters rearrange the finished pattern to match the order of the ledger entries.

The claim that a print sheet cannot reveal mark positions contradicts paragraph 2, which says the marks stay where they appear in the finished impression. A recommendation to rearrange the finished pattern is never made. Paragraph 4 uses the print sheet to identify the desired appearance and the ledger to recreate it, not to redesign that appearance.

questions.stem:
(1) In an invented kinetic installation called Drift, a ribbon crosses a lit window while two counters advance. Initially, observers assume the counters measure the same event, because both pause when the ribbon stops. Yet the counter marked Frame usually records twice as many units as the counter marked Passage during a display cycle.

(2) The designer's diagram shows one sensor at the window's entrance and another at its exit. Frame receives a signal from either sensor each time a marked band passes it; Passage receives signals only from the exit sensor. One band passing completely through the window consequently supplies two signals to Frame and one to Passage.

(3) This mechanism also explains an unusual startup result. If the display begins with a marked band already inside the window, its entry signal occurred before the counters were reset. When the band then leaves, both counters gain one unit. A complete later crossing produces the usual two-to-one increment for that crossing.

(4) The unequal totals thus reflect different sets of events being counted, rather than conflicting counts of the same event. The startup result fits this account; it requires no second mechanism. The counters' names help observers locate them, but their wiring determines what their totals represent.

Question: What is the primary function of paragraph 1?
choices: To establish the wiring arrangement that makes Frame receive signals from both of the installation's sensors.
To report that both counters pause when the ribbon stops, which is the only relationship the passage goes on to explain.
To introduce the observed difference in totals alongside an initial assumption that makes the difference seem puzzling.
To argue that one counter must be defective because two counters responding to the same ribbon cannot legitimately differ.
questions.explanation:
Paragraph 1 introduces the differing totals and the initial assumption that the counters measure the same event. That pairing creates the puzzle addressed by the sensor arrangement in paragraph 2.

Establishing the wiring arrangement belongs to paragraph 2, which identifies which sensors supply each counter. Paragraph 1 does report that both counters pause when the ribbon stops, but treating this as the only relationship explained omits the unequal counts that drive the passage and the startup case in paragraph 3. Arguing that one counter must be defective misrepresents the passage's direction. Paragraph 1 reports an observation without asserting a defect; paragraphs 2 through 4 explain the difference through what the counters count.

questions.explanation:
The puzzling-pattern account matches all four paragraphs. Paragraph 1 introduces the different counts, paragraph 2 explains the sensor connections, paragraph 3 applies those connections to startup, and paragraph 4 states that one mechanism accounts for both results.

Two rival explanations and a test between them are not presented. An initial assumption in paragraph 1 is clarified, but the passage does not describe a comparative experiment. The design-fault account likewise invents a proposed revision and a before-and-after comparison; the same installation is discussed throughout. The account of an explanation being replaced reverses paragraphs 3 and 4: the startup case follows from the earlier entry signal being outside the reset counters' totals, so no second mechanism is required.

questions.stem:
(1) In an invented kinetic installation called Drift, a ribbon crosses a lit window while two counters advance. Initially, observers assume the counters measure the same event, because both pause when the ribbon stops. Yet the counter marked Frame usually records twice as many units as the counter marked Passage during a display cycle.

(2) The designer's diagram shows one sensor at the window's entrance and another at its exit. Frame receives a signal from either sensor each time a marked band passes it; Passage receives signals only from the exit sensor. One band passing completely through the window consequently supplies two signals to Frame and one to Passage.

(3) This mechanism also explains an unusual startup result. If the display begins with a marked band already inside the window, its entry signal occurred before the counters were reset. When the band then leaves, both counters gain one unit. A complete later crossing produces the usual two-to-one increment for that crossing.

(4) The unequal totals thus reflect different sets of events being counted, rather than conflicting counts of the same event. The startup result fits this account; it requires no second mechanism. The counters' names help observers locate them, but their wiring determines what their totals represent.

Question: What does paragraph 3 contribute to the explanation in paragraph 2?
choices: It provides an exception showing that the signal connections in the designer's diagram cannot explain the installation's operation.
It proposes a new connection that would prevent the counters from producing different increments during complete crossings.
It reports that both counters gain one unit at startup but leaves that result unrelated to the described sensor arrangement.
It applies the sensor account to a different starting condition, explaining a result that might otherwise seem inconsistent with it.
questions.explanation:
Paragraph 3 applies the same sensor account to a band already inside the window when the counters are reset. Its earlier entry signal is omitted from the new totals, so the subsequent exit supplies one signal to each counter. That explains the unusual increment without changing the connections in paragraph 2.

An exception refuting the diagram is the opposite of this contribution; paragraph 4 explicitly says the startup result fits the same account. A proposal for a new connection is absent, and paragraph 3 says complete later crossings retain the usual increments. Reporting equal startup gains is part of paragraph 3's content, but claiming the result is left unrelated ignores the explanation involving the entry signal, the reset, and the subsequent exit.

questions.stem:
(1) An editor preparing a new edition of a fictional poet's Shore Songs wants to remove the opening phrase that reappears at the start of each stanza. In silent reading, she argues, the phrase supplies no new description and delays progress to the new image. Removing the repetitions would make the sequence more economical without altering its content.

(2) The surviving performance notes assign the remaining lines of each stanza to a different speaker and instruct the group to recite the repeated phrase together. In that arrangement, the phrase marks the return from a solo voice to a shared voice. A printed page cannot reproduce that change in sound, but retaining the phrase gives readers a textual sign of the recurring group response. Repetition therefore contributes to the sequence's organization even when it adds no new description.

(3) The editor's concern about slow reading is understandable, and the edition might use spacing or a note to help readers follow the changing voices. It should nevertheless retain the repeated phrase. Presenting the poem for silent readers can justify explaining an organizing feature; it does not by itself justify removing the feature identified by the performance notes. This recommendation depends on the documented function of this repetition, not a rule that every repeated expression in every poem must be preserved unchanged.

Question: Which description best captures the organization of the passage?
choices: It presents a proposal to remove repetition, endorses the proposal's account of the poem, and supplies instructions for carrying it out.
It compares two complete performances of a poem, identifies the more faithful performance, and recommends copying it in print.
It introduces historical notes, uses them to reject every adaptation for silent readers, and states a general rule against editorial changes.
It presents a proposal with its rationale, identifies a function the rationale overlooks, and recommends retention while addressing the stated concern.
questions.explanation:
The proposal, overlooked function, and qualified recommendation describe the whole passage. Paragraph 1 reports the editor's rationale, paragraph 2 identifies repetition's role in marking shared voices, and paragraph 3 recommends retention while suggesting spacing or a note to help readers.

Endorsing and implementing deletion contradicts the instruction in paragraph 3 to retain the phrase. Comparing two complete performances is not what the notes do: paragraph 2 describes the roles within one performance arrangement, not rival performances. Rejecting every adaptation also overstates the response. Paragraph 3 allows explanatory changes for silent readers and expressly limits the recommendation to this documented function rather than imposing a general rule against changes.

questions.stem:
(1) At the fictional Lumen Model Guild, members construct small paper landscapes from either a common outline or a blank sheet. Instructor Vela argues that a common outline helps beginners notice how their choices affect a finished model. She recommends using outlines in every introductory session. Her proposal still lets each member choose colors and add details.

(2) Critic Orin calls that freedom superficial. In his view, choosing the basic arrangement is itself part of learning; beginners who start from an outline lose that opportunity. He therefore recommends blank sheets from the first session, though he accepts that outlines make the instructor's comparisons easier.

(3) Orin identifies a genuine limitation: an outline fixes an important early choice. It does not follow that an outline prevents all worthwhile choices. Decisions about details can still provide practice, as Vela maintains. Whether that practice prepares members to choose a basic arrangement later has not been established.

(4) For the opening session, Vela's approach deserves a trial followed by a session using blank sheets. This sequence would allow comparison of what members learned. For now, that limited trial is warranted; a requirement to use outlines throughout the introductory program is not.

Question: Which claim does Orin grant while nevertheless opposing Vela's proposed introductory practice?
choices: Members should use blank sheets from the first session.
A common outline helps beginners notice the effects of their choices.
Common outlines make the instructor's comparisons easier.
Choosing the basic arrangement is itself part of learning.
questions.explanation:
The claim that outlines make the instructor's comparisons easier is Orin's explicit concession in paragraph (2). He accepts that advantage while continuing to recommend blank sheets. Its truth does not, for him, settle which practice is educationally preferable.

Using blank sheets from the first session is also Orin's position, but it is the recommendation he favors, not a point granted despite that recommendation. Helping beginners notice the effects of their choices is Vela's claim in paragraph (1); the passage does not show Orin adopting it. Choosing the basic arrangement as part of learning is Orin's own reason against outlines in paragraph (2), not his concession to an advantage of them. A statement can accurately describe Orin's position and still answer the wrong question about its role.

questions.stem:
(1) An editor preparing an imaginary collection of river tales has proposed grouping the tales by narrator. The editor, Saren, argues that a reader could then follow each narrator's distinctive account without repeatedly searching the volume. Saren describes that continuity as the collection's chief value and opposes an arrangement based on the tales' settings.

(2) Translator Mirel favors grouping the tales by setting. She argues that placing different accounts of the same village together would reveal contrasts that a narrator-based arrangement might obscure. She acknowledges that her arrangement would interrupt the continuity Saren values, but thinks that interruption a reasonable price for the comparison.

(3) The main ordering need not be the collection's only aid to readers. A narrator index could preserve access to a narrator's scattered tales in a setting-based collection; a setting index could support comparisons in a narrator-based one. Neither index would reproduce the experience of reading the relevant tales consecutively.

(4) An index therefore offers a partial accommodation of the competing goals. The descriptions alone give no reason to decide which experience should govern the main ordering. That decision depends on what the collection is intended to help readers do, a question its sponsors have yet to answer.

Question: Which claim is most strongly supported as a commitment of the author?
choices: An index could support a goal served less directly by the main ordering without duplicating consecutive reading.
A narrator-based ordering cannot be justified until both kinds of index have been tested.
The sponsors should give comparison priority because an index fully restores continuity.
The two arrangements would provide the same reading experience once each included an index.
questions.explanation:
Paragraph (3) describes how either kind of index could support access along the dimension not used for the main ordering, while expressly denying that an index reproduces consecutive reading. Paragraph (4) accordingly calls the accommodation partial.

Requiring tests of both indexes adds a prerequisite the author never states. The unresolved issue in paragraph (4) is the collection's intended purpose. Giving comparison priority contradicts the author's suspension of judgment about priority and incorrectly treats an index as fully restoring continuity. Equating the indexed arrangements also erases paragraph (3)'s distinction between locating scattered tales and experiencing relevant tales consecutively. The author proposes a useful accommodation while preserving a meaningful choice between orderings.

questions.stem:
(1) In the fictional town of Darel, a repair circle considers opening a table where members can bring unfamiliar devices. Coordinator Heth proposes an advice-only trial: members would describe possible repairs, but no device would be worked on at the table. He expects this separation to make it easier to tell advice from a promise that a repair will succeed.

(2) Member Cala argues that the circle should postpone even that trial until it has a written way to record which suggestions are tentative. She accepts that Heth's arrangement limits what happens at the table, but doubts that the absence of actual repairs will by itself keep visitors from treating suggestions as guarantees.

(3) Heth's distinction is useful, and Cala's concern is well founded. A statement that nobody will perform a repair does not communicate how confident a particular suggestion is. A short written record could state both the proposed approach and the uncertainty attached to it. Such a record need not resolve whether the approach will work.

(4) The circle should combine an advice-only trial with written records of that kind. Cala has not said whether she would then favor opening the table, and her stated prerequisite does not settle that question. The proposal here addresses how advice is presented; it makes no prediction about how often the suggestions will lead to successful repairs.

Question: Which claim does the author reject?
choices: A written record could communicate the uncertainty attached to a proposed approach.
An advice-only format by itself communicates how confident a particular suggestion is.
Cala might still withhold support after the circle creates a way to record tentative advice.
Uncertainty about whether an approach will work can remain even when the advice is recorded.
questions.explanation:
Paragraph (3) explicitly distinguishes stating that no repair will be performed from communicating confidence in a suggestion. The author therefore rejects the claim that the advice-only format by itself communicates that confidence.

A written record's ability to state uncertainty is the author's own proposal in paragraph (3), not a rejected claim. The possibility that Cala might still withhold support is left open in paragraph (4): fulfilling her prerequisite does not establish her subsequent position. Continuing uncertainty about success is also compatible with the author, who says in paragraph (3) that a record need not resolve whether the proposed approach will work. The author's criticism targets what a format communicates, not the possibility of useful but uncertain advice.

questions.stem:
(1) In the fictional town of Darel, a repair circle considers opening a table where members can bring unfamiliar devices. Coordinator Heth proposes an advice-only trial: members would describe possible repairs, but no device would be worked on at the table. He expects this separation to make it easier to tell advice from a promise that a repair will succeed.

(2) Member Cala argues that the circle should postpone even that trial until it has a written way to record which suggestions are tentative. She accepts that Heth's arrangement limits what happens at the table, but doubts that the absence of actual repairs will by itself keep visitors from treating suggestions as guarantees.

(3) Heth's distinction is useful, and Cala's concern is well founded. A statement that nobody will perform a repair does not communicate how confident a particular suggestion is. A short written record could state both the proposed approach and the uncertainty attached to it. Such a record need not resolve whether the approach will work.

(4) The circle should combine an advice-only trial with written records of that kind. Cala has not said whether she would then favor opening the table, and her stated prerequisite does not settle that question. The proposal here addresses how advice is presented; it makes no prediction about how often the suggestions will lead to successful repairs.

Question: Which claim should NOT be attributed to Cala on the basis of the passage?
choices: The circle should postpone the proposed trial until it can record which suggestions are tentative.
The absence of actual repairs may fail to keep visitors from treating suggestions as guarantees.
Heth's arrangement restricts the activity that occurs at the table.
Once written records exist, the circle should begin an advice-only trial.
questions.explanation:
Beginning the trial with written records is the author's recommendation in paragraph (4), not a position attributed to Cala. That paragraph explicitly says Cala has not stated whether she would favor opening the table after her prerequisite is met. Her demand for a recording method does not make that method sufficient for her approval.

Postponing until tentative suggestions can be recorded is Cala's explicit recommendation in paragraph (2). Doubting that the absence of repairs prevents visitors from hearing guarantees is also her stated concern there. Accepting that Heth's plan limits activity at the table is her concession in the same paragraph. These three claims can all be attributed to her. The incorrect attribution borrows a real recommendation from the passage but assigns it to the wrong speaker.

questions.stem:
Passage A

(A1) A stone screen at the fictional Varden Object House survives with three missing sections. Old drawings establish the screen's outer outline but do not record the carving in those sections. I favor inserting plain, removable pieces along the documented outline. The additions would help visitors follow the screen's broad arrangement without pretending to recover unknown decoration. Each insert should carry a visible date, and an adjacent drawing should show which portions are modern. The proposed material is visibly different from the old stone, so visitors could still examine the surviving work separately.

(A2) Leaving every gap open gives accidental losses too much influence over the first impression of the object. The screen was designed as a connected arrangement, and its surviving outline supplies a basis for restoring that aspect of its appearance. This does not justify inventing missing carvings or applying the same treatment whenever any fragment is lost. Where the outline itself is uncertain, an insert would embody a guess. Here, however, plain additions can distinguish the documented arrangement from unknown details. I therefore recommend the limited installation, accompanied by an account of its evidence and limits.

Passage B

(B1) Varden's proposed inserts would be recognizable as new work, and I accept that they could make the screen's outline easier to follow. Nevertheless, I oppose installing them. An open gap displays the limits of what survives, whereas filling it makes physical completeness the dominant way of presenting the object. A visitor could understand the warning labels and still receive that emphasis. My objection is therefore not that every visitor would mistake an insert for ancient stone. It concerns the choice of what the display foregrounds even when the additions are honestly identified.

(B2) The adjacent drawing can show the documented outline while the screen retains its gaps. Visitors would then be able to move between a representation of the larger arrangement and the surviving material, without making one stand in for the other. Any newly added material should always be identifiable; that safeguard is necessary but does not settle whether an addition is desirable. I also agree that unknown carvings should not be invented. These points leave our central choice open: whether restoring the documented outline in the object itself should take priority over displaying the extent of its survival.

Question: The authors disagree most directly about whether which action is appropriate for the Varden screen?
choices: Inventing carved details to make the missing portions resemble the surviving work.
Displaying a drawing that shows the documented outline beside the surviving object.
Distinguishing newly added material from the screen's surviving old stone.
Installing identifiable, plain inserts to restore its documented outer outline.
questions.explanation:
The disputed action is physically filling the gaps along the known outline. Passage A recommends the limited installation in (A1) and (A2), while Passage B rejects it in (B1) and favors leaving the screen's gaps visible in (B2). Their agreement that additions would be identifiable does not resolve this choice.

Inventing missing carvings is rejected in (A2) and (B2), so it is common ground rather than the disagreement. Both can accommodate a drawing that explains the outline and distinguishes modern work: (A1) includes such a drawing, and (B2) proposes using the drawing while leaving gaps. Both also require added material to be distinguishable from old stone, as stated in (A1) and (B2). The conflict concerns whether to install the plain pieces at all, not whether to conceal their status.

questions.stem:
Passage A

(A1) Researchers studying the imaginary nedra plant compare matched plants under two kinds of illumination. Temperature, water, and handling are held constant. The leaves curl farther under green light than under white light, and repeated switches between the lights reproduce the difference. I accept this as evidence that changing illumination can change curling under the tested conditions. It does not identify the internal process responsible. The team proposes that light affects fluid movement through narrow channels beneath the leaf surface, which in turn changes the leaf's shape. That account is a hypothesis consistent with the observations, not a directly observed sequence.

(A2) A practical question can be investigated while the internal account remains unsettled. I favor a small nursery trial to learn whether adjusting illumination reliably produces the desired leaf arrangement across the nursery's growing conditions. The trial should record failures as well as successes, rather than assume that the controlled comparison settles performance elsewhere. It would test control of arrangement, not establish improved plant health or explain the internal route. Understanding a mechanism could help explain inconsistent results, but lack of that understanding does not by itself make every limited practical trial pointless. The experimental question and the practical question should remain distinguishable.

Passage B

(B1) The nedra experiments establish a pattern that an account of curling should explain. I do not dispute the demonstrated effect of changing illumination under the conditions described. But reproducing that effect does not choose among possible internal routes. The suggested movement through channels might be required, might merely accompany a different process, or might not occur at all. Describing an unseen sequence in plausible terms cannot substitute for evidence connecting its steps. The next investigation of that hypothesis should therefore distinguish the proposed route from alternatives that could also produce the observed response to light.

(B2) One possible test would temporarily block the channels while preserving the leaf's exposure to light and holding other relevant conditions constant. If channel movement is required, the expected change in curling should be reduced or absent when that movement is prevented. Such a result would still need comparison with a procedure that causes similar handling without blocking movement; otherwise handling itself could explain the difference. This is a proposal for obtaining discriminating evidence, not a report that the test has already been performed. A clear experimental prediction makes the hypothesis answerable to further observations without pretending that the original light comparison has established it.

Question: Which claim about the nedra experiment would both authors accept?
choices: The described comparison supports an effect of illumination on curling without establishing the proposed internal route.
Repeatedly reproducing curling establishes that the channels carry fluid in response to green light.
The effect of illumination remains unsupported until the internal route has been directly observed.
The controlled comparison establishes reliable control of leaf arrangement throughout nursery conditions.
questions.explanation:
Passage A accepts an effect of illumination under the tested conditions in (A1) while treating the channel account as a hypothesis. Passage B likewise accepts the demonstrated effect in (B1) but says it does not select among internal routes. The common claim distinguishes evidence for an input effect from evidence for its mechanism.

Repeated curling does not establish movement through channels; (A1) calls that sequence unseen, and (B1) allows several possibilities concerning it. Withholding all support for an illumination effect until the route is observed contradicts the effect both authors accept. Extending the controlled comparison to reliable nursery control also exceeds both passages. Passage A proposes a separate trial in (A2) precisely because the comparison does not settle performance across nursery conditions; Passage B supplies no such performance claim.

questions.stem:
(1) The fictional Neral canal association has tested a new bell sequence for summoning maintenance crews. Because every crew acknowledged the sequence promptly, several members propose installing the bells and canceling the annual coordination exercise. That exercise interrupts ordinary work, and its cost is a legitimate concern. Nevertheless, the proposal treats two accomplishments as interchangeable: receiving a common warning and organizing a collective response to it.

(2) During the trial, crew leaders had received route cards assigning responsibilities the previous afternoon. The observers recorded how quickly each crew acknowledged the signal; they did not require crews to allocate tasks or resolve conflicting assignments. Prepared coordination was thus part of the trial's starting conditions. The trial therefore does not establish that the bell sequence could produce coordinated assignments when those assignments had not already been supplied. Its success concerned a narrower task.

(3) This limitation is not a finding that the bells would fail in every emergency. A reliable signal can contribute to preparedness without supplying everything preparedness requires. Nor must the association defend every feature of its old exercise in order to recognize the missing comparison. A different exercise might test coordination more economically, but prompt acknowledgment alone does not show that coordination practice has become unnecessary.

(4) The association should consequently consider the bells as a supplement while retaining a way to practice collective task allocation. Whether the existing exercise should be shortened, redesigned, or eventually replaced requires evidence about that function. Where crews can already coordinate independently, different arrangements may be justified; the reported trial has not established that condition. The interruption of ordinary work gives the association a reason to seek a less costly exercise, not a reason to count a test of signaling as a demonstration that no exercise is needed.

Question: What role does the conclusion in paragraph (2) about coordinated assignments play in the author's argument?
choices: It states the final recommendation that the association should decline to install the bells.
It draws a limit from the trial design that supports keeping coordination practice in the broader plan.
It presents the members' claim about the old exercise so that the author can reject that claim as too cautious.
It explains the exercise's financial burden without affecting what the trial can establish about preparedness.
questions.explanation:
The claim draws a limit from the trial design and helps support retaining coordination practice. Paragraph (2) moves from prepared route cards and the observers' narrow measurement to a conclusion about what the trial does not establish. Paragraph (4) then uses that limitation in a broader recommendation: consider the bells as a supplement while retaining a way to practice task allocation.

The recommendation to decline installation is not the author's position; paragraphs (3) and (4) preserve a possible role for the bells. The conclusion is the author's response to the members' replacement proposal, not the members' own cautious claim. The financial explanation misidentifies both its evidence and its effect. Work interruption appears in paragraphs (1) and (4), whereas paragraph (2) limits the inference from a particular trial.

questions.stem:
(1) An unsigned dramatic script from the fictional town of Avren survives in an early master copy and three later performers' notebooks. An editor attributes the original script to Sela on separate documentary evidence, then credits Sela with every passage in all four versions. The earlier attribution need not be discarded to question this extension. Establishing who composed a script and establishing who supplied each subsequent alteration are different tasks.

(2) The notebooks contain new exchanges as well as cuts. A distinctive exchange first documented in one notebook and a different exchange first documented in another both appear in the third. Independently dated rehearsal records establish the order of the three notebooks. This combination supports transmission among the documented versions, rather than three unchanged copies of the master. It does not identify whether Sela, a performer, or another collaborator introduced either exchange.

(3) The chronological qualification matters. Where the order of documents is independently established, the arrangement of shared changes can support an account of successive revision. Merely assuming that the longest version is the latest would instead build the proposed sequence into the evidence used to defend it. Here the rehearsal records provide the needed independence. Even so, an account of how versions developed can be better supported than an account naming the person responsible for every change.

(4) A responsible edition should therefore distinguish the attribution of the initial script from the documentation of later revisions, marking unknown contributors as unknown. This treatment preserves the earlier attribution while declining to convert it into comprehensive authorship. It also leaves room for new evidence to identify particular revisers. The alternative is not a choice between crediting Sela with everything and printing the entire work without attribution: the available evidence supports different degrees of specificity for different parts of the textual history.

Question: What is the primary argumentative function of paragraph (3)?
choices: To replace the attribution to Sela with the claim that the longest notebook identifies the principal author.
To show that uncertainty about the identity of revisers prevents any conclusions about relationships among versions.
To explain why the chronological evidence supports a revision sequence while preserving a limit on identifying its contributors.
To defend the editor's comprehensive attribution by arguing that every later version must have the same author as the master.
questions.explanation:
Paragraph (3) explains the independence of the chronological evidence and preserves the distinction between a supported revision sequence and unidentified contributors. It contrasts independently established ordering with an ordering assumed from length, then states that an account of textual development may be better supported than an account naming every reviser. This develops the intermediate conclusions in paragraph (2) and prepares the differentiated attribution recommended in paragraph (4).

The longest-notebook account reverses the paragraph's warning against deriving order from length and never establishes an author. The uncertainty account erases the paragraph's distinction: uncertainty about who revised does not eliminate evidence about how versions developed. The comprehensive-attribution account defends the very extension questioned in paragraphs (1) and (4).

choices: Officials should evaluate a limited remedy for an imposed shipping burden on its purpose and cost, without rejecting it solely because some advantaged studios could benefit.
Officials should reserve all assistance for studios with few resources, because otherwise the proposal cannot remove an exhibition-related barrier.
Officials should reimburse every expense of eligible entrants, because requiring models makes the exhibition responsible for equalizing all prospects.
Officials should implement the reimbursement proposal immediately, because the legitimacy of its objective settles the question of affordability.
questions.explanation:

Reimbursing every expense removes paragraph (2)'s restriction to a specified burden and contradicts paragraph (3)'s warning against assuming equal prospects. Immediate implementation goes beyond the recommendation; paragraphs (3) and (4) leave costs and competing uses of money to be evaluated.
