(1) Rae wants the next full practice session to show whether she can carry a declared return rule through the complete section sequence. She has selected an appropriate authorized form, checked its exposure history, and identified the conditions she intends to use. She has not started the attempt.

(2) A friend suggests waiting for the result before deciding which behavior the session was meant to test. Rae instead wants a plan that lets her compare the intended activity with what she actually did, including any deviations.

Question: Which action best completes Rae's protocol?
choices: Define the session's purpose afterward using whichever statistic improved most, so the protocol always emphasizes a successful result.
Record only the intended return rule and treat its presence in the plan as evidence that she executed it throughout the session.
State that following the return rule will prove her general readiness, since one complete attempt removes uncertainty about future forms.
Write the purpose and complete conditions before starting, then preserve the actual result and any departures from the declared plan.
questions.explanation: A prior statement of purpose and conditions makes the later comparison meaningful, while a deviation record separates intention from execution. Choosing the purpose after seeing the result invites selective interpretation. Merely writing a return rule does not show that Rae followed it. One complete attempt also cannot establish general readiness across future forms and conditions.

questions.stem:
(1) In November 2026, a learner plans to take the LSAT in August 2027. The official transition guidance she checks announces a new three-section format for that administration and schedules practice in that format for February 2027. Her currently available authorized forms use the earlier arrangement.

(2) She wants to keep studying now while making an accurate plan for a later full simulation. She has no separate evidence that the announced new-format materials have already become available.

Question: Which plan is supported by that information?
choices: Describe an earlier-format attempt as new-format practice now because the future publication date establishes present availability.
Combine earlier sections into a personally chosen order and identify the result as an official form for the announced format.
Label present practice by its actual format and recheck availability and version before selecting later practice for the intended administration.
Treat all present reasoning practice as unusable because a later format change prevents learning from the currently available questions.
questions.explanation: Present work can support learning when its actual format is recorded. The announcement supports a later availability check and selection of an appropriate verified version. It does not establish present availability, and a homemade rearrangement does not become an official form. A format transition also does not make reasoning practice with existing authorized material useless.

questions.stem:
(1) A planning exercise specifies a target sequence of a fifty-two-minute reading section followed by two forty-five-minute reasoning sections, with a ten-minute break between sections. A learner proposes a forty-seven-minute reasoning section, a forty-seven-minute reading section, and a forty-eight-minute reasoning section, keeping the two breaks.

(2) Both arrangements contain 142 working minutes. The learner argues that this equality alone establishes a format match. The intended purpose is to practise the specified sequence and its distribution of work, not merely to work for the same total duration.

Question: Which assessment of the learner's argument is best supported?
choices: The equal total does not establish a match because the proposed arrangement changes both the task sequence and the allocation of working time.
The equal total establishes a match because section order and separate time limits cannot matter once total working time is fixed.
The proposed arrangement matches the target because placing the longest allotted section last compensates for any changes earlier in the sequence.
The arrangements cannot be compared at all because even their stated totals and section orders cannot provide useful planning information.
questions.explanation: Both totals are 142 minutes, but the target distributes that time as 52, 45, and 45 in reading–reasoning–reasoning order. The proposal uses 47, 47, and 48 in reasoning–reading–reasoning order. Those differences defeat the claimed match for the stated purpose. No compensation principle is supplied, and equal totals do not make section details irrelevant. The explicit details do permit a useful comparison; they reveal the mismatch.

questions.stem:
(1) Before a series of planned simulations, Daniel decides to record every attempt's form, exposure history, intended conditions, and actual deviations. He expects that some sessions may be interrupted or reveal previously encountered material. He wants later comparisons to show which attempts fit the intended measurement conditions.

(2) A classmate recommends retaining only the highest results and treating them as the whole series, regardless of the conditions. Daniel is choosing his recording procedure now, before any of the new attempts has occurred.

Question: Which procedure best supports his stated comparison?
choices: Keep only the highest results, since strong results demonstrate that any recorded interruption or exposure had no effect.
Delete every interrupted attempt entirely, since a deviation prevents both qualified comparison and useful reasoning review.
Retain all attempts, define relevant condition categories in advance, and identify which results satisfy the intended comparison criteria.
Treat every completed form as equivalent, since completing the same general activity makes exposure and conditions irrelevant.
questions.explanation: Retaining all attempts and defining the relevant conditions before results are known supports an honest comparison. Qualified results can still supply learning evidence. Choosing only high results hides part of the series and does not establish that deviations were harmless. Deleting interrupted work discards useful information unnecessarily. Completion alone does not equalize familiarity, conditions, or form difficulty.

questions.stem:
(1) June has reserved an appropriate official form for a later unfamiliar full attempt. She wants to check display settings, section navigation, and whether finishing an activity reveals feedback. She has access to a tutorial and another form she has already completed and reviewed.

(2) June has not previewed the reserved form's questions. Her aim today is to learn the controls and the route to results, while keeping the planned content exposure for the later session as intact as the available tools allow.

Question: Which preparation best fits that aim?
choices: Open the reserved form's passages to test scrolling and keep calling the later attempt wholly unfamiliar if she leaves its choices unanswered.
Inspect the reserved form's explanations to learn the results screen and erase the exposure record once she closes the browser.
Avoid learning the controls from any source, since using a tutorial necessarily exposes every question in the reserved form.
Use the tutorial or previously reviewed form to inspect the controls and feedback route, then record any limitations that remain.
questions.explanation: A tutorial or training form can support the control check without deliberately opening reserved content; remaining differences can be recorded. Reading reserved passages would create exposure even without answers. Opening explanations would expose feedback, and closing the browser would not erase that history. No premise establishes that a tutorial reveals every question in the reserved form, so avoiding all preparation is unsupported.

questions.stem:
(1) For a custom learning rehearsal, not an official LSAT timing specification, Luis writes a protocol with four twenty-minute work blocks and a five-minute break after each of the first three blocks. His goal is to complete that entire planned sequence in one uninterrupted room booking.

(2) The room is available for ninety minutes, including the breaks. Setup will occur beforehand. Luis wants the record to distinguish the written protocol from any shortened activity rather than silently change the plan once he reaches the booking limit.

Question: Which planning conclusion follows?
choices: The booking fits the protocol because only the eighty working minutes count toward a room reservation that includes breaks.
The protocol needs ninety-five minutes, so Luis needs a longer booking or a separately labeled plan with a different sequence or duration.
The protocol needs ninety minutes because four work blocks require only two of the three breaks explicitly specified in the plan.
The booking fits the protocol if the final five minutes are omitted, since that omission leaves the completed sequence unchanged.
questions.explanation: Four blocks contribute 4 × 20 = 80 minutes and three breaks contribute 3 × 5 = 15 minutes, for 95 minutes. The ninety-minute booking is five minutes short. Breaks occupy the room's available interval, and the protocol explicitly includes three rather than two. Omitting five minutes changes the completed activity. Luis can arrange sufficient time or describe a different learning plan accurately without treating it as the original complete sequence.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner completes a custom session containing sixty-four original questions. At the declared cutoffs, fifty responses are correct, ten are wrong, and four are blank. The preserved answer history shows that these outcomes cover every assigned item. The session is a learning exercise with no official scale conversion.

(2) Before opening any explanations, the learner answers all four remaining questions correctly. None of the previously entered responses changes. A study partner wants to keep a single headline number and proposes using the completed answer sheet as the record of performance at the original cutoffs.

Question: Which summary accurately preserves the distinction between the two phases?
choices: The cutoff result is fifty out of sixty, and the completed result is fifty-four out of sixty-four.
The cutoff and completed results are both fifty-four out of sixty-four because the key stayed closed.
The cutoff result is fifty out of sixty-four, and the later completed result is fifty-four out of sixty-four.
The cutoff result is fifty out of sixty-four, and the later completed result is fifty-four out of sixty.
questions.explanation: The cutoff record has fifty correct among all sixty-four assigned items; the four blanks remain in its denominator. Later completion raises the correct count to fifty-four on the same sixty-four items. Fifty out of sixty measures accuracy among answered items, not the whole cutoff result. Keeping the key closed does not move later responses before their cutoffs. A completed numerator of fifty-four cannot be paired with the earlier attempted-item denominator of sixty to describe the completed set.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner is reconstructing a forty-item session from an allowed response history. Thirty-nine cutoff responses are recoverable: thirty-two correct, six wrong, and one blank. For the remaining item, the learner overwrote the response during later review, and neither the practice history nor the learner’s notes preserve its earlier state.

(2) The learner remembers hesitating over that item but cannot reliably remember selecting an option before the cutoff. The current answer is correct. A reviewer asks for the exact number correct at cutoff and suggests treating any missing historical response as an unanswered question.

Question: How should the learner handle the unrecoverable item?
choices: Keep its cutoff status unknown, preserve the thirty-nine known outcomes, and state that the exact cutoff total is not recoverable.
Classify it as blank, preserve the other outcomes, and report thirty-two correct as the exact cutoff total.
Use its current correct response as the cutoff response, since the learner remembers considering the item during the attempt.
Remove the item from the assigned set and report the result on thirty-nine questions as the complete session record.
questions.explanation: The evidence establishes thirty-nine outcomes and leaves one historical response unknown. The exact cutoff correct count could be thirty-two or thirty-three, so neither should be asserted as certain. Calling the unknown item blank invents a response state. The current correct answer does not establish what existed earlier. Removing the item conceals missing evidence and changes the original forty-item assignment rather than recovering its complete record.

questions.stem:
(1) Two permitted versions of a practice package contain overlapping material, but they use different section orders, question numbers, and option orders. A learner’s old notes say only “section two, question twelve, option B.” A newer record contains the same displayed label, and the learner wants to compare the responses across versions.

(2) The learner has not yet checked the version identifiers or established which underlying question and alternative each label denotes. One study partner argues that matching letters prove stability, while another argues that any letter change would prove the learner changed their reasoning.

Question: What must be established before interpreting the two records as a response transition?
choices: That both attempts occurred in the same month, so the learner’s knowledge was unlikely to change between them.
That the two practice packages used the same number of options, so each letter represented the same position.
That the learner spent similar time on both attempts, so differences in numbering can be ignored in the comparison.
That the exact versions, section and item identities, and selected alternatives are mapped to the same underlying question.
questions.explanation: A response transition requires paired responses to the same identified item, with the chosen alternatives understood in each version. Matching option positions does not establish matching content after reordering. Similar timing cannot repair a question-identity mismatch. Being in the same month also does not establish identity or unchanged knowledge. Until the versions and alternatives are mapped, matching or changing displayed letters alone supports neither proposed interpretation.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner follows a declared three-block practice protocol with specified intermissions. The first two blocks proceed without interruption. During the third block, a connection failure stops work for four minutes and the practice timer is paused. The learner resumes, finishes that block, and retains all responses at their actual cutoffs.

(2) The learner’s summary lists the planned active-work total but omits the connection failure. A study partner suggests that the pause can be ignored because no extra questions were answered during those four minutes. The intended comparison is performance across complete uninterrupted sessions.

Question: Which revision makes the session record suitable for honest interpretation?
choices: Describe every block as interrupted, discard the saved responses, and estimate what the learner would have answered without the failure.
Keep the first two blocks’ uninterrupted descriptions, record the third-block pause, and label the complete session as interrupted.
Keep the complete session labeled uninterrupted, but subtract four minutes from its planned active-work total to offset the pause.
Combine the first two blocks with an earlier uninterrupted third block and present the combined result as this session’s performance.
questions.explanation: The record should preserve the interruption at its actual location while identifying the whole session as interrupted. The first two blocks need not be mislabeled, and their saved responses remain useful; estimating a counterfactual would add unsupported data. Subtracting minutes does not recreate uninterrupted work or justify changing the planned allowance. Combining blocks from different days creates a composite record, not the observed complete session.

questions.stem:
(1) A fictional record-reading exercise describes a practice package whose scoring instructions designate seventy-five items for its reported result and twenty-five additional items for separate practice. These counts are stipulated for the exercise; the package is not a named official LSAT form. All one hundred items were assigned during the session.

(2) The learner answered fifty-five of the designated seventy-five items correctly and fifteen of the additional twenty-five correctly. The learner wants both a result following the package’s stated scoring instructions and a count describing all assigned work. No conversion table is supplied with this exercise.

Question: Which summary keeps both counts faithful to their stated purposes?
choices: Use fifty-five out of seventy-five for the designated scoring set and seventy out of one hundred for all assigned work, with no invented conversion.
Use seventy out of seventy-five for the designated scoring set and seventy out of one hundred for all assigned work, since every correct response adds credit.
Use seventy out of one hundred for both purposes, since a single denominator makes the two summaries easier to compare.
Use fifty-five out of one hundred for both purposes, since excluded practice responses should be retained only as incorrect items.
questions.explanation: The designated set contains fifty-five correct among seventy-five items. Across all assigned work, fifty-five plus fifteen gives seventy correct among one hundred items. Adding the extra fifteen correct responses to the designated numerator without its corresponding items changes the scoring basis. Using the all-work denominator for both purposes ignores the stated instructions. Treating excluded items as wrong likewise invents an outcome and does not follow either intended count. No supplied information warrants a scale conversion.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner preserves every cutoff response and the actual timing conditions for a practice session but records no confidence judgments. After reading explanations, the learner recognizes several mistakes immediately and remembers feeling uncertain somewhere in the final block. The response history contains no earlier confidence marks.

(2) The learner wants to examine whether low confidence predicted errors. To complete the worksheet, the learner proposes assigning low confidence to the wrong answers and high confidence to the correct answers, then labeling those judgments as observations made during the original attempt.

Question: Which treatment preserves what the available evidence can actually support?
choices: Use the proposed confidence labels because the later explanation makes the learner’s earlier uncertainty easier to reconstruct accurately.
Discard the response record because the missing confidence judgments make the known answers and timing conditions unusable.
Keep the known response and condition records, mark first-attempt confidence as missing, and label any later recollections as retrospective.
Assign low confidence to every item in the final block and treat the earlier blocks as high confidence because only the final block is remembered.
questions.explanation: The response and condition records remain available, while first-attempt confidence is missing. Retrospective recollections may be noted as such but cannot be backdated into observed confidence ratings. Deriving confidence labels from correctness builds the desired association into the data. Discarding all known responses loses useful evidence unnecessarily. A vague memory of final-block uncertainty does not establish low confidence on every final-block item or high confidence on every earlier item.

questions.stem:
(1) In an original twenty-four-item exercise, a learner’s cutoff record contains sixteen correct responses, five wrong responses, and three blanks. Before opening feedback, the learner reconsiders the set. Fifteen of the correct responses stay correct and one becomes wrong. Four wrong responses become correct and one stays wrong.

(2) Of the three blanks, two become correct and the other remains blank. The learner keeps every phase separate and asks a partner to calculate the later total. The partner counts six items that newly became correct and describes that number as the net increase over the cutoff result.

Question: What are the later correct count and the net increase?
choices: Twenty-two correct out of twenty-four, with a net increase of six because six items newly became correct.
Twenty-one correct out of twenty-four, with a net increase of five after accounting for the harmful change.
Nineteen correct out of twenty-four, with a net increase of three because answers added to blanks cannot count later.
Sixteen correct out of twenty-four, with no net increase because only responses entered before the cutoff can ever be counted.
questions.explanation: Fifteen retained correct answers plus four corrected wrong answers plus two newly correct answers from blanks gives twenty-one. Relative to sixteen, the gain is five. Counting six newly correct items without the correct-to-wrong change produces twenty-two incorrectly. The blanks’ later correct responses belong in the later total, although they must not be inserted into the cutoff total. Holding every later total at sixteen confuses preserving the original phase with refusing to describe later work.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner preserves cutoff answers for all four questions associated with a reading passage. Before independently reconsidering the passage, the learner opens the explanation for the first question. That explanation identifies the author’s central position and distinguishes it from a view reported in the passage.

(2) The learner then revisits the other three questions, including one about the author’s attitude and another about the function of the reported view. Their individual answer keys remain closed. The learner proposes labeling those three later answers as unaffected blind-review results because their keys were never opened.

Question: Which description best fits the information available during that later review?
choices: The three later answers are fresh first attempts because the learner has not opened their individual answer keys.
The first explanation must have determined all three later answers, so there is no remaining value in examining their reasoning.
The original cutoff answers are now feedback-assisted and should be replaced by the later choices in the first-attempt record.
The later review may be affected by shared-passage information from the explanation; preserve the earlier cutoff answers and record that exposure.
questions.explanation: An explanation can reveal passage-level information relevant to several questions. The later review should therefore record the exposure rather than claim it was unaffected. That does not establish that the explanation determined every answer or eliminate the value of further analysis. The preserved cutoff answers existed before the reveal and do not become assisted retroactively. The later answers are neither fresh first attempts nor feedback-free simply because their own keys stayed closed.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner plans to complete a practice session, preserve the cutoff responses, and then reconsider uncertain questions before seeing any feedback. On selecting the completion control, the permitted practice interface immediately displays the correct option for each missed item. The learner reads several of those options before recognizing what happened.

(2) The original response history remains available. The learner has not yet opened detailed explanations and wants to continue learning from the session. A partner suggests closing the page and waiting until tomorrow so the next pass can still be described as review completed without answer exposure.

Question: Which next step preserves the most accurate account of the session?
choices: Wait until tomorrow, then call the next pass feedback-free because a delay removes the influence of the displayed options.
Call the next pass blind review because correct options count as assistance only when detailed explanations accompany them.
Retain the original cutoff history, record the displayed-answer exposure, and label subsequent review accordingly while checking future workflows in advance.
Replace the original history with the next pass and report the later result as the only usable record of the session.
questions.explanation: The original cutoff history remains evidence of the earlier attempt. Recording which feedback appeared and labeling subsequent work accordingly preserves both phases; checking the workflow in advance can help plan future independent review. Waiting does not establish that revealed answers no longer influence reasoning. Correct options provide information even without explanations. Replacing the original history would erase rather than repair the distinction between earlier performance and later learning.

questions.stem:
(1) After a custom sixty-item session, a learner sees only the aggregate result: forty-two correct. The interface has not shown which items were wrong, any correct option, or any explanation. The learner’s uncertain-item list was recorded before completion and remains unchanged after seeing the total.

(2) The learner now reconsiders those uncertain items using only the questions and their own reasoning. A study partner offers two labels: completely feedback-free review or review after seeing every answer. The learner wants wording that describes the actual information available without overstating or concealing it.

Question: Which label is most accurate?
choices: Review after aggregate feedback, with individual keys and explanations still unseen.
Completely feedback-free review, because an overall score is not information about the attempt.
Review after full answer exposure, because a total score identifies every incorrect response.
A new first attempt, because the uncertain-item list was created before the aggregate result appeared.
questions.explanation: The learner has received aggregate feedback but has not seen item-level keys or explanations. Recording both facts describes the condition precisely. Calling the review completely feedback-free omits information the learner did receive. Calling it full answer exposure invents item-level information not provided by the total. Keeping an earlier uncertainty list does not make a second pass a first attempt or remove prior familiarity with the questions.

questions.stem:
(1) A twenty-four-item cutoff record contains eighteen correct answers, five wrong answers, and one blank. Before feedback, the learner reconsiders only six flagged items: two originally correct, three originally wrong, and the blank. Of those six, one correct answer becomes wrong, two wrong answers become correct, and the blank becomes correct.

(2) The other flagged answers remain unchanged. All eighteen unreviewed cutoff responses are carried forward unchanged into a later whole-set record. The learner wants to report the later count but also avoid suggesting that the entire set was independently solved a second time.

Question: Which summary accurately describes that later record?
choices: Twenty-one correct out of twenty-four, with all twenty-four independently reconsidered because each has a carried-forward response.
Twenty correct out of twenty-four, proving that the learner can reproduce every correct answer on unfamiliar material.
Eighteen correct out of twenty-four, because carrying responses forward prevents counting any successful review change.
Twenty correct out of twenty-four, with six items reconsidered and eighteen original responses carried forward.
questions.explanation: The later count is eighteen minus one harmful change plus two repaired wrong answers plus one corrected blank, giving twenty. Only six items were reconsidered; eighteen were carried forward. A count of twenty-one ignores the harmful change, and carrying a response forward is not re-solving it. The later record concerns familiar material and establishes no fresh transfer guarantee. Refusing to count changes would fail to describe the later record, even though eighteen remains the separate cutoff total.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner independently reconsiders a wrong answer while a tutor observes. Before the learner finishes, the tutor says, “Check whether your conclusion treats a statement about some members as if it concerned every member.” The learner rereads the question, changes the answer, and later finds that the new response is correct.

(2) The tutor never names an option or supplies the correct answer. The original cutoff response is still saved. The learner proposes recording the successful change as unaided blind review because selecting the final alternative required the learner’s own reasoning rather than copying a letter.

Question: How should the learner record this change?
choices: As unaided blind review, because a hint affects provenance only when it identifies a particular answer option.
As a revision made after a reasoning hint, while retaining the earlier response and specifying that the tutor did not supply an answer.
As proof that the original cutoff response was correct in substance, since the learner could repair it after a small cue.
As a wholly unusable response that should be deleted along with the cutoff answer because any assistance destroys learning value.
questions.explanation: The tutor supplied a relevant reasoning cue before the revision, so the assistance record should identify that cue while accurately noting its limited scope. An option letter is not required for help to influence an answer. The successful revision does not change the earlier wrong response into a correct one. Neither response needs deletion: the contrast can reveal a repair to test later without the cue on unfamiliar material.

questions.stem:
(1) An authorized practice platform reports a scaled practice result for a named form and configuration. A learner completed that form after studying several of its questions the previous week. During the attempt, she also paused the clock for an unplanned conversation and later resumed it.

(2) The learner saves the platform report and her condition notes. She wants to include the result in a progress record without giving the displayed number a meaning that the attempt cannot establish.

Question: Which record is best supported?
choices: Treat the displayed result as equivalent to an unfamiliar uninterrupted attempt because the platform supplied the number.
Retain the reported practice result with the repeated-item exposure and interruption, while limiting comparisons with unfamiliar uninterrupted attempts.
Delete the condition notes because a scaled practice result already adjusts for any personal interruption or previous exposure.
Convert the result into an administered LSAT score because the material came from an authorized official source.
questions.explanation: The report can be retained with the conditions that qualify its interpretation. A displayed practice result does not remove prior exposure or an interruption, and no adjustment for those factors is described. Official practice material does not turn a study session into an administered LSAT. Deleting the notes would conceal information needed for a sound comparison.

questions.stem:
(1) Two original teaching packets each contain twenty-four questions. Packet Cedar has six conditional-reasoning items, of which a learner answers three correctly, and eighteen other items, of which fifteen are correct. Packet Willow has twelve conditional items, of which eight are correct, and twelve other items, of which eight are correct.

(2) The packets are unfamiliar but have not been established as equivalent forms. The learner wants to summarize the observed counts before deciding whether a repair deserves further investigation.

Question: Which summary is accurate?
choices: The total rises from eighteen to twenty correct because the conditional correct count increases by five.
The conditional proportion declines because the learner makes more conditional errors in Willow than in Cedar.
The total falls from eighteen to sixteen correct, while the observed conditional proportion rises from three of six to eight of twelve.
The overall decrease proves that the learner’s conditional reasoning became less accurate on comparable items.
questions.explanation: Cedar totals 3 + 15 = 18, while Willow totals 8 + 8 = 16. The conditional proportions are 3/6 and 8/12, so the observed proportion rises despite the larger number of conditional errors. Adding only the conditional gain ignores the other-item decline. Different task composition and unequated questions prevent the overall decrease from proving deterioration on comparable conditional items.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner uses a practice form whose supplied instructions designate three sections for its scored total and identify another section as additional practice. The report supplies a conversion for that exact scored configuration. The learner completes all sections, preserving every response, and also keeps a separate count for the additional section.

(2) A study partner suggests adding every correct response before using the supplied conversion, arguing that every completed question required effort and therefore should increase the converted total.

Question: Which scoring approach follows the supplied information?
choices: Add all correct responses and apply the conversion because effort makes every item part of the scored configuration.
Use whichever combination of sections produces the highest converted result, provided all responses were recorded.
Apply the same conversion to an original course quiz with the same number of questions as the designated configuration.
Use only the designated scored configuration for that form’s conversion and retain the additional-section count as a separate diagnostic.
questions.explanation: The supplied conversion belongs to the specified form and scored configuration. The additional section can inform learning without being added to that conversion. Effort and a favorable total do not change the scoring instructions. Matching an item count does not establish that original questions share an official form’s conversion.

questions.stem:
(1) Across four study sessions, a learner records results but notes several differences. One form was repeated, another was unfamiliar but interrupted, and two unfamiliar forms were completed under the intended conditions. During the same period, the learner changed both a skipping rule and a passage-reading method.

(2) The most recent result is higher than the first. The learner wants to decide what the sequence can establish about the new skipping rule without discarding the records that were collected.

Question: Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: The sequence documents varied practice outcomes but does not isolate the skipping rule’s causal effect from the other changes and conditions.
The higher last result proves that the skipping rule caused the entire gain across the four sessions.
The two unfamiliar uninterrupted forms must be equally difficult because their timing conditions were the same.
The repeated and interrupted attempts cannot provide any information about particular reasoning mistakes.
questions.explanation: The conditions and two simultaneous method changes prevent a unique causal attribution. Matching timing does not establish equal form difficulty. Repeated or interrupted work can still reveal reasoning errors when honestly labeled. Retaining the series with its qualifications is more informative than either treating it as a controlled experiment or discarding its diagnostic content.

questions.stem:
(1) In a thirty-question original learning set, a learner records twenty-three correct responses, five wrong responses, and two blanks at cutoff. Four of the correct responses had been marked uncertain before feedback. The learner wants both a raw result and a review list, without changing the scoring rule after seeing the answers.

(2) A partner proposes subtracting the four uncertain answers from the numerator so the reported accuracy reflects only answers the learner felt sure about.

Question: Which report preserves both scoring and diagnostic information?
choices: Report nineteen correct out of thirty because uncertain correct answers should be scored as errors.
Report twenty-three correct out of thirty, with four uncertain correct answers separately flagged for review.
Report twenty-three correct out of twenty-eight and omit the blanks from the complete-set result.
Report twenty-seven correct out of thirty because each uncertain correct answer earns an additional confidence point.
questions.explanation: All twenty-three correct responses earn raw credit, and all thirty assigned items remain in the denominator. Uncertainty is a separate review flag, not a penalty or bonus. Twenty-three out of twenty-eight may describe attempted-item accuracy if named, but it cannot replace the complete-set result by silently removing the blanks.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner finishes a set of original Erudior questions and obtains a raw percentage. The course has not established equivalence between this set and any official practice form. The learner finds an official form’s conversion chart and observes that both sets happen to have the same number of scored questions.

(2) The learner wants to place the original result on a progress page alongside clearly labeled official practice reports, but has no evidence linking these questions to the chart’s scale.

Question: Which presentation is justified?
choices: Apply the chart because equal question counts establish equivalent score scales for any reasoning test.
Convert only the questions that look difficult because visual complexity determines their official scoring weight.
Keep the original result as a raw count with its denominator and list official practice reports separately with their form identities.
Replace the original denominator with the chart’s highest score so both records appear on one scale.
questions.explanation: The original set supports a raw count, while the official reports retain their own form-specific meaning. Equal counts and apparent difficulty do not establish a conversion. Replacing a denominator with a scale endpoint would mix incompatible quantities rather than create comparable evidence.

questions.stem:
(1) In several passage questions, a learner selects an answer that attributes a quoted researcher’s claim to the passage’s author. During review, the learner can locate both voices but explains that, under the deadline, every statement near the final paragraph was treated as the author’s own position.

(2) The learner’s current error-log entry says only “reading weakness.” A new practice block is available, and the learner wants a replacement action that directly addresses the observed step.

Question: Which repair is most closely matched to the evidence?
choices: Memorize more technical vocabulary without checking who makes the disputed claim in each passage.
Choose whichever answer quotes the last paragraph because late placement establishes author endorsement.
Avoid every answer about an author’s view because the repeated error proves such questions cannot be learned.
Before attributing a claim, identify its speaker and check whether the author endorses, qualifies, or merely reports it.
questions.explanation: The observed mechanism is an attribution error, so a speaker-and-endorsement check directly addresses it. Vocabulary study might serve other needs but is not tied to the evidence given. Late placement does not establish endorsement, and repeated errors identify a learning priority rather than an inability to learn the task.

questions.stem:
(1) An original rule says that every approved river-monitoring project has a calibration record. A learner correctly concludes that a project without such a record was not approved. In the written explanation, however, the learner says that possessing a calibration record guarantees approval.

(2) The key confirms the selected answer. The learner wants to decide whether there is anything to repair before moving to unfamiliar conditional-reasoning work.

Question: Which assessment of the response is strongest?
choices: The answer earns credit, but the explanation reverses the condition and should be repaired before testing the method on a new item.
The correct selection establishes that the stated guarantee is a valid restatement of the original rule.
The explanation is valid because a necessary condition always becomes sufficient when the answer is correct.
The response must lose raw credit because any flaw in a private explanation changes the selected answer’s correctness.
questions.explanation: Approval requires a calibration record; a record alone need not guarantee approval. The selected conclusion follows by contraposition, so it earns credit, but the learner’s converse claim is unsupported. A correct choice does not validate every explanation, and reviewing faulty reasoning does not require changing the raw scoring rule.

questions.stem:
(1) After studying an explanation, a learner reworks the same mistaken comparison question and now rejects the original distractor. The learner can state the different populations that were improperly compared. A later question uses a new topic and different wording but asks for a related comparison judgment without naming the earlier trap.

(2) The learner wants to distinguish understanding the repaired example from using the method independently when the problem no longer announces what to check.

Question: Which next step provides the more direct evidence of transfer?
choices: Repeat the corrected example until its answer is recalled instantly, then label those repetitions fresh transfer trials.
Save a first answer and explanation for the unfamiliar question before feedback, and check whether the relevant populations were compared appropriately.
Read the unfamiliar question’s explanation first so the later correct response is guaranteed to demonstrate independent use.
Assume transfer is established because the learner can now recite the original explanation without looking.
questions.explanation: An unfamiliar question answered before feedback more directly tests independent use of the repair. Repetition and recall can consolidate the familiar example but do not become fresh evidence. Reading the new explanation first changes the condition to assisted work, and reciting an old explanation does not establish use in a new situation.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner reviews ten mistakes from recent unfamiliar work. Six involve confusing an argument’s evidence with its conclusion; two involve denominator changes; two are still unexplained. The learner has time for one focused repair cycle before the next full practice session and has identified a concrete statement-role check for the six related errors.

(2) The learner wants a defensible priority, while preserving the unexplained cases rather than forcing them into the largest category.

Question: Which plan best uses the available evidence?
choices: Relabel all ten errors as statement-role errors so the largest category accounts for the complete record.
Study every topic for equal time because recurrence and an available repair cannot inform priorities.
Begin with the recurring statement-role mechanism, test the check on new work, and keep the other mechanisms and unresolved cases visible.
Guarantee that fixing the six related errors will add exactly six correct answers on the next full form.
questions.explanation: The recurring, specified mechanism and available action justify a manageable first priority. That choice does not establish the causes of the unresolved cases or guarantee a fixed gain on a different form. Equal time is not required when the evidence supports a more focused plan. Preserve the remaining errors for subsequent investigation.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner misses four questions near the end of a practice session and reports feeling tired. Two concern a technical passage, one contains a conditional reversal, and one was left blank after a long rereading loop. Earlier sections contained different question mixes and no comparable passage on the same topic.

(2) The learner wants to investigate endurance without treating section position as a complete explanation for every error.

Question: Which interpretation is best supported?
choices: Every late error was caused by fatigue because errors that occur together must share the same cause.
The technical passage proves that fatigue played no role in any part of the session.
The blank should be removed from the record because its mechanism cannot be determined from correctness alone.
Late placement and the fatigue report suggest a hypothesis, while item demands and the specific reasoning failures still require examination.
questions.explanation: The observations make endurance worth investigating but do not uniquely identify fatigue as the cause. Different item demands and identifiable reasoning failures may also matter. A technical passage does not rule fatigue out, and an unexplained blank remains part of the cutoff record and denominator.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner tests a new evidence-location check on six unfamiliar reading questions. All six answers are correct, and the written reasons cite relevant text without overstating it. The recorded attempt also takes substantially longer than the learner’s declared learning window, and the last two responses were completed after its cutoff.

(2) The learner has preserved both the cutoff record and the later completion. The goal is to assess the repair without merging these conditions.

Question: Which conclusion best matches the evidence?
choices: The explanations support progress in applying the check, while timely use remains unresolved and the cutoff result must remain separate.
The repair has achieved complete timed mastery because all six eventual answers are correct.
The late completion proves that the evidence-location check cannot improve reasoning on any future task.
The two late answers can be moved into the cutoff record because their reasoning is well supported.
questions.explanation: Correct, evidence-based explanations support the conceptual repair, but the later completion does not demonstrate that it fits the declared time condition. The cutoff and later records remain distinct. Exceeding the window does not prove the method is incapable of becoming more efficient, and valid later reasoning cannot be backdated.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner’s study calendar includes a full multiple-choice practice session and a separate original writing rehearsal. The learner plans to record the prompt identity, exposure, planning window, drafting window, and aids used for the writing task. Neither activity is an administered examination.

(2) A study partner says the writing rehearsal counts only if it begins immediately after the final multiple-choice section, even though the learner’s checked guidance describes writing as a separately administered component.

Question: Which scheduling decision is justified?
choices: Append writing immediately because any independently scheduled rehearsal cannot teach timed drafting.
Schedule writing deliberately as its own activity and preserve its conditions, without treating immediate attachment to the other session as required.
Omit writing because multiple-choice performance automatically establishes the ability to construct a complete essay.
Merge the two activities into one score so the calendar resembles a single administered examination.
questions.explanation: The described guidance supports separate scheduling and a distinct record. Immediate attachment is not required for learning, and a multiple-choice result does not establish writing performance. Combining the activities into one score would invent a scoring relationship not supplied by the tasks.

questions.stem:
(1) For an original writing prompt, a learner declares a ten-minute planning window and a thirty-minute drafting window as a custom learning exercise. The learner spends ten minutes planning, writes for twenty-five minutes, pauses for a five-minute conversation, and then completes the final five active writing minutes.

(2) The learner saves the cutoff text at the end of those thirty active drafting minutes. No rule in the declared exercise equates a paused attempt with an uninterrupted one.

Question: Which timing record is accurate?
choices: Ten planning minutes and thirty-five active drafting minutes, with forty-five elapsed minutes and no interruption.
Forty total elapsed minutes because a paused timer removes the conversation from the real duration of the session.
Ten planning minutes and thirty active drafting minutes, with a five-minute drafting interruption and forty-five total elapsed minutes.
An uninterrupted official writing simulation because the learner eventually used every declared active minute.
questions.explanation: The active phases total 10 + 30 = 40 minutes, while the five-minute interruption makes elapsed time 45 minutes. The conversation was not active drafting, and pausing a timer does not erase real elapsed time or establish uninterrupted equivalence. The windows were explicitly custom, so the record does not become an official simulation.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner wants to use two original prompts for separate first-encounter writing sessions. While preparing the first session, the learner scrolls through the second prompt’s key question and all three perspectives. No essay or explanation is visible, and the second writing session will occur a week later.

(2) The learner is keeping a prompt-exposure field so that a later comparison can distinguish unfamiliar drafting from writing about previously inspected material.

Question: Which record should be made for the second prompt?
choices: Record no exposure because only reading a model essay can make a prompt familiar.
Record exposure only if the learner can reproduce every perspective word for word a week later.
Describe the second prompt as feedback-assisted solely because its issue was read, even though no feedback was provided.
Record the prior prompt and perspective reading, and avoid labeling the later session a first encounter with that prompt.
questions.explanation: Reading the prompt and perspectives is prior exposure even without a model essay or perfect later recall. It is not itself feedback exposure, so the record should describe what happened precisely. The later session remains useful, but calling it a first encounter would erase relevant familiarity.

questions.stem:
(1) During a custom writing rehearsal, a learner’s notes include a promising response to a cost objection. At the declared drafting cutoff, the essay has a thesis and supporting reason but has not developed that response. The learner saves both the draft and the separate notes before making any edits.

(2) The learner later turns the note into a complete paragraph and wants the version record to show when the reasoning became part of the essay presented to a reader.

Question: Which treatment preserves that distinction?
choices: Keep the unfinished cutoff draft and notes separately, and record the developed paragraph in a later revision.
Paste the paragraph into the cutoff draft because an outline phrase means the full reasoning had already been written.
Delete the notes because ideas not included in the cutoff essay cannot provide any useful planning evidence.
Count the later paragraph as timed writing if it uses the same words as the original note.
questions.explanation: The note shows planning, while the cutoff essay shows what had actually been communicated. The later developed paragraph belongs to a revision. Neither copying a phrase nor recognizing that an idea was planned backdates the prose. Keeping the notes preserves useful evidence about the gap between planning and drafting.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner completes a timed draft and then makes an independent revision without feedback. A mentor subsequently points out that the proposed safeguard requires monitoring. The learner creates another version that adds a monitoring plan and acknowledges its cost, using the mentor’s observation to guide the change.

(2) The learner wants to retain all versions for review and describe which argumentative work arose within each stage.

Question: Which draft lineage is accurate?
choices: Label every version independent because the learner personally typed the final sentences.
Preserve the cutoff draft, the independent revision, and a later feedback-assisted revision that records the mentor’s contribution.
Replace the cutoff file with the final version because only the best argument belongs in a learning record.
Treat the mentor’s observation as part of the earlier independent revision because it concerns the same underlying policy.
questions.explanation: The stages have different origins and should remain distinct. Typing the sentences does not erase the feedback that guided them. Replacing the cutoff file loses evidence of the timed performance, and a later observation cannot be attributed to an earlier independent version merely because the topic is unchanged.

questions.stem:
(1) In a practice writing interface, a learner uses an external suggestion tool to generate a reply to an objection. The chosen exercise allowed assistance for learning, and the learner incorporates that reply into a revised essay. The learner’s earlier cutoff draft had been saved before the suggestion was requested.

(2) The learner now wants to use the two versions to plan a later session in which the same argumentative function must be performed independently.

Question: Which interpretation is best supported?
choices: The revision proves independent timed performance because the assistance was permitted in the learning exercise.
The saved cutoff draft should be discarded because assistance makes every earlier version meaningless.
The revision shows assisted development of the reply; a later unfamiliar, unassisted cutoff draft would provide different evidence about independent use.
The reply becomes independent if the learner changes enough words while retaining the supplied reasoning.
questions.explanation: Permission to use assistance makes the learning condition legitimate but does not make its product independent. The original cutoff version remains useful evidence, and paraphrasing a supplied reason does not change its source. A new unassisted task more directly addresses whether the learner can perform the function independently.

questions.stem:
(1) An original essay recommends making some community rehearsal rooms reservable while retaining walk-in access to others. Its reasons explain why ensembles need coordinated space and why individuals with unpredictable schedules need flexible access. The final paragraph instead says that every room should require a month-ahead reservation.

(2) The writer has also noticed a repeated adjective in the introduction. No new reason in the essay supports eliminating all walk-in access.

Question: Which revision most directly addresses the central problem?
choices: Correct the repeated adjective and keep the universal conclusion because polished language establishes a stronger argument.
Delete the discussion of individual access without explaining why its concern no longer matters.
Retain the universal conclusion because an unqualified policy is always more persuasive than a qualified one.
Align the conclusion with the mixed policy actually supported, or supply a new argument for the broader policy that addresses the lost access.
questions.explanation: The conclusion exceeds the scope of the reasons. It needs to match the defended mixed arrangement or receive a new defense that addresses its added cost. A cosmetic change leaves that mismatch intact, deleting the concern does not answer it, and stronger wording does not itself improve support.

questions.stem:
(1) A fictional archive is deciding whether to release provisional recordings with uncertainty labels. One perspective values earlier research access; another worries that incorrect attributions could circulate before corrections appear. A writer supports release and replies that anyone who worries about attribution must oppose all public research.

(2) The prompt does not say that the second perspective opposes research access in general. The writer wants to revise the response so it engages the actual competing concern.

Question: Which revision best serves that purpose?
choices: Explain how labels and a correction process could reduce mistaken reliance, acknowledge their limits, and defend release despite the remaining risk.
Repeat that research is valuable while leaving the risk of incorrect attribution unexplained.
Strengthen the claim that all critics oppose research so the disagreement appears easier to resolve.
Assert that uncertainty labels guarantee that no reader will ever circulate a mistaken attribution.
questions.explanation: The actual concern is mistaken reliance on provisional attribution. A reasoned account of safeguards and remaining risk responds to it. Repeating a benefit or exaggerating the opposing view avoids the concern, while the universal guarantee introduces an unsupported factual claim.

questions.stem:
(1) An essay recommends a trial program that lends equipment to neighborhood groups. The writer proposes checking demand and repair costs during the trial before deciding whether to expand it. The supplied prompt includes no survey or cost measurements, but the writer adds that an invented survey has already proved that expansion will save exactly forty percent.

(2) The writer wants a revision that preserves a defensible recommendation while accurately distinguishing a proposal from established evidence.

Question: Which change is best justified?
choices: Keep the invented survey because a plausible numerical estimate becomes evidence when it supports a good policy.
Remove the fabricated result and explain what the trial would measure, how that evidence could inform expansion, and what remains uncertain.
Replace forty percent with another precise percentage while retaining the claim that it has been proved.
Abandon every recommendation because proposals cannot be defended before their exact effects have been measured.
questions.explanation: A proposal can be defended through reasons, a measurement plan, and acknowledged uncertainty without fabricating results. Plausibility and numerical precision do not establish a survey, and changing the percentage does not repair its invented status. Missing exact effects do not make all reasoned policy proposals impossible.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner’s cutoff essays usually state a position and list benefits, but the strongest competing concern is first answered only during later revision. The learner has identified this pattern across three unfamiliar prompts. The next session uses another unfamiliar issue with different perspectives and a declared drafting window.

(2) The learner wants one revision target whose presence can be checked in the next cutoff text rather than a vague instruction to write better.

Question: Which target is most useful?
choices: Produce exactly the same number of paragraphs as the longest previous revised essay regardless of the new issue.
Use more elaborate vocabulary so the argument appears sophisticated even if the concern remains unanswered.
Before polishing the opening, state a relevant competing concern and develop a reasoned response to it within the cutoff draft.
Copy the old objection paragraph into the new essay without checking whether it addresses the new perspectives.
questions.explanation: The proposed target directly addresses the recurring gap and can be observed in the cutoff draft. Paragraph counts and vocabulary do not ensure an argumentative response. Copying a familiar paragraph without checking relevance may reproduce a surface form while missing the function required by the new issue.

questions.stem:
(1) After repairing an essay’s treatment of a competing perspective, a learner writes on a different unfamiliar issue. In the new cutoff draft, the opposing concern is described fairly and answered with relevant reasons. The draft is shorter than the learner’s polished earlier revision and has one awkward but understandable transition.

(2) The learner wants to evaluate the specific target without claiming that every aspect of writing is now equally strong.

Question: Which interpretation is best supported?
choices: The shorter word count proves that the targeted response became weaker despite the relevant reasoning.
The single awkward transition proves that no transfer of the targeted argumentative function occurred.
One successful unfamiliar draft establishes permanent mastery of every writing skill under any future condition.
The new cutoff draft supports progress on the targeted response function, while its clarity and other remaining features can still receive separate review.
questions.explanation: The described reasoning directly supports improvement in the targeted function. Word count and an understandable transition issue do not negate that evidence, although clarity still deserves review. One successful instance does not establish permanent, universal mastery of all writing skills.

questions.stem:
(1) A study group uses a descriptive checklist for original essays: identify the position, trace its support, examine a competing perspective, and inspect scope and clarity. The checklist has no official validation or conversion. A learner uses it to identify two specific revisions and preserves the draft versions showing those changes.

(2) Another member wants to assign a number from 120 to 180 to each essay so its review will look comparable to a multiple-choice report.

Question: Which use of the checklist is justified?
choices: Use the descriptive findings to choose and inspect revisions without inventing an official-looking writing score.
Convert the number of checked boxes directly to the LSAT scale because the same learner completed both activities.
Treat any essay with all boxes checked as a guaranteed top official writing score.
Replace the written findings with an unexplained number because numerical labels always carry more diagnostic information.
questions.explanation: The checklist supports descriptive review and specific revision choices. It does not establish an official writing scale or a relationship to multiple-choice scores. A checked box cannot guarantee an official result, and an unexplained number would discard the reasoning that makes the review useful.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner changes her intended administration from a date before an announced format transition to a date after it. Her study folder contains a confirmation for the earlier appointment, several completed reading lessons, and results from full practice sessions in the earlier format.

(2) The announcement identifies a different later session structure. The learner has not yet verified an appointment for the new date or checked which authorized practice materials are available now. She wants to update the folder without misrepresenting what it establishes.

Question: Which update is best supported?
choices: Carry the earlier appointment confirmation forward, and update only the timing labels on the completed practice records.
Discard the earlier learning records as irrelevant, and retain the appointment confirmation because registration once succeeded.
Retain the earlier learning records with their actual format, and verify the new appointment and applicable practice instructions.
Retain the earlier records as full evidence for the later format, and postpone checking the appointment until another simulation.
questions.explanation: The changed target creates new appointment and format questions without erasing earlier skill learning. The earlier confirmation does not establish a new booking. Relabeling a completed session cannot change the conditions under which it occurred. The old records remain useful when their scope is preserved, but they do not reproduce the later structure or resolve the open appointment.

questions.stem:
(1) A candidate copies a confirmed appointment into a study calendar. The original confirmation gives the date, location, time, and time zone, but the calendar entry omits the zone. She has checked that the copied date and location match the confirmation, and she still has access to the original message.

(2) Her friend says that because most fields are correct, the calendar is sufficient evidence for the intended arrival plan. The candidate wants to close only the uncertainty that remains, using information already available to her.

Question: What is the most appropriate next action?
choices: Recover and verify the stated time zone from the confirmation while retaining the already checked date and location.
Infer the time zone from the candidate’s home address while retaining the copied time as the appointment time.
Mark the whole appointment unconfirmed and repeat registration before consulting the original confirmation.
Leave the zone unstated and use the completed reasoning lessons as evidence that the appointment plan is ready.
questions.explanation: The source already contains the missing zone, so checking it directly addresses the remaining uncertainty. A home address may not establish the zone used in a confirmation. Verified fields need not be discarded merely because one copied field is incomplete. Reasoning lessons do not establish an appointment time or its time zone.

questions.stem:
(1) A general testing page describes multiple delivery possibilities without identifying a particular cycle. A dated official page states a narrower rule for the cycle a learner intends to use. The learner also holds an individual approval whose wording may affect that rule, but she has not checked its scope.

(2) The learner wants a defensible administration record. The documents come from the official organization, yet their dates, generality, and possible individual exception are not identical. She cannot resolve the approval’s applicability from the text she has reviewed.

Question: Which approach best addresses the evidence?
choices: Use the general page because a rule covering more candidates must supersede a rule for one testing cycle.
Use whichever document offers the preferred arrangement and label that preference an individual authorization.
Ignore the individual approval because a cycle-specific page necessarily cancels every previously granted condition.
Compare the cycle-specific rule with the approval’s scope and seek official clarification of the unresolved applicability.
questions.explanation: The cycle-specific rule is relevant, but the individual approval’s actual scope still needs clarification. Generality does not make a page controlling for every cycle. Preference supplies no authorization, and the scenario gives no cancellation of all individual conditions. The record should retain the unresolved issue until applicable evidence settles it.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner requests an adjustment to a testing condition. The official system acknowledges receipt and assigns a tracking number. The acknowledgment explicitly says that a decision will follow. The learner has no separate decision notice and no other approval covering the requested adjustment.

(2) He has practised using the requested condition because it helps him work through the material. He now wants his administration record to distinguish those learning sessions from the conditions currently established for his actual appointment.

Question: Which entry follows from the available evidence?
choices: The request was approved when the tracking number appeared, and practice now confirms the approved condition.
The request was received, the decision remains pending, and practice under the requested condition does not establish approval.
The request was denied because no decision has arrived, and all learning from the adjusted practice should be removed.
The request requires no decision because the learner has already demonstrated that the condition improves his practice.
questions.explanation: Receipt is established and a decision is explicitly pending. A tracking number records the request rather than its approval. The absence of a decision does not show denial. Helpful practice neither grants an adjustment nor becomes worthless because the official status remains open; it should retain its actual conditions.

questions.stem:
(1) A fictional appointment checklist requires a confirmed booking, an acceptable identification document, and a completed equipment check for the assigned modality. A learner has a current booking confirmation. Her official instructions establish that her identification document is acceptable, but her equipment check is still incomplete.

(2) Her latest unfamiliar practice result is her strongest so far. She wants to identify the particular open checklist item without turning the practice result into administrative evidence or reopening items already supported by current records.

Question: Which conclusion is justified?
choices: The practice result closes the equipment item; strong performance demonstrates that every assigned setup requirement is met.
The equipment check remains open; the supported booking and identification entries can retain their confirmed status.
The incomplete equipment item makes the booking and identification evidence invalid until the next practice result.
The booking confirmation closes the equipment item; a confirmed appointment establishes every prerequisite automatically.
questions.explanation: Only the equipment check lacks the required evidence in this scenario. A reasoning result does not establish a setup check, and a booking confirmation is not described as certification of all prerequisites. An open item does not erase the current evidence for the distinct booking and identification requirements.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner reviews seven entries in her administration worksheet. Three have matching current confirmations. Two actions have been submitted and are explicitly awaiting decisions. One entry contains contradictory instructions whose applicability she has not resolved. The final entry concerns a modality that her current confirmation does not assign.

(2) The worksheet labels confirmed, pending, unresolved, and inapplicable are descriptive study labels. The learner has checked why the last entry does not apply and wants a count that preserves the differences among the remaining states.

Question: Which count accurately summarizes the seven entries?
choices: Five confirmed, none pending, one unresolved, and one inapplicable.
Three confirmed, three pending, none unresolved, and one inapplicable.
Four confirmed, two pending, one unresolved, and none inapplicable.
Three confirmed, two pending, one unresolved, and one inapplicable.
questions.explanation: The three confirmations support confirmed status. Submitted actions awaiting decisions remain pending. Contradictory instructions create a distinct unresolved applicability issue. The final entry is inapplicable for a checked reason, not another completed requirement. Counting submissions or inapplicability as confirmation would collapse different evidence states.

questions.stem:
(1) A repeat test taker has an earlier writing sample in her account. Her current instructions permit an acceptable prior sample to meet the writing requirement, but she has not checked whether this particular sample remains acceptable. She has also written two strong practice essays during the current course.

(2) She wants to decide whether another administered writing session is needed. The account’s mere display of the earlier sample does not include the acceptance information she needs, and the practice essays were ordinary learning activities.

Question: What should she establish before closing the writing requirement?
choices: Whether the earlier sample satisfies the current applicable requirement, using its actual status and current official guidance.
Whether one practice essay is stronger than the earlier sample, using that comparison as a substitute for official acceptance.
Whether the earlier sample is still visible, treating visibility alone as proof that it satisfies every current requirement.
Whether she prefers the earlier topic, treating that preference as the criterion for needing another administered session.
questions.explanation: Current applicability and acceptance determine whether the prior sample satisfies the stated requirement. The scenario does not establish them from visibility alone. Practice quality can inform learning but cannot replace official acceptance, and topic preference does not settle whether another administered sample is required.

questions.stem:
(1) A candidate’s applicable score-release instructions require both an approved writing sample and the absence of account holds. His account shows an approved sample. It also shows a hold that he has not resolved. He has completed the multiple-choice test and is waiting for the scheduled release process.

(2) A study partner says the approved sample proves that all release requirements are met. The candidate wants to summarize only what the two account entries establish under the rule supplied in his instructions.

Question: Which summary correctly applies the stated rule?
choices: Both stated conditions are met because approval of one component necessarily removes any account hold.
Neither stated condition is met because an account hold proves that the approved writing sample has been withdrawn.
The writing-sample condition is met, but the visible hold means the other stated release condition is not yet established.
The two conditions are alternatives, so the approved sample is sufficient regardless of the recorded hold.
questions.explanation: The stated rule requires both conditions. Approval establishes the sample condition but does not remove the hold. The hold does not, by itself, withdraw sample approval. Treating the requirements as alternatives changes the rule and makes one satisfied condition do work it cannot do.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner has confirmed that her multiple-choice appointment will take place at a test center. The current instructions describe writing as a separate remote component with its own equipment and workspace requirements. She has not checked the computer she intends to use for writing.

(2) She has become comfortable with the reasoning interface during practice and assumes that the test-center confirmation covers every technical preparation issue. She wants to identify what the confirmation actually resolves and what still needs attention.

Question: Which interpretation is supported?
choices: The confirmation resolves both setups because a test-center assignment supplies the equipment for every component.
The writing setup can be treated as verified because comfort with the reasoning interface establishes equipment compatibility.
The multiple-choice booking must be canceled because a separately remote component is incompatible with test-center delivery.
The confirmation resolves the stated multiple-choice location, while the separate writing setup still needs its own applicable checks.
questions.explanation: Separate delivery creates separate setup questions. The confirmation establishes the described multiple-choice location, not the learner’s writing equipment. Interface familiarity does not prove compatibility with the required writing system. Nothing in the scenario makes a test-center appointment incompatible with a separately remote writing component.

questions.stem:
(1) During ordinary writing study, a learner uses a browser extension to suggest revisions. Before an administered session, she reads current official instructions that prohibit that extension unless a relevant individual authorization applies. She has no such authorization and has not yet changed her setup.

(2) Her last practice draft was clearer after using the extension. She wants to prepare for the administered session while preserving an honest record of what the earlier practice draft demonstrates and which setup change is required.

Question: Which action follows the supplied instructions?
choices: Leave the extension active because a clearer practice draft supplies evidence that the tool is authorized.
Prepare the administered setup without the prohibited extension and retain the practice draft’s assistance history.
Remove the assistance note from the practice record because disabling the extension later makes that draft independent.
Treat the writing session as an ordinary study task because the same learner will type both versions.
questions.explanation: The explicit rule governs the administered setup in the absence of an applicable authorization. Helpful study output does not authorize a tool. Disabling it later does not erase its earlier contribution, and personal authorship does not make administered requirements identical to ordinary study conditions.

questions.stem:
(1) A learner saves three writing records: an original course essay, a notice confirming submission of an administered sample, and a later account entry saying review is pending. For this scenario, the current requirement is an approved sample, and the learner has no other accepted sample on file.

(2) The learner wants a record that preserves the value of the practice essay while accurately describing the administrative status. She has not received any notice converting the pending review into approval.

Question: Which entry is best supported?
choices: The practice essay and submitted sample together establish approval because two writing activities exceed a one-sample requirement.
The submitted sample should be marked approved because the pending entry confirms that official processing has begun.
The practice essay supports learning review; the administered sample is submitted, and the approval requirement remains pending.
The practice essay should be discarded because a pending official review prevents it from showing any writing skill.
questions.explanation: The records support different conclusions: practice can inform learning, submission establishes receipt, and pending review does not establish approval. Counting two activities does not satisfy a requirement defined by approval. A pending administrative decision does not erase the practice essay’s descriptive learning value.

questions.stem:
(1) A fictional candidate checks the official page relevant to her writing sample. It describes a processing period that can extend beyond immediate submission. Her planned submission is very close to another deadline, and she has not verified whether the sample would be approved by that deadline.
