E. The museum once displayed the pump without allowing visitors to move either its original components or its replacement handle.

references.title: Reconciling observations and comparing explanations
references.body:
## Identify the requested task

- For an apparent paradox, accept both observations and identify the background expectation making their combination surprising. Seek information defeating that expectation without denying either observation.
- Compare explanatory hypotheses by identifying observations that bear differently on them. Fitting the initial observations does not settle the comparison.
- Preserve population, time, units, and strength. A candidate can help explain a result without proving the actual historical cause or excluding every alternative.
- A proposition and its direct negation about identical contents, definitions, and the same instant form a contradiction. An ordinary added fact cannot make both true under those stipulations.

## Find the missing connection

- Counts and totals: forty leaks losing ten liters each yield 400 liters; twenty losing thirty each yield 600. Greater loss per event can outweigh fewer events.
- Distinct units: fewer people can produce more attendance events if they return often enough. More tickets can produce less revenue if a sufficiently lower price offsets the larger ticket count.
- Components and totals: faster repairs can coexist with longer total waits when extra queue time exceeds saved repair time. Specify matching populations before adding averages.
- Mixtures: changing subgroup proportions can alter an aggregate rate even when each subgroup improves. Use appropriate weights and verify that groups cover the target without overlap.
- Detection and history: a greater reporting share can raise recorded incidents despite fewer actual incidents. Previously damaged items can remain damaged while newly treated items deteriorate more slowly.

## Compare actual predictions

- Separate factors that initially occurred together. If all affected labels were batch R in warmth, observing more R labels in warmth repeats the original overlap.
- For two narrow accounts, one predicting curling only for R at either tested temperature and another predicting curling only in warmth with either batch, test R in cool conditions and S in warmth. Their predictions differ there.
- Hold relevant background conditions fixed, including material, handling, moisture, and observation time. Explain which result favors which stated account instead of inventing numerical probabilities.
- A condition expected similarly under both rivals may do little to distinguish them. It can still support their shared starting point or challenge another account.

## Interpret missing results carefully

- Check every required condition and auxiliary assumption before calling a prediction unsuccessful. Unknown sample acidity, inadequate exposure, or faulty equipment can leave the test unsettled.
- Match the observation period to the prediction. Stopping at ten minutes cannot reject a result requiring forty minutes. Observe throughout the relevant interval if an event might appear and disappear.
- With all required conditions and reliable detection stipulated, failure of a guaranteed result refutes that guarantee. A merely probable prediction can survive an unfavorable result.

## Keep the conclusion proportionate

- Distinguish possible reconciliation, support over a named rival, and proof of an actual sole cause. Production records establishing a common source do not establish copying of every sentence or deceptive intent.
- Acknowledge revisions that change predictions. A revised account may deserve testing, but it did not predict the old result unchanged. Ask what evidence could now count against it.
- Avoid forced exclusive causes. Sorting and printing delays can both contribute to a late dispatch when the recorded sequence supports both contributions.

references.title: Parallel patterns, methods, and statement roles
references.body:
## Start with the target

- Parallel reasoning compares support relationships. Parallel-flaw questions compare specific unsupported moves. Method questions ask what authors do with reasons; role questions ask what particular statements contribute. Identify the target speaker.
- Locate the main conclusion and any intermediate conclusions. Map support connections before labeling categories. Preserve a consistent correspondence wherever a category recurs. Sentence order and subject matter can change while the reasoning stays parallel.

## Preserve the structure

- Keep logical connections intact. Either authorization or a waiver guaranteeing entry supplies two independently sufficient routes. Authorization and a waiver together guaranteeing entry supplies a joint input. The same familiar words do not make those rules interchangeable.
- Preserve quantifiers, the group being counted, scope, and conclusion strength. Some is not most; most researchers need not mean most editors. Probably contributing to an outcome differs from being its guaranteed sole cause. A recommendation adds a different kind of conclusion.
- Preserve support direction and links. A sample used to estimate a population differs from a population rule applied to a member. Two facts jointly establishing eligibility, followed by eligibility supporting review, differ from two facts separately supporting eligibility and review.

## Test the exact match

- Follow a witness in a valid quantified pattern. No restricted records are public; some new arrivals are restricted. Therefore, some new arrivals are not public. A candidate must preserve the exclusion, the existence statement, and the limited negative conclusion.
- Transfer a countermodel for an invalid pattern. Priority status or prepayment guarantees service; an item lacks priority status; therefore, it gets no service. A nonpriority prepaid item receiving service defeats the conclusion. A rule whose sufficient input combines both properties has a different form, even if an attempted inference shares an inverse-error label.
- A shared flaw label is only a starting point. Before-and-after evidence and an association between groups can support different causal leaps. Match the evidence and the move. An invalid argument can happen to have a true conclusion; actual truth does not repair the original support.

## Describe the operation

- Name an action and its target: applies a rule to a case, uses a relevant similarity to extend a feature, supplies a counterexample to a universal claim, or distinguishes two measures. An example may illustrate a definition without proving a generalization.
- One qualifying counterexample defeats an unrestricted universal. It does not establish a typical failure rate or prove that a recommendation lacks every possible justification. Criticizing the offered reason and rejecting the conclusion are different moves.
- A temporary supposition is not an accepted fact. Deriving a contradiction with fixed premises can support rejecting that supposition. An inconvenient consequence is not automatically a contradiction.
- Elimination establishes a remaining option only when the supplied alternatives are exhaustive and the rivals are actually excluded. Discrediting someone's reason for an option does not itself eliminate the option.

## Describe the statement's role

- Separate content, offered role, and adequacy. Weak evidence can still be offered as evidence. A true statement can be irrelevant.
- An intermediate conclusion receives and supplies support. A concession grants an opposing point without necessarily accepting the opposing conclusion. A qualification limits scope or strength. Check every part of a description, including speaker and endorsement.

references.title: Passage structure and viewpoint checks
references.body:
## Establish the inquiry

- Name the topic, then ask the organizing question that connects the passage's parts. “How do these designs handle changing requirements?” gives more direction than “designs.” Keep the question broad enough for the whole account and specific enough for its actual development.
- Distinguish description, explanation, and argument without forcing the passage into one fixed template. A classification need not rank its categories; an explanation need not recommend a policy. Mixed passages can perform several activities within one larger inquiry.
- Finish reading before fixing your first map. Later material may qualify an apparent conclusion or reveal that an opening position belonged to someone else.

## Map contributions at the right level

- Pair a content hook with a function: “inspection case: illustrates the limitation.” Use an action and its object, rather than a list of nouns. Check what relationship the paragraph adds to the surrounding discussion.
- Separate a sentence's role, its paragraph's main contribution, and the whole passage's organization. A paragraph can concede one benefit before developing an objection. A genuine detail may be too narrow to answer a function question without being false.
- Ask what connection would disappear if a paragraph were removed. This is a diagnostic aid, not proof that the paragraph is logically necessary.
- Investigate structural pivots. However can introduce a small contrast inside an example; therefore can introduce a reported speaker's conclusion. Neither word settles the overall structure independently of its content and attribution.

## Track speakers and commitments

- Record speaker, proposition, and response. “Planner: favors full adoption; author: accepts a limited trial” preserves a distinction that “adoption supported” erases.
- Follow names, pronouns, quotation boundaries, and the reasoning around them. A paragraph break does not automatically change speakers. One paragraph may report a claim and then assess it.
- Reporting is not endorsement. An author commitment requires evidence that the author accepts the claim or adopts reasoning that supports it. Dramatic language inside a quotation belongs to its speaker unless the author also adopts that appraisal.
- Treat calm criticism as criticism when the reasoning warrants it. Neutral sentence structure does not erase a definite judgment about an inference's limits.

## Measure the extent of agreement

- Identify the precise proposition accepted or disputed. Local agreement with a benefit need not endorse a speaker's recommendation. A concession can acknowledge that benefit while the paragraph argues against adoption.
- Preserve population, conditions, certainty, and time. Firm support for a restricted proposal is different from either hesitation about everything or unrestricted approval.
- Establish disagreement on one shared proposition. “The guide helps beginners” and “the guide is expensive” can both be true. Different concerns do not automatically conflict.
- Record silence as an unexpressed position. Questioning whether evidence proves a claim does not necessarily deny the claim itself.

## Test the map on a small case

A planner proposes assigning every photograph one event label, with no supplementary references, to simplify browsing. A reviewer accepts that benefit but notes that some photographs depict two events. The author also accepts simpler browsing as a benefit, favors one main label with supplementary links, and leaves the extra staff time unmeasured.

The development is proposal with benefit, limitation, then a modified arrangement. The author agrees about simplicity without endorsing one-label-only classification. The main point combines a principal label with additional links; the purpose is to defend that revision. Neither the cost of the revision nor its superiority for every collection is established.

## Before choosing

State the requested level, name the relevant speaker, and return to an exact textual anchor. Use the map to locate evidence, then check the whole answer for changed relationships, omitted qualifications, or an unsupported claim attached to an accurate clause.

references.title: Plans and evaluation questions
references.body:
## Trace the proposed route

- Action and objective: distinguish installing a system from the outcome it is supposed to achieve. Equipment counts do not automatically measure saved time or improved access.
- Implementation: identify practical requirements such as staff, equipment, supplies, and access. Meeting one requirement removes an obstacle without proving the final benefit.
- Uptake: ask whether the intended users can and actually do use the change. Favorable opinions about a name or appearance do not establish the relevant behavior.
- Limiting stage: faster label printing need not increase completed dispatches when unchanged packing capacity remains the bottleneck under the stated workload.
- Horizon: match the promised period. A launch delay can undermine this month's result without ruling out later benefits.

## Measure the outcome the argument claims

- Net effect: eight fewer waiting minutes plus ten additional booking minutes yields two more minutes overall when all other pickup components remain fixed. The narrower waiting improvement still occurred.
- Displacement: evening visits can replace afternoon visits without increasing distinct weekly users. Count people without duplication and investigate whether the plan reaches previously excluded users.
- Recommendation: costs and other trade-offs matter through the stated decision criterion. A new charge can weaken an adoption argument while leaving a shorter-queue prediction intact.
- Feasibility: practical capability and expected demand are separate links. Enough qualified staff makes operation possible; it does not by itself establish customer attendance.

## Test opposing possible answers

- Identify the unresolved issue: record the conclusion and the connection the candidate question would investigate. A question already answered by a premise adds no unresolved information.
- Hold facts fixed: imagine one answer, explain its effect, then imagine a contrasting answer. Do not change the reported result or add another condition to make the question matter.
- Allow asymmetry: yes may supply a competing cause while no only removes that particular alternative. A useful question need not prove or disprove the entire conclusion with either answer.
- Check attribution: asking whether a separate team began preloading parcels bears on attributing increased courier output to new routes. Both answers preserve the observed increase and equal shift lengths.
- Check sources: two reports copied from one unchecked notice do not provide two independent confirmations. Ruling out that copying route does not automatically establish independence.

## Locate the relevant boundary

- First-year costs: saving 100 credits, paying 40, and incurring only an additional setup charge gives a net saving of sixty minus that charge. Positive saving requires a charge below sixty.
- Exact negation: a no answer to below sixty means at least sixty, including the zero-saving boundary. Do not exclude equality when testing a strict reduction.
- Useful contrast: a below-200 question can leave both a ten-credit charge and a 150-credit charge possible. The actual sixty-credit boundary resolves the sign more directly.
- Final relevance: compare answers against the specified measure and period. Decorative facts or a different year's expense cannot replace the question about this argument's remaining gap.

references.title: Quantifiers, witnesses, and majority overlap
references.body:
## Read quantity and existence together

Keep the stated domain and the complete property fixed. Being trained is not the same property as performing a job.

- All A are B: every A is B. This rules out an A outside B, without asserting that any A exists.
- Some A are B: at least one member has both properties. “Some” allows all; it does not mean “some but not all.”
- No A are B: the groups are disjoint. This also gives no B are A. Either group may be empty.
- Some A are not B: an existing A lies outside B. This gives “some things outside B are A,” not “some B are not A.”
- Most A are B: in the course's finite groups, more than half of A belong to B. This establishes overlap and a nonempty A group. It allows all A to be B; it does not establish most B are A.

## Negate the entire statement

- All A are B. Negation: some A are not B.
- Some A are B. Negation: no A are B.
- No A are B. Negation: some A are B.
- Some A are not B. Negation: all A are B, including the possible empty-A case.
- Most A are B. Negation: at most half of A are B. For twelve reviewers, “most approve” is negated by at most six approving. Six approving and six not approving defeats “most approve” without establishing “most do not approve.”

## Keep the same witness

Some A are B supplies one existing member of both groups. If all B are C, that same witness establishes some A are C.

Separate existential claims may concern different members. Some A are B and some B are C do not establish some A are C. One member can be A and B but not C; another can be B and C but not A. Both premises hold without the proposed overlap.

## Check the counting base

Two majorities of the same finite group must overlap. Exact counts can give a minimum: among eighteen trainees, eleven with skill P and twelve with skill Q require at least five with both. Only seven trainees remain outside P, so five of Q cannot fit there. The overlap might be larger.

Majorities of different groups do not form that argument. Most editors being proofreaders and most proofreaders being illustrators need not produce an editor who illustrates. Identify the population counted by each “most.” Words such as “many” supply no fixed majority threshold without additional context.

references.title: Quantitative flaws — counts, bases, and weights
references.body:
## Attach a measure to every number

- Identify whether the conclusion concerns a count, a share, an event rate, a change, or an average. Correct numbers can still measure something different from the conclusion.
- For a finite group's share, let n be the qualifying count and N the total. Require N greater than zero and n between zero and N. The share is n/N; the percentage is 100n/N percent.
- Keep population, period, units, and counting definitions fixed. Errors per shipment and errors per working hour use different exposure bases and answer different questions.
- Multiple events can occur per unit, so an event rate may exceed one per unit. A percentage of objects with a feature cannot exceed 100 percent under the stated finite-group definition.

## Connect shares and counts

- Count equals share times total. A smaller percentage need not mean a smaller qualifying count when the total changes; a larger count need not mean a larger share.
- Complete inventories with an unchanged definition show 48 rare volumes among 240, then 72 among 600. The share falls from 20 to 12 percent while the count rises by 24.
- Do not invent a missing-base flaw when the base is supplied. Of 200 inspections each period, twelve and then eight find at least one error: the shares fall from six to four percent.

## Keep changes distinct

- Percentage points subtract percentages directly. A rate moving from 30 to 36 percent rises six percentage points. Relative change divides the change by its positive starting value: six divided by thirty is 20 percent.
- Absolute change uses the original quantity's units. Thirty objects becoming thirty-six is six additional objects, not six percentage points. Relative change from zero is undefined under the usual division formula.
- Successive percentages usually use successive bases. Eighty cards increasing 25 percent becomes 100; decreasing that new total 25 percent leaves 75. The final decline from eighty is 6.25 percent.

## Ask “of which group?”

- A conditional proportion attaches one feature to a specified group. Sixteen illustrated translations among twenty translations gives 80 percent illustrated within translations.
- If the collection contains 100 illustrated works altogether, translations form only 16 percent of illustrated works. Reversing the described group changes the denominator even when the overlap count stays sixteen.
- Check the base rate and contributions from every relevant category. Flagging most members of a small category does not by itself establish that most flagged cases belong to that category.

## Combine with appropriate weights

- For disjoint groups covering the target population under one feature definition, add qualifying counts and group totals. Nine of ten plus fifty-four of ninety gives sixty-three of 100, or 63 percent.
- Averaging the subgroup percentages equally gives 75 percent in that example. Equal group weights need justification; equal group sizes justify them, and matching subgroup rates can also make the results agree.
- Inspect group composition. Fixed subgroup cancellation rates of 10 and 40 percent combine to 13 percent with a 90/10 group mixture and 37 percent with a 10/90 mixture. Neither subgroup rate worsened.
- Diagnose the specific numerator, denominator, unit, or weight mismatch. When constructing a counterexample, preserve every supplied number and show the claimed conclusion can fail.

references.title: Rare-error audit and response decisions
references.body:
## Use this after preserving the attempt

This worksheet organizes a small number of consequential reasoning or execution problems without treating their rarity as proof of mastery. Keep the original response record, cutoff, exposure history, and review phases. Select uncertain corrects and questionable reasoning as well as wrong answers. A correct response earns its raw credit even when its reasoning needs repair.

Start with a bounded record: the task or form identity, date, conditions, complete-set denominator, and the reason each item entered the audit. If you selected only difficult or changed answers, say so. An error count among selected items does not establish an error rate across every opportunity in the full session. When an earlier choice or reasoning step was not recorded, mark it unknown instead of reconstructing a convenient history from the key.

## Reconstruct a mechanism

For each audited item, record the requested task, the relevant source claim, your original inference, your selected response, and the evidence used during each later review phase. Then state the smallest supported description of the problem. “Reading question” identifies a broad task. “Converted a claim about some observed sites into a claim about every site” identifies an inference that can be inspected and repaired.

Construct a counterexample where appropriate. Suppose a fictional rule says that every approved night survey has a current permit and a trained leader. A learner concludes that every survey with both features is approved. A survey can possess both features yet fail a separate approval requirement. That possibility satisfies the stated rule and defeats the converse. The repair is to preserve the direction of the implication, not to memorize the original answer phrase.

Keep alternative explanations alive when the record cannot decide among them. A wrong response might follow a misunderstood rule, a misread task, or a selection slip. A later polished explanation does not prove what happened at cutoff. State a mechanism hypothesis, the evidence for it, and what additional observation would distinguish it from a plausible rival.

## Preserve changes and denominators

The following fictional paired record contains every one of twenty-four assigned items at both phases, with the same scoring basis. It has no blanks or missing responses.

| Response pair | Items and meaning |
|---|---|
| Right to right | 18 items; correct in both phases |
| Wrong to right | 3 items; a correct response appears later |
| Right to wrong | 1 item; a harmful change occurred |
| Wrong to wrong | 2 items; incorrect in both phases |

The first phase has nineteen correct out of twenty-four; the later phase has twenty-one. Four responses changed correctness status, with three gains and one loss, producing a net gain of two. This is an observed paired record. It does not prove that changing answers is always beneficial, that every gain used valid reasoning, or that every unchanged correct answer was secure.

If four right-to-right items had been marked uncertain before feedback, they would remain correct and receive an additional review flag. They would not become four extra items or lose raw credit. If the later phase followed explanations, label that assistance. A correction after feedback cannot be backdated to the first phase.

## Write one useful next action

For a changed answer, identify the reason for changing and whether it supplied new task-relevant evidence. A justified change can follow discovery of a missed restriction or a counterexample. Discomfort alone does not establish that a previously supported response became false. Review right-to-wrong and wrong-to-right changes under the same standard rather than praising every change that happened to end correctly.

Finish each priority entry with a replacement action, an unfamiliar verification opportunity, and a possible cost to observe. For example: restate the rule's direction before inferring membership; then inspect unfamiliar applications for both reversals and unnecessary checking time. Keep familiar repair practice separate from fresh transfer evidence. The audit should make the next action more precise while leaving unresolved causes and limits visible.

## Fields to complete

- Attempt identity, exposure, conditions, cutoff, and complete denominator.
- Selection reason, original response, and contemporaneous reasoning if available.
- Review phase, assistance, changed response, and paired scoring basis.
- Supported mechanism, rival explanation, and missing evidence.
- Replacement action, unfamiliar follow-up, and costs or omissions to monitor.
- Decision after review: retain, narrow, modify, or gather more evidence.

references.title: Readiness evidence and decision record
references.body:
## State the decision before selecting the evidence

Use this record to explain what recent performance supports, what remains uncertain, and what action you will take next. It is not a score predictor or an official readiness certification. Identify the intended administration, the question you are trying to answer, the period of records being reviewed, and the reasons that period is relevant.

Define eligibility for a comparison before choosing the most favorable results. A particular comparison might require an unfamiliar complete official practice form, a recorded form identity and scoring configuration, and the intended practice conditions. Another question might concern a small original repair set. Both can be useful, but they answer different questions and need their own denominators and labels.

Do not erase ineligible records. Retain them with the reason they are outside the particular comparison. Reviewed material may show whether you can explain a repair. Interrupted work may reveal a mechanism. Missing exposure information may motivate a history check. Those purposes do not make the record equivalent to an unfamiliar uninterrupted attempt.

## Inventory each session

Record the source and form or task identity, date, prior exposure including repeated components, actual conditions, cutoff responses, omissions, interruptions, and assistance. For an official practice result, preserve the exact form's own supplied report or scoring configuration. For original course work, retain raw correct counts and complete denominators. Do not use a conversion from a different form or infer one from matching question counts.

Separate performance from the quality of the evidence. A low result under relevant conditions remains relevant. A high result after reviewing the answers remains exposed. If part of the history is unknown, mark it unknown rather than assigning whichever label makes the series look consistent. Missing records can limit conclusions, especially when only successful sessions were saved.

## Worked inventory

These are fictional learner records and fictional labels, not published form identifiers or a conversion table. Assume each reported number came from that session's exact official practice report. The learner's stated comparison requires unfamiliar complete attempts under the intended recorded conditions.

| Session and result | Relevant history |
|---|---|
| A — 171 | Complete; unfamiliar; intended conditions recorded |
| B — 174 | Previously studied components |
| C — 169 | Unfamiliar; substantial unplanned pause |
| D — 172 | Complete; unfamiliar; intended conditions recorded |

Sessions A and D meet this particular comparison rule. Their observed results are 171 and 172, a one-point spread. B and C remain in the inventory with their qualifications. Selecting B because it is highest would change the evidence rule after seeing the result. Dropping C from the inventory entirely would conceal the interruption and any diagnostic information its work supplies.

Two eligible observations do not establish the range of future outcomes. An observed minimum and maximum are descriptions of these records, not a personalized probability interval. LSAC's [score-band guidance](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/lsat-scoring/lsat-score-bands) concerns measurement uncertainty in officially administered scores. A private practice range is not that official score band. Do not attach an invented confidence level or guarantee to either the course's original raw results or this fictional series.

## Inspect functions as well as totals

Record whether the learner's approach operated as intended across the session, whether omissions or harmful changes appeared, and which mechanisms repeated. Inspect uncertain correct responses without subtracting them from the raw result. Retain evidence of functioning skills as well as weaknesses. A single total may hide a gain in one task and a cost in another.

Give writing a separate descriptive entry: prompt and exposure, planning and drafting conditions, cutoff draft, treatment of competing perspectives, later revisions, and assistance. Do not average an essay judgment into a multiple-choice score. Track official writing approval in the administration record rather than confusing it with the quality of a practice essay.

## Conclude with a bounded decision

Write a short decision statement: the evidence supports this action for these reasons; these uncertainties remain; this next observation or change would prompt reconsideration. Possible actions include retaining a practised approach, targeting a specific repair, gathering missing whole-session evidence, or revising the schedule around current constraints.

Do not require a universal number of practice tests or impose an invented score cutoff. The sufficiency of evidence depends on the decision, its consequences, and the quality of the records. A learner can acknowledge substantial preparation and remaining uncertainty in the same statement. The useful outcome is a reasoned plan whose basis can be checked.

references.title: Reading map, viewpoint, and scope
references.body:
After each paragraph, record its job in a short phrase: introduces a dispute, explains evidence, reports an objection, tests an explanation, or qualifies a recommendation. Use your labels to locate evidence; a label does not replace the passage.

## Separate five questions

| Question | What to record |
|---|---|
| What is the topic? | The subject under discussion, usually a noun phrase. |
| What is the main point? | The author's overall claim about that subject. |
| Who holds this view? | The author, a named thinker, critics, or a hypothetical speaker. |
| What does this detail do? | An example, counterexample, qualification, objection, or supporting reason. |
| How strong is the claim? | Its quantifier, certainty, comparison group, and stated limits. |

"Some critics say" reports a viewpoint. "However" signals a turn whose target must be identified. A concession accepts a point while limiting what follows from it. An inference must be supported by the passage; a plausible fact from outside the passage is not enough.

## Two passages

Write each author's position separately before comparing them. Identify the precise common question. Two authors can share a goal while disagreeing about a method, threshold, or tradeoff. If one author never addresses an issue, silence alone does not show agreement or disagreement.

## Eliminate by reason

Explain why a rejected choice fails: wrong speaker, reversed relation, outside scope, excessive strength, or a true detail that misses the question. "It sounds wrong" is not a transferable explanation. A choice with "always" is not automatically wrong; it fails only when the passage does not support that strength. Similarly, "sometimes" establishes at least some occasions; it does not alone establish that there are exceptions.

For every answer, return to the relevant sentence or relationship. Your memory supplies a location; the text supplies the evidence.

references.title: Purpose, tone, and textual evidence
references.body:
## Distinguish three global questions

- Topic names the subject. Main point states the central claim or overall account. Primary purpose describes what the author principally does with it: explains a mechanism, compares approaches, challenges an interpretation, or defends a restricted proposal.
- Give purpose an action and an object. “To discuss change” often says too little; an imagined motive such as impressing an employer says something the text may never support.
- Check global coverage. A main point should make the major paragraphs intelligible as parts of one project. A true illustration may be too narrow; a sweeping maxim may be too broad. The last sentence can be a conclusion, consequence, example, or open question, so determine its function before adopting it.

## Match attitude to its evidence

- Specify the object, direction, and intensity of tone. Doubt about a study's conclusion is different from contempt for its researchers. Qualified approval is not automatic neutrality.
- Use evaluative language together with reasons. Promising suggests a favorable but limited appraisal; a reasoned rejection can be firm even when its syntax is restrained. Match force to evidence instead of treating strong words as automatically wrong.
- Attribute emotional wording before using it. A speaker's angry quotation does not establish the author's anger. Check whether the author adopts, limits, or disputes the reported assessment.

## Locate details with enough context

- Identify the requested person, event, period, and outcome. Return to a textual anchor, then widen the span when a pronoun, comparison, or qualification depends on nearby sentences.
- An explicit detail can appear in an accurate paraphrase. Familiar vocabulary does not rescue an answer that changes the action, speaker, or time.
- Resolve a referent through grammar and meaning, not proximity alone. For contextual meaning, substitute the proposed sense and check the sentence's purpose. “Marks a variant for comparison” does not by itself mean “condemns a variant as false.”

## Connect evidence without enlarging it

- For a cross-paragraph inference, identify each needed claim and explain their connection. Check that the same people, objects, dates, and conditions are involved. Separate groups cannot silently become one group.
- For a must-follow task, seek a permitted case where the evidence remains true and the proposed conclusion fails. Finding one defeats necessity; failing to imagine one is not itself a proof.
- For a best-supported task, compare positive evidence for the alternatives and retain the text's uncertainty. Mere compatibility or cautious wording is insufficient.
- Preserve scope. Permission is not action; one observed condition is not every condition. Missing measurements, omitted records, and absent discussion do not automatically establish failure, nonexistence, or disagreement.

## Apply the checks together

An account says that all four panels of a folding screen stayed upright in an indoor trial. Those panels were not tested outdoors. The writer calls the indoor result promising and recommends an outdoor trial before recommending garden use.

The detail concerns all four tested panels indoors. The main point connects that limited success to further investigation; the purpose is to justify the next trial. The tone is favorable toward the indoor result while withholding a garden-use recommendation. All is supported within the stated group. Guaranteed outdoor success is not supported, and untested does not mean proven failure.

## Compare complete answers

Explain whether a rejected alternative contradicts the passage, adds an unsupported claim, changes a relationship, or gives a true statement that answers another question. Check every clause. A matching topic or one accurate phrase cannot compensate for an altered qualification, wrong speaker, or invented result.

references.title: Untimed reading and evidence review
references.body:
## Set a clear record

Use an untimed set to practice coordinating structure, attribution, purpose, tone, details, and inference. Record whether the passage and questions are unfamiliar or previously studied. Preserve first answers, their reasons, and any confidence recorded before reconsideration. Keep these notes yourself when needed; an evidence ledger is a study method, not a claim about an automatic app feature.

The original passages teach reasoning skills. Their results do not provide a calibrated conversion to an official LSAT score. Evaluate the actual answers and evidence under the conditions you recorded.

## Read for structure, then select the task

- Build a brief, revisable passage map: subject, organizing question, major functions, and speaker changes. Keep exact details available for retrieval rather than trying to memorize them all.
- State a provisional main point and primary purpose. Revise them if later paragraphs reveal a limitation or change your understanding of the opening.
- Identify the question's operation. Organization connects parts; viewpoint attributes a commitment; tone matches an attitude; detail retrieves stated information; inference explains a supported step.
- Form a short prediction, then compare the full choices. A prediction is useful only while the text supports it. Revisit the evidence when a choice exposes an overlooked condition.

## Make an evidence ledger

For an uncertain or missed item, record:

- The item ID and the task actually asked.
- The first answer and its reason, plus recorded confidence.
- Any blind-review answer and its reason, recorded before feedback.
- A paragraph number and the phrase or span supporting the defended answer.
- The connection from that evidence to the requested conclusion.
- Why the strongest competing choice fails by content.
- Whether reconsideration occurred before or after feedback.

Record answer content, not only a displayed letter or position. Useful diagnoses include wrong speaker, changed group, lost qualification, unsupported causal claim, or a true detail answering the wrong question. “Careless” does not identify what to repair. A correct selection with a weak explanation still deserves attention.

## Work through one review entry

A writer reports an architect calling a new gate elegant, then says its effect on queues remains unmeasured. A learner selects a description saying the author celebrates the gate's elimination of queues.

The task is author attitude. The anchors are the attribution of elegance to the architect and the author's explicit limit on the queue evidence. The chosen description changes both speaker and evidential force. A repair separates aesthetic praise from an unresolved practical effect; it does not turn unmeasured benefit into proven failure. Preserve the initial selection, then mark whether this analysis was reached independently or after an explanation.

## Keep exposure and improvement distinct

Blind review means reconsidering before seeing the relevant solution or explanation. A changed answer after feedback is a feedback-assisted correction. Preserve the first answer and reason and the blind-review answer and reason separately; add feedback-assisted corrections without overwriting either record. If confidence was not recorded beforehand, do not present a later reconstruction as an original rating.

Several questions about one passage are several assessment items, not several independent first readings. Familiarity can help with later questions. Feedback on one item may disclose a relationship useful for another, so record when explanations became available.

Module reviews reuse questions from the bank. Changed display order does not make familiar items or passages fresh evidence. Repeated work can strengthen retrieval and explanation while still being labeled as repeated work.

## Choose a specific next practice

Name one repair that can be applied again: track the returning pronoun, preserve the tested population, distinguish author from quoted speaker, or separate omitted data from a negative result. First explain that repair on the reviewed passage. Then use unfamiliar text and new questions to examine transfer, preserving the new first attempt and its exposure conditions.

references.title: Original repair check — key and repair notes (open after attempt)
references.body:
## Preserve the attempt before using this key

Open this reference after freezing all eight responses from the questions-only reference and any planned review before feedback. These are the fixed A–E choices in that manual set, not shuffled app choices. Opening the passage analysis can assist every later question on that passage; record the exposure if any independent work remains.

Count correct responses out of four for R11-01 through R11-04, out of four for R11-05 through R11-08, and out of eight overall. Keep blanks in each full denominator. Correct but uncertain responses earn raw credit and can also receive a review flag. Retain cutoff, later independent work, and feedback-assisted changes as separate records. This original set has no official scaled-score conversion or established equivalence to a practice form.

The mechanism notes below are hypotheses to compare with your actual reasoning. A chosen distractor does not by itself diagnose why you missed an item. Explain the exact inference, evidence search, or decision that produced your response before choosing a repair. The suggested checks call for unfamiliar material; repeating these eight items is useful rehearsal but does not restore a first encounter.

## R11-01 — C

Night Market lacks a catalog number. Because every recording available for listening must already have such a number, Night Market is not available for listening. Its newly deposited status and rights that remained cleared through the review’s close would require availability then unless a temporary hold had been requested. All rules were followed, so the hold request must have occurred.

A contradicts the explicit statement that the rights remained cleared without cancellation through the review’s close. The absence of a catalog number cannot override that stated fact.

B is undetermined. The rules expressly allow preservation copying during a hold, but neither require nor prohibit a copy in this case.

C follows by combining the catalog requirement with the cleared-rights rule and its stated exception.

D reverses what can be inferred about this recording into an unsupported rule about every held recording. A held recording could already have a catalog number.

E adds a second-clearance requirement. The passage gives no such rule for later availability.

Possible mechanism: A mistaken response may reflect reversing a one-way rule, overlooking the time at which the rules apply, or treating permission to copy as proof that copying occurred. Reconstruct your actual reasoning before selecting a diagnosis.

Repair: Write the directions separately: availability requires a catalog number; a newly deposited, cleared recording without a requested hold must be available by the review close. Use the absence of the necessary catalog number before applying the exception.

Next check: On unfamiliar material, derive the consequence of an absent necessary condition and distinguish that consequence from the converse. Check that any unless clause and stated deadline are both preserved.

## R11-02 — E

The combined percentage weights each depot by its parcel count. Under the proposed distribution, spring has 20 damaged northern parcels and 20 damaged southern parcels: 40 of 1,100, about 3.64 percent. Autumn has 1 damaged northern parcel and 100 damaged southern parcels: 101 of 1,100, about 9.18 percent. Each depot improves, but far more parcels go through the depot with the higher remaining damage rate.

A could help explain why each depot’s percentage fell. It does not explain why the combined percentage rose despite both declines.

B states the ordinary denominator for each reported depot percentage. It supplies no change in the relative numbers of northern and southern parcels.

C concerns the monetary cost of damage, not the fraction of parcels damaged. Both quantities could move differently.

D concerns customer-order grouping, while the report counts individual parcels. It does not establish the needed shift in parcel weights.

E supplies a concrete change in the mixture of parcels. The resulting calculations reproduce the reported pattern with the same total shipment count.

Possible mechanism: A mistaken response may treat an aggregate rate as an unweighted average of subgroup rates or confuse a cost measure with a frequency measure.

Repair: For every subgroup, identify both the rate and its denominator. Convert rates to counts when denominators are known, add the relevant counts, and then divide by the combined denominator.

Next check: Use a fresh comparison with different subgroup sizes. Explain how changing the mixture could change the combined result even when each subgroup moves in the same direction; then verify the arithmetic with actual counts.

## R11-03 — B

The unusable island provides a competing reason for nesting pairs to relocate, and the band records connect most of the additional pairs to that lost nesting area. The reserve’s increased count could therefore reflect displacement rather than, or in addition to, reduced disturbance. The trail may still have contributed; weakening the attribution does not require proving it had no effect.

A supports the proposed intermediate mechanism by confirming reduced proximity to walkers. It does not supply a competing explanation for the count increase.

B links an independent change in nearby nesting availability to the additional pairs and thereby weakens the director’s attribution.

C holds two aspects of visitor access constant. It does not identify an alternative cause of the nesting increase.

D gives analogous observations compatible with the director’s explanation. Those observations alone do not resolve causation here, but they are not the stated competing cause.

E concerns reproductive output after nesting, rather than what brought additional pairs to the reserve. Similar output does not explain the rise in the number of pairs.

Possible mechanism: A mistaken response may substitute evidence that disturbance fell for evidence that this change caused the entire nesting increase, or demand complete disproof when the task asks only for weakening.

Repair: Name the claimed cause, the observed outcome, and a concrete alternative route to that outcome. Explain how the new information changes confidence in the attribution without asserting more than it establishes.

Next check: On a new causal argument, separate evidence about the proposed mechanism from evidence distinguishing that mechanism from alternatives. Identify what comparison or additional observation would help distinguish them.

## R11-04 — A

The booth contributes 1,200 dollars after its stated costs. The only possible additional financial effect is a change in other contributions to the usual appeal. For the library to finish with more money because of the booth, any reduction in those other contributions must be less than 1,200 dollars. Negating the selected assumption permits a reduction of at least 1,200, which cancels or exceeds the booth’s surplus and defeats the conclusion.

A states the necessary limit on displaced contributions. A fall of exactly 1,200 would leave no gain; a larger fall would produce a loss.

B is stronger than required and concerns donor history. A previous donor could make a genuinely additional contribution at the booth.

C concerns preferences without establishing how much money was added or displaced. No numerical majority of such donors is required.

D compares two gross receipt totals. The booth can increase total funds even when the usual appeal collects a larger amount.

E rules out every donor’s reduction, which is unnecessary. For example, a total reduction of 500 dollars would still leave a 700-dollar gain. The argument needs a bound on the net reduction, not zero displacement.

Possible mechanism: A mistaken response may compare the booth’s receipts only with its direct costs, omit the counterfactual funding source, or select a stronger assumption than the conclusion requires.

Repair: Define the comparison with the no-booth case. Combine the direct surplus with the change in other contributions. Test the negation of a proposed necessary assumption against that net difference.

Next check: For an unfamiliar plan argument, identify benefits that may replace rather than add to existing benefits. State the weakest required bound and distinguish it from an unnecessary zero-loss requirement.

## R11-05 — D

The author conditionally favors placing plausible alternatives in the main text when the gap affects a consequential historical claim. The editors in the opening paragraph defend placing the leading completion in the main text and keeping alternatives in notes to preserve flow. The selected statement identifies that presentation disagreement without making the author endorse unfiltered alternatives everywhere.

A conflicts with the author’s warning that ranking does not establish the original word. It also exceeds what the opening editors are said to claim.

B contradicts the evidential filter in paragraph 2 and the final paragraph’s rejection of every imaginable completion.

C is unsupported. Neither position requires deleting all damaged passages to obtain coherence.

D captures the author’s qualified support for inline alternatives at consequential gaps and the opening editors’ reason to question that presentation.

E is unsupported. The passage treats intact dates as information that readers can report without resolving the missing cargo word.

Possible mechanism: A mistaken response may attribute a reported editorial preference to the author or turn the author’s conditional endorsement into an absolute rule.

Repair: Attach each position to its speaker. Record the opening editors’ preference, Vale’s proposal, and the author’s conditions separately before comparing them.

Next check: On a fresh passage with several viewpoints, find a proposition on which the author and a reported speaker differ. Quote or paraphrase the relevant limits before choosing an answer.

## R11-06 — C

Readers shown alternatives more often identified a historical claim’s dependence on the gap. The experiment did not identify the original cargo word: no intact copy settled it, and the measured outcome concerned readers’ interpretations. The supported conclusion stays within that distinction.

A overstates the measured benefit. Accuracy on reporting intact dates did not differ between groups.

B confuses failure to establish the correct restoration with proof that both candidates were wrong.

C combines the reported interpretive benefit with the explicit limit on what the trial establishes about restoration accuracy.

D turns one comparative result into a universal claim that a conventional edition can never succeed. The text does not support that scope.

E replaces “more often” with all-versus-none. No such individual-level totals are reported.

Possible mechanism: A mistaken response may confuse an improved reading outcome with a verified historical restoration, or strengthen a comparative result into a universal claim.

Repair: Name the variable actually measured. Keep it distinct from the fact the researchers could not independently verify, and preserve the comparison’s stated scope.

Next check: Use another passage about a study or proxy measure. Identify exactly what improved and which tempting broader conclusion remains unestablished.

## R11-07 — A

Paragraph 2 presents Vale’s alternative, illustrates why a missing word can affect an economic account, and restricts acceptable candidates using surviving marks and securely dated terminology. It supplies a proposal and its rationale before the trial evaluates a consequence of that proposal.

A accurately captures the paragraph’s proposal, motivating example, and evidential restrictions.

B invents a determination that stone was the original word. The paragraph presents grain and stone as plausible competing restorations.

C reverses the paragraph’s requirements: surviving marks and dated documents constrain the candidates rather than become unnecessary.

D assigns the next paragraph’s trial discussion to this one and adds an unsupported claim about every conventional-edition reader.

E expands a local uncertainty into total skepticism about the ledger. The passage later distinguishes gaps from intact evidence.

Possible mechanism: A mistaken response may select a topic description or an asserted fact instead of the paragraph’s argumentative role, or assign a later paragraph’s evidence to an earlier proposal.

Repair: Describe what the paragraph does in the developing argument using a short action phrase. Then check each part of an answer against this paragraph and its relation to the next one.

Next check: For a new multi-paragraph passage, map the sequence of problem, proposal, evidence, limitation, and conclusion without assuming every passage uses all five roles.

## R11-08 — B

The trial reports better recognition of a claim’s dependence on the gap but no group difference on reporting intact dates. Together those findings support a bounded benefit rather than general improvement on every task. They fit the author’s recommendation to choose a presentation by the evidence and the reader’s task.

A mistakes no difference in date accuracy for a decline. The reported comparison does not show that intact information became harder to report.

B preserves both observations and limits the benefit to the supported domain without claiming an improvement on the date task.

C equates readers’ agreement about a claim’s dependence with recovery of the original word, which paragraph 4 expressly separates.

D imposes an unstated all-tasks standard. A method can have a useful limited advantage without improving every measured outcome.

E turns the findings into categorical rejection of notes and mandatory alternatives at every gap, contrary to the final paragraph’s conditions.

Possible mechanism: A mistaken response may interpret an unchanged result as a cost, require universal improvement before recognizing a limited benefit, or generalize beyond the measured tasks.

Repair: State the direction of each reported result separately: one comparison favors the alternative display, while the other shows no group difference. Explain what their combination supports and what it leaves open.

Next check: On unfamiliar mixed evidence, distinguish improvement, no observed difference, and deterioration. Test a proposed conclusion against all reported outcomes rather than only the favorable one.

## Make one repair concrete

Choose one explanation that matches your preserved reasoning. Write the proposed action, the unfamiliar material you will use, the conditions and any skill cue, and what observable result would count against the repair hypothesis. Keep the full result, including harmful changes and remaining errors. Eight-item success or a better repeat alone does not establish that the repair will hold across an unfamiliar full session.

references.title: Original repair check — questions only
references.body:
## Before opening the questions

This original eight-item exercise supports a small check of a proposed reasoning repair. All scenarios, participants, and research described here are invented for practice. It is not a full LSAT simulation, an equivalent official form, or a source of scaled scores. Its first four questions use separate sources; its last four share one passage.

Before starting, record previous exposure, the repair you intend to test, and your chosen conditions. An untimed attempt is acceptable; if you choose a time limit, write it before beginning. No time in this reference is an official per-item target. If a teacher, topic label, or earlier discussion has already identified the likely skill, record that cue: success on a known focus is different from recognizing an uncued problem in mixed work.

Keep the separate key closed until you have frozen responses to all eight items, including blanks. Use one row per item, R11-01 through R11-08, and keep any later completion or independent reconsideration in another column. If you plan a review before feedback, finish it before opening the key. An explanation for one reading question may reveal information useful for the other questions on that passage. The A–E labels below are fixed within this manual reference.

Afterward, use the key to count the first block out of four, the reading block out of four, and the complete set out of eight. Keep uncertain correct responses in the correct count while flagging their reasoning for review. A result on eight items cannot establish a stable difficulty level, an official score, or general readiness.

## Questions R11-01 through R11-04

### R11-01

(1) At the close of each monthly review, a sound archive must make every newly deposited recording with cleared rights available for listening, unless its depositor has requested a temporary hold. Every recording made available for listening must by then have received a public catalog number. A temporary hold does not prevent staff from making a preservation copy, and some recordings with catalog numbers are unavailable while equipment is repaired.

(2) The October review has closed, and all these rules were followed. The recording called Night Market was newly deposited, its rights were cleared during that review and remained cleared without cancellation through its close, and it still has no public catalog number.

Question: Which of the following must be true?

A. Night Market’s rights clearance was canceled before the October review closed.

B. The archive has not made a preservation copy of Night Market.

C. Night Market’s depositor requested that it be placed on a temporary hold.

D. Every recording on a temporary hold lacks a public catalog number.

E. Night Market can become available only if its rights are cleared a second time.

### R11-02

(1) Marrow Shipping operates only two depots. In spring, 2 percent of parcels leaving the north depot and 20 percent leaving the south depot were damaged in transit. In autumn, those percentages fell to 1 percent and 10 percent, respectively. Each parcel was assigned to exactly one depot, and the company used the same definition of damage throughout both seasons.

(2) Nevertheless, the percentage of all company parcels that were damaged was higher in autumn. The company shipped the same total number of parcels in both seasons, so the pattern cannot be attributed merely to growth in its overall parcel count.

Question: Which of the following, if true, most helps explain the reported pattern?

A. Both depots adopted stronger packaging before autumn, and neither changed its definition of a parcel.

B. The company calculated each depot’s percentage using only parcels assigned to that depot in the relevant season.

C. The average repair cost for a damaged parcel fell at both depots between spring and autumn.

D. Only a small number of customer orders in either season contained parcels shipped from both depots.

E. North handled 1,000 of the company’s 1,100 parcels in spring but only 100 of its 1,100 autumn parcels.

### R11-03

(1) A coastal reserve moved a heavily used visitor trail farther from its nesting shore. In the following spring, observers counted sixty-seven nesting pairs, compared with forty in the previous spring. Counts had remained close to forty for three years before the trail was moved. The reserve’s boundary, observation period, and counting method remained unchanged.

(2) The director concludes that reducing disturbance from walkers caused the increase in nesting pairs. The new trail does place visitors farther from the shore, but the director has supplied no information about changes in other nesting areas or the prior locations of the additional pairs.

Question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the director’s causal inference?

A. The move reduced the number of walkers who passed within a short distance of nests on the reserve’s shore.

B. A nearby nesting island became unusable that winter, and band records identify most additional pairs as former nesters on that island.

C. The old and new trail routes were both open during the same hours, with the same admission charge.

D. Several other reserves have reported that moving trails away from nesting sites was followed by more nesting pairs.

E. The additional nesting pairs at this reserve produced at least as many young per pair as the pairs counted the previous year.

### R11-04

(1) A neighborhood tool library ran a donation booth at a street fair. The booth received 2,000 dollars in contributions. Supplies and permits cost 800 dollars, and these were all the expenses attributable to the booth. Volunteers staffed it without pay; their time would not otherwise have generated money for the library. No goods or services were sold.

(2) The library also continued its usual donation appeal. Any further financial effect of the booth could occur only through changes in contributions to that appeal. Its treasurer argues that, because the booth’s receipts exceeded its costs by 1,200 dollars, running the booth must have left the library with more money than it would have had without the booth.

Question: The treasurer’s argument depends on which of the following assumptions?

A. The booth did not cause other contributions to the library to fall by 1,200 dollars or more.

B. None of the people who donated at the booth had ever contributed to the library before.

C. At least half of the booth’s donors prefer making donations in person to making them online.

D. The booth’s total receipts exceeded the receipts from the library’s usual donation appeal.

E. No person who donated at the booth reduced any other contribution they would otherwise have made to the library.

## Passage for R11-05 through R11-08

(1) Editors of damaged shipping ledgers face a problem that clean digital type can conceal. A missing word in an old receipt may admit several plausible restorations, yet an edition often prints one completion as if it were intact. Some editors defend placing the best-supported completion in the main text and relegating alternatives to notes. They argue that readers need a coherent account and that repeated interruptions can make even secure information difficult to follow. The computational tools now used to rank candidate words have made producing a fluent edition easier.

(2) Historian Nera Vale favors a different presentation for consequential gaps. If a missing cargo name could be either “grain” or “stone,” the choice may affect an account of the port’s economy. She proposes showing the plausible alternatives in the main text while marking the gap. Her approach does not give every computer-generated suggestion equal standing: an alternative must fit the surviving letter marks and the terminology used in securely dated documents. Ranking candidates remains useful, but a ranking should not silently become a statement that the top candidate is known to be correct.

(3) In a trial, eighty-four history students were assigned by lot to read one of two editions of the same damaged entry. One printed the leading completion in the text, with uncertainty described in a note. The other displayed the two plausible alternatives at the gap. Readers of the second edition more often identified which proposed account of the port depended on the missing word. The groups did not differ in their accuracy when reporting dates that survived intact in the entry.

(4) This finding supports a limited advantage of displaying alternatives: readers in the trial more readily located a dependency between an uncertain restoration and a historical claim. It does not show that either displayed word was the word originally written. No intact copy was available to settle that question, and the trial assessed readers’ interpretations, not the accuracy of the restoration itself. Better communication of uncertainty is compatible with continued uncertainty about the underlying text.

(5) An edition should therefore make the importance of a gap visible without burying readers in every imaginable completion. Where competing plausible restorations change a consequential claim, Vale’s approach deserves consideration. Where the surviving text settles the relevant question, multiplying alternatives may add little. The decision should follow the evidence and the reader’s task, rather than a general preference for either seamless prose or conspicuous doubt.

### R11-05

Question: Which position would the author most likely accept and the editors described in paragraph 1 most likely question?

A. A computational ranking is sufficient to establish which word originally appeared in a damaged entry.

B. Editors should present every computer-generated completion to readers without filtering it through surviving evidence.

C. A coherent edition is possible only when all damaged passages have been removed from the published text.

D. Plausible alternatives that affect a consequential historical claim may belong in the main text despite interrupting its flow.

E. Readers should disregard intact dates until every missing cargo name in the same ledger has been restored.

### R11-06

Question: Which statement about the trial is most strongly supported by the passage?

A. Displaying alternatives improved readers’ accuracy on every task that the researchers assessed.

B. The trial established that neither of the two displayed cargo names could have been the original word.

C. The alternative display helped readers identify a claim’s dependence on the gap, without establishing the correct restoration.

D. The trial showed that a single completion with an explanatory note can never communicate uncertainty successfully.

E. Every reader shown alternatives identified the dependent claim, while no reader shown a single completion did so.

### R11-07

Question: Paragraph 2 primarily serves which function in the passage?

A. It introduces an alternative editing practice, explains why a gap can matter, and identifies limits on which candidates deserve display.

B. It establishes that the cargo named in the damaged entry was stone rather than grain by applying a reliable computational test.

C. It rejects the need for surviving marks and dated documents once a computer has ranked the available completions.

D. It reports the trial’s results and explains why all readers who received a conventional edition misunderstood the entry.

E. It argues that uncertainty about one word prevents historians from drawing any justified conclusions from the entire ledger.

### R11-08

Question: How do the two reported trial findings in paragraph 3 relate to the author’s conclusion?

A. They show that improved recognition of a gap’s importance necessarily makes intact information harder to report.

B. They support a benefit for recognizing one kind of uncertainty without showing a corresponding improvement on the intact-date task.

C. They establish that the original cargo word is recoverable whenever readers agree about which historical claim depends on it.

D. They refute Vale’s approach because an editing change must improve every measured task to have any useful purpose.

E. They demonstrate that notes are never useful and that every uncertain word should always receive several alternatives in the main text.

## Stop and preserve the record

Freeze all eight responses before opening Original repair check — key and repair notes. Keep later changes, feedback exposure, and any interrupted conditions visible. A repeat of this set remains a repeat even if its answers are no longer easy to remember.

references.title: Statement roles and author viewpoints
references.body:
Use this sheet after reading a whole argument. Roles describe what a statement does in a particular passage; they are not permanent properties of a sentence.

## Find the target, then trace its support

1. State the author's final target in the supplied passage.
2. Identify the reasons actually offered for it.
3. Ask which reasons are themselves supported by earlier claims.
4. Track who holds each view and whether the author accepts it.
5. Paraphrase without changing certainty, conditions, or scope.

A conclusion need not be the last sentence. "Therefore" inside an opponent's quoted statement can introduce that opponent's conclusion. A recommendation can be the main conclusion even if you think its reasons are weak.

- **Main conclusion:** Where does the offered support finally lead? It need not be last.
- **Intermediate conclusion:** Is this supported, then reused as a reason? It has two roles.
- **Premise:** For which claim is this offered as a reason? Relevance alone is insufficient.
- **Background:** Does this only place the discussion in context? It may support a different argument.
- **Reported view:** Who holds this position? Reporting is not endorsement.
- **Concession:** What point does the author grant? A granted point may support a narrower proposal.
- **Objection:** What claim or step is challenged? The author may accept part of it.
- **Rebuttal:** What response is offered to the challenge? Answering one objection need not prove the proposal.

## Establishing a claim or explaining an event?

If the participants dispute whether the conservatory cooled overnight, temperature records can be evidence that it did. If they accept the cooling and ask why, an open vent can be a proposed explanation. Evidence about the vent can then support an argument for that explanation. The same discussion can contain both functions.

Do not classify by "because" alone. State what is accepted for the discussion, what remains at issue, and which statement is being offered in support of which other statement. An accepted event need not be independently verified merely because the discussion treats it as given.

## Check your paraphrase

Compare the original and your version on four dimensions:

- Subject: the same people, objects, and comparison group.
- Strength: "may" remains possible; "must" remains required or necessary in its context.
- Scope: "some" is not silently changed to "all" or "not all."
- Condition: an "if" clause is not dropped.

Also distinguish an obligation from its fulfillment. "The room is required to close" is not the same statement as "the room has closed." Keep that distinction when joining steps in an argument.

## One final role question

Ask: "According to this author, this statement is offered as what kind of support for which claim?" That question prevents you from substituting what you think a sensible argument should have said.

references.title: Rule chains, witnesses, and consistency
references.body:
## Build a route through complete conditions

- Chain: A → B and B → C yield A → C. The rules alone do not establish an actual A.
- Reverse reasoning: not C → not B → not A follows by contraposition. C alone does not establish A or B.
- Matching middle: preserve the full property, subject, time, and domain. “Eligible for review” does not match “approved”; January indexing does not match February indexing.
- Shared consequence: A → C and B → C do not connect A to B. They provide sufficient routes to C, without saying that either route is required for C.

## Distinguish branches and required inputs

- Branch: A → B and A → C make both results follow from A. They do not establish B → C. A false, B true, C false is a counterexample to that proposed connection.
- And input: (B and C) → D requires both inputs to use this route. B alone establishes neither D nor not D; C is unestablished, and D could also have another route.
- Or input: (B or C) → D allows either input to activate the rule. “Or” is inclusive, so both inputs are also permitted.
- Backward check: from (B and C) → D and not D, infer not B or not C. Add B true and C must be false. Do not conclude both inputs fail without further information.

## Carry one subject through the rules

Some A are B, all A are C, and all B are D establish some C are D. One existing witness has both starting properties and receives both consequences. Two unrelated “some” statements may supply different witnesses.

For named objects, Aster's indexing cannot combine with Birch's scanning to satisfy a rule requiring one document to be both indexed and scanned. Keep outer conditions too: “While M, printing requires loading” restricts the combination M and printing, not printing outside M.

## Test a proposed conclusion

A counterexample must preserve every rule and stated fact while making the proposed conclusion false. For A → B, B → C, and C true, use A false, B false, C true to defeat the claim that A must hold. A true, B false, C true is unusable because it breaks the first rule.

Consistency means that the supplied statements can all be true together. A → B, A true, and B false are jointly inconsistent for the same case. Identifying that clash does not determine which statement should be corrected. Do not invent an exception to make the exercise work.

Classify conclusions as required, ruled out, or unresolved. An unfinished proof does not establish the conclusion's negation.

references.title: Full-simulation planning and runbook
references.body:
## Choose the evidence you want

Use this runbook before opening a practice form. A faithful full simulation aims to observe performance across the intended complete multiple-choice format and applicable conditions. A custom endurance session, interrupted attempt, or targeted training block can also teach useful skills; record its actual design and purpose. The original Erudior bank and generic app Exam mode are learning tools, not official full LSAT simulations.

Use official practice through LawHub or another appropriately authorized source. Access permission, format suitability, and unfamiliarity are separate questions. Owning a practice resource does not show that it fits the intended administration or that its questions are new to the learner. Keep official test content in its authorized environment; the worksheet needs identifiers and observations, not copied passages or answer explanations.

## Verify the intended administration

Primary guidance checked November 3, 2026:

- Through June 2027, the standard multiple-choice format has four thirty-five-minute sections: two scored Logical Reasoning, one scored Reading Comprehension, and one unscored variable section. A ten-minute intermission follows the second section.
- From August 2027, LSAC announces a fixed order: Reading Comprehension for fifty-two minutes, then two forty-five-minute Logical Reasoning sections. A ten-minute intermission follows each of the first two sections. Unscored questions are embedded within the sections.
- The announced Reading Comprehension section has six passages and forty questions; each Logical Reasoning section has thirty-two questions. These are workload counts, not a direction to guess which items count toward the score.
- Practice in the announced format is planned for February 2027. At this November 2026 check, that future announcement does not establish current availability. Recheck the official practice inventory before selecting a form.

Individual approved accommodations and current administration instructions govern actual timing, intermissions, tools, and other conditions. Record them as part of the target protocol. Do not suppress an approved condition to make a practice record look standard. Do not rearrange old material and call the resulting collection an official new-format form.

The stated standard work intervals sum to 140 minutes in the four-section format and 142 minutes in the announced format. Adding only the listed ten-minute intermissions gives arithmetic subtotals of 150 and 162 minutes. These subtotals exclude setup, check-in, other transitions, and any applicable individual conditions. They are not exact appointment durations or a claim about the official change in total appointment length.

## Complete the plan before revealing content

Write a session ID, intended administration, purpose, source, form identifier and version, format, and known exposure. Exposure includes earlier question attempts, passage reading, explanations, and overlapping content encountered in a different collection. Mark an uncertain history as uncertain. Do not resolve uncertainty by silently calling the form fresh.

Record the section order, allowed time for each section, intermission placement and duration, clock behavior, aids, and approved conditions being reproduced. Describe how responses and omissions will be preserved at each cutoff. Use only recording actions compatible with the chosen practice setup. Retrospective estimates belong in the record as estimates; do not invent precise timestamps afterward.

Check the interface using a tutorial or a different training resource. Confirm how the chosen practice mode handles submission, score display, answer review, and navigation. If independent reconsideration is desired, determine in advance whether the permitted workflow can preserve it before feedback. Do not assume an instant-scoring platform will conceal feedback. If feedback appears, record its scope and conduct an honestly labeled assisted review.

Choose a realistic block of time for the session and allow separate time to preserve records and review. Keep unfamiliar forms in an inventory with intended uses rather than spending them casually on interface exploration. A plan can change; retain the original plan and explain the reason for the change.

## Run the declared sequence

Follow the selected form's applicable instructions, section boundaries, and intermissions. Do not use an intermission to study explanations or correct a finished section when the intended protocol excludes that work. Follow current guidance about permitted intermission activity; this course does not replace administration rules.

Apply a reasoned skip-and-return policy within allowed navigation. During the administered LSAT, scored and unscored work is not identified to the test taker. For practice, complete the assigned workload even if its scoring instructions identify work excluded from the reported score.
