Do not use guesses about scoring status to decide which items deserve no effort. Preserve blanks at cutoff. Do not manufacture an apparently complete attempt by moving later responses into the earlier record.

If a disruption occurs, record what happened, where it occurred, its known duration, clock behavior, and any content or help seen. Use applicable official directions during an actual administration. For practice, choose whether to stop or continue for learning and label that choice. Neither adding nor subtracting interruption minutes establishes equivalence to the intended uninterrupted session.

## Close, review, and choose the next task

Preserve the cutoff responses and any platform report before editing a personal worksheet. Review the evidence through the simulation-record reference. Use the exact official practice form's scoring instructions for a converted practice result; keep original-course results raw. Treat practice results as evidence with conditions, not guarantees of an administered score.

Choose a repair only after inspecting the reasoning behind priority answers and omissions. Reserve a later unfamiliar task to test its use. Schedule Argumentative Writing practice separately with its own prompt, phases, cutoff draft, and revision record; it does not have to follow every multiple-choice session immediately.

## Primary sources

- [LSAC — Official LSAT Practice Tests](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/prepare/official-lsat-practice-tests)
- [LSAC — Specifications of the LSAT and LSAT Argumentative Writing](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/register-lsat/accommodations/specifications-lsat-and-lsat-argumentative-writing)
- [LSAC — Format changes beginning August 2027](https://www.lsac.org/lsat-will-look-little-different-starting-august-2027)
- [LSAC — Official practice features](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/prep)

Recheck these sources for the intended administration and again before publishing or relying on a future practice format. The learning procedures in this sheet are original course guidance; they are not additional LSAC rules.

references.title: Full-session record and review worksheet
references.body:
## Use one identity throughout the record

Create a session ID and keep it on the plan, cutoff responses, report, review, and repair notes. Record in your own worksheet or permitted practice environment. This reference is a manual template; it does not create an automatic diagnostic session or store the filled record in Erudior.

Before starting, fill in:

- Purpose and intended administration.
- Authorized source, form identity, version, and format.
- Exposure to questions, passages, explanations, or overlapping forms, including unknown history.
- Section order, allowed times, intermissions, clock behavior, permitted aids, and applicable individual conditions.
- Planned response-saving and feedback sequence, including what the interface actually permits.
- A specific observation to investigate, such as repeated late attribution errors, without assuming its cause.

Keep protected official material in its authorized source. A form/section/item locator and your own reasoning note are enough to connect the record to later review without copying the question into this course.

## Preserve the attempt as it happened

For each section, save every cutoff response, including blanks. Record the start and cutoff time if available, working time, and section role under that form's scoring instructions. Keep the full workload visible even when some practice items are excluded from a converted result. Do not try to identify unscored items during the attempt.

Record intermissions and interruptions separately. For an interruption, identify the point in the session, known duration, whether the timer continued, and any assistance or feedback received. If a detail was not recorded, write unknown or an explicitly labeled estimate. Precision invented afterward makes the record less useful.

Save a platform report under its actual conditions. Do not recalculate a modified report and overwrite the original. A follow-up completion or review uses a separate response column or copy with its own time and assistance notes.

## Separate review stages

Before feedback, independent reconsideration may be possible if the selected workflow permits it. Save the revised responses and explanations before opening results or help. If a score, answer status, key, explanation, or relevant hint has already appeared, describe what was exposed and which later judgments could be influenced. Do not promise that all platforms provide a hidden-feedback stage.

Exposure can extend beyond one item. An explanation of a passage's structure may help answer other questions on that passage. A general method suggested by a tutor can also guide later work. Record the relevant scope without falsely claiming that seeing a total score means every answer explanation was seen.

For each priority item, record:

1. Cutoff response and any pre-feedback confidence flag.
2. Independent later response, if one was actually made before relevant feedback.
3. Key outcome and the applicable source of that key.
4. Relevant feedback or other assistance and when it arrived.
5. The learner's reason for the original choice, the supporting evidence, and the unsupported step if identified.
6. A proposed repair and an unfamiliar verification task.

## Worked record: a custom learning session

This fictional example uses three original learning blocks of twelve, ten, and eight questions. It is not an official form or an LSAT timing specification. The declared working windows are twenty, eighteen, and fifteen minutes, with two five-minute intermissions. A six-minute interruption pauses the second block's clock. The learner completes all three blocks and keeps the key closed until a separate independent review is saved.

The work totals fifty-three active minutes. Planned intermissions add ten minutes, and the interruption adds six, for sixty-nine elapsed minutes if there are no other gaps. The interruption's effect is unknown. Subtracting six produces a duration calculation, not an uninterrupted equivalent.

| Block | Right | Wrong | Blank |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A: 12 items | 9 | 2 | 1 |
| B: 10 items | 6 | 3 | 1 |
| C: 8 items | 5 | 2 | 1 |
| All: 30 items | 20 | 7 | 3 |

The complete cutoff result is twenty correct out of thirty. Twenty out of twenty-seven describes attempted-item accuracy only. The three blanks remain part of the complete denominator. All three blocks count in this original exercise; there is no official conversion.

During independent review, three initially wrong responses become correct, two blanks become correct, and one initially correct response becomes wrong. The remaining responses do not change. The resulting total is 20 + 3 + 2 − 1 = 24 correct out of thirty, with five wrong and one blank. Five problems became correct, but the net gain is four because one change was harmful.

Preserve all transitions: nineteen correct-to-correct, one correct-to-wrong, three wrong-to-correct, four wrong-to-wrong, two blank-to-correct, and one blank-to-blank. These counts total thirty. This transition record explains the net change without merging the twenty-correct cutoff result into the twenty-four-correct review result.

Suppose two successful corrections repaired a lost speaker distinction, while the harmful change replaced a qualified answer with an absolute one. Record both mechanisms. Do not attribute every improvement to having more time or every initial miss to fatigue. The next repair can target speaker attribution while a separate note preserves the scope error.

## End with a concrete decision

Write the chosen mechanism, replacement action, reason for prioritizing it, and next verification task. Specify whether that task is familiar practice, a cued original exercise, or unfamiliar official practice. State its timing and feedback conditions before beginning.

A record is useful even when it contains uncertainty or an interrupted session. Its value comes from preserving what happened and supporting a narrower, testable next question. It should not manufacture a clean attempt, an official conversion, or a diagnosis that the evidence does not establish.

references.title: Linked, independent, and serial support
references.body:
A support map records the author's reasoning. It does not establish that the premises are true, that the inference succeeds, or that one event causes another. Keep the full statements beside short diagram labels.

## Three patterns

- **Linked support:** Premises are used together in one line. Does the intended inference need their combination?
- **Independent support:** Separate lines aim at the same claim. Does another offered reason remain when one line is set aside?
- **Serial support:** A supported claim is used for a further claim. Which conclusion is intermediate, and what is the final target?

These patterns can coexist. Two linked premises may establish an intermediate conclusion; that conclusion can join another premise to support the final target. Another line might separately support the same final target.

## Shared background matters

Suppose a fictional contest says a display qualifies if it passes either a stability check or a visibility check. With that rule fixed, passing stability and passing visibility are two separate routes to qualification. In an explicit deduction, each result is paired with the shared rule.

If the rule instead requires both checks, the two results must work together. Do not infer the support pattern from the number of sentences or from a picture alone.

## Use removal carefully

Temporarily set one claim aside while preserving the remaining information and its stated background. Do not replace the removed claim with its opposite. Ask which particular line of support remains, rather than whether the conclusion is now impossible.

A surviving reason need not be decisive. A linked premise may still have some relevance on its own even when the intended complete inference is lost. If the prose is ambiguous, describe the uncertainty instead of inventing a rule to force a classification.

## Keep three distinctions

- Separate support lines are not automatically statistically independent evidence. Two speakers may repeat the same underlying report.
- Chronological order is not support direction. A later measurement can be evidence about an earlier event.
- A missing bridge is not permission to invent an asserted premise. Qualification for an award does not itself guarantee receiving it.

A restatement of the conclusion provides no separate basis merely because it uses different words. To evaluate a map, examine the actual claims and connections after reconstructing them.

references.title: Two original prompts for timed writing and revision
references.body:
## Prepare two separate attempts

These are original Erudior prompts for manual practice, with no required policy position or automatic essay score. Use one prompt per attempt. Record prior exposure, your planning allocation, your drafting allocation, and your revision reserve before beginning. Keep the second prompt unread if you want to use it for a later unfamiliar attempt.

Write an essay that defends your position with connected reasons and addresses at least one serious competing consideration from the perspectives.

LSAC's standard writing allocations, checked November 3, 2026, are fifteen minutes for prewriting and thirty-five minutes for essay writing, with adjustments for approved accommodations. Verify the applicable instructions through [LSAC's writing overview](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/about/lsat-argumentative-writing) and the timing-check reference. Treat the phases separately; do not assume unused planning minutes extend drafting. Label shorter or otherwise modified practice conditions explicitly.

## Freeze, review, and test a repair

At the writing cutoff, save the draft exactly as it stands. Before feedback, check whether it contains an identifiable position, connected reasons, fair treatment of a competing view, and a conclusion consistent with its scope. Name the most consequential missing or unsupported step.

Save an independent later revision separately and explain one substantive change. Label further changes prompted by feedback. On the second unfamiliar prompt, test a specific planning or revision adjustment, such as choosing a provisional thesis earlier. Compare the recorded behavior and completeness while acknowledging that the prompts have not been equated for difficulty.

## Prompt 1: Recognition at a science festival

The fictional Merin youth science festival invites participants to display investigations and explain their methods. Organizers want the festival to encourage careful inquiry and continued participation. They must decide whether to retain a small number of competitive awards, replace them with detailed feedback for every project, or adopt a combination. What policy should guide recognition at the festival?

Perspective 1: Public awards can make standards visible. Recognizing a project for a clear method, a carefully tested explanation, or an honest response to contrary evidence shows what the festival values. Competition need not reward a flashy result if its criteria focus on the quality of inquiry.

Perspective 2: A project reflects opportunities as well as effort. Participants may have unequal access to equipment, advice, or time. Ranking their products can obscure those differences and discourage someone whose investigation represents substantial learning. Recognition should emphasize development and useful next steps for every participant.

Perspective 3: Inquiry also depends on exchange. Participants who ask helpful questions or share a method can improve other projects without producing the highest-ranked display. A recognition system should consider whether it encourages such contributions. At the same time, an extremely broad set of honors could make the festival's standards difficult to understand.

Planning questions: Which policy would you defend, and what should count as achievement under it? Explain one connection between your criteria and the festival's purpose. Select a serious objection involving opportunity, motivation, clarity, or cooperation and plan a direct response. Do not invent an experiment proving how all young participants respond to awards.

## Prompt 2: Shared use of a regional park

The fictional Iven regional park includes a central lawn, walking paths, and quieter areas beyond the lawn. Community groups request permission for organized public events. Other visitors seek an accessible place for quiet recreation. The park cannot remove every conflict by creating new space. What principle should guide its policy for organized events?

Perspective 1: A public park should support shared civic life. Open events can give residents a reason to visit and participate with people they would not otherwise meet. A policy that treats organized activity as an intrusion may reserve a public resource for only one kind of visitor.

Perspective 2: Quiet is also a form of access. Some visitors cannot readily travel to a more remote outdoor space, and sound may carry beyond the site of an event. Keeping a quiet zone on a map does not guarantee that visitors can experience it. Event decisions should account for effects outside the booked area.

Perspective 3: Predictable limits and observable follow-up can make competing uses more manageable. Published conditions on location, frequency, and intensity allow groups to plan and visitors to anticipate changes. However, rules that are difficult to monitor can promise a balance the park cannot actually maintain.

Planning questions: State whether and under what conditions you would permit events. Explain why your chosen priority or compromise deserves its weight. Address a concern about spillover effects, exclusion, or enforcement without claiming that a written rule guarantees compliance. Label any imagined event outcome as hypothetical.

references.title: Timing, format, and practice-condition check
references.body:
## Choose the administration before the timer

Format information checked November 3, 2026. Recheck the linked primary guidance before choosing a simulation or relying on these details. The intended administration, current instructions, and individual approved accommodations determine the relevant conditions. A course learning window is a separate choice and should be labeled accordingly.

For administrations through June 2027, LSAC describes four 35-minute multiple-choice sections: two scored Logical Reasoning sections, one scored Reading Comprehension section, and one unscored variable section. The standard intermission is ten minutes after the second section. See [LSAC's current specifications](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/register-lsat/accommodations/specifications-lsat-and-lsat-argumentative-writing).

For administrations beginning August 2027, LSAC has announced this fixed sequence:

- Reading Comprehension: 52 minutes, six passages, forty questions.
- Ten-minute intermission.
- Logical Reasoning: 45 minutes, thirty-two questions.
- Ten-minute intermission.
- Logical Reasoning: 45 minutes, thirty-two questions.

In that announced format, unscored questions are embedded and not identified. The announced counts are twenty-seven scored and thirteen unscored Reading Comprehension questions, with twenty-five scored and seven unscored questions in each Logical Reasoning section. Do not try to identify unscored questions; apply the same evidence-based answering and skip/return decisions throughout. LSAC plans new-format LawHub practice for February 2027; that future availability must not be described as already present in November 2026. Verify both the materials and their intended format through [LSAC's transition guidance](https://www.lsac.org/lsat-will-look-little-different-starting-august-2027).

## Keep writing phases separate

LSAC's current Argumentative Writing guidance describes a standard fifteen-minute prewriting period and thirty-five-minute essay-writing period, adjusted for approved additional-time accommodations. Moving past prewriting is permitted after five minutes have elapsed. This permission does not establish that unused prewriting time increases the essay allocation. Follow the actual phase rules and interface.

The writing task is separately administered and unscored. It calls for a position engaging ideas from supplied perspectives. Use [LSAC's writing overview](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/about/lsat-argumentative-writing) for current task and administration information. A complete cutoff draft and a later revised essay are different records; the course does not automatically grade either.

## Record the condition you actually used

Before practice, record the source and form identifier, intended format, previous question or passage exposure, selected duration, pause rule, and planned breaks. Identify any authorized accommodations used. Prefer appropriately authorized official materials for an administration-matched simulation. Combining older sections or inventing new time limits can create a learning exercise, but it does not establish an official new-format form.

At the cutoff, preserve every response, including blanks. Record interruptions and actual duration. Keep later independent review and feedback-assisted changes separate. A paused clock can show active working time without demonstrating equivalence to uninterrupted work. A familiar passage with unfamiliar questions also needs a mixed exposure record.

## Interpret the result within its limits

[LSAC's scoring explanation](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/lsat-scoring) reports no deduction for incorrect answers. For official multiple-choice practice, use the applicable instructions and make a response to each question when possible; distinguish a reasoned answer from a guess in your learning notes. Do not let a return plan conceal unanswered items at the cutoff.

The original Erudior questions and separate pacing set supply raw learning results, without an official scaled-score conversion or established equivalence to official forms. The app's generic timer and completion threshold are course settings. A higher percentage on different original material may reflect changed difficulty or conditions as well as improved reasoning. Keep counts, denominators, exposure, and the specific repair visible.

references.title: Writing-session record and two original prompts
references.body:
## Prepare the record before opening a prompt

Choose one prompt below and record its identity, previous exposure, purpose, planning window, drafting window, clock rules, and permitted aids. These are original course exercises, not official prompts or automatically scored essays. A timed rehearsal should use conditions appropriate to its stated purpose. For a faithful official-interface rehearsal, use appropriately authorized official writing practice and current instructions.

LSAC's guidance, checked November 3, 2026, describes writing as separate and unscored, with standard prewriting and drafting phases of fifteen and thirty-five minutes. Approved accommodations and current directions govern individual conditions. The option to move past prewriting after five minutes does not mean unused prewriting time should be assumed to extend drafting. Sources: [LSAC Argumentative Writing](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/about/lsat-argumentative-writing) and [LSAC specifications](https://www.lsac.org/lsat/register-lsat/accommodations/specifications-lsat-and-lsat-argumentative-writing).

## Freeze, review, and choose a later target

At cutoff, save the essay exactly as written and keep planning notes separate. Record unfinished portions, actual phase durations, interruptions, and assistance. Create another version for any independent revision. Once a tutor, model, suggestion tool, or explanation informs a change, preserve that contribution in the next version's assistance record.

Review descriptively: state the position; identify its principal support; examine the treatment of a relevant competing perspective; compare the conclusion's scope with the reasons; then review organization, clarity, and mechanics. Cite a sentence or paragraph from the learner's own draft when recording a finding. Do not invent an official writing score from this checklist.

Choose one revision target that a later cutoff draft can show. It might be answering a serious competing concern before polishing the introduction or checking that the conclusion does not exceed the defended policy. Rework the familiar draft to understand the repair. Use the other prompt as a later unfamiliar check only if it has not been previewed. Scrolling past it and reading its perspectives counts as exposure.

The prompts offer different positions rather than a required answer. Develop your own position, support it with reasoning, and engage at least one relevant supplied perspective. Distinguish proposals and hypothetical examples from established facts; do not invent research findings. The guided questions support planning but do not require a fixed essay structure.

## Prompt 1: Permanent places or rotating opportunities? — W11-01

A neighborhood food market has a limited number of stalls. Its organizers must choose how much space to assign to vendors with renewable long-term places and how much to reserve for short rotating placements. They want a market that serves residents, supports viable small businesses, and allows unfamiliar offerings to be tried. They have not yet collected reliable evidence about the effects of a particular allocation.

Key question: What approach should guide the market's allocation of long-term and rotating vendor places?

Perspective 1: A stable place lets a vendor build customer relationships, plan supplies, and invest in improving the stall. Residents also benefit when they know where to find essential products. Organizers should give established vendors a dependable basis for planning rather than making continuity depend on repeated contests for space. A vendor's willingness to make a sustained commitment should receive substantial weight.

Perspective 2: A market's public value includes opening opportunities to people who do not already possess a place. Long-term assignments can let an initial group keep scarce access while new vendors wait indefinitely. Rotation allows residents to encounter different products and gives newcomers a chance to demonstrate demand. Organizers should treat access as an opportunity to share rather than a permanent reward for arriving earlier.

Perspective 3: Neither continuity nor turnover alone establishes whether the market serves residents well. Some products may require stable availability, while others may benefit from trials. Organizers should explain their criteria, collect evidence about service and unmet demand, and allow allocations to be reconsidered. Review also has costs: a complicated procedure could consume resources that would otherwise support vendors and customers.

Planning questions: Which objective should carry the most weight, and why? What would your approach preserve or sacrifice? Which competing concern presents the strongest challenge? What evidence would justify changing the allocation later?

## Prompt 2: A shared foundation or a self-designed degree? — W11-02

A university is revising how undergraduate students choose courses outside their main field. One proposal creates a common group of required introductory courses. Another lets students design individualized programs with advising. The university values intellectual breadth, meaningful choice, and students' ability to connect ideas across fields. The prompt supplies no evidence that one exact number of required courses produces the best result.

Key question: How should the university balance common educational requirements with students' freedom to design their own studies?

Perspective 1: Students cannot always recognize the value of a field before encountering it. A shared foundation introduces methods and questions that an individually chosen program might avoid. It also gives students common intellectual experiences that support later discussion across specialties. Requirements can therefore expand meaningful choice by revealing possibilities, even when they initially restrict which courses a student takes.

Perspective 2: Students bring different interests, preparation, and goals. Requiring everyone to follow the same introductory route can repeat what some already know and displace courses that would deepen an unusual interest. Responsibility for constructing a program can itself be educational. Advising should help students justify coherent choices rather than assuming that identical courses are the only route to breadth.

Perspective 3: The relevant question is whether a program demonstrates the desired capacities, not whether every student's timetable looks the same. The university could define learning goals and permit different ways to meet them. Yet flexible pathways demand clear standards and accessible advising; otherwise, students with more guidance may gain options that others cannot use. A proposal must address how its flexibility would work in practice.

Planning questions: What should a university require students to demonstrate? How does your position respond to the strongest concern about either uniformity or unchecked choice? Which proposed safeguards have costs? Where should your conclusion remain qualified?
